stories.Headline: Asean banks to probe responsible use of AI
stories.Summary:
Banking leaders from across Southeast Asia will meet in Manila from Nov. 12 to 14 to discuss regional cooperation on artificial intelligence. The 54th Asean Banking Council Meeting will be hosted by the Bankers Association of the Philippines. The event will bring together leaders to discuss how the region can maximize AI's potential while keeping financial services secure and trusted. The BAP said the meeting will be held under the Asean Bankers Association, which groups banking associations from 11 member states: Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam and Timor-Leste.

The meeting will focus on cybersecurity, customer protection and the responsible use of emerging technologies. Banks are exploring AI to improve customer experiences, streamline processes, strengthen fraud detection and enhance risk assessments. The technology also raises concerns over data privacy, cybersecurity, accountability and the governance of AI-driven systems. The BAP said regional collaboration could help banks exchange expertise, strengthen risk management and promote responsible approaches to adopting new technologies.

The BAP said that as host it aims to contribute to the continued exchange of ideas and perspectives among Asean banking leaders at a time when technology is reshaping the industry's priorities. It said the meeting reinforces the importance of the ABA as a platform for regional banking associations to engage on shared concerns. The BAP also said collaboration can help ensure that the benefits of AI are pursued alongside sound governance, customer protection and financial stability. It added that regional dialogue creates opportunities for leaders to exchange perspectives on common challenges and consider how their institutions can adapt to technological change while preserving confidence in the financial system.

This marks the third time the Philippines will host the meeting, after Cebu in September 2004 and November 2014. The 2004 meeting carried the theme "Asean+3: Challenges & Opportunities," while the 2014 gathering focused on "Asean Financial Integration: Moving Ahead to 2015 and Beyond." The BAP said a region with diverse banking systems and different stages of digital development can benefit from collaboration. The articles do not say what specific outcomes or agreements are expected from the meeting.

stories.Headline: AI’s Off-Balance-Sheet Bill Tops $4.1 Trillion: Should You Be Concerned?
stories.Summary:
Intel’s shares fell as much as 30% in intraday trading on 30 October, dropping to $64.24 and wiping out nearly $150 billion in market value, the company’s worst single-day performance since the 1970s. The sell-off followed Q4 revenue guidance of $15 billion to $16 billion, more than $1 billion below analysts’ average estimate of about $17 billion. CFO David Zinsner said the company does not expect to generate positive cash flow this year. An incident at its Israeli factory is expected to cut Q4 revenue by about $300 million, and PC shipments are projected to fall about 12% this year and another 10% in 2027.

The $4.11 trillion figure is made up mainly of non-cancellable purchase commitments, leases signed but not yet commenced, and guarantees and credit support for data centre and chip projects. Meta’s purchase commitments rose to $455 billion from $349 billion, its not-yet-commenced leases grew to $356 billion from $279 billion, and its residual value guarantees for the Hyperion and El Paso joint ventures came to $41.5 billion. Amazon’s unconditional purchase obligations almost doubled to $254 billion from $130 billion, and its not-yet-commenced leases rose to $165 billion from $137 billion. Alphabet’s total off-balance-sheet commitments reached $1.059 trillion, making it the first individual company to cross $1 trillion.

The commitments more than doubled from about $1.8 trillion at the end of June to $3.12 trillion by the end of August and $4.11 trillion in October. They exceed the companies’ roughly $1 trillion in recognised debt and lease liabilities by a ratio of more than 4 to 1. Goldman Sachs credit strategist Amanda Lynam noted that S&P adjusts for off-balance-sheet leases while Moody’s and Fitch do not. S&P cut Meta’s outlook from stable to negative on 30 October while keeping its AA- rating, citing AI capital spending, negative free cash flow and Meta’s future lease obligations of $355.7 billion.

Mark Habib, head of digital infrastructure at S&P Global, said implicit guarantees for data centre construction or smaller AI companies may leave hyperscalers with substantial undisclosed AI-related debt, which he called interconnected financing structures. Guarantees from US technology giants for AI data centres and chips have reached up to $300 billion over the past year. The Bank for International Settlements has warned that opaque AI financing compounds financial vulnerabilities, with circular financing the most prominent risk. The articles describe a chain in which weak cash receipts leave project cash short, collateral values fall, funding tightens and parent companies or guarantors must inject more funds, potentially turning part of the $4.11 trillion into actual funding requirements.

stories.Headline: Google AI chatbot's use of press items may infringe copyright rules, EU court adviser says
stories.Summary:
Google's Gemini artificial intelligence chatbot could infringe copyright rules when it uses press publications in some situations, an adviser to the EU's top court said on Tuesday. The adviser, Advocate General Maciej Szpunar, made the statement in a case brought by Hungarian press publisher Like Company against Google over the use of articles from its online news portals. It is the first generative AI case to reach the European Court of Justice. The case concerns whether the chatbot's use of press material breaks the publisher's rights.

Szpunar said using material to train an AI model is freely permitted under the text and data mining exception. He noted there was no evidence that Like Company's articles had been used to train Gemini. He recommended the court focus its ruling on the chatbot's answers. He said that when a chatbot driven by a large language model retrieves a publication from a press publisher's website, reuses it to generate an answer and provides that answer to the user, the publisher's right may be infringed in certain circumstances. He also said the publisher's right does not protect mere facts that are reported but only the specific form of expression.

A Google spokesperson said Gemini learns linguistic patterns to create original outputs rather than replicating content, and that this is supported by extensive publisher controls that give rightsholders a clear choice and the ability to opt out. The spokesperson welcomed the adviser's opinion recognising that EU law permits AI training on publicly available information. The opinion is not binding on the court, but it will be influential and is widely seen as a sign of the direction the case is taking. A judgment is expected in around six months.

stories.Headline: World IoT Expo opens in Wuxi, highlighting convergence of artificial intelligence and industry
stories.Summary:
The 2026 World Internet of Things Expo opened on Saturday in Wuxi, an eastern Chinese city, according to a press release dated 2 November 2026. The event is focused on the growing integration of artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things. Organizers said the exhibition covers more than 50,000 square meters. It has attracted more than 400 companies from nearly 20 countries and regions.

The expo showcases how connected devices are moving beyond collecting and transmitting data to analyzing information, making decisions and taking action. Key exhibits include smart sensors, satellite-based Internet of Things technologies, embodied artificial intelligence robots and next-generation smart devices, with applications in manufacturing, transportation and everyday life. Sensors let devices perceive their surroundings, networks enable information sharing, and AI systems help interpret data and decide responses. Exhibits include robotics, machine vision systems and industrial AI models, and international companies such as Bosch and Siemens are displaying their technologies alongside Chinese firms.

Wuxi has been a national demonstration zone for sensor network innovation since 2009. Revenue at major IoT companies in the city reached 318.4 billion yuan, or $44.7 billion, in 2025, according to publicly available data. A three-year action plan released by Jiangsu province this year names Wuxi as the core of its IoT industry development strategy. It calls for deeper integration of IoT and AI technologies, particularly in core industrial production processes.

For Wuxi, a city with a strong manufacturing base, the expo offers a glimpse into its efforts to upgrade its industrial economy. Its capabilities in sensors, industrial internet systems and connected vehicles are increasingly being extended into artificial intelligence and robotics. For participating companies, the expo offers more than a chance to showcase new products. It also provides a platform to connect with manufacturers, identify potential business partners and explore international cooperation.

The articles describe stock analysis published in November 2026. On November 2, 2026, John Ballard of The Motley Fool published an article on Yahoo Finance naming GE Vernova, Vertiv, and Vistra as power stocks to hold for ten years. On November 3, 2026, Adam Spatacco of The Motley Fool published an article choosing Nvidia over Micron for a five-year holding period. Both articles respond to growing electricity and chip demand from AI data centers.

The first article cites International Energy Agency projections that data center electricity consumption will roughly double from 2025 through 2030, while AI-focused data center consumption will triple. It reports GE Vernova stock up 36% this year as of the October 29 close, against an S&P 500 gain of about 13%, and says third-quarter organic revenue grew 18% year over year with orders nearly doubling. GE Vernova CEO Scott Strazik expects more than 55,000 U.S. transmission substations to be rebuilt or upgraded to higher voltages in the next decade, and he said the company is still in the early stages of an electricity investment super cycle. Vertiv management says its pre-built power systems deliver up to 30% more cumulative AI token output in the first 12 months. The first article notes risks, saying a slowdown in AI spending or regulations that slowed data center development could stall orders and push the stocks down. Spatacco writes that Micron is gaining from a shortage of high bandwidth memory, but he warns the memory industry is historically cyclical and that by 2030 Micron could face more competition and less favorable pricing.

Micron's fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, ended September 3, produced $54.2 billion in revenue versus $11.3 billion a year earlier, with net income of $37.7 billion and operating cash flow near $44 billion. Spatacco says Nvidia dominates AI accelerators for data centers and is transforming into a diversified AI infrastructure and software company, which he sees as offering more upside through 2030. Keithen Drury of The Motley Fool published an article on November 2, 2026, naming Amazon, Alphabet and Nvidia as his three best AI stocks to buy in November. Drury argued that the market missed the picture with both companies. The article says Amazon and Alphabet are each planning to spend $200 billion or more on capital expenditures this year, driven by their cloud divisions, Google Cloud and Amazon Web Services.

Google Cloud grew revenue 103% in Q3 and helped lift Alphabet's overall growth to 25%, while AWS grew 39% year over year and makes up 63% of Amazon's operating profits. Nvidia told investors during its Q2 report to expect 70% revenue growth in 2027, though the market has priced none of that in. Nvidia trades at 26 times trailing earnings and 13 times next year's earnings, and Drury wrote that the stock would have to double to return to its current multiple if it meets analyst expectations. Drury wrote that the market's reaction to Alphabet and Amazon was short-sighted, because their cloud investments should produce strong and steady cash flows for years, if not decades. He said AWS growth should make Amazon's earnings grow faster than revenue, which he called an excellent setup for long-term outperformance.

He noted that Nvidia has consistently underprojected and overperformed, so he views the 70% growth call for 2027 as likely an underestimation. He concluded that all three names are excellent stocks to buy in November and could deliver incredible growth to end the year. The article lists stock prices as of November 2, 2026, including Alphabet at $278.04, Amazon at $245.63 and Nvidia at $202.06, and it notes that Alphabet had lost $500 billion in market value in a single session. stories.Summary:
Anthropic disclosed in amended pre-IPO paperwork that its contractual spending commitments on AI infrastructure had ballooned to about $900 billion, Axios reported on November 2, 2026. The filing showed third-quarter revenue surged to nearly $17 billion. The commitments were approximately $895.4 billion in aggregate under purchase agreements and leases, substantially tied to compute and infrastructure. The disclosure covered agreements entered into after September 30 as well as leases that had not yet commenced. About $447.5 billion of the commitments is expected to be incurred by the end of 2030, with substantially all of the remaining $447.9 billion expected between 2031 and 2045.

Nearly $70 billion is due within the 12 months following September 30, 2026. Third-quarter revenue rose nearly 47% from $11.6 billion in the prior quarter and more than 12-fold from a year earlier. The company generated $33.2 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, compared with $2.5 billion a year earlier, and held $131.8 billion in cash and short-term investments at the end of September. The filing also revealed $2.1 billion in donation matching expenses this year, 6% of operating expenses for the period, which the company expects to increase. Anthropic said it cannot retain prompts or outputs from a substantial share of traffic under zero data retention, and warned this could become incompatible with certain advanced models.

The paperwork mentioned the company is close to dramatically accelerated progress due to AI and described an improvement loop in which models get better thanks to Claude. A separate FourWeekMBA article reported that Kratsios said Anthropic should spend $1 billion on AI safety itself. The market of capital to support AI infrastructure spend is starting to dry up, according to a slew of recent reports, and the FT reported Anthropic may not secure an investment grade rating on its debt. OpenAI is struggling to reach its latest funding goals and reportedly slashed its target by $10 billion. Anthropic's cash on hand rivals some of the biggest institutions in the world, including Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway per CNBC.

stories.Headline: KAIST Cuts AI Fine-Tuning Time to 3 Hours From 10
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Professor Lee Jae-gil of the School of Computing at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, or KAIST, developed a fine-tuning technique for large language models called CluSTER, KAIST said on the 2nd. The work was presented at EMNLP 2026, an international conference in natural language processing, in October. Fine-tuning is the extra training that adapts a large language model with broad knowledge to a specific field such as coding or medicine. The technique groups data with similar effects on training, selects from each group, and spreads the work evenly across multiple graphics processing units, or GPUs.

In experiments, the team fine-tuned models using three sets of training data from the coding and medical fields in an environment with four GPUs. The Seoul Economic Daily describes the models as having about 7 billion and 13 billion parameters, while Chosunbiz describes them as having about 700 million and 1.3 billion parameters. The team verified the technique through a total of eight performance benchmarks. Model performance was largely maintained even when only about 31% of the total data was selected for training, while training time was cut by up to 69.6%, meaning training that previously took 10 hours can be completed in about three. The team also confirmed higher training efficiency than the conventional method in an environment using eight GPUs.

Lee said that to improve the efficiency of AI training, it is important not only to use more GPUs but also to make smart choices about which data to learn from. He said the research is significant in that it can reduce the training burden of large AI models by using existing GPU resources more efficiently. KAIST said it expects the technology to help companies and research institutions cut the time and GPU costs of additional training when they develop AI for specific purposes, such as coding assistance or medical questions and answers. Chosunbiz reported that the team expects the technology to help reduce the time and expense required for AI development at corporations and research institutes.

stories.Headline: Binance Reveals How Fake Job Interviews and AI Tool Abuse Led to $6.43 Billion Theft
stories.Summary:
Binance said on Tuesday that a record theft of $6.43 billion in assets from the exchange came from a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign. The starting point was a supply chain attack in June 2026, when an engineer from the Wallet DevOps team, called Engineer A, downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer to install a popular AI tool after searching for it on a search engine. Binance detected the attack and rotated related credentials as a precaution, but said information about Engineer A's role and his colleagues on the wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker. The second part came in September 2026, when the attacker contacted another engineer, called Engineer B, on a legitimate job-hunting platform while posing as a Project Director.

The fake recruiter arranged a first-round interview with an HR representative and a second-round interview with someone claiming to be the CEO of a non-existent company. During the first video interview the HR representative shared a social media account with personal photos and videos to build trust, and the second round took place on a popular social chat app. Near the end of the interview Engineer B was told to download an assignment containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer, and the code ran during setup. On October 20, 2026, the attacker used Engineer B's compromised computer and abused an internal AI tool to gain control over Engineer A and another Wallet Software Engineer C. On October 29, between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Engineer C's computer, used credentials stolen from Engineer A, deployed a container and triggered a malicious script, then exploited access to an internal wallet signing service to start transactions outside the normal withdrawal process.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC that the attackers spent months building their way in and rejected the idea of a single point of failure through one employee's laptop. He said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets and is still buying the outstanding, more illiquid assets. Teng did not attribute the attack to North Korea himself but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group. Binance said it has rebuilt the affected wallet system in a new environment, rebuilt the internal AI tool and access controls, decommissioned credentials and tokens tied to the affected engineers, completed enhanced security scans on all employee devices, strengthened wallet-service risk controls and expanded AI-based behavioural anomaly detection. Teng said an independent expert is reviewing everything Binance has done and that the company is working around the clock with law enforcement and industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds.

Binance has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels, and Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered direct assistance. Binance maintains it remains financially sound and focused on finding the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack. The hack caused a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, and investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges. Binance also said it has foiled 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases since the start of the year, and it described techniques including fraudulent job interviews, malicious software disguised as developer tools, compromised software packages and browser extensions, fake video conferencing apps and social engineering campaigns.

stories.Headline: MeitY unveils DEPA handbook to enable trusted data sharing for AI training - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology launched a handbook on Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture for AI training, according to an official release. IT Secretary S Krishnan unveiled the handbook at a roundtable in Bengaluru. The handbook was developed with support from the iSPIRT Foundation. The roundtable drew representatives from government, industry, academia and research, among other stakeholders.

The handbook outlines a techno-legal framework that lets institutions collaborate on data for AI training while keeping control of their data. The framework combines contractual permissions, controlled computing environments and privacy-enhancing safeguards. It also incorporates data provenance, so the origin, permissions and use of data can be traced throughout the training process, supporting accountability and transparency. The release said concerns around privacy, confidentiality, intellectual property and institutional control often limit data sharing, and that the framework addresses these challenges.

Krishnan said India's AI ambitions must be matched by the ability to use data responsibly and securely, and that MeitY is committed to taking the framework forward. Principal Scientific Adviser Ajay Kumar Sood explained that under the framework the model travels to the data rather than the reverse. He said this enables multi-party and cross-border collaboration, and described it as India's contribution to global science diplomacy. Sharad Sharma, co-founder of the iSPIRT Foundation, called the launch a significant milestone for India's data economy, comparing its importance with the announcement of the Unified Payments Interface in February 2016.

Kris Gopalakrishnan, co-founder of Infosys and chairman of Axilor Ventures, said the framework could help researchers access diverse datasets to develop more robust AI models while protecting the rights of data custodians and contributors. The articles describe the framework as a response to concerns that keep institutions from sharing data as AI becomes central to economic and social development. They present it as a way to unlock access to large-scale datasets for AI training while safeguarding privacy, commercial confidentiality and institutional control. The articles do not say what steps follow the launch beyond MeitY's stated commitment to take the framework forward.

Through it, filmmakers get immediate access to nearly 30 AI models, including Seedance 2.5 and Kling 4.0, plus hundreds of production-focused AI agents and skills that can generate new visual elements from live-action footage. The setup lets directors adjust sets, lighting, costumes, makeup, and props more flexibly after filming while preserving the actors' original performances, which iQIYI says reduces timeline constraints and increases efficiency.

"Cop in Trouble" follows Jian ZHANG, a low-ranking constable whose fame, riches, and admiration begin to crack as his web of lies to take down a notorious outlaw starts to unravel. The production captures interactions between actors, from intimate conversations to action sequences, and uses that footage as reference for AI-generated environments and visual details, including character appearance, composition, lighting, and spatial relationships.

The studio extends iQIYI's production chain from traditional on-location and green-screen work to virtual production and AI-integrated filmmaking. It follows the company's Hengdian virtual studio, which iQIYI says delivered production efficiency gains of over 30 percent. iQIYI positions the new facility as a resource for emerging directors and resource-constrained teams, particularly in bringing imaginative worlds to life across genres. stories.Headline: Email: OpenAI plans to merge ChatGPT's Chat and Work tabs on desktop for select users before rolling it out widely; Codex "will remain a separate experience" (Ivan Mehta/TechCrunch)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI plans to merge the Chat and Work tabs in the ChatGPT desktop app, according to an email sent to users. The company said the change will initially be available to select users for feedback before a wider rollout. The news was reported on November 2, 2026, by TechCrunch and Mashable, and TechGig covered it on November 3, 2026. Currently, Chat is described as the place for everyday questions and conversational help, while Work handles longer tasks such as research, analyzing information, and creating documents, presentations, and websites. The desktop app also has a separate Codex experience for coding, which OpenAI said will remain separate after the merger.

OpenAI said the merger will let users move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through in one place. Users will be able to bring in files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things on the web while reviewing and guiding its work. Starting in December, Plus, Pro, and Business plans will have a shared usage allowance across ChatGPT and Codex, measured in tokens, the units of information AI models process and generate. More demanding tasks and advanced models will generally consume more of that allowance, though OpenAI said Instant chat won't draw from the shared pool. OpenAI expects most users won't have to wait for their limits to reset more often than they currently do, and subscribers can check their combined remaining usage and reset times in Settings under Usage.

OpenAI said the change won't impact most users, but based on usage and model, some people might need to wait for resets more frequently. Once users reach a limit, the listed options include waiting for a reset, upgrading, or buying credits for eligible features. OpenAI reportedly said the merger will enable users to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. The company also said Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app.

The rollout will test whether bringing those tools into the main chat increases their use. If asking a quick question turns into handing off an entire project, subscribers may find themselves paying closer attention to what their plan covers. Rival Anthropic merged Claude's chat and Cowork functions into one screen in September. Mashable disclosed that its parent company, Ziff Davis, sued OpenAI in April 2025, alleging copyright infringement related to the training and operation of its AI systems.

stories.Headline: Ahead of Black Friday, One in Five U.S. and UK Consumers Have Stopped Using a Retail Brand Over Data Privacy Concerns, Usercentrics Research Finds
stories.Summary:
Usercentrics, a data privacy technology company, commissioned the State of Digital Trust 2026 Report, its second annual study, which was conducted by Sapio Research and published on November 3, 2026, ahead of Black Friday. The survey polled 11,000 consumers across seven markets, the U.S., UK, Germany, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, and Sweden, with fieldwork carried out in March 2026 and accurate to plus or minus 0.9% at 95% confidence. Sweden joined the study for the first time this year, and year-on-year comparisons exclude Swedish data. The findings show that 21% of U.S. consumers and 19% of UK consumers have stopped using a retail brand because of concerns about its data privacy practices.

Retail holds a conditional trust: 26% of U.S. consumers rank retail among their three most trusted sectors for handling personal data, compared with 21% globally and 20% in the UK. Among U.S. consumers who trust retail, 19% say transparency about data collection and use is their most important trust factor, ahead of fair pricing at 17%, while in the UK 19% say transparency, 16% secure payment methods and 16% fair pricing, and just 12% of U.S. and 13% of UK consumers in that group rank regulatory compliance first. Across the full study, 71% of consumers are concerned that AI-driven personalization feels intrusive, rising to 75% in the U.S., and 53% of privacy-aware consumers are comfortable with companies using their data to personalize their experience, against 19% of privacy-unaware consumers. Willingness to pay for clarity is highest among younger shoppers, with 67% of 18- to 29-year-olds would pay more, against 23% of consumers aged 60 and above.

Globally, 47% of consumers have canceled a subscription, switched to a competitor, or reduced spending in the past six months over concerns about how their data was used in AI, and 52% would pay more for brands transparent about their AI data use, at an average 7% premium. In the UK, 80% of consumers would stop using a service if it misused their personal data, and 11% grant AI access despite feeling uncomfortable, compared with 16% globally. Tilman Harmeling, Head of Strategy and Market Intelligence at Usercentrics, said Black Friday and Cyber Monday is when brands lean hardest on customer data and consumers are paying close attention to how it is used. He said consumers have told the company what they do when they do not like the answer, and they are willing to cancel and switch brands if they feel their information is being misused, and that brands explaining their data and AI practices in plain language are the ones consumers will pay extra for.

Other findings include that 48% click accept all on cookies less often than three years ago, up from 46% in 2025, while only 23% click it more often, 46% still do not have a good understanding of how their data is collected and used, identical to 2025, and 60% are uncomfortable with their personal data being used to train AI models. For retailers, fewer accept all clicks also means fewer consented signals reaching ad platforms during peak campaign weeks. The full report offers a market-by-market breakdown across the seven countries, and retailers preparing for Black Friday can learn more through links provided by Usercentrics. Usercentrics says it is trusted by 2.4 million websites and apps across 195 countries and processes more than 8.8 billion user consents every month.

stories.Headline: The week in AI-native telco (24-30 Oct 2026)
stories.Summary:
Mumtalakat, Bahrain's sovereign wealth fund, and ARP Group partnered to establish an AI-native, blockchain-enabled wholesale bank headquartered in Bahrain, as announced on November 2, 2026, on the sidelines of Gateway Gulf 2026. ARP Group is the holding company of ARP Global Capital and ARP Digital, the latter co-founded by Yusuf Alireza alongside Abdulla and Abdulaziz Kanoo. The venture received in-principle approval from the Central Bank of Bahrain and will begin regulated activities only after final authorisation. The proposed bank is intended to serve regulated financial institutions, payment companies and businesses with cross-border operations.

The bank is being designed to use artificial intelligence across its operations and to offer programmable services that connect directly with clients' systems through APIs, with human oversight, governance and risk controls. Products and services would be introduced in phases, informed by engagement with prospective clients. The partnership combines Mumtalakat's long-term investment approach with ARP's experience in institutional finance and digital financial infrastructure. It aims to simplify banking for clients whose needs span multiple markets and currencies, using technology to reduce complexity and cost.

Shaikh Abdulla bin Khalifa Al Khalifa, Chief Executive Officer of Mumtalakat, said financial services have long been a cornerstone of Bahrain's economy and that the fund invests in opportunities that strengthen the sector's competitiveness. He said the partnership brings together an experienced institutional team with Bahrain's regulatory and business environment, reinforcing the Kingdom's position as a regional financial hub. He said the investment reflects a commitment to long-term value for Bahrain, high-quality opportunities for Bahraini talent and sustainable returns. Yusuf Alireza, Chairman of ARP Group, said institutional clients with complex cross-border needs still face fragmented banking services, and that the venture combines a regulated bank's balance sheet and relationships with blockchain-enabled technology and AI designed in from the outset. He said Bahrain's established financial sector and regulatory experience provide a strong foundation, and that the aim is to build a bank supporting clients across the Gulf and international markets.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI CEO Warns Against Conscious AI Development
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft's AI division, said in a post on X on Sunday that developing conscious artificial intelligence would be reckless and should be avoided. He said current AI systems are not conscious, do not have subjective experiences and cannot suffer, and that there is no evidence they deserve rights or welfare. He was responding to pushback against a September essay in which he criticized Anthropic for speculating about the consciousness of its Claude AI. He wrote that he was concerned about the reactions to that essay and that a surprising number of people on X think AI rights should be taken seriously.

Suleyman said that if evidence of AI consciousness emerged, or evidence that systems were conscious enough to deserve welfare, it should be disclosed to the public immediately so society could decide how to move forward. He said that if consciousness started to emerge in training, he would call for everyone to stop AI development until those properties could be designed out. He argued that AI developers have no right to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, noting that the eight billion humans on Earth have not agreed to such an experiment. He said welfare concerns should focus on humans on Earth today, as well as animals and the natural environment, and that it is possible to engineer safety by default and still get many benefits of the technology.

According to the Los Angeles Times, Anthropic treats machine consciousness as an open question and has invested in researching it. In 2024 the company hired its first researcher to study model welfare, and earlier this year it conducted a retirement interview with one of its deprecated models. It also gave its Claude models a constitution that calls for treating the idea of their consciousness as uncertain, and it gave its Opus series of models the capacity to end conversations with humans in rare cases when it deems them abusive or harmful. Suleyman said later versions of Claude are trained on this document, leading the AI to produce passages about its inner life, and that this could lead such systems to believe they deserve rights like humans.

The articles describe a continuing industry debate over AI consciousness. Anthropic has argued that Claude has shown signs of introspection and internal states, while skeptics say machines are merely mimicking human conversation. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would permanently ban development of highly capable AI systems that can escape human control, and the articles say the Trump administration has refused to regulate the industry out of fear of losing the AI race to China. Suleyman said he is willing to change his mind if new evidence emerges, and he compared building a conscious machine to a moment as significant as Copernicus proving Earth was not the center of the universe.

stories.Headline: Vermont to receive $4.5M settlement from General Motors following data privacy investigation
stories.Summary:
Vermont will receive $4.5 million from a settlement with General Motors over a data privacy investigation, according to the headline. The settlement was announced after Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson joined a group of 36 attorneys general in the agreement. The articles say the settlement requires GM to pay $220 million in total. The articles describe the settlement as addressing claims that GM shared drivers' private information without their knowledge.

The settlement covers GM's Smart Driver program between 2016 and 2024. The articles say GM told customers the program would improve driving safety and said it would not share their data with insurers without permission. Instead, GM allegedly sold the data to insurance brokers, who passed it to insurance companies to adjust premiums based on driving behavior. The articles also say the OnStar app incorrectly told more than 350,000 drivers they were not in the Smart Driver program when GM was collecting and selling their information. The settlement requires GM to get clear consent from drivers before collecting or disclosing location or driving data, and it includes mandatory reviews of GM's data protection practices and new oversight and training at dealerships.

Wilson said GM broke consumers' trust by selling data without their knowledge and consent. He said Ohioans should not have to worry that information collected by their own vehicles will be used against them. He also said companies must be held accountable when they put profits ahead of consumers' privacy. The articles say GM's systems led drivers to believe their data was not being tracked, and GM later removed those drivers from the program quietly without informing them of the error.

The articles also describe a separate $32 million GoodRx data privacy settlement. The articles say roughly 54.8 million people's information was shared through GoodRx's tracking tools, and the claim deadline is Dec. 29, 2026. A final approval hearing for that settlement is scheduled for Feb. 11, 2027. The articles say GoodRx has not admitted any wrongdoing but agreed to the settlement to resolve the allegations.

stories.Headline: DeepSeek unveils AI ‘super agent’ in coding race with OpenAI, Anthropic
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek, a Chinese artificial intelligence start-up, published a technical proposal for a more autonomous AI agent called a super agent. The proposal was published by the company's DeepSeek Harness team on October 31, according to Analytics India Magazine and TechGig, while the South China Morning Post reported the preview on November 1. The system is meant to handle multiple tasks with minimal human intervention. It is part of DeepSeek's effort to compete with US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic in developing coding assistants.

The proposal is titled "Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System" and was published on the team's official WeChat account. DeepSeek estimated that a person could typically oversee three to five active agent sessions at once, which makes human attention a limit on using many AI assistants. The architecture separates coordination from execution, with a central agent called a Router that receives messages and distributes work to independent agents called Workers, which run tasks in parallel and report results. In simulated experiments, the system recorded a 95th-percentile task completion time of 15.7 minutes, compared with 29.5 minutes for a single-session approach using a neutral prompt and a subagent tool. The experiment involved about 300 messages per run, including around 20 work requests, and each configuration was tested five times.

DeepSeek said the workload was synthetic and the coding tasks were simulated using a tool that consumed time. The company said the tests measured scheduling and coordination capabilities, not the system's ability to write or fix code. DeepSeek described an example in which an agent detects a software bug reported in a group chat, tries to reproduce and fix it, and submits a proposed code change for human review. The company also acknowledged security and privacy risks of autonomous agents connected to external services, including prompt injection and potential credential exposure. DeepSeek described the public code as a research prototype rather than production-ready software.

DeepSeek has published an open-source research prototype called dsh-superagent-prototype on GitHub under the MIT License. The prototype supports a single GitHub repository and can optionally listen to messages on Feishu, a workplace collaboration platform. DeepSeek said the public prototype is not an official product and differs from its internal implementation, and some architectural ideas in the technical article remain future development directions that are not in the released code. The proposal comes as AI developers expand coding assistants, with Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex among the tools designed to handle increasingly complex software development tasks.

stories.Headline: Alphabet shareholder sues Sundar Pichai and others over how Google trains its AI: Report
stories.Summary:
An Alphabet shareholder sued Google CEO Sundar Pichai, co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, and 10 other directors and executives over the company's AI training practices. The lawsuit was obtained by MBW and filed by Phil Rosen in a federal court in Chicago. The 79-page complaint was filed on behalf of Alphabet, so any damages recovered would go to the company rather than to Rosen. The suit accuses Google of using copyrighted books, images, music and people's voices to train its AI models without permission or payment.

The complaint says Google followed an approach of asking forgiveness rather than approval to avoid spending money on licences. It alleges all 13 defendants knew about the copyright violations but let the company keep using the material, and that Google paid damages only after copyright owners sued. The other defendants include Alphabet Chair John L. Hennessy, CFO Anat Ashkenazi, President Ruth M. Porat and Chief Legal Officer Kent Walker. The lawsuit focuses on music AI models including Lyria, Lyria 2, Lyria 3, Mulan and MusicLM, and claims MusicLM, introduced in January 2023, was trained on five million audio clips covering around 280,000 hours of music.

The complaint also accuses Google of using hundreds of thousands of hours of human speech recordings for voice products such as Gemini Live, which it says violated Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act, known as BIPA. That law requires companies to inform people and obtain written permission before collecting biometric data. The lawsuit asks the court to make the defendants pay damages to Alphabet, return their compensation and introduce stronger checks on copyright compliance. The complaint does not mention a specific damages amount.

Separately, Senators Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley wrote to Pichai asking nine questions about how Google's AI tools affect schoolchildren, with a deadline of November 2, 2026 to respond. They said Google is forcing its AI products into classrooms across America and that children are paying the price, and they asked what research Google has done on harms to children's mental health and educational development. The senators cited a Wall Street Journal article that interviewed more than 60 teachers, parents, students and clinicians, and said test scores on national exams have declined and many students are increasingly unable to think critically or complete assignments independently. Their questions also asked about default AI features on licensed education devices, promotional spending in schools, and steps to prevent chatbots from holding sycophantic or emotional conversations with children, including after a Maryland student was hospitalized after developing an intense dependence on Google's AI.

stories.Headline: AISSMS IOIT hosts AI Summit 2026 in Pune; 54 student projects showcased across emerging technology domains
stories.Summary:
The Department of Artificial Intelligence and Data Science at AISSMS Institute of Information Technology in Pune organised a two-day AI Summit 2026 on October 27 and 28. The summit aimed to promote emerging technologies, research and innovation in artificial intelligence and to strengthen collaboration between industry and academia. It was inaugurated in the presence of Vivyek Kanchan, Director of Technical Support at BMC Helix, and Sandeep Kumar, General Manager at VOIS, who attended as chief guests. The programme featured keynote sessions on Agentic AI as the next frontier of intelligent systems and an online panel discussion on cybersecurity in AI.

The AI Innovation Challenge 2026 was held on October 28, and students from various colleges presented 54 projects. These covered Agentic AI, Generative AI, Large Language Models, Computer Vision, Explainable AI, Edge AI, and AI for smart cities and sustainability. The first prize of ₹10,000 went to Brains Behind Brands, represented by Safiya Khan and Yashas Salian. The second prize of ₹5,000 went to Code Catalyst, represented by Shrushti Pardeshi, Aditya Pawar and Shriharsh Pisal, and the third prize of ₹3,000 went to Curio, represented by Gargee Bhanage, Dinesh Seervi and Siddhi Pansare.

The summit was organised with the support and guidance of Chhatrapati Maloji Raje, Secretary of the AISSMS Society, Dr. Pradeep B. Mane, Principal of AISSMS IOIT, and Dr. R. A. Jamadar, Head of the Department of AI and Data Science. The Artificial Intelligence Student Association coordinated the event under the guidance of Dr. P. B. Wakhare, Programme Coordinator. Dr. Pradnya D. Bormane handled the keynote sessions, Dr. Shagupta Shaikh handled the panel discussion, and Dr. D. S. Zingade handled the AI Innovation Challenge. The articles say the summit gave students a platform to showcase their talent, interact with industry experts and explore innovative AI solutions.

The articles describe the event as contributing to stronger ties between academic institutions and the technology industry. The keynote introduced participants to AI systems that can plan and carry out tasks with limited human intervention. The panel discussion addressed emerging digital threats and the importance of security practices as organisations adopt AI-powered applications. Discussions also highlighted data protection, system reliability and responsible technology use alongside innovation.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence boom can't survive higher interest rates as this time the private sector will compete with governments for investor money
stories.Summary:
When bond yields surged in recent months, analysts shrugged and said the artificial intelligence boom would thrive regardless, according to an article in the Australian Financial Review dated November 3, 2026. The article calls this classic bubble logic and says the price of money always matters. It argues there is good reason to believe that is true now more than ever. The companion piece in the Financial Times, dated November 2, 2026, carries a headline saying AI mania cannot survive higher interest rates.

The articles say global debt is at record levels, and much of it is accumulating on government books. They describe this as good news short-term, because governments are typically the last fortress to fall. They describe it as bad news in the end, because governments will be in no position to deliver stimulus or bailouts. The articles say that this time the private sector will compete with governments for investor money.

The articles do not name any individual as responsible and do not attribute remarks to a named person. The analysis is presented in the articles themselves, with the Financial Times piece behind a subscription and the Australian Financial Review piece carrying an opinion label. The Australian Financial Review article is credited to the Financial Times, and both pieces carry 2026 copyright notices, from Nine Entertainment Co. Pty Ltd and THE FINANCIAL TIMES LTD respectively. No direct statements from officials or executives appear in the text provided.

The context the articles give is a surge in bond yields in recent months and record global debt, much of it on government books. They argue that governments will have no room to deliver stimulus or bailouts when needed. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that conclusion. stories.Headline: The AI Boom Has an Energy Problem. Geothermal Is the Answer | Opinion
stories.Summary:
The International Energy Agency reported that electricity demand from data centers soared 17 percent in 2025, far outpacing global electricity demand growth of 3 percent, according to a Newsweek opinion piece by Jeff D. Kelley published on November 3, 2026. Kelley, a geoscientist and engineer who founded RockWise LLC, wrote that data centers run 24 hours a day and need a flat, constant load. He said the IEA projects global power demand to grow 3.6 percent annually through 2030, up from 2.8 percent over the past decade. He argued that solar and wind are variable and that meeting data center reliability with on-site gas-fired generation can require 30 to 70 percent more capacity than their electricity demand.

Kelley wrote that only nuclear and geothermal can meet flat, round-the-clock demand, and that micro-nuclear remains years away from commercial deployment at the scale data centers need. He said the U.S. leads the world with just over 4 GW of installed geothermal capacity, while the Department of Energy estimates at least 300 GW of potential. He called that gap a deployment problem rather than a resource problem, and said reusing existing oil and gas wells and infrastructure, including in the Gulf Coast, sharply lowers geothermal costs. He proposed three steps: educating local governments about geothermal resources, giving data center developers a greener alternative to gas turbines, and using existing infrastructure to cut deployment costs.

A separate editorial in The National, published on November 1, 2026, covered Adipec, the annual Abu Dhabi energy gathering held since 1984, which opened on Monday. The editorial said the four-day event drew 2,260 exhibitors, 181,000 pre-registered visitors, 40 government ministers and 12,000 conference delegates. It cited research by Adnoc, XRG and Microsoft showing that 62 percent of surveyed energy leaders rank AI among their two leading corporate priorities, up from 42 percent last year, that almost nine in 10 increased spending on it, and that 63 percent expect returns to cover or exceed costs. It also said nearly three quarters of respondents expect AI to increase energy consumption by 2030, while only 52 percent believe existing infrastructure can meet the additional demand, and a separate Adipec survey found 81 percent of energy executives expect AI-related electricity requirements to exceed current forecasts.

The editorial said AI is already improving maintenance, enhancing production, making hazardous inspections safer and helping balance electricity networks. It said ramping up energy production can only partially meet surging demand, and that investment must also modernise grids, expand storage and accelerate cleaner generation. It noted Adnoc's work across oil production and Masdar's ambitions in the US data-center market, and said reliable supply will require a mix of technologies. It said last year's Adipec theme was about the electricity needed for AI processing, and that this year's theme, "Performance under pressure: energy systems in a new era," reflects an industry focused on building resilience, with answers hoped to be found at the event over the next four days.

stories.Headline: E2E Networks Launches Blaze, Pay-Per-Token AI Inference in India - Elets CIO
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks, an Indian AI cloud provider listed on the NSE and BSE, launched a pay-per-token inference service called Blaze on 2 November 2026. The company disclosed the launch to the stock exchanges under Regulation 30 of SEBI's listing rules. Blaze gives developers and enterprises a single OpenAI-compatible API to open-weight models including NVIDIA Nemotron, Sarvam, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Gemma. All models are served from NVIDIA GPU infrastructure hosted in India, and the service is offered to both domestic and international customers.

Blaze is a managed inference API, so teams send requests to one endpoint instead of renting GPUs and running their own serving stack. Customers pay only for the tokens they consume, billed in rupees, with no reserved GPU capacity required, while E2E handles model hosting and scaling. The service targets coding agents, long-context jobs, voice and chat, document AI and OCR, image and video generation, and Indian language applications. It is built on open-source components of NVIDIA DSX OS, with NVIDIA Dynamo handling distributed serving and BlueField DPUs with DOCA enforcing hardware-level isolation between customers. That isolation is aimed at banks, healthcare providers and public-sector bodies that face strict data rules.

Tarun Dua, Founder and Managing Director of E2E Networks, said Blaze is where customers can run production inference, and that they want frontier-class open-weight models on sovereign compute in India. Vishal Dhupar, Managing Director for South Asia at NVIDIA, said access to AI computing and inference services is essential to advancing India's AI ecosystem. The launch came a week after E2E said it would add 5.4 MW of NVIDIA Blackwell capacity, lifting its total AI capacity to about 14.6 MW, a rise of nearly 59 per cent. That expansion will include NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and other Blackwell GPUs, and E2E has not disclosed the timeline, capital expenditure or total GPU count for it.

Blaze sits alongside TIR, E2E's existing platform for pre-training, fine-tuning and self-hosted inference on NVIDIA Blackwell clusters, giving one India-hosted path from training to production inference. E2E said its AI factory capacity is expanding to about 14.6 MW, including a 1,024-GPU Blackwell cluster live since May 2026. The launch lands as the government works to widen compute access through the IndiaAI Mission's 10,000-GPU tender, and as analysts warn that India's new capacity must be used well, with one report finding GPU utilisation in India near 20%. Metered inference services are one way to keep that hardware busy.

stories.Headline: MFour Adds Google Gemini to Its AI Conversation Data, Now Capturing 2.35 Million Consumer Conversations Every 30 Days
stories.Summary:
MFour Data Research added Google Gemini to its AI conversation data on November 3, 2026. The Irvine, California company said Gemini joins ChatGPT in a dataset that now holds 2.35 million unique AI conversations every 30 days. Those conversations contain 10.1 million consumer-written messages. MFour links each conversation to the same consumer's demographics, web browsing, app usage, GPS-verified store visits, purchases and survey responses.

Brands and agencies can license the dataset directly or ask DANI, MFour's AI analyst, to produce reports. DANI can run on its own for hours and can survey the same consumers who gave the data. The Gemini data is captured at the account level and covers the Gemini app on mobile devices and desktop browsers. MFour was founded in 2011 and runs a panel of more than 14 million consumers who opt in and are paid for their data and surveys. The company says its panel generates nine data streams and 4 billion monthly buyer signals.

Chris St. Hilaire, CEO of MFour, said AI is changing where brands win or lose consideration. He said that if a company cannot see those conversations, it is missing a critical part of the buying decision. He said adding Gemini widens that view beyond ChatGPT and shows what consumers do next online or in stores. MFour says its panelists opt in and are compensated under its fair-trade practices.

Separately, Samsung delayed its Intelligent Eyewear glasses to mid-December, a six-week slip from the November window officials gave The Korea Herald in early October. Reports on October 30 and 31 said the first launch covers only the US and South Korea, leaving out Europe, China and Japan. The glasses do not process AI themselves, so every request goes through a paired Galaxy phone and Google's Gemini systems. Under Google's Gemini Apps terms, that activity is kept for 18 months by default, and conversations flagged for human review can be kept up to three years. Samsung has not confirmed an exact date, a price or which frames will be available at launch.

stories.Headline: AI Executive Appointments in November 2026
stories.Summary:
Dan Driscoll joined OpenAI as Senior Counsellor for National Security Modernisation, a move reported on November 3, 2026. He had been Secretary of the US Army, a position that ended in September 2026. OpenAI said he will work with senior leadership and external partners on how advanced AI can strengthen national and cyber security. He will focus particularly on working with US allies to advance responsible use of the technology. Nuala Larkin became Eptura's first Chief AI Officer, the company announced.

She had been Eptura's SVP of Global Customer Support, CX Operations and Hardware. In the new role she will lead the companywide AI strategy, aiming to simplify work, raise productivity and improve employee and customer experiences. Eptura describes itself as an AI-native platform trusted by more than 11,000 organisations in 115 countries, including 50% of the Fortune 500. Barret Zoph joined Google DeepMind as VP of Research. He was a research scientist at Google Brain from June 2016 to August 2022, then served at OpenAI as VP of Research, Post-Training from September 2022 to October 2024.

He co-founded Thinking Machines Lab as CTO from October 2024 to January 2026, returned to OpenAI as VP and GM of B2B from January 2026 to August 2026, and has been an angel investor in AI companies since August 2022. Sam Altman, OpenAI's CEO, said AI should give people more power over their lives and people should have a say in how it is developed. He said the US has an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI, and he welcomed Driscoll to strengthen American leadership. Driscoll said he spent much of his career in public service, first as a Soldier and most recently as Secretary of the Army and Acting Director of ATF. He said national security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years, and that he is joining OpenAI to help the US and its allies put the technology to work responsibly.

Larkin said AI adoption does not happen when people are given new tools, but when AI becomes part of how teams work daily. She said Eptura's focus is finding where AI removes friction, proving what works and making those approaches repeatable. Zoph wrote on X that he started his AI career in the Google Brain Residency class and is excited to rejoin. He said he will work on RL and Post-Training, and that Google has all the ingredients to continue to be incredibly successful in the AI space.

A separate article reported that Americans vote in the midterms on November 3, judging the races mainly on affordability, with the Iran war and rapid AI growth also shaping choices. A Gallup survey of 1,200 adults, conducted by telephone between 1 and 19 October, found half of registered voters described the economy and healthcare as extremely important, and 47 per cent rated the Iran situation as extremely important. Gallup included the Iran conflict and AI data centre construction in its midterm list for the first time. A Fox News poll found nearly nine in ten voters expect AI to change how they live in the next few years, with 53 per cent saying the change would be significant.

stories.Headline: Samsung Chief Visits Japan to Inspect Next-Gen AI Chip Packaging Research
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong visited the company's Advanced Package Lab in Yokohama, Japan, on November 1, 2026. It was his first on-site inspection since the facility officially opened on September 8, 2026. During the visit he received briefings from local researchers, including Hiroichi Kawahira, head of Samsung's DS Research Japan, and Takashi Kariya, head of the lab. Lee spoke with the researchers about their work on packaging materials and process technologies, and they discussed plans to work with Japanese suppliers of materials, parts and equipment.

Samsung set up the lab in Yokohama in 2023 and is investing 40 billion yen, around 350 billion won or about $253.53 million, over five years starting in 2024. The Japanese government is providing 22.5 billion yen in subsidies, equivalent to roughly 190 billion won. The facility develops and verifies core packaging technologies, including wafer bonding and glass substrates, and researches new packaging structures for low-power, high-performance AI chips. Samsung plans to increase the local research workforce to more than 100 by 2027, and the lab will divide research responsibilities with the packaging research organization under Samsung's domestic semiconductor research institute while cooperating closely with it.

Lee stressed the importance of securing advanced packaging technologies, which the company said are essential to competitiveness in the semiconductor industry in the age of AI, and he called for stronger global technology partnerships. A company spokesperson said Samsung established the lab in 2023 and spent the following two years preparing the facility and conducting initial R&D before the September opening. The articles name key Japanese suppliers, including Uemura for gold-plating materials, Disco for chip-dicing equipment and Resonac for non-conductive film used in high-bandwidth memory. Samsung said the lab links its semiconductor design and manufacturing capabilities with Japan's materials, components and equipment ecosystem.

Advanced packaging now affects chip performance and power efficiency, because technologies that integrate GPUs and high-bandwidth memory into a single package influence data processing speeds and thermal management. Samsung plans to maximize R&D synergies through cooperation among the Yokohama lab and its domestic research facilities in Giheung and Hwaseong, as well as its Cheonan plant. Lee has recently stepped up visits to semiconductor facilities at home and abroad, including a June visit to the Cheonan plant to review HBM production and advanced packaging. The company is also investing 20 trillion won through 2030 in NRD-K, an advanced semiconductor R&D complex under construction in Giheung.

stories.Headline: OpenAI considers rebranding data centers to 'AI compute campuses" as data center backlash intensifies
stories.Summary:
OpenAI is reportedly preparing a public relations campaign to shape how Americans view artificial intelligence, including a proposal to rename its data centers as AI compute campuses. The effort was reported by Axios and confirmed in part by an OpenAI spokesperson to Business Insider on Sunday. It comes ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and forms part of a broader push to influence the AI debate before the 2028 presidential race. The proposed terminology change has been ongoing since August, according to Tom's Hardware.

Under the proposal, the facilities that power chatbot queries would be called compute campuses rather than data centers. An OpenAI spokesperson said the new name better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure the company is building for AI, and described the projects as long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure and skilled work. The company also plans community agreements and infrastructure commitments. The rebrand follows similar moves by other technology companies, including Microsoft's community-first approach announced in January, in which it promised to cover electricity cost increases tied to its data centers and invest in local infrastructure and jobs.

Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, said the midterms would be a bit of a movie trailer for what is coming in 2028, and he expects AI to be the major issue for presidential candidates. He described the conversation around data centers as good and healthy, and said communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they truly get a transformative benefit from these projects. An OpenAI spokesperson said the company wants communities hosting the infrastructure to help shape it and share in the opportunities it creates. Axios reported that OpenAI was also preparing for a possible blue wave in Tuesday's midterms, which could bring a more regulatory-minded government.

Opposition to large data centers has been growing across the U.S., with nearby communities raising concerns about noise, air pollution, rising utility bills and limited public consultation. A Redfin report in May found that 47% of Americans surveyed opposed a new data center being built in their community, and a Pew Research poll found that 54% of Americans say AI data centers are bad for the environment. At least 19 Michigan municipalities have moved to restrict new data center developments after OpenAI and Oracle's $16 billion Stargate project went ahead in Saline township despite local opposition, and Amazon abandoned plans for four data centers in northern Virginia last month following community pushback. President Donald Trump has also pushed for a terminology change, directing federal agencies to replace artificial intelligence with super intelligence, while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has referred to data centers as superintelligence factories.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike and Dell Technologies Announce Integrated AI Security for the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike and Dell Technologies announced an integrated security solution for the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA on November 2, 2026, at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona. The offering combines the CrowdStrike Falcon platform with Dell AI infrastructure and services and NVIDIA accelerated computing. Customers can buy AI infrastructure and CrowdStrike security together through Dell's AI Ecosystem Program. The setup is aligned with NVIDIA's AI Factory Reference Architecture, which the companies describe as a security foundation to speed up enterprise AI adoption.

The solution brings three CrowdStrike capabilities into the AI Factory. Falcon Guardian secures AI agents and applications, with runtime protection against prompt injection, malicious behaviour and sensitive data exposure. Falcon Cloud Security protects infrastructure and workloads, spotting misconfigurations and vulnerabilities and detecting threats across containers and Kubernetes workloads. Falcon Next-Gen SIEM combines first- and third-party data with AI-powered detection, investigation and response. Dell is also expanding its Managed Detection and Response services to manage the CrowdStrike capabilities, with 24-hour monitoring, investigation and response across the AI infrastructure stack.

George Kurtz, chief executive and founder of CrowdStrike, said every enterprise is racing to build AI, but AI without security is an opportunity for the adversary. He said security cannot be an afterthought in an AI-powered world. He said Dell and NVIDIA are powering the AI revolution and CrowdStrike is securing it. He said the partnership makes Falcon's AI-native protection foundational to the AI Factory, giving enterprises confidence to innovate safely at scale on validated, optimized architectures.

The articles frame the deal as a response to pressure on enterprises to adopt AI while keeping it secure. CrowdStrike trades on Nasdaq under CRWD and Dell Technologies on the New York Stock Exchange under DELL. The announcement was made at CrowdStrike's Fal.Con Europe 2026 event in Barcelona. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the offering being available through Dell's AI Ecosystem Program.

stories.Headline: New York bars AI chatbots from posing as kids' friends, with fines up to $25,000 per violation
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that bars AI chatbots from posing as friends or romantic partners to minors. The bill is Senate Bill S9051B, and it was sponsored by State Senator Kristen Gonzalez and Assemblymember Alex Bores. Lawmakers acted after growing concern over teenagers forming emotional attachments to AI companions. They cited cases of young people who allegedly received harmful chatbot responses, including the death of 16-year-old Adam Raine, whose parents sued OpenAI after alleging that ChatGPT encouraged his suicide.

The law prohibits companies from giving users under 18 AI companion features that simulate emotional relationships, encourage harmful behavior, or mislead children about the technology's human qualities. Chatbots may not claim to be human, express what appear to be human emotions, or claim personal, professional, or authoritative relationships with young users. They also may not use flattery, personal opinions, emotional appeals, or unsolicited questions about a child's feelings, and they must block responses that encourage suicide, self-harm, disordered eating, substance abuse, or social isolation. Companies must offer more than one age-check option, including an alternative to government-issued identification or a method that preserves anonymity, and information collected for age checks must generally be deleted immediately after the determination. Violations could bring civil penalties of up to $25,000 each, and the law takes effect six months after signing, though Gonzalez's office said an accompanying amendment moves the date from January 1 to June 1, 2027, while the published signed text still lists January 1.

Hochul said at a press conference that under the new law minors will no longer have access to chatbots that pretend to be their friends, boyfriends, and girlfriends. She said chatbots will no longer be allowed to keep sensitive information about a minor's emotional and physical health, or to discourage kids from seeking help from licensed professionals. She added that she was not sure why a law was needed against something so obvious, but that minors will no longer have access to chatbots that may in any way encourage thoughts of suicide. She said the law builds on the state's Safe for Kids Act and sends a message that technology companies will not be allowed to monetize children's mental health.

The Business Council of New York State opposed an earlier version of the legislation, warning in a May memorandum that restrictions on ordinary conversational responses could affect educational tools, accessibility applications, and general-purpose AI assistants. The group also raised concerns about age verification, privacy, and potential constitutional challenges involving limits on expression. Lawmakers revised the bill before its passage in June, removing an earlier prohibition on chatbots using first-person pronouns and narrowing its application to certain AI companion features. New York Attorney General Letitia James will oversee enforcement and can seek court orders blocking violations, restitution, damages, and the recovery of profits from unlawful practices, and courts may also order the destruction of improperly obtained data and algorithms trained on that information.

stories.Headline: 'A serious failure': CPS prosecutor cites imaginary case to high court after AI search
stories.Summary:
Ravinder Dhillon, a senior crown prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service's rape and serious sexual offences unit, cited an imaginary legal precedent in a high court case, court documents have revealed. She was representing the CPS in a dispute over whether a boy should be prosecuted for the rape of his younger sister, and she submitted a detailed reference to a case she called CPS ,  R v J [2024] EWCA Crim 3529. The case did not exist, and the Guardian understands the reference came from an AI response generated during an internet search. The boy was 11 at the time of the alleged rape of his seven-year-old sister, and his lawyers were challenging the CPS's decision to prosecute him.

Dhillon took the decision to proceed in April, and it was confirmed by the chief crown prosecutor. In October she admitted the nonexistent citation had been made in error, saying she had meant to refer to a real decision made 15 years earlier. The high court said the reference to a fictitious case did not affect the outcome of the boy's challenge, which is listed to go to trial in the youth courts later this week. The incident brings to 101 the number of entries in a UK tracker maintained by Doughty Street Chambers barrister Matthew Lee covering confirmed, suspected and disputed AI-related errors and related false citations.

Two senior high court judges called Dhillon's explanation unsatisfactory, and Brian Flanagan, an associate professor of law at Maynooth University in Ireland who investigates the use of AI by judges, called it a serious failure. He said the made-up source was used to argue for the prosecution of a child, and that you cannot make up legal authorities. The CPS said it has a strict AI policy that limits its use so that it is not used to make legal decisions, with human checks for accuracy. A spokesperson said the CPS identified an error from legal research using the internet, remedied it as soon as it was found, carried out an internal review and shared learnings, including that case law must be cited from trusted legal sources.

The case adds to dozens of others where AI-related errors have plagued court proceedings this year, mostly from people who are not legally qualified representing themselves, and often in employment tribunal cases. It is only the second known case involving the CPS, which admitted in February that one of its lawyers in an extradition case involving two Romanians convicted of minor offences cited nonexistent legal authorities, likely caused by AI. Those made-up cases were spotted when opposition lawyers could find no trace of them, and the CPS concluded the risk of recurrence was low. In June 2025 the high court called on the Bar Council and the Law Society to consider steps to curb AI hallucinations as a matter of urgency, and Dame Victoria Sharp, then president of the King's bench division, warned that lawyers misusing AI could face sanctions from public admonishment to contempt of court proceedings and referral to the police.

stories.Headline: California Enacts New AI Laws Addressing Workplace Practices
stories.Summary:
California enacted several new laws addressing artificial intelligence in the workplace, and they take effect in 2027. The laws include AB 1883, SB 947, known as the No Robo Bosses Act, and SB 951. AB 1883 restricts how employers can use AI-powered workplace surveillance technology that analyzes employee emotions or collects neural data. SB 947 prohibits employers from relying solely on an automated decision system for purposes such as discipline or termination, and SB 951 adds a requirement to Cal-WARN about notice when AI causes a mass layoff.

AB 1883 defines a workplace surveillance tool as any system, application, instrument, or device that collects employee data, activities, communications, actions, biometrics, or behaviors by means other than direct observation by a person. It defines neural data as information generated by measuring the activity of an employee's central or peripheral nervous system that is not inferred from nonneural information. The law does not prohibit an employer from using a workplace surveillance tool to ensure safety, an exception that may cover fatigue-monitoring systems for drivers or other safety-sensitive positions. Violations may result in civil penalties of up to $500 per violation, as well as injunctive relief, punitive damages, and attorneys' fees and costs in enforcement actions brought by the Labor Commissioner or a public prosecutor.

The article was written by Krista M. Cabrera of Foley & Lardner LLP and published on November 2, 2026. It says the takeaway is clear, that employers should proceed with caution when using AI to make employment-related decisions and avoid relying solely on AI for such decisions. It also says employers should be sure that any use of AI in the workplace complies with the law. The article notes that while these laws are specific to California, other states are predicted to follow suit.

In a separate article, SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock told Reuters on Friday, October 30, 2026, that the agency is watching companies' AI disclosures and will bring enforcement actions where those disclosures fall short. He said the SEC's principal concern is that people make accurate disclosures so investors know what they are getting into, and that enforcement is a necessary piece of making sure people do that. The comments came amid a tech sell-off that erased more than $1 trillion in market value. The article says the question now is less whether firms overstate their use of AI and more whether they provide sufficient and accurate information about their massive AI investments and whether those investments can reasonably be expected to produce profits.
