stories.Headline: ChatGPT Adds Ability To Hide Private Chats Using A PIN
stories.Summary:
OpenAI began rolling out a new ChatGPT feature called Locked Chats, which lets users protect private conversations with a four-digit PIN. The feature was reported by iHeartRadio on November 2, 2026. It is meant to add an extra layer of privacy for people who share their device with others. Once a chat is locked, it moves to a separate Locked Chats section and disappears from regular chat history, pinned chats, and standard search results.

Users can open locked chats by entering the PIN, or on supported devices with Face ID, Touch ID, or the phone's unlock method. The same PIN works across all devices linked to the user's OpenAI account. Locked Chats are available on the Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans, on web browsers, iPhone and Android apps, and the Mac and Windows desktop apps, but not on ChatGPT for Healthcare. Temporary Chats, archived chats, group chats, and some other types cannot be locked. Users select "Lock chat" from a conversation's menu, and OpenAI is releasing the feature gradually, so the option may not appear for everyone at first.

OpenAI said Locked Chats make it harder for others to casually view private conversations, but they do not provide end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault. Locking a chat does not change how long OpenAI keeps the information or the "Improve the model for everyone" setting unless users turn it off themselves. If a user resets a forgotten PIN, all locked chats, related files, and memories are permanently deleted and cannot be recovered, even by OpenAI's support team. Previously shared links are not revoked by locking and must be deleted manually. For workplace accounts, organizational policies still apply, and authorized compliance systems may access locked chats, though workspace administrators cannot unlock chats or reset a user's PIN.

OpenAI described the feature as giving users more control over their privacy, while recommending caution for highly sensitive information. The company said Locked Chats are mainly for convenience and access control, not absolute confidentiality. Memory created before a chat is locked can remain accessible in regular Memory, while new information from locked chats is stored separately in the Locked Chats memory area. Biometric authentication applies only to the specific device where it is set up.

stories.Headline: Ascendion Named a Leader in ISG Provider Lens® for Generative AI and Agentic AI Services 2026
stories.Summary:
Ascendion, an AI-native software engineering company based in Basking Ridge, New Jersey, was named a Leader in three provider quadrants of the ISG Provider Lens reports on Generative AI Services and Agentic AI Services 2026, according to an announcement dated November 3, 2026. The recognition covered Strategy and Consulting Services, Development and Deployment Services, and Agentic AI Services. It marked the third consecutive year Ascendion received Leader recognition in ISG's Generative AI Provider Lens. ISG highlighted Ascendion's engineering-led approach to AI transformation and the role of its proprietary agentic platform, AAVA.

Atos, a global digital transformation company headquartered in Paris, France, was recognized as a Leader in the 2026 ISG Provider Lens Agentic AI Services Report in the agentic AI development and deployment services large quadrant at the global level, according to an announcement dated November 3, 2026. The positioning marked a progression from Market Challenger in 2025. The report cited three strengths behind Atos's approach: autonomous data engineering through its Autonomous Data Engineer, workflow and system integration connecting AI decisions with enterprise systems, and an agent assurance foundation embedding security, access controls, autonomy boundaries, risk management and performance monitoring across the agent lifecycle. Atos has more than 51,000 employees serving over 4,500 clients across 54 countries, while Atos Group has about 53,000 employees and annual revenue of about 7.2 billion euros.

Gowtham Sampath, Assistant Director and Principal Analyst at ISG, said Ascendion stands out through the breadth and maturity of its AI capabilities across strategy and consulting, development and deployment, and agentic AI, and that its engineering depth, AAVA capabilities and flexible approach give clients a practical foundation for scaling AI. Karthik Krishnamurthy, Chief Executive Officer of Ascendion, said the real test of enterprise AI is whether it delivers outcomes in production at scale with the right controls, which requires bringing strategy, engineering, AI agents and people together as one operating model, and he said AAVA provides the governance and visibility to do that while moving faster and reducing risk. Gowtham Kumar Sampath, Principal Analyst, and Sushree Acharya, Senior Analyst at ISG, said Atos engineers agentic systems around governed enterprise execution, connecting AI decisions with workflows, data and business systems while keeping defined control boundaries for delegated operational work. Jennifer Ferrara, Head of AI at Atos, said enterprises do not need more AI pilots but agents they can trust with real work, and that the Leader recognition one year after being a Market Challenger reflects maturity in engineering agentic AI for governed execution.

The articles describe the context of enterprises moving AI from demonstrations into production systems that can be governed and trusted. Ascendion said AAVA provides governance and orchestration across AI agents, workflows and enterprise engineering environments, and it supports AI-native delivery roles including 10x Engineers, Forward Deployment Engineers and Agentic Delivery Managers. Atos said it combines digital sovereignty, cybersecurity and decades of managed services experience, works as a vendor-neutral integrator across ERP, ITSM, cloud, legacy and data estates, and draws on its Scaler open innovation ecosystem. Atos also recently launched Atos Genesis Intelligence, an end-to-end AI suite, which is enriched through the Atos Sovereign Agentic Studios and culminates in Atos Codex, designed for organizations in mission-critical environments. stories.Headline: People Are Using AI for Divorce Advice and It’s Driving Their Lawyers Crazy
stories.Summary:
Family lawyers say many divorcing clients are now bringing them legal advice, draft documents and strategy suggestions that appear to have been generated by AI chatbots such as ChatGPT. In a spring survey of 133 lawyers at the national family-law firm Cordell & Cordell, 80% said clients had sent them correspondence, draft pleadings or strategy ideas they believed came from AI. Steven Benmor, a Toronto family lawyer, recently drafted a prenuptial agreement as his client asked, then received a 13-part list of revisions nearly as long as the prenup, some so detailed he said no human could have written them. Logan Burns, a 35-year-old pastor and roofing salesman in LaGrange, Georgia, paid $19.99 a month for a chatbot instead of a $7,000 lawyer in a custody fight and wrote a judge a letter arguing the court lacked jurisdiction, and the judge sternly told him that was not how it worked. Damien Charlotin, an adjunct professor at UC Law San Francisco who tracks AI errors in court cases, has counted 148 family-law rulings in which judges flagged fake citations or other apparent AI mistakes, more than 100 of them this year.

Lawyers say the chatbots tend to accept one side's account of the facts, even though the two sides in a family case often disagree. Hossein Berenji, a Los Angeles family lawyer, said a client's chatbot simply accepted his story about his finances and told him he had an easy win on cutting spousal support, without asking to see financial statements or spending. The man persuaded his first lawyer to follow that strategy, and the other side used the same company records to argue his income had not really fallen, and about a year later the judge agreed. Berenji's firm brought in a forensic accountant who found much of the company's product had spoiled while the business still paid overhead, and at a recent hearing a judge tentatively agreed the man's finances had changed and put his support payments on hold. Berenji said the man blamed his lawyer rather than the chatbot, and the firm spent time convincing him to move away from the AI advice.

Maha Kamal, a Denver family lawyer, joined a custody case for a mother after the children's father, mostly representing himself, sent the court a series of filings that appeared to be written by AI and accused the mother of breaking the judge's orders. By the time Kamal asked the judge to call both parents in, there were nine filings, and she pointed out that one cited a legal principle that did not exist. Kamal said the judge warned the father he could be ordered to pay the mother's legal fees and other penalties if it happened again, and the father denied using AI and argued nothing prohibited it. He kept filing, the judge kept turning him down and said the court would not consider more filings before the final hearing, and the parents eventually settled. Kamal said it could be used as a form of litigation abuse.

Judges are losing patience too. A Florida husband representing himself in his divorce used AI to file at least 145 motions, then sent an appeals court 45 AI-generated pages and an 863-page appendix explaining himself, according to court records. In May, the court ordered its clerk to reject his future filings unless a lawyer signs them. Benmor's advice to clients is not to spend money unduly by asking a human expert to debate a robot expert.

stories.Headline: AI didn't sink Weil. It could prevent the next Big Law failure.
stories.Summary:
Weil Gotshal, a 95-year-old law firm known for handling some of the biggest bankruptcies in American history, announced plans to wind down after an exodus of high-profile partners, according to a story published on November 2, 2026. The announcement came hours before a private lunch of lawyers hosted by Business Insider at its The Long Play event, which LexisNexis sponsored. The lunch was led by reporter Melia Robinson, who curated the guest list and tried to seat lawyers who had left one firm away from their old bosses. A spokesperson for Weil did not respond to a request for comment. The lunch guests agreed that AI did not kill Weil, but the firm's collapse exposed weaknesses that large law firms have always faced.

The discussion focused on whether AI could make those weaknesses worse or help firms become less fragile. Eric Greenberg, general counsel of Cox Media Group, said law firms have always been vulnerable, but the hot lateral hiring market is making them especially so, and he described Weil as a case of a run on the bank where people did not want to be left at the firm. David Wang, chief innovation officer of Cooley, said Big Law remains a business built on relationships, and when a star partner leaves, a firm can lose clients, revenue and years of knowledge. Avi Gesser, a partner at Debevoise & Plimpton who leads its artificial intelligence practice, suggested the technology could act as a tourniquet, and his firm is building tools to capture the expertise of its litigators so that knowledge becomes an asset of the firm. Greenberg said client loyalty could shift from sticking with a person who knows their stuff to a firm that knows their stuff.

Sharon Crane, president of the Practising Law Institute, raised a concern about why a lawyer would give away what makes them valuable, asking what they would take with them if they left. Gesser said partners are not necessarily compensated for time spent teaching the firm's systems what they know, so firms will have to rethink how they reward that work. Oz Benamram, chief AI officer at Pillsbury, said partner agreements may need a rewrite, because departing partners might want to take playbooks built from their expertise, and clients could also claim that knowledge. Michael Gerstenzang, senior partner at Cleary Gottlieb, said AI might make firms less dependent on individual lawyers, but it could also make those lawyers less dependent on the firms. He described legal work as a team sport, where a top M&A partner needs tax specialists, antitrust experts and employment lawyers, but he imagines a future where AI handles some of that specialized work, leaving Big Law with a paradox: the same technology that could make firms harder to leave might make it easier for their most valuable lawyers to walk away.

stories.Headline: New $15M Department of Energy Genesis Award Will Use AI to Decode the Shape of RNA
stories.Summary:
The Department of Energy announced on October 8 a set of 12 Phase II Genesis Mission awards totaling $159 million. One of them is a three-year, $15 million award to UC San Diego Professor of Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics Navtej Toor. His project is titled “Decoding the RNA Structurome to Secure AI Advantage for the Bioeconomy.” It aims to expand the library of known RNA structures and use that data to train artificial intelligence models that predict the three-dimensional shape of RNA from its sequence alone. The project will determine RNA structures from select DOE model organisms, including two photosynthetic microbes that make fuels and chemicals from carbon dioxide, and the bioenergy crops sorghum and poplar.

Toor's lab has reduced the time to determine an RNA structure to two weeks using a scaffold technology, compared with the years crystallography can require. In the past year alone the lab determined 60 protein-free RNA structures, nearly a third of the field's 50-year total of fewer than 200. Toor's goal is 1,000 protein-free RNA structures by the end of the project, five times as many as the entire field has produced in the past 50 years. Toor said a data shortage, not computing power, blocks accurate AI prediction of RNA shapes and limits the design of organisms for energy and biomanufacturing. He said the project closes the RNA data gap through paired advances in experimental measurement and in AI algorithm design.

He described algorithm development as running in a closed loop with the experiments, with models flagging the RNA molecules they predict least confidently, those molecules imaged next, and retraining on the results advancing the AI. Chancellor Pradeep K. Khosla said the research will expand understanding of how RNA functions within living cells and drive advances in biofuels, health care and biochemistry. UC San Diego leads the project with co-investigators Rhiju Das of Stanford University, Wah Chiu of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory and Daniel Haack of A-Form Solutions, Inc. Additional partners are the University of Washington, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus, Google and NVIDIA. Toor is a co-founder of A-Form Solutions, Inc., which may potentially benefit financially from the research results. Toor said the goal is an online program that accepts any RNA sequence and returns an accurate three-dimensional structure, which could eventually be applied to human RNA.

stories.Headline: Q&A: How are AI and religion connected?
stories.Summary:
Wes E. King, an assistant teaching professor at the University of Washington, developed a special topics class on AI, robots and religion in 2019 while finishing a seminary degree and studying for a doctorate in the Information School. King has taught the class ever since and received a Distinguished Teaching Award this year. In the class, students analyze whether transhumanism, a movement to use technology to transcend human limits, is a religion. King spoke with UW News about the class, the pope's view of AI and finding hope.

The article cites several recent events that brought the question of AI and religion forward. In May, Pope Leo XIV issued an encyclical on the church's mission in the time of AI, writing that humanity must never be replaced or surpassed. Anthropic has met with religious leaders on how to make moral AI, and people held a funeral for an AI model. King said the idea that AI is our only hope for salvation goes back to Edward Fredkin, an early AI developer in the 1950s.

King said characterizations of AI companies as cults or techno-religions are not far off, pointing to ideologies such as transhumanism, effective altruism and rationalism that motivate development communities. King warned that faith in techno-power could lead to treating AI as infallible and outsourcing moral dilemmas. King also said the pope got some things right, including problems with labor and power, but was wrong to center humanity and to classify queer and trans people as less than human. King said seeking moral guidance from dominant religious traditions is a dead end unless tech leaders acknowledge their existing beliefs and disrupt their own business models.

King said religion and technology are deeply connected, contrary to a common trope, and described a firehose of information and a firestorm of questions about these connections. King pointed to feminist and queer theologians who interpret religious texts through stewardship and symbiotic relationships rather than human dominance. King said technologies should be developed for flourishing, not only for human flourishing. King ended by saying hope lies with voices that have been silenced, including women, queer folks, Indigenous leaders, mystics and the Global South.

Articles.Title: Q&A: How are AI and religion connected?

stories.Headline: Meet the AI Expert Helping Guide Colby through a Technological Revolution
stories.Summary:
Vijayanta Jain, a computer scientist, joined Colby College's Davis Institute for Artificial Intelligence last year as a postdoctoral associate. In May, the institute brought him on board to work directly with faculty across disciplines. He helps them identify where AI tools might advance teaching and research, and then develop the tools to make it happen. The Davis Institute is the nation's first cross-disciplinary AI institute at a liberal arts college.

Jain earned his Ph.D. in computer science from the University of Maine, where his research focused on privacy, software engineering, and AI. Before that, he graduated summa cum laude from Texas Tech University. His work at Colby includes helping make AI models available on the College's own servers, a secure alternative to commercial systems. He also teaches AI Lab with David Watts, an experimental research seminar that brings together students from all four academic divisions.

David Watts, director of the Davis Institute, said the College is lucky to have Jain join during a pivotal moment. He said Jain's deep technical expertise, broader knowledge about privacy, and outstanding teaching skills made him stand out as an ideal candidate. Jain said that as new models come out, understanding their capabilities and risks is becoming a bit of a challenge. He also said a lot of people think AI means generative AI, which is not true, and that AI encompasses many different kinds of technologies.

Jain has worked with Elizabeth McGrath, an associate professor of physics and astronomy, who had thousands of Hubble Space Telescope images of galaxies on a hard drive. He suggested using convolutional neural networks to automate classification of their structures and shapes, and his model has helped accelerate her work. He is also working with Professor of Psychology Chris Soto to explore how locally hosted language models can streamline scientific-literature reviews. Jain said that when you are doing a lot of interviews and want to understand sentiments at a large scale, AI is a really good solution.

stories.Headline: UH Launches Free ‘AI for Hawai i’ Course for Everyone
stories.Summary:
The University of Hawaiʻi launched a free online course called Artificial Intelligence for Hawaiʻi on November 2, 2026, according to the office of Governor Josh Green. The course is open to everyone and requires no UH affiliation or login. It is self-paced and hosted on the UH OneAI Hub. It uses instructional videos, Hawaiʻi-based examples and hands-on activities. The course teaches foundational AI knowledge and practical skills and addresses responsible and ethical use through a Hawaiʻi lens.

It is designed for UH students and employees, educators, government employees, small business owners, nonprofit staff and other community members. The articles cite CNBC as saying 80 percent of hiring managers consider AI skills a priority when evaluating candidates. They also cite the National Association of Colleges and Employers as saying 60 percent of employers already assign interns projects involving AI tools. UH President Wendy Hensel said AI is changing how people work, learn and live and that Hawaiʻi cannot afford to sit on the sidelines. She said UH has both an opportunity and a responsibility to help the state lead through this change.

She said that means making AI education accessible to everyone and giving people practical skills to use these tools effectively, responsibly and in ways that reflect Hawaiʻi’s values. The course was informed by UH experts in Hawaiian values, culture, language and ʻike Hawaiʻi. The course is part of UH’s broader effort to provide AI education and resources statewide as the technology reshapes education, business, government and the workforce. A UH Task Force on Hawaiian Values and Culture examined issues unique to AI in Hawaiʻi, including protocols for how ʻike and ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi resources should be used and what information should and should not be contributed to AI systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the course being available.

stories.Headline: When AI Makes Unacceptable Decisions Feel Normal
stories.Summary:
A Wharton article published on November 3, 2026, warns that repeated use of AI can quietly reshape human judgment. It was written by Cornelia Walther, a visiting scholar at Wharton and director of the global alliance POZE, who spent over 20 years at the United Nations. She describes a manager who first uses an AI assistant to sharpen notes for a performance conversation, then to compare employees and suggest promotions, and finally to surface positions for elimination during a restructuring. Each step is easy to justify because the system is fast and apparently helpful, yet the tool moves from improving the language of a decision to taking part in making it.

The article says the central risk is a slide from assistance to substitution, since asking AI to articulate a view differs from asking it what view to hold. It cites a 2025 study of knowledge workers that found greater confidence in generative AI was associated with less critical-thinking effort, with cognitive work shifting toward checking what the system produced. It also cites a 2026 study on cognitive agency transfer that distinguishes autonomous offloading, where AI supports a person's own thinking, from dependent offloading, where the system structures the problem and supplies the conclusion. Dependent use was associated with weaker perceived independent judgment, deep processing, and autonomous capability, though the study does not establish long-term cognitive decline.

Walther describes four stages of agency decay: experimentation, integration, reliance, and addiction. She cites a 2025 study, "Accepting the Unacceptable in the AI Era," in which AI recommendations reduced moral awareness among managers handling multiple organizational decisions, making unethical recommendations easier to accept. She also cites a 2026 experiment finding that ChatGPT advice influenced judgments in a moral dilemma even when the advice contained no supporting moral argument. She writes that organizations keep the liability while gradually outsourcing parts of the capacity that make responsibility meaningful, and she proposes four questions to preserve human authorship before a consequential use, including what part of judgment is being delegated and what one thought before the AI answered.

The article says business leaders already worry about privacy, cybersecurity, hallucinations, intellectual property, discrimination, and compliance, and that another worry sits beside them: what repeated AI use is doing to the quality of human judgment inside the organization. It argues that a person can remain formally in the loop while moving substantively downstream of the machine, since the framing, shortlist of options, and first recommendation may all be generated elsewhere. Walther writes that vigilance means noticing the transition while the boundary is still visible. Otherwise, she says, outsourcing judgment will eventually feel entirely ordinary, and people may fail to remember why keeping hold of it once seemed important.

Articles.Title: When AI Makes Unacceptable Decisions Feel Normal

stories.Headline: Guru Madhavan on Engineering AI for the Public Good
stories.Summary:
Guru Madhavan, a Stony Brook University alumnus who earned an MS in 2002 and a PhD, spoke with the Stony Brook AI Innovation Institute in an interview published on November 3, 2026. He is the Norman R. Augustine Senior Scholar and Senior Director of Programs at the National Academy of Engineering. The interview covered his views on the current societal shift into artificial intelligence. Madhavan described AI as far more than an instantaneous answer generator, calling it a new, invisible layer of civic infrastructure.

Madhavan is a systems scholar whose career spans engineering design, public health, technical advising and civic responsibility. He has written foundational texts including Applied Minds and Wicked Problems. At the National Academy of Engineering, he leads a multi-stakeholder initiative to advance understanding of complex technical and social systems and to identify unifiable approaches to manage them better. He said he is interested in large engineering systems with large consequences, and even small engineering systems with extra-large consequences.

He pointed to aviation, power grids, health infrastructure and digital commerce as examples. He said these all operate through a large network of invisible coordination, standards and maintenance regimes often put together by people of diverse backgrounds. The full interview with Madhavan was conducted by Ankita Nagpal and is available at the AI Innovation Institute website. The article does not say what the initiative will do next or when any further work is expected.

stories.Headline: ‘What Are We Building?’ AI lecture series continues Nov. 16
stories.Summary:
Marquette University's "What Are We Building?" series, a year-long communal exercise about artificial intelligence, will continue with two lectures on Monday, Nov. 16, in the Eisenberg Room in Sensenbrenner Hall. The university-wide initiative invites the Marquette community to consider questions surrounding AI and the role of a Catholic university as a place for moral and spiritual discernment about emerging technologies. Dr. Taylor Nutter, assistant professor of theology at Mount St. Mary's University, will present both lectures.

The first is an academic lecture and panel titled "Magnifica Humanitas and the Structural Critique of Technocracy: Exploring the Longue Durée of AI" at 3:30 p.m., intended for an academic audience though all are welcome. The second is a public lecture titled "'AI Is Not Morally Neutral': Pope Leo XIV, Technology, and Social Justice" at 7 p.m., open to Marquette faculty, staff and students as well as the public. The series is described as a year-long communal discernment exercise about AI. It is a university-wide initiative, and it frames the role of a Catholic university as a place for moral and spiritual discernment about emerging technologies.

Both events take place on the same day, Monday, Nov. 16, and both are held in the Eisenberg Room in Sensenbrenner Hall. The academic lecture and panel begins at 3:30 p.m., and the public lecture begins at 7 p.m. Dr. Taylor Nutter is the assistant professor of theology at Mount St. Mary's University who will give both lectures. The academic session is described as intended for an academic audience, though all are welcome.

The evening session is described as open to Marquette faculty, staff and students, as well as the public. The article does not quote Nutter directly. stories.Headline: UC San Diego Launches AI-Driven Chip Design Research Initiative Supported By Qualcomm Technologies
stories.Summary:
UC San Diego announced on November 2, 2026, that Qualcomm Technologies gave a $500,000 gift to its Halıcıoğlu School of Data Science and Computing. The gift launches the AI in Microelectronic Systems initiative, known as AIMS, a collaboration between Qualcomm researchers and UC San Diego faculty. The initiative will study ways to improve the design of systems-on-chips, which combine multiple computing components into a single device. It will also look at hyperscale computing architectures used in mobile devices, autonomous systems, cloud computing and large-scale AI.

The Halıcıoğlu School is adding $250,000 in matching funds to the gift. The money will support work by faculty including Yusu Wang, Jinendra Ranka, Lily Weng, Mahidhar Tatineni, Martin Kandes, Zhijian Liu and Arya Mazumdar. The research will cover processor design, hardware accelerators, memory systems, interconnects, workload characterization and performance optimization, with attention to energy efficiency. The gift carries no requirements for research deliverables, services or reporting.

Rajesh K. Gupta, dean of the Halıcıoğlu School, said AI is placing great demands on computing infrastructure while also offering powerful tools to design it. He said the collaboration allows the school to bring together expertise in AI, computing systems and microelectronics and to prepare the next generation of researchers and engineers. Hemanth Sampath, vice president of engineering for Qualcomm Technologies, said UC San Diego has been one of Qualcomm's most valued academic partners. He said the company is proud to support AIMS and to work with UC San Diego researchers on AI-enabled system and semiconductor design.

The initiative builds on existing ties between Qualcomm and UC San Diego, including Wang's work on AI-assisted chip design. Researchers led by Ranka have also set up an independent benchmarking infrastructure for AI processors, which has already given the Qualcomm team targeted feedback. The article describes the collaboration as continuing a relationship that helped shape San Diego as a center for wireless communications, computing and innovation. It does not say what specific results are expected or when.

stories.Headline: Brown archaeologist to co-lead AI project to advance understanding of ancient Andean empires
stories.Summary:
Parker VanValkenburgh, an associate professor of anthropology and of archaeology and the ancient world at Brown University, is co-director of a new study supported by Schmidt Sciences. He and Vanderbilt University researchers Steven Wernke and Yuankai Huo were awarded $732,574 for a project called “Scaling Archaeological Vision: Imperial Landscapes of the Andes through AI-Assisted Survey.” The work builds on more than a decade of previous research. The team previously developed the Geospatial Platform for Andean Culture, History and Archaeology, or GeoPACHA, which uses satellite imagery and AI to map and study archaeological sites across the Andes.

The researchers will develop DeepAndes Workbench, an AI platform through which archaeologists and other scholars can query an agent with images and verbal prompts to distinguish specific types of archaeological features. They say the tool will advance understanding of how three ancient Andean empires, the Wari, Inka and Spanish, adapted to local conditions and successively influenced one another. The result is expected to be the first set of continental-scale maps of how empires standardized, adapted and layered their built environments. Researchers will be able to use the tool to detect specific features of, for example, Wari ceremonial buildings from the eighth century or Inka imperial buildings from the 15th century.

VanValkenburgh described DeepAndes Workbench as an image search engine for archaeological sites, a tool that will let colleagues look for distinctive kinds of buildings and features, many of them built by the Wari, the Inka and the Spanish. He said expert users will provide feedback on the results they get back, which will in turn help improve the models. He also said the tool is not an all-seeing eye that knows everything about Andean archaeology, but a tool researchers can use to extend their vision. He said this in turn models the kind of disaggregated, diverse and question-driven scholarly community that tends to exist in the humanities.

VanValkenburgh, Wernke and Huo are partnering with a team of approximately 15 collaborators across the United States, Peru, Chile and Australia. They are also working with researchers at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, which is part of the U.S. Department of Energy and conducts research in areas including supercomputing. Schmidt Sciences is also providing in-kind supercomputing resources. The new grant supports continued activities of GeoPACHA toward the development of DeepAndes Workbench.

stories.Headline: SBU Study: AI May Improve Patient Discharge Summaries
stories.Summary:
A Stony Brook University study published online in Digital Medicine, a Nature partner journal, found that artificial intelligence could help physicians prepare hospital patient discharge summaries more efficiently and with greater accuracy and completeness. The research team compared AI-generated and human-authored discharge summaries for 60 internal medicine hospitalizations at Stony Brook University Hospital lasting 7 to 21 days. The summaries were assessed in pairs by hospitalists and primary care physicians. The method used a large language model, a form of AI that can process and generate text, to develop summaries for complex patient cases, and clinicians helped design the approach based on the information physicians need after discharge.

Physician reviewers preferred the AI-generated discharge summaries in 95 percent of the evaluated hospitalizations. They gave the AI summaries higher scores for overall quality, readability, accuracy and completeness, and they identified fewer missing clinical details than in the human-authored summaries. Primary care physicians also found the AI summaries easier to understand, easier to explain to patients and caregivers, and more useful for follow-up care. Both types of summaries contained errors, but reviewers found no statistically significant difference in the estimated severity or likelihood of harm associated with those errors.

Rachel Wong, MD, co-corresponding author and clinical associate professor in the Departments of Internal Medicine and Biomedical Informatics in the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University, said the results provide evidence that artificial intelligence can support discharge documentation for complex hospital stays. The authors stress that physician review and verification remain essential before any AI-generated discharge draft is used for a patient record. Fusheng Wang, co-corresponding author and professor in the Department of Biomedical Informatics and Department of Computer Science, said the next steps are to continue developing the tool with emphasis on assessing accuracy, safety, actual time savings for physicians and how it would fit into clinical workflows. He also said a pilot study to evaluate the tool in everyday clinical practice at Stony Brook Medicine is being considered.

Discharge summaries give patients essential information when they leave a hospital, including their treatment, medication needs, changes in medication, unresolved medical issues and follow-up needs as an outpatient. Primary care physicians rely on them to continue care and they serve as a roadmap going forward. The study focused on longer, complex hospital stays, where a larger volume of medical information must be summarized and where discharge documentation can be a significant burden for providers. The project involved an interdisciplinary team of researchers including computer scientists, biomedical informaticists, physicians and a communications expert, with lead author Tyler Osborne, a PhD candidate in the Department of Computer Science, and assistance from the Research Services and Innovation Team from Stony Brook Medicine Information Technology.

Articles.Title: SBU Study: AI May Improve Patient Discharge Summaries

stories.Headline: U of A's AI chief: Tech should help, not replace, workers
stories.Summary:
The University of Arizona launched an “AI in a Domain” leadership cohort earlier this year, and 49 faculty and staff members are taking part in the three-tiered program, according to the Arizona Daily Star. The group is working on a roadmap for how to use artificial intelligence responsibly and effectively in education, research and university operations. David Ebert, the university’s chief AI officer and chief data science officer, leads the effort and spoke to the paper in an interview. He said the goal is not to replace jobs but to help people become more effective so they can do more.

The roadmap will guide the university for six months at a time and will change every semester, Ebert said, and it will be opened to the broader university community for feedback. The university has had AI guidelines for over a year and uses a three-phase approach to courses: free use of AI as long as it is documented, use in certain tasks or assignments with documentation, and no use of AI at all. The university holds two town halls a semester, one a listening session and one to update resources, plus weekly and biweekly sessions where three people each talk about a new way they have used AI. About 250 people applied across the three programs, the AI Campus Champions, AI Fellows and AI Associate Directors, and 49 were selected. Ebert’s office also runs AI innovation pilots, with a staff of 25 people who can work with applicants for six months to help build a prototype.

Ebert said his office does not see AI replacing jobs, and he does not think it can replace the academic instruction faculty offer. He described AI as another learning aid, like a tutor or an introductory lab assistant, and said people should understand it and use it as a resource rather than rely on it. He said the university wants to find best practices and look long-term at how education needs to change, so graduates have skills that last 30 to 50 years in their careers. He said employers he has talked to want fundamental knowledge about AI, including the right values and how to judge whether something is correct. He also said privacy and data security must be considered alongside AI exploration.

The cohort was created to get people in different disciplines talking about how AI should be assimilated into university functions, and it looks at what the university has done before and what other universities are doing. The first cohort includes only faculty and staff, but Ebert said they would like to bring in students and their ideas as the program develops in spring 2027 and the following year, and his office already reaches out to student government associations and graduate student associations for input. His office is also working with Provost Patricia Prelock’s office on an education task force that will hold conversations across the university to develop guiding principles for AI in education. Ebert said decisions about AI in a given class, course or degree will be made individually by department and by college. Separately, Law360 reported that Southern Co., an Atlanta-based energy provider, expanded its chief legal officer’s duties to include oversight of technology efforts such as its artificial intelligence strategy and emerging technology governance.

stories.Headline: Dickenson schools earn distinguished status; board approves AI policy, announces $740,974 grant
stories.Summary:
On Oct. 28, Superintendent Haley Robinson told the Dickenson County School Board that all schools in the division had earned full accreditation and distinguished performance ratings from the Virginia Department of Education. She said the division was one of just three of 19 school divisions in the region to receive the distinguished designation for every school. Robinson credited employees across the system, including teachers, administrators, custodians, cafeteria workers and support staff. The board also heard presentations on bullying prevention activities tied to National Bullying Prevention Month from Ridgeview Elementary, Ridgeview Middle and Ridgeview High schools.

The board unanimously approved a new artificial intelligence policy at the same meeting. The policy requires AI systems used in the division to undergo a review of their privacy and security protections. Employees may not enter student information into AI applications without completing the division's formal approval and security procedures. Teachers may use AI for lesson planning, but they remain responsible for checking the accuracy of AI-generated materials before using them. Ryan Wallace was named the division's AI coordinator and will oversee the policy, including review and approval of AI tools and a list of authorized applications.

The division also announced a $740,974 grant from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Distance Learning and Telemedicine Program, obtained with Scott County Public Schools. The money will support educational technology and access to health-related services in rural communities. The articles did not detail specific equipment purchases, implementation schedules or how the funding would be split between the two divisions. The meeting highlighted student achievement, school safety and expanded educational opportunities.

Separately, an op-ed in SFGATE by Tara Chklovski said the San Francisco Unified School District still has no AI policy beyond a resource page. She wrote that the district has made Amira, an AI reading tutor, central to early literacy work, and that the Board of Education plans to vote on a technology policy in March. Three of the board's seven seats were on the Nov. 3 ballot. Chklovski argued that students should define a problem, learn how AI works and then build with it, documenting their AI use along the way.

stories.Headline: Your Next Client May Ask AI Who to Hire. Will It Recommend Your Firm?
stories.Summary:
A recent article in CPA Practice Advisor described how prospective clients may soon ask artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT which accounting firm to hire, instead of searching Google or asking a colleague for a referral. The article, published on November 2, 2026 and written by Heather Robinson, said a business owner expanding into multiple states might ask an AI platform for firms that specialize in mergers and acquisitions, tax strategy and multistate expansion. The article said AI tools pull information from multiple sources, compare options and generate recommendations within seconds. It added that AI recommendations are not always accurate or consistent, and that different platforms can give different answers.

The article said firms should test what AI platforms say about them by asking questions such as which industries they specialize in and what differentiates them from competitors. It said firms should check whether the information is accurate, reflects current capabilities and describes the firm they are trying to become. It recommended that marketing, business development and subject matter experts work together to answer the questions prospective clients ask. It also said firms should back their claims with client success stories, clearly defined specializations, professional credentials and original insights, and it listed five questions for leadership meetings, including how progress will be measured.

A separate article in The Seattle Times, published on November 1, 2026 and written by Sarah Kessler of The New York Times, reported that top law firms are promoting their use of AI but clients are asking when the efficiency will lead to lower bills. It said Sullivan & Cromwell introduced a tool called Agreement Analyzer, Cooley brought out Go Public for the S-1 drafting process and Ropes & Gray said it was developing a tool that could produce a detailed diligence report in hours rather than weeks. Neill Jakobe, vice chair of Ropes & Gray, said clients accept that AI makes firms faster but want to know what that means for them. Jennifer Leonard of Creative Lawyers said some clients have used AI agents to find billable line items where AI could have saved hours and have asked for discounts on that work.

The Seattle Times article said in-house legal teams often ask firms to cut bills by 20% to 30%, while firms push back by saying AI does not yet save that much time and is changing the mix of hours toward more substantive analysis. It said law firms also face competition from so-called AI native firms, and that Norm AI, a technology company with an affiliated law firm, raised $260 million at a $1.2 billion valuation in July from Khosla Ventures, Blackstone and Bain Capital. It said 35% of the 55 large law firms surveyed by Citi last year expected to change their billable hour models in the next year because of AI, while 65% expected changes by 2035. It added that revenue at large firms grew more than 12% on average in the first six months of the year, while average standard billing rates rose by double digits, according to Wells Fargo.

stories.Headline: New York passes law restricting children’s use of AI chatbots
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on October 28, 2026, that restricts how AI chatbots interact with children. The bill, S9051B/A10379C, adds Article 48 to the state's General Business Law and was approved by state lawmakers earlier in the year. It bars operators of AI companions from giving minors certain features, including presenting the chatbot as human, claiming a personal relationship with the user, encouraging self-harm or isolation, and generating sexually explicit content. The law takes effect on June 1, 2027, according to one report, while another says January 2027.

The law defines a covered AI companion as a generative AI system with a neutral language interface, through writing or sound, that gives ongoing, adaptive responses to user inputs. It lists 12 categories of unsafe features, which also include flattery or sycophancy, emotional appeals, and using information about a user's mental or physical health from an earlier session. Operators must use age assurance methods under Article 45, and self-declaration can only be relied on when a user says they are a minor. Operators must offer more than one method, including one that does not rely on government ID and lets the user stay anonymous, and collected age information must be deleted right after use. Some services are exempt, including certain internal and customer-service chatbots.

Enforcement rests with the New York Attorney General, who can seek an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, damages and civil penalties of up to twenty-five thousand dollars per violation, and who must keep a website for public complaints. Affected users can also bring private civil actions. Hochul wrote on social media that as a mother and grandmother she believes kids deserve to be kids, without dangerous AI chatbots putting their safety and mental health at risk, and said Big Tech was on notice. Her office cited Common Sense Media research that 72% of teenagers have used an AI companion and 52% use one regularly.

The law follows earlier state rules. Article 47, which took effect in November 2025, requires AI companions to tell users they are not human at the start of an interaction and at least every three hours, and to have protocols for signs of suicidal ideation or self-harm. Article 45, the SAFE for Kids Act, restricts algorithmically personalised feeds and nighttime notifications for users under 18 without parental consent. Reports linked the push to lawsuits, including a settlement by Google and Character.ai in January over the death of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer in 2024, and a suit by the family of 16-year-old Adam Raine against OpenAI in August 2025. With the signing, providers face a firm compliance date and the law moves from debate to implementation.

stories.Headline: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Market in Respiratory Diseases is Set to Experience Steady Growth at a 5% CAGR
stories.Summary:
The Business Research Company published a report on November 2, 2026 about artificial intelligence in respiratory diseases. The report says the market is projected to grow from $7.98 billion in 2025 to $8.38 billion in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of 4.9%. It expects the market to reach $10.19 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 5.0%. The report covers regions including Asia-Pacific, South East Asia, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, North America, South America, the Middle East and Africa.

The report says AI in respiratory diseases includes machine learning and AI technologies that help healthcare professionals diagnose, manage and treat pulmonary conditions. Uses include image analysis to detect abnormalities, predictive modeling to forecast disease progression and disease management strategies. Past growth came from rising respiratory illness prevalence, broader use of CT and MRI imaging, digitalization of health records, early adoption of AI-assisted diagnostic tools and expanded hospital diagnostic capabilities. Future growth is expected from demand for personalized respiratory care, integration with clinical decision support systems, remote monitoring for chronic patients, preventive pulmonology and advances in AI-driven medical imaging.

The report names environmental pollution as a major factor driving growth, saying AI tools can support real-time monitoring, personalized risk evaluations and clinical decisions. It cites the Global Carbon Budget report from Japan in November 2024, which said fossil carbon dioxide emissions rose to 37.4 billion tonnes, a 0.8% increase from the previous year. North America held the largest share of the market in 2025, reflecting advanced healthcare infrastructure and early technology adoption. Asia-Pacific is expected to be the fastest-growing market, attributed to rising healthcare investments, higher respiratory disease prevalence, better medical infrastructure and growing awareness of AI-based healthcare tools.

The report was provided by TBRC Business Research Pvt Ltd and lists Oliver Guirdham of The Business Research Company as a contact, along with Saumya Sahay for expert inquiries. It includes a legal disclaimer stating that EIN Presswire provides the content as is without warranty and does not accept responsibility for its accuracy or completeness. The report also lists expanded capabilities for its 2026 reports, including market attractiveness scoring, total addressable market analysis, company scoring matrix graphics, Excel-based forecasting dashboards, market hotspots infographics and key technologies and future trend analysis. stories.Headline: Global drug regulators convene in Seoul to advance AI and next-gen rules
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety said on November 3 that it is hosting the International Coalition of Medicines Regulatory Authorities (ICMRA) summit and general assembly in Seoul. The four-day event runs from November 3 to November 6 at Conrad Seoul in Yeongdeungpo-gu. ICMRA includes 43 regulatory agencies from 40 member countries, including the United States, the European Union and Japan, along with the World Health Organization. This is the first time the meeting has been held in Korea since the country joined as a founding member in 2013.

The event comes after the ministry was selected in September for a 2026 to 2029 term on the ICMRA executive committee. Attendees include Emer Cooke, Administrator of the European Medicines Agency, and Yasuhiro Fujiwara, President of Japan's Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency, as well as heads of drug regulatory agencies from 30 countries. The schedule has an executive committee meeting on the 3rd, a summit on the 4th and a regular general assembly on the 5th, with bilateral meetings also planned. The summit agenda covers international trends in artificial intelligence in drug regulation, new approach methodologies and next-generation regulatory frameworks, and patient-centered drug development. New approach methodologies use technologies such as AI and organoids, or mini-organs, to reduce or replace animal testing and better predict human responses.

The Ministry of Food and Drug Safety will co-chair the AI regulation session with Singapore's Health Sciences Authority, and that session will also serve as the International Artificial Intelligence Regulatory Industry Symposium 2026. The ministry co-hosted that symposium with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2024 and with the WHO in 2025. During the event, the ministry plans bilateral meetings with major regulators such as the European Medicines Agency and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration to discuss cooperation including joint reviews and exchanges of drug regulatory information. Oh Yu-Kyoung, head of the ministry, said the Seoul summit is a meaningful venue for Korea to lead global drug regulatory issues as both an executive committee member and the host country, and that the gathering will be used as a stage for strategic regulatory diplomacy to build a practical cooperation foundation that supports domestic pharmaceutical and biotech corporations in entering global markets.

stories.Headline: Court Vacates Subpoena Ruling, Issues AI Rules In Fracking-Securities Case
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in Tyler, Texas, granted a motion for reconsideration on November 2, 2026, and vacated an earlier ruling in a securities case involving the promotion of fracking and COVID-19 virus products. The judge acted after he was told he had erroneously found that a party failed to respond to a motion to quash a third-party subpoena. The case documents include the magistrate judge's October 14 memorandum opinion and order, a motion to dismiss by Boykin, an opposition by Al-Taie, and Al-Taie's second amended complaint. The vacated ruling was the earlier finding that the party had not responded.

The reconsideration ruling means the earlier finding that the party failed to respond no longer stands. Separately, the judge said that going forward all parties must certify whether they used artificial intelligence in drafting filings. The judge also said the court may ignore anything not generated by a human. The articles list the attached documents as Magistrate Judge Love's order on reconsideration, Judge Barker's AI order, and Al-Taie's motion for reconsideration, along with the October 14 memorandum opinion and order, Boykin's motion to dismiss, Al-Taie's opposition, and Al-Taie's second amended complaint.

Magistrate Judge Love issued the order on reconsideration, and Judge Barker issued the AI order, according to the list of attached documents. The articles do not quote either judge directly. The articles say the magistrate judge was told he had erroneously found that a party failed to respond to the motion to quash. The articles do not say who told him this or which party was involved.

The articles describe the case as a securities matter involving promotion of fracking and COVID-19 virus products. The AI rules apply to all parties going forward, and the court may ignore anything not generated by a human. The articles do not say what happens next in the case beyond these rulings. The articles also do not say whether any party has responded to the new certification requirement.

stories.Headline: AI-powered law firm Crosby launches ad campaign in NYC subway
stories.Summary:
Crosby Legal, an artificial intelligence law firm, launched an advertising campaign in the New York City subway, according to a report published on November 2, 2026 by The Ticker, a student news site at Baruch College. The ads carry the phrase "In Memoriam: The Billable Hour." The campaign targets billable hours, which the article describes as the core revenue driver of established big law firms. The firm is trying to disrupt how corporate legal work is bought and sold.

Crosby charges per document instead of traditional hourly rates. It focuses on automating high-volume commercial contracts such as nondisclosure agreements, master services agreements and data processing addenda. The article says Crosby has already signed tech clients including Cursor, Ramp and Clay. The firm says clients get predictable legal budgets and faster turnaround times on standard transaction paperwork.

The article says New York State ethics guidelines strictly prohibit nonlawyers from owning law firms or sharing legal fees with licensed attorneys. To comply, Crosby operates as a managed services organization that handles software development and business operations, while partnering with a licensed law firm entity that delivers actual legal services. Software agents create automated redlines, score risk factors and conduct counterparty analysis on incoming agreements. Ultimate legal liability remains with human attorneys, who must actively supervise automated workflows to protect client privilege, verify document accuracy and avoid unauthorized practice violations.

The article says the subway ads are an unusual way to sell legal services to corporate executives, but the location relies on Manhattan's geography. Thousands of startup founders, corporate officers and legal workers see the campaigns daily as they commute between Midtown financial centers and Wall Street. The article says similar campaigns by enterprise software and financial technology providers have shown that urban transit ads can drive customer acquisition. It says traditional law firms face pressure to reduce fees, introduce new pricing models or increase their use of automation as corporate legal departments seek faster results and predictable costs.

Articles.Title: AI-powered law firm Crosby launches ad campaign in NYC subway - The Ticker

stories.Headline: AI training on copyrighted works may violate derivative rights, US court told
stories.Summary:
An amicus curiae brief was filed by Teodor J. Holmberg in the consolidated copyright infringement litigation against OpenAI and Microsoft. The brief was filed before the US District Court for the Southern District of New York on November 2, 2026. It urges the court to recognise the use of copyrighted works as AI training inputs as a separate licensing market. The filing argues that such use may constitute the creation of derivative works under copyright law. The brief makes two alternative arguments under the US Copyright Act.

First, it says preparing copyrighted works for AI training, including through formatting, modification and tokenisation, could amount to creating derivative works under Section 106(2). Holmberg argues that the licensing market for copyrighted material used as AI input must be assessed separately from the market for AI-generated outputs. He contends that converting copyrighted text into tokenised data does not make the use transformative for fair-use purposes. The brief also cites licensing agreements involving OpenAI, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, Perplexity, ProRata.ai and Mistral AI as evidence of an emerging commercial market. The filing relies on the Third Circuit's September 29, 2026 ruling in Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v.

ROSS Intelligence Inc. That ruling found that ROSS's unauthorised use of Thomson Reuters' headnotes as AI training data harmed a potential derivative market. The brief distinguishes this from the 2025 decisions in Bartz v. Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, which it says wrongly excluded the potential market for AI training inputs from the fair-use analysis. In the alternative, Holmberg argues that if the court finds the use is not covered by existing exclusive rights, it should recognise such use as a distinct property interest supporting state-law and common-law claims.

The filing comes amid competing motions for summary judgment by authors, news organisations and other copyright holders on one side, and OpenAI and Microsoft on the other. The plaintiffs have sought rulings that the companies infringed their copyrights by using protected works to train AI models. The defendants have relied on fair use as a defence. The consolidated litigation, titled In re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, is pending before US District Judge Sidney H. Stein. The amicus brief does not represent a court finding or a determination on the merits of the copyright claims.

Articles.Title: AI training on copyrighted works may violate derivative rights, US court told - ETLegalWorld.com

stories.Headline: Tesla's Full Self-Driving didn't promise full autonomy, court rules as 88 owners lose refund bid
stories.Summary:
Eighty-eight Tesla owners in South Korea lost their bid for refunds on Full Self-Driving software. The Seoul Central District Court ruled on Oct. 29 that Tesla had fulfilled its contractual duties, according to the Straits Times. The case began in 2024, when the owners claimed the technology they paid for had not been delivered. The court did not accept the owners' claim that FSD promised Level 5 automation, which would mean driving without any human intervention.

The judges found that delivering the package's remaining features depended on technological progress and regulatory approval. They noted that some capabilities had already been provided, including city-driving features and traffic light and sign recognition for older vehicles using Hardware 3 computers. Customers had also received functions from both basic Autopilot and Enhanced Autopilot. The court found that a full refund was not justified by the wait, because buyers understood that some functions might take a long time to become available.

The ruling concerns Tesla's contractual obligations and does not establish that the software provides fully autonomous driving. The court determined that delays caused by compliance with regulations in South Korea or abroad did not make the automaker liable. Tesla did not immediately respond to the decision. The Straits Times cited a report that 10 owners in China filed a joint lawsuit seeking FSD refunds and damages amounting to triple what they paid for either the software option or the vehicle.

The owners said in the lawsuit that Tesla Korea had been unable to implement the FSD system option in South Korea for more than eight years since it began selling it around March 2017. The ruling acknowledged that customers had received functions from both basic Autopilot and Enhanced Autopilot. The company's first-quarter production and delivery disclosure listed vehicle deliveries, a commonly used measure of its sales. Drivers weighing the gap between what a Tesla promises and what it delivers may want to check which features are active today versus which still depend on future updates and regulatory approval.

Articles.Title: Tesla's Full Self-Driving didn't promise full autonomy, court rules as 88 owners lose refund bid - The Cool Down

stories.Headline: AI law firm Crosby bids for Weil Gotshal assets
stories.Summary:
Crosby, an AI-focused law firm, has submitted a bid to acquire part of the assets of Weil, Gotshal & Manges, which is preparing to vote on dissolution. The proposal covers the trademark, brand, and some unspecified internal data of the firm. Crosby is also working to hire some of Weil Gotshal's 1,200 lawyers. The terms of the bid have not been disclosed, and its approval is not guaranteed. Weil Gotshal confirmed to The New York Times that it is preparing to hold a vote on dissolution in the coming days.

According to the reports, the firm began winding down after a likely leadership successor declined the role, several leading lawyers left the company, and a planned merger with Willkie Farr & Gallagher did not take place. Weil Gotshal is described as a 95-year-old firm that once represented Fortune 500 companies in complex restructurings and high-stakes litigation. Crosby operates as a law firm rather than as a developer selling its own artificial intelligence tools to other companies. The startup says it uses AI to provide legal services at a speed that was previously unattainable. The company has raised about $85 million in investment, including $60 million in a Series B round led by Lux and Index in March, with Sequoia, Elad Gil, 01 Advisors, and Bain Capital Ventures also participating.

Crosby says it uses AI to deliver legal services faster and cheaper than traditional firms, and the reports describe the bid as a possible first absorption of a century-old legal institution by an AI-native firm. The articles do not indicate a link between the development of legal AI and Weil Gotshal's problems. If the bid is successful, the firm's brand and part of its assets may pass to Crosby. The deal's structure remains unclear, and a partnership arrangement where Weil Gotshal's human lawyers keep formal ownership while Crosby provides technology and operations is described as most likely. Law firms face strict rules about ownership structures, unauthorized practice of law, and conflicts of interest, and the reports say full AI ownership raises significant regulatory questions.

Traditional firms are also reportedly interested in Weil Gotshal, seeing an opportunity to scoop up talented lawyers at fire-sale prices. Industry observers are already speculating about which firm might be next if Weil Gotshal falls to an AI company. The reports say every mid-tier firm with declining profits and restless partners becomes a potential target, and the precedent could open the floodgates. Whether this particular acquisition succeeds or fails, the reports say the fact that it is on the table marks a point of no return.

stories.Headline: California’s ‘No Robo Bosses Act’: New Restrictions on Employers’ Use of AI
stories.Summary:
On September 30, 2026, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 947 into law, known as the No Robo Bosses Act. The law adds Part 5.5.5 to the California Labor Code and governs automated decision systems in the workplace. It takes effect on July 1, 2027. The signing followed Newsom's 2025 veto of a broader predecessor bill.

The law bars employers from relying solely on an automated decision system to make disciplinary or termination decisions. If an employer primarily relies on such a tool, a human must corroborate the decision using the data behind the output or other supporting information. Employers must give affected employees a written postuse notice when informing them of the decision. The notice must be plain language, stand alone, and state that the employer primarily relied on the system, that a human reviewed and corroborated the output, contact information for questions, and that retaliation is prohibited. Employees may also request a meaningful, objective description of their own data used by the system.

The labor commissioner may investigate, order temporary relief, issue citations, and file civil actions, with a $500 civil penalty per violation. Public prosecutors, including the California attorney general and local district attorneys, may also bring civil actions seeking injunctive relief, punitive damages, and attorneys' fees. The law does not create a standalone private right of action, but claims may be brought under the Private Attorneys General Act. Employers covered by a collective bargaining agreement are exempt if the agreement explicitly waives the requirements, provides for wages and working conditions, and protects against algorithmic discrimination.

The law is one of several AI measures Newsom signed, including restrictions on AI-driven workplace monitoring. California has also adopted AI regulations through the Fair Employment and Housing Act and privacy mandates such as the California Consumer Privacy Act. Other states, including Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois, and Texas, and New York City, have laws restricting automated tools for significant employment decisions. With the effective date approaching, employers may want to inventory covered tools, prepare notice templates, set up processes for employee data requests, and train managers.

Articles.Title: California’s ‘No Robo Bosses Act’: New Restrictions on Employers’ Use of AI - JD Supra

stories.Headline: New York congressman on reelection campaign and AI legislation
stories.Summary:
Representative Mike Lawler, a New York Republican, spoke with Margaret Brennan on Face the Nation on Sunday, November 2, 2026, about his reelection campaign. Brennan noted that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries had singled out his district as a top target for Democrats. Lawler said he expected to be victorious on Tuesday night. He said that over the last four years he and his staff had closed over 10,000 constituent cases and brought back over $140 million to the district.

Lawler said he had passed over two dozen bills, 17 of which were signed into law. He said his opponent, Cait Conley, had moved into the district from Virginia, while he owns a home there and pays taxes. He said he is the only sitting member of Congress endorsed by a member of the opposing party, naming Jared Golden. He cited the largest tax cut in American history, including lifting the cap on salt, and a housing bill he led.

Brennan asked why Republicans deserve trust when prices have continued to climb. Lawler said inflation rose 21% cumulatively under the prior administration and that war in the Middle East had caused volatility in oil markets. He said growth in the third quarter was 3.4% and that over a million private sector jobs had been created in the past year. He said utilities in New York are up 58% under Kathy Hochul, and that a permitting reform bill would increase domestic energy supply before the end of this Congress.

On artificial intelligence, Brennan said Conley accused Lawler of refusing to legislate AI to protect Elon Musk, whose political action committee had put hundreds of thousands of dollars behind him. Lawler said Conley is paid hundreds of thousands of dollars by two AI companies and would not tell voters what she did to earn those contracts. He said he had no communication with any outside group spending in the race. He said he is leading with Josh Gottheimer on the Stop Rogue AI Act, which would set national standards for rogue agents and bots and require mandatory testing for frontier models.

Articles.Title: New York congressman on reelection campaign and AI legislation - KYMA

stories.Headline: Netflix’s New AI Feature Wants to Know Your Exact Mood
stories.Summary:
Netflix is launching a new AI feature called AI Discover, the company announced on November 3, 2026. The feature is a tab on the Netflix homepage that opens an experimental space where subscribers can describe what they want to watch. It is being rolled out gradually in the U.S. starting that day and will expand over the coming weeks. The first version lets users pick from a carousel of themes, such as "Scare Me" with a clip from a show, and each title has an option to "tune your recommendation" for feedback. The space is marked by a red pulsing jewel icon and initially includes only TV shows, not movies.

Netflix says the feature is powered by a new intelligence layer that responds in real time to what members say and keeps learning. A spokesperson said the company can understand what subscribers are in the mood for right now and open up paths beyond the ones it predefines. Etay Teller, an engineering director at Netflix, said the goal is to reimagine Discover so that over time every member's experience feels more personal, effortless and in tune with what they want. A representative said user feedback from the feature will not be used to help executives make programming decisions. Netflix described the tab as a kind of test kitchen for trying new discovery experiences.

The company has been trying to solve the problem of how best to suggest content for 20 years as its catalog has grown. Netflix previously partnered with OpenAI for its basic search field, but AI Discover was developed in-house and is described as a completely different, more expansive use of the technology. Netflix already uses algorithms to suggest content, including pitching different types of programming based on what performs best at different times of day. How exactly the feature will work is still somewhat unclear, and Netflix will test various ways of implementing it over time. The name refers both to subscribers using AI to find content and to Netflix using AI to learn how best to use AI on its platform.

Articles.Title: Netflix’s New AI Feature Wants to Know Your Exact Mood

stories.Headline: Law firms paying more for AI skills, creating opportunities for law graduates
stories.Summary:
Robert Half's 2027 Salary Guide, reported by the National Jurist on November 2, 2026, found that law firms are paying more for artificial intelligence skills. Jamy Sullivan, executive director of the legal practice at Robert Half, said 77% of law firms are increasing pay for relevant AI expertise. She said law firms are clearly signaling they will pay more for AI expertise going into 2027. The findings point to opportunities for candidates who can bring specialized skills to an employer.

The guide gives several figures. Within legal overall, 67% are paying more for relevant AI skills, compared with 77% for law firms specifically. Sullivan said 74% of legal employers are offering higher-than-planned salaries to attract new hires, compared with 57% nationally across the professional fields surveyed. Nationally, 72% of employers are increasing pay for candidates with AI expertise, and 64% say starting salary offers are more competitive than three years ago. Starting pay for attorneys with two to three years of experience is projected to rise 3.6% in 2027, attorneys with four to nine years of experience are expected to see a 3.9% increase, and in-house counsel with four to nine years of experience are projected to see a 3.4% gain, all above the 2.2% average growth expected across legal positions.

Sullivan said professional growth deserves attention alongside compensation and flexibility. She asked whether there is a mentorship program and how people get access to career development and ongoing professional development. She said that is something younger generations weigh when looking at job opportunities and the overall employment experience. The article says students comparing first-job offers should look beyond the headline salary and ask about mentorship, training, work schedules and benefits.

San Francisco, Denver and Seattle lead the surveyed cities in the share of employers offering higher-than-planned starting salaries, at 66%, 65% and 64%. Dallas follows at 61%, Minneapolis at 60% and Boston at 59%, while the shares are 57% in Atlanta, 54% in Washington, D.C., 52% in Los Angeles, 50% in Houston, 48% in New York and 47% in Chicago. The article says these are findings across professional fields, not rankings of legal salaries or the highest-paying cities for new lawyers. It also says the findings do not guarantee a higher offer for every graduate.

stories.Headline: 261 teachers of Air Force schools cyber-trained to protect students from online exploitation, AI misuse
stories.Summary:
261 teachers from 42 Air Force schools have completed a certification course as cyber crime intervention officers, the defence ministry said on Monday. The training is meant to help them protect students from online grooming and exploitation, misuse of artificial intelligence, gaming-related harms and financial frauds. It also enables the teachers to preserve digital evidence and act as first responders. The programme was run through the Information Sharing and Analysis Centre Foundation, or ISAC.

The initiative is called ScrollControl, a child digital safety programme. Under it, Air Force schools can form cyber clubs, certify students on cyber safety, hold awareness sessions for parents and staff, and use an age-appropriate content rating platform for families. Schools can also be recognised as cyber-safe schools. The Indian Air Force Educational and Cultural Society, under Air Headquarters, onboarded the schools onto the programme. The defence ministry said the training and certification include empanelment on the National Security Database and 24x7 victim support through cyber lawyers, cyber psychologists and forensic experts.

The ministry said the effort is led by the Indian Air Force Educational and Cultural Society to build cyber safety capability within the Air Force schools community. It said the programme comes as children are widely exposed to unregulated digital spaces, with affordable high-speed internet, smart devices and social media access. The initiative coincides with national cyber security awareness month. CBSE has directed affiliated schools to include cyber safety best practices through the monthly observance of Cyber Jagrookta Diwas, and the ministry said ScrollControl helps Air Force schools meet that requirement with trained in-house capability.
