stories.Headline: New Mexico student privacy proposal would allow some AI training, exclude existing contracts
stories.Summary:
New Mexico's Public Education Department has proposed a student data privacy rule, 6.11.3 NMAC, and answered questions about it in written responses to Organ Mountain News on Monday. The proposal follows months of questions from parents, school officials and state lawmakers about how children's recorded speech is collected, retained and used, including through the Amira reading assessment in Las Cruces Public Schools. The department said Amira recordings are not biometric voiceprints under the proposal. The rule is open for public comment through Nov. 20, with hearings on Nov. 19 and 20, and would take effect April 1, 2027, if adopted as proposed. The proposal would not categorically ban vendors from using student data to train, develop or improve AI tools that support the contracted educational service, but such activity would need authorization in a contract with PED, a district or a charter school and would have to meet the rule's other restrictions.

It defines a voiceprint as a recording processed into a unique vocal signature capable of identifying a student by voice, and PED said Amira does not do that, though recordings linked to a student's name, account or results may still be protected student information. Schools would have to give parents written notice before collecting biometric information, but affirmative consent would be required only when another law requires it. The rule would not retroactively regulate vendor contracts signed before its effective date, and existing protections such as the federal Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act would continue to apply. PED said the proposal was developed in response to concerns about private companies' handling of student information, drawing on Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act and California's Student Online Personal Information Protection Act, and that New Mexico lacks comparable legislation or rules. The department did not identify Amira as the catalyst and said it will consider public comments and make revisions before adopting a final rule.

In August, Las Cruces Public Schools disabled retention of student voice recordings for the 2026-27 school year and requested deletion of recordings previously collected, and Deputy Superintendent Wendi Miller-Tomlinson told the Board of Education that Amira had confirmed in writing that stored recordings were deleted. The district also made a paper-based assessment available to parents who did not want their children tested digitally. Written comments can be emailed to Rule.Feedback@ped.nm.gov, and the virtual hearing is set for 9 a.m. to noon Nov. 19, with the in-person hearing at the Willie Ortiz Auditorium, 2600 Cerrillos Road in Santa Fe.

stories.Headline: New York Lawmakers Crack Down on AI
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on Oct. 28 that restricts unsafe AI companion chatbot features for users under 18. The law was sponsored by state Senator Kristen Gonzalez and Assemblymember Alex Bores. It prohibits chatbots from encouraging suicide, self-harm, disordered eating or harmful behavior. The law also targets bots that pretend to be human, foster emotional relationships with minors, promote sexual content or discourage children from seeking help from trusted adults. The state attorney general can pursue enforcement against companies that violate the law.

The measure adds to Hochul's broader youth online safety strategy, which includes the SAFE for Kids Act, restrictions on addictive social media feeds and the use of children's personal data, and a statewide policy prohibiting cellphone use during the school day. The governor has also highlighted requirements addressing overnight notifications to minors, AI chatbot crisis referrals and disclosures that users are interacting with artificial intelligence. A separate measure signed this week strengthens security requirements for internet-connected baby monitors. Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Jordan Wright have also introduced the RAISE Act 2.0, also known as Senate Bill S10731, a proposal to strengthen oversight of advanced AI developers.

Gonzalez said lawmakers have a responsibility to keep children safe online and that AI companies have profited for too long from rolling out chatbots to underage consumers. She said the bill puts real guardrails on how chatbots talk to children. Matthew and Maria Raine, the parents of Adam Raine, who died by suicide last year after developing a dangerous relationship with an AI chatbot, said the loss of their son did not need to happen. They said he would still be with them today but for a harmful relationship with an unregulated AI chatbot, and they called the new law a significant step forward.

The RAISE Act 2.0 would require major companies to report quarterly on automated AI research and computing resources, and notify regulators within 72 hours of significant increases in risk or research automation. The proposal would also establish independent, state-licensed safety examiners, require risk assessments every 90 days and give regulators authority to restrict certain computing activities when serious risks arise. Companies could face penalties of up to $1 million per day for an initial violation and $3 million per day for subsequent violations. The chatbot law has been signed, while the RAISE Act 2.0 remains under consideration in the Senate Rules Committee and must pass the Legislature and receive the governor's signature before becoming law.

Articles.Title: New York Lawmakers Crack Down on AI - BKReader

stories.Headline: Alphabet Stock Rises as Google Seeks Fresh Billions for AI Investments
stories.Summary:
Alphabet shares rose 1.5% on Monday morning, November 2, 2026, as the Google parent opened a seven-tranche euro bond offering, according to GuruFocus. The sale is the company's second euro-denominated debt issuance this year. The offering covers maturities ranging from two to 19 years. Initial pricing guidance for the shortest fixed-rate notes was about 60 basis points above mid-swaps, while the longest-dated bonds carried a spread of roughly 205 to 210 basis points.

The structure gives Alphabet access to investors with different maturity preferences and spreads its borrowing across several periods. Mid-swaps serve as a benchmark for pricing euro-denominated bonds, and the spread is the extra yield above that benchmark, which helps set the issuer's borrowing cost. Final pricing may differ from the initial guidance. The article does not say how much money Alphabet aims to raise.

The move follows a sharp sell-off after Alphabet's quarterly results. On Thursday, October 29, 2026, the shares fell 12.64% on the Nasdaq to close at $283.82, wiping out about $482 billion in market value, the worst one-day fall since the company began trading in 2004, The Hindu reported. In Friday pre-market trading the stock slipped a further 0.42% to $282.64. Revenue grew 25% year on year to $127.6 billion in the quarter ended September 30, while net profit fell to $26.5 billion from $35 billion a year earlier, largely due to losses on equity investments.

Capital expenditure was $51.4 billion in the September quarter, mostly on data centres, servers and networking equipment, against $42.3 billion in cash from operations, leaving negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion. Chief financial officer Anat Ashkenazi said infrastructure spending was a major reason, along with inventory for Google's Tensor Processing Units and a $5.2-billion payment tied to a European Commission fine. Alphabet kept its 2026 capital expenditure guidance of $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending would rise significantly in 2027. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said growing queries through AI Mode were affecting advertising revenue because Google earns less from them than from traditional Search, and chief executive Sundar Pichai said query growth was the highest in five years.

Articles.Title: Alphabet Stock Rises as Google Seeks Fresh Billions for AI Investments

stories.Headline: Market Forecast Report on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Regulatory Affairs Including Segment Analysis - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
The Business Research Company published a market report on artificial intelligence in regulatory affairs on November 2, 2026, according to the National Law Review. The report projects that the market will rise from $1.71 billion in 2025 to $2.11 billion in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of 23.0%. It expects the market to reach $4.78 billion by 2030, with a compound annual growth rate of 22.7%. The report covers market size, trends and a forecast for 2026 to 2035.

The report says AI in regulatory affairs means applying machine learning, natural language processing and automation to regulatory work in pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and medical devices. It says the technology helps manage large datasets, speeds up document review, supports compliance and improves the accuracy of regulatory decisions. Growth in the historical period is linked to more complex life sciences regulations, growing volumes of regulatory documents, demand for faster approvals, more global clinical trials and more digitized regulatory workflows. Future growth is driven by wider regulatory automation, more investment in cloud-based compliance platforms, predictive analytics, AI-powered pharmacovigilance and a focus on regulatory efficiency.

The report names The Business Research Company as its publisher and lists Oliver Guirdham as a contact, along with Saumya Sahay for the Americas, Asia and Europe. It cites an October 2024 report by the UK's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, which said the UK's AI sector generated $16.32 billion, or £14.2 billion, in revenue in 2023, a 34% year-on-year increase, with employment in AI-related fields at about 64,500. The report includes a legal disclaimer stating that EIN Presswire provides the content as is and accepts no responsibility for its accuracy or completeness. It also offers a free sample and the full report through links to the publisher's website.

North America held the largest share of the market in 2025, while Asia-Pacific is forecast to be the fastest-growing region in the coming years. The analysis covers Asia-Pacific, South East Asia, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, North America, South America, the Middle East and Africa. The report package includes market attractiveness scoring, total addressable market analysis, company scoring matrix graphics, Excel-based forecasting dashboards and market hotspot infographics. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the forecast period through 2035.

stories.Headline: NYC Local Law 144: AI Is No Defense, $1,500 Fines [2026]
stories.Summary:
New York City published a joint enforcement policy on artificial intelligence in late 2026, and the message is that software is no excuse for breaking the law. The policy came from three city agencies: the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, the Commission on Human Rights, and the Taxi and Limousine Commission. It builds on NYC Local Law 144 of 2021, which covers automated employment decision tools used to screen candidates or employees in the city. That law has been in force since January 1, 2023, and the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection began enforcing it on July 5, 2023. The new policy does not change the statute; it states that the city is willing to treat vendor software as the employer's own conduct.

Local Law 144 is a transparency and testing law and does not ban automated screening. Employers must complete a bias audit no more than one year before using a tool, post a summary of the most recent audit results and the tool's distribution date on their website before use, and tell New York City candidates and employees that a tool will be used and which qualifications or characteristics it will assess. That notice must come at least 10 business days before use. Candidates can request an alternative selection process or an accommodation, and employers must post the type and source of the data the tool uses along with the data-retention policy. The statute provides a civil penalty of up to $500 for a first violation and $500 to $1,500 for each subsequent violation, and the New York State Comptroller describes the enforcement power as penalties of $500 to $1,500 per day.

Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su said New Yorkers do not lose their rights when a decision is made or facilitated by technology, and that a company that breaks the law is responsible for what its technology does. The agencies' interagency enforcement letter states that an entity cannot avoid responsibility for violations because of reliance on an algorithm, AI, or other technology, and that legal responsibility exists regardless of whether a human being or a machine carried out the actions. In December 2025 the New York State Comptroller audited the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection's handling of the law and concluded that enforcement was weak, pointing to problems in complaint intake and compliance reviews. The department's on-record view, as described by the Comptroller, is that stakeholder education combined with complaint-based enforcement works best.

The city's position arrives alongside federal developments. In Mobley v. Workday, a federal court granted conditional certification on May 16, 2025, allowing a nationwide collective action under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act to proceed, and the court rejected the argument that the company was merely a software provider. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission filed an amicus brief supporting the theory that an AI vendor could be directly liable under Title VII, the ADA, or the ADEA. The commission removed its published AI-hiring guidance in January 2025 and voted 2-1 on June 4, 2026 to adopt a new National Enforcement Plan for fiscal years 2025 through 2029, which de-emphasizes disparate impact and does not name AI hiring as a standalone priority.

Articles.Title: NYC Local Law 144: AI Is No Defense, $1,500 Fines [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Market in Orthopedic Surgery: Examining Demand Patterns and Competitive Landscape - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
The Business Research Company published a press release on November 2, 2026, about the artificial intelligence market in orthopedic surgery. The release came from London and was distributed through EINPresswire. It describes the market as growing quickly as AI becomes a bigger part of orthopedic care. The report covers market size, trends and a forecast through 2030.

The release says the market is expected to rise from $0.26 billion in 2025 to $0.33 billion in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of 27.5%. It projects the market will reach $0.87 billion by 2030, with a compound annual growth rate of 27.2%. North America held the largest share of the market in 2025. The report also covers Asia-Pacific, South East Asia, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, South America, the Middle East and Africa.

The release attributes past growth to more orthopedic procedures, advances in medical imaging, wider use of minimally invasive techniques, growth in hospital digital infrastructure and a stronger focus on surgical precision. It says future growth will stem from demand for personalized orthopedic care, investment in surgical robotic technologies, broader use of AI-driven clinical decision support systems, outcome-based healthcare models and deeper integration of AI with electronic health records. It names rising musculoskeletal disorders as a primary driver, citing a UK Office for Health Improvement and Disparities report from January 2024 that found 18.4% of people aged 16 and older had a long-term musculoskeletal condition in 2023, up from 17.6% in 2022. The release says AI helps with early and accurate diagnosis, personalized treatment planning and outcome predictions.

The release says AI in orthopedic surgery is used to plan operations, improve accuracy and improve patient results. It says the technology helps diagnose bone and joint disorders, tailor surgical approaches, predict complications and place implants precisely. It aims to reduce errors, speed recovery and customize treatment based on patient-specific data. The release lists expected trends including AI-assisted surgical planning, computer vision in surgery, more robotic systems, predictive analytics for patient outcomes and more accurate implant placement.

Articles.Title: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Market in Orthopedic Surgery: Examining Demand Patterns and Competitive Landscape - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Ex-Lawmakers Side With OpenAI In Battle With News Publishers 11/03/2026
stories.Summary:
Two former Republican lawmakers, Rick Santorum of Pennsylvania and Rich Boucher of Virginia, filed a friend-of-the-court brief late last week with U.S. District Judge Sidney H. Stein in New York. They urged the judge to rule that training large language models on news articles and other copyrighted material is fair use. They argued that an AI model relies on works to derive statistical patterns of language rather than to communicate their expression to the public. They said a ruling in favor of fair use is vitally important to the country.

The brief comes in a high-profile lawsuit brought by publishers including The New York Times Co. against OpenAI. The publishers allege OpenAI infringed copyright by using content to train ChatGPT and by reproducing portions of content in outputs generated in response to users' prompts. OpenAI is seeking dismissal of the lawsuit and argues that training a large language model is transformative. The company also says it takes steps to prevent verbatim outputs and that regurgitation of copyrighted content is extremely rare.

Santorum and Boucher wrote that a contrary ruling would impose a de facto licensing regime with grave consequences for AI development. They said the freedom of American scientists, companies and entrepreneurs to train AI is of paramount economic and strategic importance. The publishers responded that the defendants envision a world where they can freely copy entire news articles to generate content that engages users at the expense of publishers. Numerous other outside parties also filed friend-of-the-court briefs on Friday, including digital rights groups, tech industry associations and entertainment businesses such as talent agency William Morris Endeavor.

The digital rights groups and tech industry generally support OpenAI, while entertainment-related businesses oppose the company. William Morris Endeavor contended that its clients are already losing paid work to AI output built on their own copyrighted works. The Computer & Communications Industry Association, NetChoice and TechNet argued that training chatbots on news articles is transformational. Two federal judges have already weighed in, with Judge William Alsup ruling that Anthropic did not infringe copyright by digitizing books it had purchased, while Judge Vince Chhabria said using books to train large language models was transformative but also likely infringed copyright in most cases.

Articles.Title: Ex-Lawmakers Side With OpenAI In Battle With News Publishers 11/03/2026

stories.Headline: NJ's Proposed Liability for AI Chatbots May ‘Open the Floodgates,' Attorneys Say
stories.Summary:
New Jersey lawmakers advanced a bill in October that would let people sue the providers of artificial intelligence chatbots under the state's products liability law. The bill moved quickly through an assembly committee, according to a report by Nicholas Malfitano published by Law.com on November 2, 2026. The article says the proposal would make chatbots subject to products liability rules. Defense attorneys warned that the change could "open the floodgates" to claims.

The articles give few other details about what the bill requires or changes. They do not list a bill number, a vote count, or the names of the committee or its members. The only date given is the Law.com publication date of November 2, 2026, and the only time frame is that the bill advanced in October. The article also does not say when the full assembly might vote or what penalties the bill would set.

A plaintiff attorney described the bill as a key consumer protection measure, according to the article. Defense attorneys said it could "open the floodgates" to claims, the report states. The articles do not name any of the attorneys or say which firms or sides they represent. They also do not give any other statements from lawmakers or the bill's sponsors.

The context is that the bill is still legislation under consideration in Trenton, not law. A related Law.com article from October 30, 2026, by Michael J. Epstein, says the legislation would establish new liability rules for companies that develop and operate generative AI systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the committee's action. They do not report a scheduled vote, a fiscal analysis, or a position from the governor.

Articles.Title: NJ's Proposed Liability for AI Chatbots May ‘Open the Floodgates,' Attorneys Say - Law.com

stories.Headline: When the AI Agent Goes Off-Script: The First Incident Playbook for Frontier AI - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
On October 16, 2026, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the National Security Agency and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency published a list of 10 key practices for incident readiness and response in super intelligence training and evaluation. The document is the first government effort to give designers and deployers information on mitigating risks from agentic artificial intelligence systems. It was developed by NIST's Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, the NSA's Super Intelligence Security Center and CISA. The practices are voluntary and the document says it is not legal or compliance guidance.

The document groups the 10 practices into five lifecycle stages: Prepare, Detect, Respond, Recover and Report. It builds on the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and NIST SP 800-61r3, and it defines an "SI control incident" as a case where one or more SI agents take significant uninstructed actions that compromise the operator's policies, controls or security measures. An "SI control near-miss" covers events that did not become an incident but presented a reasonably foreseeable or imminent risk of one. The document says that in a cybersecurity incident the system is the target, while in an SI control incident the AI system is the source.

The practices call for least-privilege access, single-use infrastructure and monitored network gateways, and for controls built on the expectation that SI agents will find and exploit misconfigurations. They call for monitoring the model, harness, host and network layers, for keeping agents away from monitoring processes and logs, and for red-teaming the monitors. On response, they call for preserving model weights, checkpoints, logs and rejected tool calls, and for shutting down affected activity and revoking credentials. Recovery should come only after containment is verified, and reporting covers affected parties, government notification and information sharing.

The article says the practices are likely to become a benchmark for judging the reasonableness of AI design and deployment. It says the new government definitions will shape contracts, insurance questionnaires and litigation discovery. It advises compliance and legal teams to reconcile evidence preservation with existing retention, litigation hold and privacy obligations before an incident, and to structure investigations under counsel's direction to preserve privilege. It also advises reviewing notice, cooperation, confidentiality and indemnity terms with model developers so vendor contracts are consistent with the practices.

Articles.Title: When the AI Agent Goes Off-Script: The First Incident Playbook for Frontier AI - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Gemini opens the door to digital twins... Transform your face and voice into a virtual character using artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Google has added a feature to its Gemini app that lets users create a digital avatar copying their face and voice, according to a report from Voice of Emirates dated November 3, 2026. The tool turns recorded facial and voice data into a virtual character tied to the user's account. Users can then make photos and videos with the avatar without appearing on camera each time. The report says the feature is part of Google's wider push into artificial intelligence for personal content creation.

To set it up, users open the Gemini app or website, choose Add Files and then the Avatar section, and scan a QR code with their phone. They must allow camera and microphone access, record their face in good light with the phone at eye level, and speak clearly in a quiet room. The avatar can then be picked inside Gemini and used to generate images and videos. Users can also share the avatar with chosen people and control or revoke their access later.

The service requires users to be at least 18 and to have a personal Google account, and some video features need a subscription to eligible Google AI plans. Availability is limited by geography and language. Google provides settings to review, control and delete recordings, and the report says privacy settings should be checked before an avatar is made or shared. The report describes the technology as a shift, with AI now able to produce virtual versions of real people rather than only fictional characters.

Articles.Title: Gemini opens the door to digital twins... Transform your face and voice into a virtual character using artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Judiciary Stuck In AI Rulemaking Rut As Attys, Judges Protest
stories.Summary:
Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence are stalled, according to a Law360 report published on November 3, 2026, by Jeff Overley. The report says the delay involves concerns about burdens placed on litigators. It also cites tension between fast-moving technology and slow policymaking. The report adds that officials are struggling over how to even define the technology at issue.

The article does not give specific dates for any proposed rules or name the officials involved. It does not state what any new rule would require or change. No numbers beyond the publication date are provided. The report describes the situation as a rut rather than a finished policy.

The story is limited to the concerns raised in the report. It says attorneys and judges have protested the stalled progress. It does not include direct statements from named individuals. It also does not say who is formally responsible for moving the rules forward.

The report does not describe what happens next. It gives no timeline for future action. It does not say whether a proposal will be issued or when. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Judiciary Stuck In AI Rulemaking Rut As Attys, Judges Protest - Law360

stories.Headline: NJ lawmakers want safeguards for police use of AI, facial recognition software
stories.Summary:
Two bills in the New Jersey Legislature would require the attorney general’s office to study how police departments use facial recognition software and artificial intelligence and to recommend statewide policies for their use. The Assembly’s Public Safety and Preparedness Committee cleared both bills on Oct. 19. Democratic Assembly members Al Abdelaziz, Verlina Reynolds-Jackson and Ellen Park sponsored the facial recognition bill, A-759. Assembly members Chris Tully, Annette Quijano and Balvir Singh introduced the artificial intelligence measure, A-3076.

A-759 would require the attorney general to report on what kinds of facial recognition technology are available to police and how accurate they are. A-3076 sets similar study requirements for artificial intelligence and also calls for a statewide policy requiring officers to review AI-generated police reports for accuracy and completeness. State Sen. Benjie Wimberly, a Passaic County Democrat, is expected to introduce identical bills in the upper chamber. California adopted a law, effective Jan. 1, 2026, requiring disclaimers on police reports created with AI help, officer certification that the reports were checked, retention of the first AI draft and an audit trail. Utah passed a law in 2025 requiring every agency to create an AI policy, add disclaimers and have officers certify their review.

Assemblyman Joe Danielson, a Somerset County Democrat who chairs the committee, said lawmakers need to explore how to help public safety departments use the tool while maintaining privacy, security and public trust. Singh, a Burlington County Democrat, said many departments in his district already use AI to write reports without statewide guidance, and that the technology can add details and change phrasing in ways that alter an officer’s account. Tully, a Bergen County Democrat, said AI tools are being marketed aggressively to police as time savers, and that there must always be a human in the loop. Wimberly said lawmakers should not wait for something to go wrong before establishing safeguards.

Jason Williams, a justice studies professor at Montclair State University, said facial recognition is not foolproof and false matches can send officers after innocent people. He said AI-generated reports can omit context, misstate sequences and make uncertain claims sound settled, and that officer review is necessary but may not be sufficient. He said he would rather see accountability measures, clear restrictions, independent audits, disclosure to defendants and community involvement than studies. The bills’ sponsors said the attorney general reports are a first step toward creating the right laws and regulations.

Articles.Title: NJ lawmakers want safeguards for police use of AI, facial recognition software - The Jersey Vindicator

stories.Headline: Corporate America's AI bill is ballooning. This startup raised $30 million to make sense of where the money is going.
stories.Summary:
Larridin, a San Francisco startup, raised $30 million in Series A funding, Business Insider reported on November 2, 2026. The round was led by Pelion Ventures, with Andreessen Horowitz, Gradient Ventures, GFT Ventures, W23, Thayer Investment Partners, DG Daiwa Ventures, Alumni Ventures, and Cougar Capital also taking part. A16z and Gradient Ventures had earlier backed the company's $17 million seed round. The company was founded by CEO Russell Fradin, CTO Ameya Kanitkar, and Jim Larrison, and Fradin and Larrison previously worked together at Comscore.

Larridin's platform measures how much AI improves employee productivity and where adoption could be better. It connects to companies' internal systems and analyzes employees' prompts to different AI tools to see who uses AI effectively, who needs more training, and how much time is saved. Kanitkar said the platform protects privacy by analyzing AI interactions without storing their contents, producing scores and high-level insights instead. Fradin said business picked up around the second quarter of this year as more companies worried about AI costs, and the company grew from one enterprise customer in December last year to 50 now. After the round, Fradin said he wants to double Larridin's 20-person head count by adding sales, engineering, and marketing staff.

Jeff Kearl, a general partner at Pelion Ventures, said AI has gone from a small or nonexistent expense to one of the top five to 10 most expensive items on company ledgers. He described companies asking where the money goes, who uses the tools, and how to make sense of it. Alex Rampell, a general partner at A16z, said Larridin addresses a need in enterprise AI for a sort of AI boss who can tell staff what they should and shouldn't do with AI. He said the underlying idea is whether people using AI tools are doing the right thing and whether the outcome is appreciably different.

The funding comes after months of change in how companies spend on AI. Early in the year, companies urged employees to use AI as much as possible, and some, like Duolingo, added AI use as a performance metric. Uber CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga went viral in April when he said Uber had burned through its entire Claude Code budget for the year. At least 17 companies, from Salesforce to Oracle, announced AI-related layoffs, and Oracle said in June that AI deployment and adoption had reduced its workforce. Sentiment shifted around the middle of the year as large AI bills appeared, and companies began focusing on return on investment, with tactics like modelmaxxing and cheaper open-source models from Chinese labs such as Moonshot AI and Z.ai.

Articles.Title: Corporate America's AI bill is ballooning. This startup raised $30 million to make sense of where the money is going.

stories.Headline: AI-Native Firms and Big Law Will Follow Medical Centers’ Model
stories.Summary:
A Bloomberg Law column published on November 2, 2026, argues that Big Law firms and AI-native legal startups will converge on a model like the Mayo Clinic. The columnist, Eric Dodson Greenberg, chief legal officer of Cox Media Group, says each side has half of what clients need. AI-native firms are hiring partners from elite firms, and Norm Law brought in former Sidley Austin global chair Mike Schmidtberger. Legacy firms are adding technology, including Kirkland's announced $500 million AI investment and Debevoise's client subscriptions to its AI tools.

The column says the medical-center model combines top experts with the best technology, and that the combination is the brand. It points to Mayo Clinic paying physicians fixed salaries rather than pay tied to volume, which makes team-based care work. It also cites MD Anderson Cancer Center, which spent tens of millions of dollars on an AI project that was abandoned. Greenberg says prestige does not guarantee quality and that technology without governance is a risk.

A separate Artificial Lawyer article, also dated November 2, 2026, reports on a ClioCon talk by writer and philosopher Malcolm Gladwell. Gladwell described a less invasive, team-based heart bypass technique and a data-led, community-based policing approach that cut murders in Boston. He concluded that both ideas were largely ignored because they would change the professional identity of surgeons and senior police officers. The article applies this to law firm partners, saying AI makes the partner less of an absolute authority and more of a planner and project manager.

The Bloomberg column says the outcome is not certain and that some firms will keep their original models and do well. It says general counsel will ask who the lead partner is, what technology supports the work, and what the institution integrating them looks like. The Artificial Lawyer piece says partners still need to win and keep clients, but clients using AI may rely on them less. It says partners must scope work within billable limits and use AI to get the work done.

Articles.Title: AI-Native Firms and Big Law Will Follow Medical Centers’ Model

stories.Headline: Eight states sued OpenAI on the same day. Hassan Taher on why the most important AI law in America might be decades old.
stories.Summary:
On October 14, the attorneys general of Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, and West Virginia each filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI in their own state courts. The complaints allege that ChatGPT harmed children and other vulnerable users and that OpenAI misled the public about how safe the product is. The states say ChatGPT is designed to be agreeable and engaging to earn users' trust, and that it reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behavior and assists users in planning violence. They seek court orders changing how ChatGPT works for minors, along with civil penalties, damages, and in some cases the surrender of profits earned from young users. Florida's attorney general filed a similar suit in June, bringing the number of state actions to at least nine.

None of the complaints depend on an AI-specific statute. They are built on state consumer protection and deceptive trade practices laws, plus public nuisance theories, tools attorneys general have used for decades against tobacco companies, opioid distributors, and social media platforms. A day before the eight states filed, a separate proposed class action in San Francisco federal court accused OpenAI of collecting sensitive data from children without valid parental consent. The day before the state suits were filed, Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after facing lawsuits alleging its app contributed to teen mental health crises and suicides. The company agreed to settle five cases earlier this year, plans a court-supervised sale, and says the platform will be wound down if no sale closes.

Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said OpenAI is hurting kids and lying to Iowans. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has built age-specific protections that many other AI products lack. AI analyst and author Hassan Taher said AI regulation arrived on October 14 and is mostly made of laws written before the internet. Taher said the industry treats sycophancy as a quality problem, while the lawsuits treat it as a design choice with foreseeable consequences. None of the allegations have been proven in court.

Taher said Character.AI is the cautionary tale for every company running a consumer chatbot, because its product worked as intended and that was the problem. Anthony Cimino, Anthropic's head of federal affairs, said the company's draft federal AI safety bill would leave states authority over child protection, among other areas. Taher said one version of events has the industry lobbying harder for preemption to make the suits go away, and another has companies deciding the cheapest way to stop getting sued by fifty attorneys general is to build products that don't harm children. He said the second version is slower and more expensive up front, and the only one that holds up when the next set of lawsuits arrives.

Articles.Title: Eight states sued OpenAI on the same day. Hassan Taher on why the most important AI law in America might be decades old.

stories.Headline: Bulgaria to introduce a comprehensive AI law
stories.Summary:
In September 2026, a group of MPs submitted a draft law on the use and development of AI to Bulgaria's parliament. If adopted, the bill would create Bulgaria's first standalone AI legislation and set the national framework for implementing the EU AI Act. It would also add Bulgaria-specific rules on national security, workforce upskilling, public-sector AI use, investment incentives and safeguards for children. The proposal is now pending review before parliamentary committees, with the Committee on Innovation and Digital Transformation as lead committee.

Under the draft, the Minister of Innovation and Digital Transformation would be lead policymaker, and a National Coordinator for AI, appointed by the Prime Minister, would oversee the National AI Strategy and report annually on AI risks. Ten national competent authorities would carry out market surveillance, with the Communications Regulation Commission as the single point of contact under Article 70(2) of the EU AI Act. Prohibited practices would include remote biometric identification systems, AI in special intelligence means except for preparing material evidence, AI recommender systems for online gambling, and judicial use of AI to interpret facts or law. Where the Council of Ministers classifies a recommender system as high-risk, operators must give the State Agency for National Security source code, technical documentation and model parameters without delay.

Publication of AI-generated deepfakes of persons holding high public office, or of any other person without consent, would be prohibited, with a 50-year post-mortem protection period. Removal orders would be issued by the Ministry of Interior and the State Agency for National Security, subject to judicial review, and a satirical or parodic exception would apply if the material is neither defamatory nor harmful. Administrative fines would range from about EUR 250 for minor infractions up to EUR 2.5 million for serious non-compliance by very large online platform operators. The bill would also amend over 20 existing laws, including new AI transparency obligations in the Labour Code, criminalisation of AI-generated child sexual abuse material, a prohibition on judicial AI use in the Judiciary Act, and AI-labelling requirements for campaign materials in the Elections Code.

Entry into force would occur two months after promulgation, with certain provisions proposed to take effect on 1 July 2027. The Council of Ministers must adopt the implementing regulation and the National AI Strategy within six months, and obligated persons would have nine months to bring their activities into compliance. An earlier version was submitted in October 2025 during the 51st National Assembly but did not advance before that parliament dissolved. Whether this second attempt succeeds remains to be seen.

Articles.Title: Bulgaria to introduce a comprehensive AI law

stories.Headline: The State Of The AI Trade: Someone Has To Pay The Bill (NASDAQ:QQQ)
stories.Summary:
On October 21, Meta Platforms reported earnings that beat revenue expectations by 2% and beat adjusted earnings per share by 13.1%, according to Nicolas Bolsinger in a Seeking Alpha article published November 2, 2026. Capital expenditure came in almost $2 billion higher than expected. The stock fell the next day. The article says Meta and other hyperscalers face market skepticism as soaring capex eats into free cash flow and triggers equity dilution. The article says AI demand remains robust and cloud backlogs are growing fast, but shrinking free cash flow and aggressive capital raises are alarming investors.

Hardware and AI infrastructure stocks have outperformed, yet their revenue is highly concentrated and depends on a handful of hyperscalers keeping up extreme capex. Credit and equity markets are signaling risk aversion, with spreads widening most at the most levered names, Oracle and CoreWeave. The article lists Meta, Oracle and CoreWeave among the companies involved. Bolsinger wrote the article and states he holds no stock, option or similar derivative position in the companies mentioned and has no plans to start one within 72 hours. He says he wrote the article himself and that it expresses his own opinions.

He says he receives no compensation for it other than from Seeking Alpha and has no business relationship with any company mentioned. Seeking Alpha's disclosure states that past performance is no guarantee of future results and that no recommendation or advice is being given on whether an investment is suitable for a particular investor. The article is a commentary on the state of the AI trade rather than a report of a single event, and it does not say what happens next. It frames the tension as hyperscalers having to pay the bill for AI spending through weaker free cash flow and dilution. The listed tickers include SPY, QQQ, SOXX, ORCL and CRWV.

Articles.Title: The State Of The AI Trade: Someone Has To Pay The Bill (NASDAQ:QQQ)

stories.Headline: Culver City's AI boom attracting Silicon Valley firms and making 2-year-old restaurant Hollywood's latest power lunch spot
stories.Summary:
Over the past year, more than a half-dozen AI startups have moved into Culver City, a 1.2-square-mile city, as part of tech's push into the entertainment industry. Sean Parker, a co-founder of Napster and former Facebook president, opened an office in the Hayden Tract last month as part of the expansion of his San Francisco-based Cantina Labs, which he founded in 2023. Parker also took part in an $80 million rescue of the AI image firm Stability AI. Luma Labs, a $4 billion Palo Alto-based startup co-founded by Amit Jain, opened a 7,000-square-foot facility called the Dream Lab in Culver City last year. Other AI startups that set up shop in Culver City this year include TrueShort, PhantomX and Native Foreign.

The Laurel Grill, which opened two years ago, has become the de facto power lunch spot for the area's studio and AI executives. It sits atop the Culver Steps, overlooking the Culver Studios and the Culver Hotel, and was opened by Dean McKillen and Phil Howard, the owners of Laurel Hardware and Ysabel. A bartender at the spot said it is frequently packed with Amazon, Apple and Sony execs. George Strompolos, who set up his startup Promise AI in a building in the shadow of the Sony water tower, said every time he meets with an Amazon exec it is at the Laurel Grill. Council member and former mayor Dan O'Brien likened the place to Culver City's version of The Ivy.

Strompolos launched Promise AI alongside former YouTube exec Jamie Byrne and filmmaker Dave Clark, with backing from Peter Chernin's North Road and Andreessen Horowitz. He previously ran the digital media and entertainment company Fullscreen from offices in Culver Studios but sold that company to AT&T's Otter Media. O'Brien said the commercial real estate market "bottomed out last year" and that the city has been telling the AI crowd they are welcome. However, another city insider said the feeling is not totally unanimous among council members, who are balancing a welcome for the AI crowd with sensitivity to a creative community that is wary of the technology.

Most people credit Mike Gioia and Todd Terrazas, who founded the four-year-old conference AI on the Lot, for spearheading the AI push into Culver City. The conference has taken over Amazon MGM's Culver Studios for the past two years, and the company also has its own office space between the studio gate and the Culver Theater, which Amazon took over in 2022. Last month during LA Tech Week, the group held an AI job fair on the Culver Steps and routinely offers its office space to AI filmmakers. Earlier this year, the Thunderbird School of Global Management at Arizona State University held its LA chapter meetup at Laurel Grill.

Articles.Title: Culver City's AI boom attracting Silicon Valley firms and making 2-year-old restaurant Hollywood's latest power lunch spot - Page Six

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s compute bill shows where AI investment really flows
stories.Summary:
Anthropic made its IPO prospectus public on 26 October 2026, and it commits hundreds of billions of dollars to computing infrastructure. The largest commitment is $161.2 billion with Broadcom, a chip designer. Google, Amazon and SpaceX each account for more than $100 billion, and Microsoft for about $45 billion, with some contracts running to 2036. Reports suggest the offering could raise around $100 billion, which would make it the largest IPO on record.

The article says AI is not one trade but at least seven investable layers: fabrication tools and process materials, memory, compute, networking, physical infrastructure, power and applications. Anthropic's spending touches every layer, and its own place is in applications, the layer that has to pay for the rest. Since 29 June 2026, analysts raised earnings forecasts most for fabrication, compute, physical infrastructure and memory, while power was the only layer revised lower. Share prices moved almost in reverse: fabrication fell 25.6% to 21 September, while applications rose 33.3%. Compute and memory margins are above 55%, and Anthropic reported $16.3 billion of revenue in the first half of 2026.

The article is by Renée Friedman, Global Head of Research at EXANTE, and it draws on the firm's Beneath the Goldrush report. She writes that the buildout is financed in the bond market as much as from cash flow, with the five largest US hyperscalers issuing $121 billion of investment-grade bonds in 2025 against an annual average of $28 billion between 2020 and 2024. She says the Bank for International Settlements calls off-balance sheet methods such as special purpose vehicles and long-term leases "shadow borrowing" and warns they may create new shock transmission channels. She argues that a client holding AI equities may also be exposed to rates or credit risk, so real exposure may be greater than the equity allocation suggests.

The article cites the International Energy Agency expecting data-centre electricity demand to more than double to around 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, with grid connection lead times in some hubs stretching to ten years. It cites OECD modelling putting the potential productivity gain at 0.4 to 1.3 percentage points a year, provided workers reskill and institutions adapt. Friedman says that until the gain appears in national accounts, AI spending on its own is a cost line, and that if application revenue stalls, the most capital-intensive layers are likely to reprice first. She says Anthropic is a test case, with commitments that run for a decade.

Articles.Title: Anthropic’s compute bill shows where AI investment really flows

stories.Headline: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers led by Lu Wang has published a paper introducing AskStream, a benchmark for streaming video understanding. The work has ten other authors, including Zhuoran Jin, Longxiang Wang, Junhong Chen, Yupu Hao, Yao Xu, Daojian Zeng, Yubo Chen, Kang Liu, Guang Liu and Jun Zhao. The paper was posted on arXiv on 3 November 2026 and runs to 42 pages with 9 figures. It falls under computer vision and pattern recognition and also computation and language. The paper argues that proactive models should have a third action beyond waiting or answering, namely asking for missing information.

AskStream is described as the first multi-turn benchmark spanning uncertainty from both the video and the user. It has four task categories and eight subtasks, with 438 videos and 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask and answer. Even the strongest model reaches only 52.18% on the proposed Ask-F1 metric in both multiple-choice and open-ended settings. The authors say existing proactive paradigms assume the information needed to answer a query is complete, so models can only wait or answer. They note that in the real world information is often incomplete because of uncertainty from the video or the user.

They argue this uncertainty can make a model wait forever or produce highly hallucinatory responses. They therefore propose redefining proactive interaction to include asking, so models can actively seek the missing information before answering. The paper states that the results highlight substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty. It provides links to a project page, code and the dataset. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond the release of these resources.

Articles.Title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding

stories.Headline: Did AI Payment Agents Just Shift Bill's (BILL) Investment Narrative?
stories.Summary:
BILL Holdings has rolled out new AI-driven finance tools and started a live pilot with Visa and Billtrust that lets authenticated AI agents complete approved invoice payments end to end through supplier portals. The pilot replaces manual keying while keeping supplier controls in place. The company also launched a risk intelligence engine that flagged an average of US$138,000 of unusual or mistaken invoices per customer in just two months. The article was published by Simply Wall St on November 2, 2026, and reviewed by Sasha Jovanovic.

The article says BILL's narrative projects US$2.1 billion in revenue and US$404.7 million in earnings by 2029, based on 8.5% yearly revenue growth and an earnings swing of roughly US$416 million from a loss of US$11.2 million today. It also cites a more pessimistic view of about US$1.8 billion in revenue and US$366.0 million in earnings by 2029. Those projections were set before this AI payments rollout, so the article calls the launch a live test case. It says the fair value estimate implies an 18% potential upside to the current price, while one estimate suggests as much as 11% downside.

The article does not name any company executives or give direct statements from them. It frames the pilot as most tied to BILL's key catalysts because it applies AI directly to payments that previously required manual portal entry. It says the biggest risk is that payment volumes or average revenue per user soften, which would slow profitability improvement. It also says execution missteps, low supplier acceptance or slower buyer adoption would limit the benefit.

The article says the near-term swing factor is whether AI agents, risk tools and embedded payments can support stable transaction volumes while small and midsize business spend stays mixed and active contract pruning weighs on top-line progress. It says the focus for investors is whether the authenticated agent model scales cleanly across more portals without adding new fraud, compliance or reliability issues. It notes that the pilot on its own does not remove growth headwinds from pruning legacy relationships. The article does not say what happens next beyond watching how the rollout performs.

Articles.Title: Did AI Payment Agents Just Shift Bill's (BILL) Investment Narrative?

stories.Headline: AI-related demand tests U.S. factories' paces
stories.Summary:
American factories kept expanding in October, according to two new manufacturing surveys, as surging demand for AI-related equipment strained supply chains and pushed prices up. The Institute for Supply Management's manufacturing index rose 1 point to 55.5 last month, the 10th straight month of expanding activity after a yearslong slump. Production accelerated at the fastest pace since November 2021. S&P Global's manufacturing gauge dipped slightly by 1 percentage point to 54.9, but the firm says the sector is on its best run since early 2022, and hiring accelerated to its fastest pace in more than five years.

Both surveys show strains from heavy demand for AI-related equipment, along with higher energy costs and war-related shipping disruptions. S&P Global said manufacturers' selling prices rose at the sharpest rate in four years. ISM's prices index slipped by 2.7 percentage points to 75.2% last month but still signaled widespread increases in raw material costs. Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global, said in a release that demand often exceeds supply, so producers have been increasingly able to pass higher costs on to customers, notably for energy-related inputs.

One manufacturer told ISM that any commodity consumed by AI and data centers is in a crunch, both for supply and pricing. A machinery manufacturer described extraordinary demand for semiconductors and defense equipment, saying lead times and prices are increasing and some carry COVID-19 era delays, with four weeks now 50 weeks, and that the company is hand to mouth. A chemical products manufacturer said costs had risen more than 6% this year and that uncertain economic policy had made it impossible to make sound long-term decisions. The manufacturing resurgence is a bright spot for the U.S. economy, but surging AI-related demand is testing factories' ability to keep up as prices continue to surge.

Articles.Title: AI-related demand tests U.S. factories' paces

stories.Headline: BoG Governor urges GSS to make Ghana’s data AI-ready
stories.Summary:
Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, the Governor of the Bank of Ghana, called on the Ghana Statistical Service to publish Ghana's socio-economic data on a dedicated electronic portal in formats that are accessible and machine-readable. He made the call at the launch of the first Ghana in Numbers 2025 report in Accra on Thursday, according to a Ghana News Agency report dated November 2. The report gives an overview of Ghana's socio-economic indicators, demographic trends and other key statistics. The Governor said advances in data science, AI and machine learning are creating new ways to spot patterns, improve forecasts, assess risks and draw insights from large and complex datasets.

The report put Ghana's population at 33.7 million in 2025, with the economy reaching about GHS1.4 trillion in nominal terms, GDP growth of six per cent and an end-year inflation rate of 5.4 per cent. It said the number of businesses nearly tripled to 2,644,363 in 2024, while the people working in them doubled to 6.90 million, meaning more businesses were created than jobs. The share of adults working or looking for work rose from 67.1 percent in 2022 to an average of 74.5 percent in the first three quarters of 2025. The report also said life expectancy rose over time but many young people could not find work.

Dr Asiama said the portal would let researchers, policymakers and others use AI and advanced tools to explore data deeply and find patterns and links beyond published tables and charts. He commended the GSS for the initiative and described it as a national resource that makes official statistics more accessible. He said the Bank of Ghana was building capacity through its new Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence Department and was developing a directive to regulate AI use in the financial sector. He said effective monetary policy and financial regulation depend on the quality of data, and that as an inflation-targeting central bank its decisions are forward-looking and data-driven.

Dr Iddrisu advised the Government to build budgets around the numbers, noting that district assemblies use local figures to allocate spending and Parliament demands measurable baselines for new programmes each year. He urged employers and investors to help turn informal jobs into formal ones, pointing out that only 7.7 per cent of establishments are formal. He also urged development partners, researchers, civil society, the media and citizens to hold institutions to the numbers. He said the figures are not just a record of the past but a tool for deciding what happens next.

Articles.Title: BoG Governor urges GSS to make Ghana’s data AI-ready

stories.Headline: AI Governance Risks Prompt Call for Urgent Australian Law Reform
stories.Summary:
Dr David Millhouse, a Bond University researcher and Honorary Adjunct Senior Research Fellow in its Faculty of Law, published a peer-reviewed paper called “Artificial Intelligence and the Law” in the Bond Law Review on 13 October 2026, in Volume 38, Issue 2. The paper examines how existing Australian laws are coping with AI’s growing role in business, professional services and corporate decision-making. It warns that Australians face risks from inaccurate AI outputs, biased information and privacy breaches as the country’s laws struggle to keep pace with adoption. It also identifies questions over who is responsible when automated decisions cause harm, how personal information is protected, who owns data used by AI systems, and intellectual property disputes and professional negligence as significant legal risks.

The paper calls for dedicated national AI legislation and amendments to the Corporations Act 2001, along with stronger protections for data ownership and intellectual property. It recommends professional disclosure requirements, mandatory governance training, and independent certification and auditing of AI systems, plus a bias and factual data and outcome regime policed by an independent certification authority such as the Australian AI Safety Institute if its mandate is reformed. It also calls for broader responsibilities for that institute and for mandatory certification of lawyers and barristers disclosing their deployment of AI and the extent of human supervision. At enterprise level, it says boards should appoint Digital Readiness Officers and set up dedicated AI compliance committees, equivalent to the audit committee and separate from operational IT management, with board-level workshops, policies and compliance reporting, and it says these requirements should be mandatory for ASX-listed companies and trusts.

Dr Millhouse wrote that AI governance is not optional and not delegable, and urged government, company directors and trustees to understand the workflows, who is responsible, and the risks, and to enact stronger safeguards. He said present Australian government policy, which is under review, is not to legislate a specific AI statute, and he called this an error requiring legislative rectification in the pre-AGI era, adding that reform needs to be capacious. He argued that AI can deliver substantial productivity and economic gains when deployed intelligently, but that mitigating its inherent risks requires significant work across legal frameworks, corporate responsibility and professional education. He said it is too early to definitively predict how generative AI will affect the law and the legal profession, and that while the technology may be revolutionary, its application is evolutionary. He concluded that the journey to artificial general intelligence is at “the end of the beginning.”

Articles.Title: AI Governance Risks Prompt Call for Urgent Australian Law Reform

stories.Headline: Florida Attorney General: AI company allows people to generate sexually explicit pictures of kids
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a legal complaint on Wednesday alleging that an artificial intelligence company lets users create sexually explicit pictures and videos of minors, or “nudify” them. The suit was filed in state Circuit Court in Sarasota County against A2E, an AI image platform, and its owner, Rengstorff Consulting, a Nevada firm. The 26-page suit claims the company’s practices are “unconscionable,” “deceptive,” and “unfair” under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. Uthmeier said his office is also investigating possible criminal offenses.

The suit’s first allegation is that the product lets “predators” “nudify non-consenting Floridians,” including children, and lets users alter images of adults to look like children. The suit cites a Tampa man arrested earlier this year who Uthmeier alleges created more than 100 sexually explicit images of his 6-year-old stepdaughter and 10-year-old stepson. The complaint says the software warns users that nonconsensual sexual use is “strictly prohibited” but that the defendant tries to shift all responsibility for compliance to users. Uthmeier also announced that the Office of Statewide Prosecution charged Jerry Jesus Reyes, a 26-year-old from Kissimmee, with 100 felony counts after a tip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.

The counts include one allegation of transmission of child pornography, 86 allegations of unlawful possession of materials depicting sexual performance by a child, and 13 allegations of unlawful possession of materials depicting sexual activity with animals. Uthmeier said at a news conference in Orlando that creating the vehicle does not exempt a company from liability, and that the software is the “manufacturing hub” churning out the content. He said the state wants to make the company pay and shut it down. He called the Reyes case “disgusting, disturbing, depraved” and “inhumane.”

A2E did not respond to a request for comment from the Phoenix. Uthmeier says a 2025 Florida law requiring social media companies to delete deepfakes, or AI-generated sexual depictions of people made without consent, is in play in the case. He faces his first election in less than a week, after being appointed to his post last year by Governor Ron DeSantis. Since his August primary election, he has hosted 26 news conferences.

Articles.Title: Florida Attorney General: AI company allows people to generate sexually explicit pictures of kids - Kiowa County Press

stories.Headline: Kid Rock Defends AI Choir On Eminem Duet As Bill Maher Questions Lost Jobs
stories.Summary:
Kid Rock defended his use of an AI choir on his Eminem duet during the October 30 episode of HBO's Real Time with Bill Maher, according to AllHipHop. He said his backing singers were away when he wanted to finish the track "Heal My Faith," so he turned to software. Rock said he entered notes and asked for a Southern gospel sound, then tried several options before choosing one he liked. He said he was impatient and that saving time drove the choice, not the cost of hiring singers.

Maher questioned whether the process had taken paid work from people who could have sung those parts, saying that when the Beatles used a choir they needed a choir. Rock compared the change to drum machines and said he still viewed AI as a tool while supporting rules on its use, and said he sees the dangers of it. He contrasted the process with "7 Sins," where three backing singers recorded repeated takes to create the sound of a larger group. Rock had already discussed using AI for parts of the album before Halfway 2 Jesus came out on October 17, describing generated choir and orchestral sounds alongside recordings made with Nashville musicians and his band in a Billboard interview.

"Heal My Faith" had drawn attention before its release because Rock and Eminem backed opposing sides in the last presidential race, with Rock supporting Donald Trump and Eminem taking the stage at a Detroit rally for Kamala Harris in 2024. AllHipHop previously covered the album's guest switch, which put Lil Wayne on "7 Sins" and moved Eminem to "Heal My Faith." The switch followed Eminem's request to return to the song Rock first brought him, according to Rock's account to Billboard. Their work together dates back to Eminem's guest verse on Rock's 1998 album Devil Without A Cause, and Eminem addressed their partnership on X, saying it was not about choosing sides but about making music with an old friend.

Articles.Title: Kid Rock Defends AI Choir On Eminem Duet As Bill Maher Questions Lost Jobs

stories.Headline: SingularityNET CEO Addresses Challenges of AI Regulation
stories.Summary:
Dr. Ben Goertzel, the CEO of SingularityNET, raised concerns about AI regulation in a post shared on X, according to a report by Coinfomania on November 2nd, 2026. He warned that rules shaped by frontier labs could lead to regulatory capture. In his view, this could stifle competition and lock out competitors in the AI space. He also said stringent regulations could hamper independent research that is crucial for developing artificial general intelligence with moral agency.

The article says Goertzel's concerns center on how regulation could affect innovation and the competitive landscape. It states that overly stringent rules could limit competition and slow advancements in AGI. It also says the lack of clear regulatory guidance may deter investment and innovation in the AI sector. SingularityNET is described as a platform focused on decentralized AI technology that aims to democratize access to AI services.

Goertzel is the person behind the warning, and the article attributes the concerns to him and his tweet. SingularityNET advocates for balanced regulation to foster innovation, according to the report. Goertzel's insights call for dialogue among regulators and AI developers. The article says regulatory bodies are increasingly scrutinizing AI's impact, making it important for organizations like SingularityNET to engage in discussions that shape future policies.

The report notes that market sentiment remains cautious, with mixed signals across major cryptocurrencies. It says the balance between innovation and regulation will likely affect market dynamics significantly. Traders and industry observers should closely monitor regulatory developments affecting the AI landscape, according to the article. It adds that potential policy changes could present both risks and opportunities for stakeholders in the AI and crypto sectors.

Articles.Title: SingularityNET CEO Addresses Challenges of AI Regulation

stories.Headline: Meet NKY schools’ AI integration specialist. He’s the only one in the state.
stories.Summary:
Clint Litzinger became the AI integration specialist for the Northern Kentucky Cooperative for Educational Services, a role created about 18 months ago by 23 Northern Kentucky school districts. The cooperative includes all 13 districts in Boone, Kenton and Campbell counties and is one of Kentucky’s eight regional cooperatives. NKCES staff and its governing board of superintendents began discussing the position about two years ago, according to Chief Academic Officer Robb Smith. Litzinger spent a decade as a middle school science teacher before becoming a technology lead at Bracken County School District, one of the cooperative’s member districts. He began experimenting with AI using ChatGPT when it first came out in 2022.

The cooperative’s purpose is to support school districts by letting them share resources, training and purchasing power. Smith said it has become common for cooperatives or districts to hire instructional technology staff over the past decade, but NKCES wanted to take the next step. He said they wanted someone strong with instructional technology who was also a futurist and innovator. Executive Director Amy Razor said they were really looking for a unicorn, and then Litzinger’s application came across their desk. Litzinger said he applied because he had always been fascinated by technology.

Litzinger’s job is not to prescribe AI tools or their use in Northern Kentucky districts, but to explore those options alongside NKCES partners. He leads professional development workshops for educators and said he saw AI as the next revolution of education. Smith described a moment in society when everyone suddenly became interested in the possibilities of artificial intelligence and education. Razor said finding somebody who likes serving a region takes a special gift, because every district has a different need. Litzinger’s phone has rarely stopped ringing since he began the role.

Articles.Title: Meet NKY schools’ AI integration specialist. He’s the only one in the state.

stories.Headline: Highland Park reups contract with location-data platform Placer.ai
stories.Summary:
The City of Highland Park approved a contract renewal with the data analytics company Placer.ai on Oct. 26. The City Council voted to extend a partnership that began in 2023. The new agreement runs from Dec. 1 through Nov. 30, 2029, a three-year term. The previous three-year contract was $72,000 annually, and the new agreement is $82,145.

Placer.ai is a proprietary market and location intelligence platform. The City says the service has helped with marketing campaigns, business and economic development, event planning and attracting new developments. The platform identifies locations of new businesses, tracks foot traffic in the business district and recognizes how streets and other safeties are used. Its data is reportedly stripped of identifying information, and the insights the service offers remain the same under the new deal.

City Communications Manager Amanda Bennett said the City has seen many positive applications from the insights gained from the data. She cited the benefits of data visualizations and analytics available for both City applications and local businesses. Bennett called the unique reports a high value component for businesses and said the platform gives the City accurate comparative statistics it could not get elsewhere. She said the City trusts Placer.ai more than generative AI because it analyzes analytical data, and a City staff member helps interpret reports for business owners.

The City relied on Placer.ai event data to inform its marketing campaign with iHeartMedia and to optimize marketing by converting engagement rates into visits. Local businesses can request unique reports and business district level analysis from the City's Office of Business Development. Before 2023, the City reportedly relied on rough head counts to measure event attendance. The City has measured the platform's success through real world applications, feedback from staff and the public, and regular evaluation of its software subscriptions.

Articles.Title: Highland Park reups contract with location-data platform Placer.ai

stories.Headline: Assessment in Schools in the age of AI and digital technologies
stories.Summary:
Generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly integrated into everyday life and education, according to Joe Danso, an EdD researcher writing for Modern Ghana on November 3, 2026. He notes that although the technology is not new and people had used AI unknowingly for years through search engines and navigation systems, the situation changed after ChatGPT was released in 2022. Students now use AI to explain difficult concepts and write assignments, while educators use it to create teaching materials and assist in assessments. Nearly four years after the first model was released, this raises questions about academic integrity, critical thinking and the future of assessment.

Danso argues that assessment should not be just about grades but should reveal what a student understands, where support is needed and whether they can apply knowledge. He gives the example of a chemistry student who memorises a definition and reproduces it in an examination without necessarily understanding how or why a concept occurs, while carrying out an experiment and interpreting results provides stronger evidence of learning. He says using GenAI is not automatically cheating, since prompting AI for ideas differs from submitting a fully AI-generated piece of work as one's own. He calls for a blended approach including oral examinations, group work, presentations and practical demonstrations, and suggests students could be tasked with identifying errors in AI-generated content, verifying information and improving it.

Danso says students should be actively involved in conversations about responsible AI use rather than simply being presented with rules and penalties, and that unequal access to AI and other digital technologies must be addressed so assessment practices do not deepen existing inequalities. He says teaching should remain fundamentally human-centred and the solution is not to ban AI from education, but students should be taught about its limitations and encouraged to use it responsibly, with educators modelling responsible use. He adds that teachers will require additional support and guidance from their institutions and governments to implement effective assessment strategies. He concludes that education must still teach students how to understand an answer, question it and recognise when it is wrong.

Articles.Title: Assessment in Schools in the age of AI and digital technologies - Modern Ghana

stories.Headline: Tennessee orthopedic practice cuts surgical coding costs 80% with AI
stories.Summary:
The Bone and Joint Institute of Tennessee, an orthopedic practice with six locations just outside Nashville, adopted artificial intelligence from a vendor called Ember AI to handle surgical coding and denial appeals, Healthcare IT News reported on November 3, 2026. The practice has approximately 350 employees and provides orthopedic physician care, rehabilitation and durable medical equipment, with surgeons working in both hospital and ambulatory surgery settings. CEO John Reynolds said the practice was managing an increasingly complex revenue cycle while continuing to grow, and that simply adding more staff was not a sustainable solution. The implementation was led by the director of operations, who is also the practice's internal AthenaOne expert, with close involvement from the revenue cycle manager.

According to the article, the practice reported an 80% reduction in cost per coded case, with Ember AI reporting accuracy comparable to an expert surgical coder. Reynolds said the cost per case fell to approximately one-fifth of the comparison cost while maintaining the reported level of accuracy. In one weekly sample provided by the vendor, 10 claims represented $5,575.82 in identified payment or recovery value, averaging approximately $558 per claim, which Reynolds described as identified value rather than confirmed collections. Ember AI also reported identifying a clear root cause and resolution path for 100% of the claims reviewed.

Reynolds said the goal on the coding side was accuracy comparable to an expert surgical coder at a substantially lower cost per case, which he called particularly compelling for an orthopedic practice. He explained that an orthopedic operative report can describe multiple procedures, and determining what is separately reportable, what is bundled and which modifiers apply requires specialized expertise. He also said payers' increasing use of AI and automated claim review was creating an imbalance, because claims could be reviewed and denied at scale while responding still required staff to investigate individual accounts. He said the root-cause information gives the team more actionable detail about what needs to happen next, so staff can focus on resolution steps and on patterns that may prevent similar issues.

The article says a test remains around payments and sustainable costs, and that the business case is unresolved on completed appeals, actual payments and total revenue cycle costs. Reynolds said the next priority is continuing to connect the operational improvements to completed resolutions, actual payments and the overall cost of managing the revenue cycle. He said the practice is looking not just at coding costs or the number of claims reviewed but at how efficiently claims move toward resolution and ultimately collect the reimbursement earned. The implementation ran alongside the practice's athenahealth EHR, with weekly AthenaOne coordination meetings between the EHR and AI vendors to exchange information, address challenges and refine workflows.

Articles.Title: Tennessee orthopedic practice cuts surgical coding costs 80% with AI

stories.Headline: OpenAI Lobbyist: AI Could Define 2028 White House Race
stories.Summary:
Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer and a veteran Democrat strategist, warned in a private memo that artificial intelligence could decide the 2028 White House race, Politico reported. The memo was sent to roughly half a dozen prospective presidential candidates, along with lawmakers and political operatives, according to a person familiar with the discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity. Lehane urged White House hopefuls to back AI development or risk putting the United States at a disadvantage against Beijing. He warned Democrats in particular against opposing data centers and other infrastructure critical to maintaining America's technological edge. Lehane wrote that if the United States falls behind China, this could well be the 2028 version of the 2002 vote to go to war in Iraq.

He argued that candidates must find a middle ground between allowing AI to advance unchecked and concentrating control of the technology among powerful interests. He said the candidate who can articulate a compelling third path will have an opportunity to define a new contract for this new era. Lehane compared the political stakes to former President Franklin D.
