Roosevelt's New Deal in 1932, arguing that the next president could redefine the relationship between people and a transformative new force in their lives. Lehane, a former press secretary to then Vice President Al Gore, predicted that by 2028 AI will become an even bigger political issue as its capabilities expand and Americans grow more familiar with the technology. His memo urged candidates to address protecting children, keeping humans in control of major decisions, overhauling taxes, and ensuring AI makes life more affordable.

He also warned against allowing the Chinese Communist Party to dictate the future of AI. Lehane wrote that policymakers must solve problems such as higher electricity costs rather than treating infrastructure itself as the problem. The warning comes as data centers face growing public opposition ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections, with Americans increasingly concerned about rising electricity costs and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. In the memo, Lehane said those disputes are part of broader voter anxiety over affordability, economic uncertainty, and a social contract that many believe has been fractured. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the memo and the midterm elections.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Lobbyist: AI Could Define 2028 White House Race

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania AI Ad Law Covers Voices and Radio Spots
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed Senate Bill 806, the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, on 22 October. It became Act 99 of 2026 and takes effect 60 days later, on 21 December. The bill’s sponsor, State Senator Nick Pisciottano, told KDKA in Pittsburgh that the point is to protect consumers. He also said the technology will only get better and better, and that Pennsylvania moved fast on this.

The law defines synthetic content to include an audio clip that has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence. An advertiser may not knowingly, recklessly or willfully run an ad that uses synthetic content to create a false consumer perception about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised without clear and conspicuous disclosure. When a label is needed, it must say the ad contains content that was modified or generated using artificial intelligence. It has to appear the first time the synthetic content is presented, in the same medium, and where technically possible it should be permanent or very hard to strip out. The bill’s definition of clear and conspicuous includes audio delivered at a volume and pace a listener can hear and follow.

There are three exceptions: content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary or criticism, and anything limited to text. Enforcement belongs to the Attorney General or a district attorney, who can seek an injunction, and a court can add a civil fine of up to $3,000 plus legal costs. The law firm Loeb & Loeb noted there is no private right of action, so a listener cannot sue under the act on their own. Libby O’Neill of Loeb & Loeb said an AI-altered real person giving a fake endorsement, which New York and California do not reach, may be covered. She also said an AI spokesperson delivering accurate information may not require disclosure in Pennsylvania.

New York’s law took effect in June and covers synthetic performers, digital humans that look like they are performing, but not audio ads. California’s SB 1050 names the off-camera narrator, but its definition only covers a synthetic performer who is not recognisable as a real person, so a clone of an actual voice falls outside it. Ballard Spahr’s Alan Kaplinsky and John Culhane told advertisers in a 2 November alert to implement appropriate disclosure controls before the December 21 effective date and to check the controls used by their agencies and vendors. The act starts on 21 December, in the middle of holiday ad season, and California’s law follows on 1 January 2027. Neither state has put out guidance on what a spoken tag should sound like, so the first versions will be written by advertisers’ lawyers, and the first test cases will come from state prosecutors rather than listeners.

Articles.Title: Pennsylvania AI Ad Law Covers Voices and Radio Spots - Voice Over Talent Industry News - Voice Over Herald

stories.Headline: Krafton launches Kiff AI chat app with Fifty Fifty character
stories.Summary:
Krafton launched an AI character chat service called Kiff on Monday, Nov. 2, according to the Korea JoongAng Daily. The service started with the girl group Fifty Fifty, known for its 2023 hit song "Cupid," as its first artist. Users can talk to Wenny, Fifty Fifty's official character, which the group's members helped create, from its personality to its look. The character remembers each user's preferences and earlier conversations and reflects them in later chats.

Kiff is available in Korean on Apple iOS and Android for users aged 14 or older. Users can chat for free up to a daily limit, and a monthly subscription of 3,900 won, or about $2.90, unlocks unlimited chatting. The service has two modes, a chat mode for texting with the character and a character mode where the on-screen character moves along with the conversation, such as waving when a user says hello. Kiff can also turn a day's conversations into a picture diary, and Wenny can share news about the artist and continue the conversation based on that news.

Park Jae-min, head of Krafton's AI Frontier Division, said the company had researched AI for a long time so that characters in games communicate naturally with users. He said that experience was used to create a new way for fans to enjoy an artist's world up close. Park also said that starting with Kiff, Krafton will expand its AI business to more artists and wider markets. Krafton plans to add more artists and features and expand the service to more countries.

Articles.Title: Krafton launches Kiff AI chat app with Fifty Fifty character

stories.Headline: Seoul Music Forum explores humanism in AI age, with one in four K-pop acts now virtual
stories.Summary:
The 2026 Seoul Music Forum took place on Sunday and Monday in western Seoul, hosted by the Record Label Industry Association of Korea, which has run the event since 2015. The theme was "Independent, Connected, Global: The Next Chapter for Music Labels." Josh Jordan, founder of the Manila-based consultancy Crosscurrent, gave a keynote speech titled "Building Worlds of Their Own: Fantasy, Identity and Connection in Asian Gen Z Culture." Music critic Lim Hee-yun presented research done with Crosscurrent showing that one in four newly debuting K-pop acts this year are virtual.

Jordan said AI media often focuses on optimization and perfection, while Gen Z in Asia searches for emotional connection in artificial worlds. He named three trends among Gen Z in Asia: seeking human connection in digital worlds, a shift toward multipolar cultural exchange in Southeast Asia as shown by acts such as Filipino boy band SB19, and interest-led online socializing that leads to offline gatherings. He cited virtual boy band Plave as an example of perfect, never-aging idols whose fans know real humans are underneath. Lim said that since all these acts debuted only this year, not all are popular, but the one-in-four figure has major significance, describing the appeal as an "inhuman-human combination."

Tinko Georgiev, founding growth architect of Shanghai-based CRxAI, said a major change from AI is that high-quality content will no longer be scarce. He said that even if intellectual property and copyright laws stay unchanged, so much content will exist that copyrighted content will never generate the revenues it has over the past 50 to 60 years. He suggested artists use technology and digital platforms to expand fan engagement and offer more localized interactions. Yang, co-founder of the Asian Music Industry Festival, said breaking into the United States remains difficult for Asian acts, though social media offers smaller artists an opening, citing Chinese rapper Lan Lao, who gained global popularity through a viral dance challenge. LIAK President Park June-seok said in opening remarks that the industry is changing rapidly due to technology, platform shifts and global market expansion, and that beyond responding to trends, the industry must consider how to protect the value of music and creators' rights and build a sustainable ecosystem.

Articles.Title: Seoul Music Forum explores humanism in AI age, with one in four K-pop acts now virtual

stories.Headline: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer
stories.Summary:
Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer published an opinion article in The Guardian on 2 November 2026 calling for wealth taxes on billionaires and for blocking new tech IPOs. They wrote that the billionaire class gained 40% more wealth in just two years, and that nearly 3,000 global billionaires now hold combined wealth equal to one-fifth of the world's yearly output. Nearly 1,000 billionaires live and do business in the United States, they said. They pointed to Elon Musk becoming an instant trillionaire when SpaceX went public earlier this year, and said he is funding Republican midterm campaigns with a small share of those gains.

The authors said Oracle's Larry Ellison, seventh on the Forbes billionaires list, backed the Paramount-Warner Brothers merger, and that Google's Sergey Brin spent $100m opposing California's Prop 40, a one-time wealth tax for healthcare and public services. They said Anthropic and OpenAI intend to go public soon, that both recently had major security flaws exposed, and that both openly acknowledge huge debts. They argued that when a company goes public, regular Americans end up carrying its risks through their retirement accounts without consent. They called for wealth taxes starting in California and New York, and for legal and legislative avenues to stop the IPOs.

The authors placed responsibility on the Trump administration and tech investors, saying they present IPOs as market success stories while regular people shoulder the risks. They said the 10 most valuable public companies are in tech, leaving the economy dependent on one industry with a history of bubbles, crashes and, in extreme cases like Theranos, fraud. They warned that if the AI bubble bursts it will take everyone down, while billionaires will walk away relatively unscathed. Their first step is passing wealth taxes, and they closed by urging readers to tax the billionaires and block the IPOs.

The article describes a divided country in crisis, with millions struggling to find and keep jobs, rising living costs and lost health insurance despite a sunny forecast from the Trump administration. It cites June's highly contentious SpaceX IPO as already carrying great risk for regular investors, and warns that more speculative tech companies going public would be too much for the market to bear. The authors say the survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires. They call for collective action and real change to stop new billionaires being minted and to keep the AI industry's risks from being transferred onto the public.

Articles.Title: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer

stories.Headline: US Midterm Elections: Bill Ackman Says AI Pause Talk May ‘Win a Few Votes’ But America ‘Can’t Slow Down’
stories.Summary:
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman said on Tuesday that calls to pause artificial intelligence development might help some candidates in the midterm elections, but he warned that the United States cannot afford to slow down. He made the comments in an interview with CNBC. Ackman is the CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management. His remarks come amid growing debate over the cost and scale of the data center buildout supporting AI.

Ackman said AI development is part of a strategic competition the United States cannot afford to lose, describing it as a global race for superintelligence that is existential to the country. He said opposition to data centers in some places would not stop the buildout, noting that many states would welcome the jobs and that the country has a lot of landmass. He compared efforts to slow AI infrastructure to restricting access to a basic utility. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan called for a pause on AI development last week, aligning him with Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Greg Casar of Texas, who co-sponsored the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. Companies including Amazon and Meta Platforms are investing heavily in infrastructure, raising questions about energy use, local opposition and whether the spending could become a political issue.

Ackman pointed to housing finance and energy prices as areas where the midterms could affect markets. He said resolving Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is one of the few significant economic policy things President Donald Trump can get done, and that it can be done by executive order even if the midterms go against the president. He said the administration may be waiting until after the midterm election to act. On energy, he said the war with Iran pushed up prices, creating a political headwind for Republicans, and called higher oil and energy prices a temporary phenomenon that is very helpful to the Democrats. He added that a divided Congress would make it harder for Trump to advance legislation, but played down the long-term consequences, saying it matters more who the next president is than the outcome for the next two years.

Articles.Title: US Midterm Elections: Bill Ackman Says AI Pause Talk May ‘Win a Few Votes’ But America ‘Can’t Slow Down’ - TradingView

stories.Headline: Mathews Phosa urges lawyers to be wary of using AI in court papers
stories.Summary:
Mathews Phosa, an ANC heavyweight and former Mpumalanga premier, spoke on Tuesday at the Future of Law Conference hosted by LexisNexis in Sandton, Johannesburg. He warned lawyers that using AI to draft court papers irresponsibly could put their careers at risk for lying to court when AI cites case law that does not exist. The conference was looking into the AI phenomenon in the legal and justice sector. Two judgments were delivered recently in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal in which lawyers cited fake case law. Judges reported legal practitioners to the Legal Practice Council for using AI without disclosing it in court and for misleading the court by citing cases that do not exist.

Phosa said the legal fraternity cannot avoid AI because it is already used in the profession. He said technology can now produce legal arguments in seconds, analyse complex contracts and process information on a scale previously unimaginable. He said responsible use of AI is important to lawyers so as not to put their careers at risk. Speaking to Business Day after his presentation, he said a lawyer who quotes case law that does not exist makes a statement knowing it is not true and must be reported to the LPC and charged for unethical conduct. He said there has been an invention of case law that does not exist and that this is dangerous.

Phosa said citing non-existent case law can be problematic, particularly when judgments have to be delivered urgently. He said that in existing South African cases where lawyers used non-existent case law, judges were able to pick up the discrepancies when writing judgments. He asked how one convinces a judge with a lie, saying they will check and the lawyer will be exposed for a lack of professional ethics. He said lawyers carry the responsibility that their whole profession may be on the line if they deviate from responsibility and integrity. He said lawyers must accept that AI is an imperfect tool and that everything it produces needs to be checked.

The government has been grappling with regulating the use of AI, and there is a judicial committee looking into a policy to regulate how judges can use AI. This year, judge Ingrid Opperman delivered a judgment about an acting judge who cited non-existent law or incorrect cases, suggesting AI use was a key factor. Legal bodies such as the LPC and the Black Lawyers Association have also warned about the reckless use of AI. Phosa said regulation needed to look into protecting confidential information, citing the Protection of Personal Information Act and the Cybercrimes Act as important safeguards. He said Africa must not remain a passive recipient of technologies and must generate AI sovereignty, noting that China is producing AI at a speed that cannot be calculated and America is doing the same with six companies.

Articles.Title: Mathews Phosa urges lawyers to be wary of using AI in court papers - Business Day

stories.Headline: Singapore’s STT GDC eyes $3.1 billion loan, adds to AI debt binge
stories.Summary:
Singapore-based data centre operator STT GDC is in talks with banks for a $3.1 billion syndicated loan, according to sources familiar with the matter. The banks working on the planned borrowing as global coordinators, mandated lead arrangers and book runners include Standard Chartered, UOB, OCBC Bank and DBS Bank. The sources asked not to be identified because they were discussing private details. A group led by KKR and Singtel completed its acquisition of STT GDC in September, after earlier agreeing to buy the data centre company for $6.6 billion.

The three-year borrowing pays an interest margin of 165 basis points over the Singapore Overnight Rate Average and comes with an extension option of up to two years. Proceeds will be used as financing for STT GDC's assets, the sources said. DBS, OCBC and UOB earlier took part in a $5 billion sustainability-linked loan for the purchase. STT GDC was established in 2014 and is one of Asia's largest data centre operators, with facilities across 12 countries, including India, South Korea, Japan and Malaysia, as well as Britain, Germany and Italy.

Representatives from STT GDC, Standard Chartered, DBS, KKR and UOB declined to comment, while Singtel and OCBC did not respond to a request for comment. The deal adds to a wave of debt financing driven by the artificial intelligence boom, which has raised worries among investors as the binge pushes up bond yields and increases scrutiny of what many see as lofty valuations of AI-linked companies. Globally, the AI borrowing binge has flooded markets with more than US$650 billion of debt since the start of 2025, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Moody's Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion of data centre-related investments over the next five years.

Articles.Title: Singapore’s STT GDC eyes $3.1 billion loan, adds to AI debt binge

stories.Headline: Report addresses AI use to prepare documents in UK civil proceedings
stories.Summary:
A working group of the UK's Civil Justice Council released the second of two reports on the use and regulation of artificial intelligence for preparing court documents in civil proceedings. The report was published on Nov 3, 2026, and was written by Bernise Carolino. It makes recommendations on litigants-in-person, witness statements and expert evidence. The group had published an interim report on Feb 17, 2026, and considered consultation responses before developing its recommendations.

The report says the Solicitors Regulation Authority, the Bar Standards Board, the Legal Services Board, other professional regulators and legal representatives should regulate AI use in this context. It says a practice direction from the Civil Procedure Rule Committee should guide that regulation, using a functional and risk-based approach. The direction should consolidate and clarify the court's current approach to the accuracy of, the verification of and the responsibility for legal representatives' AI use. It should also offer guidance on existing sanctions for AI misuse and on AI use in specific contexts such as witness statement preparation and disclosure. The report says the Civil Justice Council should urgently address AI use by litigants-in-person, while the rule committee should revise the practice direction as needed.

Sir Colin Birss, the working group's chair, said in a foreword that the group thanks all those who contributed. He said it was greatly assisted by the many responses to the interim report and consultation, and that all responses and the points they raised were considered carefully. For witness statements, the group recommended no new rules for a legal representative preparing and signing a statement. A witness of fact should make a specific declaration that they did not prepare the statement with an AI tool that generated or influenced the substantive content, and the report said this would not prevent the use of any particular AI tool.

For expert witness evidence, the group recommended amending the Civil Procedure Rules by adding a declaration about AI use and revising the AI use guidance for experts. The report says these recommendations aim to help the court and opposing parties scrutinize and test expert evidence. Otherwise, the report opposed introducing declarations regarding AI use. It also did not recommend requiring parties to apply for permission to use AI when preparing materials for submissions in civil proceedings.

Articles.Title: Report addresses AI use to prepare documents in UK civil proceedings - Canadian Lawyer

stories.Headline: Telangana plans AI-enabled transactions in agri. market yards
stories.Summary:
The Telangana government is planning to make the state's agricultural markets AI-enabled for the first time in the country, according to Minister for Agriculture Tummala Nageswara Rao. He made the announcement at a meeting with agricultural marketing and agriculture department officials in Hyderabad on Monday. The minister said the AI technology would check for irregularities in transactions in market yards. Tenders for introducing AI technology in the market yards' transactions would be called within a week.

The minister suggested bringing all transactions related to farmers into a single digital system, from the farmer entering the market with produce through sale, payments and exit. He listed the tasks to be handled on one platform, including listing of farmers' details, allocation of an identity number to every lot or crop, assessing crop quality, fixing price, digital bidding, online auction, farmer's consent, weighing, sale bills, market charges, payments to farmers, recording of gate exit, and issuance of e-receipts and e-permits. The management information system should also hold details of commission agents, traders, price patterns and auction details so they can be cross-checked in future. The Minister told officials to study digital marketing systems being implemented elsewhere in the country.

The new digital system would also cover attendance of marketing department officials, including biometric attendance registering. Market yards should have closed-circuit camera systems to monitor maintenance of godowns and daily activities. Digital screens should be arranged so farmers could know about prices elsewhere in the country. On the Koheda integrated fruit market, the Minister asked officials to ready at least the first phase by March next. He expressed dismay over the delay in taking up the tendering process, stating that it would delay completion of the market.

Articles.Title: Telangana plans AI-enabled transactions in agri. market yards

stories.Headline: Big Tech Spent $200 Billion on AI in Just Three Months
stories.Summary:
Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta reported another quarter of strong revenue growth and record spending on AI infrastructure, according to an article on LinkedIn dated November 2, 2026. In the September quarter, Amazon spent $77.3 billion on property and equipment, Alphabet spent $51.4 billion, Microsoft spent about $45.2 billion and Meta spent $33.9 billion. Together their combined quarterly capital expenditure exceeded $200 billion. Despite strong revenue growth, the four companies collectively lost nearly $900 billion in market value as investors questioned whether the AI investments would deliver returns fast enough.

Amazon reported third-quarter revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12% year-over-year, and operating income of $28.1 billion, up from $17.4 billion a year earlier. Its cloud business, AWS, grew revenue 39.3% to $46 billion, its fastest growth in nearly five years, and generated $17.8 billion in operating income. Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for its fiscal first quarter, up 19%, with Azure growing 48% to $33.2 billion. Alphabet reported revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25%, with Google Cloud revenue more than doubling to $30.7 billion, while Meta reported revenue of $64.6 billion, up 26%.

Sundar Pichai said Google's year-over-year Search query growth rate was the highest in five years, including growth in commercial queries, and the company said its Gemini app had crossed one billion users. Mark Zuckerberg's AI ambitions are expanding beyond recommendation systems and advertising, with the company launching its first frontier models, Muse and Muse Wonder, as it pushes towards personal superintelligence. Meta's operating income fell 37% to $13 billion, which the article attributes mainly to a $9.89 billion legal charge related to an agreement with 52 US state attorneys general. Meta expects full-year 2026 capital expenditure to reach $135 billion to $145 billion.

The article says the dominant question has been who can build the largest AI infrastructure footprint, and the more important question now is who can generate enough revenue from that infrastructure to justify the investment. It says AWS growth, Google's improving Cloud profitability and Microsoft's Azure momentum show that enterprise demand for AI infrastructure and cloud services is translating into real revenue growth. It adds that growing revenue is different from generating attractive returns on capital, and that more data centres, GPUs and custom chips do not automatically translate into sustainable profits. The article says the next few quarters will reveal whether AI becomes a durable growth engine across these businesses or an expensive infrastructure race in which revenue takes longer to catch up with investment.

Articles.Title: Big Tech Spent $200 Billion on AI in Just Three Months

stories.Headline: State bill allows consumers to hold AI chatbot providers liable
stories.Summary:
New Jersey lawmakers introduced Bill A5607 on Oct. 5, 2026, according to the ABA Journal. The bill targets artificial intelligence chatbots and aims to make them subject to the state’s product liability laws. It would create several content and data privacy requirements for AI chatbot providers. The legislation also characterizes chatbots as products, which means product liability claims would cover them.

Providers found to violate the state’s products liability laws would face $5,000 per violation. The New Jersey attorney general’s office could also take potential action against them. The bill was introduced in the state legislature and has not yet become law. The ABA Journal reported on the bill on Nov. 3, 2026, citing a story from Law.com.

Scott S. Christie, a partner at McCarter & English who focuses on intellectual property and data privacy, spoke to Law.com about the bill. He said the legislation would open the floodgates for lawsuits if it passes. He said that with $5,000 in statutory damages per violation and no need to prove harm, plus a strict liability standard, lawsuits could reach hundreds of thousands and perhaps millions of dollars. He also said that if a chatbot provider is violating the statute as to one user, it is probably violating as to all users.

The articles do not say what happens next with the bill, such as whether a committee vote or floor vote is scheduled. They also do not say whether Gov. Phil Murphy supports or opposes the measure. The ABA Journal notes only that the bill was proposed and has not passed. More to follow.

Articles.Title: State bill allows consumers to hold AI chatbot providers liable - ABA Journal

stories.Headline: AI Spending Has Gone From $140 Billion to $740 Billion in 3 Years, and Ackman Is Buying
stories.Summary:
Bill Ackman and Ryan Israel, chief executive and chief investment officer of Pershing Square, sent a letter dated November 2, 2026, arguing that Big Tech's capital spending boom is an offensive growth investment with attractive returns. The letter's figures cover combined capital spending at Microsoft, Meta Platforms, Amazon and Alphabet, which rose from about $140 billion in 2023 to about $740 billion in 2026 on company guidance, a calculated 5.3 times. The letter does not break out AI's share of that spending. Pershing owns Microsoft, Meta and Amazon, so the letter argues for Ackman's own holdings.

Capital spending was nearly 12% of the group's revenue in 2023 and an estimated 38% in 2026, per the letter, a shift that pressures free cash flow. Consensus cited by Pershing calls for another 35% increase in 2027, and about $1.5 trillion once other AI builders are included. Pershing estimates one gigawatt of AI data center capacity costs $40 billion to $50 billion and produces $15 billion to $20 billion of annual revenue, which at a 50% incremental margin implies a pre-tax return on invested capital of 15% to 25%. Pershing says revenue could run 15%-plus to 35% above consensus after three years, and if it falls short, the letter argues the companies will cut spending and free cash flow will beat consensus anyway.

By June 30, Pershing had added 552,652 Microsoft shares, a 9.8% increase to 6,206,730, and 535,201 Meta shares, up 20.1%. It cut Amazon by 25.2% to 8,563,857 shares and sold out of Alphabet. The letter does not say Pershing added during October's selloff, and Pershing Square Holdings' net asset value was down 6.9% for 2026 as of October 31. On November 2, Microsoft fell 2.83% to $507.12, Meta slipped 1.34% to $606.73 and Amazon rose 2.2% to $245.63.

The bull case rests on contracted demand, with Microsoft's commercial remaining performance obligations growing 73% to $677 billion and AWS backlog reaching $578 billion. The bear case is twofold: Pershing's return math is its own estimate, while Meta is funding its expansion with negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter and a reported bond sale of at least $20 billion. Ackman and Israel host a call at 9:30 a.m. ET on November 3, and the third-quarter 13F is expected in November. It will show whether Pershing kept adding to Meta before its October drop, and a cut there would weaken the letter's case.

Articles.Title: AI Spending Has Gone From $140 Billion to $740 Billion in 3 Years, and Ackman Is Buying - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: Over 2.5 billion daily Siri requests put Apple's AI overhaul in perspective
stories.Summary:
Apple reported its fiscal fourth-quarter results on November 2, 2026, and CEO John Ternus repeated that Siri handles more than 2.5 billion requests a day. The figure is not new: Lilian Rincon, Apple's vice president of product marketing for artificial intelligence, first revealed it at the September 9 iPhone event. At WWDC 2024, Apple had reported 1.5 billion daily voice requests. The company has not said whether the two numbers measure the same kinds of interactions, since the 2024 figure counted voice requests while the newer figure does not specify what is included.

Apple's Siri AI overhaul began reaching customers in September with iOS 27. The redesigned assistant uses Apple Intelligence to understand personal context, handle more complicated questions, and take actions across apps, and it can pull information from messages, emails, and photos. The features are not available to everyone: Siri AI remains in beta, eligible users must join a waitlist, and some features that depend on server-based AI models have daily usage limits, with broader access expected to require payment eventually. Apple added five languages on October 26, so Siri AI now supports French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish alongside English, though regional restrictions still apply.

The 2.5 billion daily requests also include traditional Siri interactions such as setting alarms, sending messages, and controlling smart-home devices. Apple has not revealed how many people use the newer AI features or what share of daily requests they account for. Rincon first gave the 2.5 billion figure, and Ternus repeated it during the earnings discussion. After the conference call, Apple shares fell $8.79, despite a large quarter and expectations of about $148 billion in the next.

Articles.Title: Over 2.5 billion daily Siri requests put Apple's AI overhaul in perspective

stories.Headline: AI Cloud Stocks Fall as Big Tech Capex Comes in Light: Fastly Sinks 6%, Oracle and Nebius Drop 3%
stories.Summary:
On October 28, Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases for its first quarter of fiscal 2027, below the Wall Street consensus of $50.7 billion and short of its own $50 billion target. Alphabet reported $51.36 billion in capital expenditures against a consensus of $55.09 billion. The next day, AI cloud stocks fell, with Fastly down 6% at $25.43, while Oracle at $140.57 and Nebius at $177.56 each dropped 3%. Alphabet stock fell 11% to $287.67, and Microsoft slipped 1% to $523.30.

Microsoft chief financial officer Amy Hood said some third-party capacity deliveries expected in the quarter were delayed. She said she expects capital spending of more than $50 billion next quarter and about $170 billion for the calendar year, and she maintained that customer demand continues to exceed available supply. On October 28, Oracle stock had rallied 11% to close at $144.54 after its investor day, where it forecast $30 billion in free cash flow by fiscal 2029. Oracle capped new financing through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, split evenly between equity and debt, and reaffirmed a $225 billion revenue target for fiscal 2030 along with $664 billion in remaining performance obligations.

Those Oracle targets followed negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026, and the funding cap helped ease debt concerns. Fastly is up 150% this year after six straight quarters of earnings beats, and on August 5 it lifted its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $732 million to $746 million. Nebius is up 112% this year, and three customers made up 24%, 21% and 14% of its revenue in the second quarter of 2026. CoreWeave stock was at $64, up 0.1% and essentially flat, and it is down 11% year to date.

The next test for Microsoft is whether its delayed third-party capacity arrives in the second half of its fiscal year, as Hood expects. A smooth transition could restart the revenue ramp for Nebius and CoreWeave, while another slip could stretch their revenue schedules further. Upcoming spending updates from other cloud giants could either confirm that worry or ease it. For Oracle, the open question is whether it stays within its new funding cap while it keeps building data centers, and Fastly's growth rests more on AI traffic and security demand than on hyperscaler budgets.

Articles.Title: Oracle Stock Falls After Launching $20 Billion AI Funding Plan

stories.Headline: Bill Gates Says AI Makes Nuclear Weapons 'Look Like Nothing'
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates said artificial intelligence has crossed danger thresholds in biological and cyber capabilities, and he called it the most dangerous thing humans have ever gone near. He made the comments on the Ezra Klein Show in an interview published on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. He said the technology makes nuclear weapons look like nothing, and that the world met the moment with complete silence. The Microsoft co-founder said AI could empower a bioterrorist to kill hundreds of millions of people. He also said it could carry out a cyberattack that scrambles all bank accounts and shuts down the electric grid.

Gates pointed to AI's code abilities as his evidence, saying recent models found flaws in code that humans had reviewed for over 20 years. He said a model can spot in minutes where to inject an attack, at a complexity that makes people agree once they see it. He said only nation states once had the resources for such things, and that power now sits with a small group using the latest AI tools. The article also described a Zcash case, in which security engineer Taylor Hornby used Anthropic's Opus 4.8, released the day before, in an audit of the Orchard circuit on May 29. He found a flaw live since Orchard launched in May 2022 and wrote an exploit that minted undetectable counterfeit ZEC in testing, according to Shielded Labs, and an emergency fix followed within days.

Gates said relying on the AI industry to regulate itself is just insane, and he called self-regulation insane while saying there is no supervisory layer today. He said he almost could not believe he was asked whether corporate incentives were enough to keep humanity safe. The interview was published the same day tech CEOs signed a voluntary safety accord at the White House. Anthropic's December 2025 study found AI agents identified $4.6 million of exploitable smart contract vulnerabilities. CertiK put first-half losses at $1.32 billion and said attackers revisiting dormant codebases were likely assisted by automated tooling.

The article said whether attackers have used AI in real-world exploits is not yet established, but it is highly suspected. Blockstream refused to pay a ransom over the Sept. 6 Liquid Network theft and said the world is a different place with the advancements of AI, hinting that AI could have been used in the exploit. Shielded Labs said the Zcash flaw had evaded years of scrutiny by many of the world's best cryptographers. The article did not say what happens next beyond those events.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates Says AI Makes Nuclear Weapons 'Look Like Nothing' - CoinMarketCap

stories.Headline: Three questions that will define AI's political power
stories.Summary:
The 2026 midterms will be the first test of how voters feel about the AI race, according to Axios. The article says the results will show whether campaigning on AI regulation, or aligning with tech figures like Elon Musk, helps or hurts candidates ahead of 2028. It also says candidates can no longer afford half-baked AI agendas. The piece lays out three questions about AI politics and names the races it is watching on Election Day.

Some groups want to make AI policy itself a campaign issue rather than backing candidates based on their AI positions. Guardrails Alliance, a pro-regulation group, launched ads targeting Republicans and Democrats over AI positions in Arizona, Montana, North Carolina and California, and backed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who called AI the most important issue and tied it to jobs and affordability. Democratic group Tomorrow Together ran ads against Republicans' AI records in Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. Competing groups Public First and Leading the Future spent more than $50 million through affiliated super PACs in nearly 50 races, but their ads largely avoided AI itself.

Musk was the biggest donor in the midterms by far, contributing more than $400 million, and his spending, involvement in DOGE and ties to the Trump administration made him both a powerful backer and a target for Democratic attacks. In Texas' 10th District, Republican Chris Gober, who represented Musk in connection with DOGE, faces Democrat Caitlin Rourk. In Kansas' 1st District, Democrat Lauren Reinhold has leaned on her DOGE experience and criticized Musk's influence in her challenge to Republican Rep. Tracey Mann. Other races watched include Ohio's Senate contest, where Republican Jon Husted benefited from Musk's America PAC spending against Democrat Sherrod Brown, and the Texas Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.

A few candidates aligned with stronger AI safeguards could shape whether the next Congress has a louder bloc pushing back on industry efforts to limit regulation. In Michigan, El-Sayed wants a cabinet-level federal agency to regulate AI and a ban on super intelligence, and he has attacked Republican Mike Rogers, who benefited from Musk-affiliated spending. In Colorado's 8th district, Democrat Manny Rutinel sponsored the nation's first comprehensive AI bill, and in California's 11th district, Democrat Scott Wiener's AI transparency legislation was at the center of a regulatory fight that divided the industry. In Minnesota's 2nd district, Democrat Matt Little would add a voice to the push to ban data center construction and non-disclosure agreements nationally. The article says competing AI factions will be quick to claim victories, explain away losses and draw lessons about what worked ahead of 2028.

Articles.Title: Three questions that will define AI's political power

stories.Headline: Oracle stock slides as it borrows another $10 billion for AI spending
stories.Summary:
Oracle kicked off a $10 billion bond sale on Monday, November 2, 2026, and at the same time filed to sell $10 billion of stock, raising the full $20 billion in a single day. That was every dollar of new debt and stock Oracle said at its investor day the week before that it would raise through fiscal 2030. Investors did not like the speed, and Oracle stock fell nearly 9% that Monday, its worst day since June, to its lowest close since July 29. The drop wiped out what was left of an 11% pop after the investor day, and over three sessions Oracle was down nearly 18%, its worst three-day stretch since 2002 by Yahoo Finance's calculations. Oracle has lost more than half its value over the past 12 months.

Oracle burned through about $24 billion in cash in its last fiscal year and owed about $125 billion as of August, nearly twice its shareholders' equity. Monday's bonds add $10 billion more, and it costs about five times as much to insure Oracle's debt against default as Microsoft's, using credit default swaps. Oracle's bonds due 2066 yield about 8.4%, compared with about 6.1% for Apple's and Microsoft's bonds due 2062, according to a BofA note cited by The Market Ear. CoreWeave, a debt-heavy AI cloud provider, pays more than 14%.

Fitch kept Oracle's BBB credit rating, two notches above junk, and said in a statement Monday that it does not expect Oracle to raise material incremental capital over the rating horizon following this capital raise. Moody's affirmed its rating too but kept its outlook at negative, a sign a downgrade is still possible. Futurum CEO Daniel Newman called Microsoft the AI adults in the room, the company that has really done this with the least collateral damage to their balance sheet. Fitch thinks Oracle is done asking, for now, while lenders are still charging like they are not so sure.

Oracle is not the only one tapping lenders, as Alphabet sold euro bonds Monday for the second time this year. BofA economists warned Monday that a lasting AI sell-off is one of the biggest risks to the economy, adding that all that AI borrowing is part of why interest rates are up. After Oracle's nine previous three-day plunges of 12% or more since 2016, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta fell over the following month only four times, by Yahoo Finance's calculations. At the tops of the dot-com bubble in 2000 and the pandemic boom in 2021, Oracle peaked after the Nasdaq, not before.

Articles.Title: Oracle stock slides as it borrows another $10 billion for AI spending

stories.Headline: Casap, whose AI tools automate dispute and anti-fraud operations for banks, raised a $56M Series B led by Base10 Partners, bringing its total funding to $90M (Jeff John Roberts/Fortune)
stories.Summary:
Casap, a financial AI startup, announced on Wednesday a $56 million Series B funding round led by Base10 Partners, bringing its total funding to $90 million since it launched in 2023. The company declined to disclose a valuation. Synchrony and Experian joined the round as strategic investors. Casap was founded by CEO Shanthi Shanmugam and Saisi Peter, a Chime veteran.

Casap's AI tools handle disputes and chargebacks for banks and card companies. The company says its customers have cut first party fraud losses by as much as 51% and raised their chargeback win rate to 96%, compared with a 60% industry average. Shanmugam says disputes are resolved in 8 days on average, versus up to 90 days with traditional methods. A human still reviews each case, often in 1 to 2 minutes. Casap does not disclose all the indicators it uses, but Shanmugam said they include the physical location of a card and spending patterns.

Shanmugam said the shift comes back to people thinking it is a victimless crime and telling what they see as white lies. She said the rules governing disputes are written in a way that almost assumes no one lies. She said banks often resolve disputes below a threshold, typically around $30, in the customer's favor, and sometimes the cutoff is much higher. Casap plans to use the new funding to move into customer complaints and collections. Its other investors include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Emergence and Primary.

Separately, the five biggest tech companies spent $556.9 billion on capital projects, mostly AI data centers, in the first nine months of 2026, while their combined operating cash flow reached $542.9 billion. Capital spending had never topped operating cash flow in data going back to 2011. Alphabet spent $9 billion more than it earned in the third quarter and covered the gap with $41 billion from share sales and new debt. The five companies cut buybacks 83% to $14 billion.

Articles.Title: Casap, whose AI tools automate dispute and anti-fraud operations for banks, raised a $56M Series B led by Base10 Partners, bringing its total funding to $90M (Jeff John Roberts/Fortune)

stories.Headline: States to Congress: Don’t Pull Back on Cybersecurity Funding as AI Raises the Stakes
stories.Summary:
State technology leaders from Florida, New York and Tennessee urged Congress to keep investing in state and local cybersecurity at a May hearing before the House Homeland Security Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection. They called for reauthorization of the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program. The officials warned that artificial intelligence is making cyberattacks faster and more sophisticated. Colin Ahern, New York's director of security and intelligence, said the states are on the front lines of multiple cyber conflicts.

Tennessee CIO Kristin Darby described a dangerous imbalance between highly sophisticated attackers and severely resource-constrained defenders. She said Tennessee has used federal grant funding to secure nearly 90,000 endpoints across local government networks. That has given many communities access to cybersecurity capabilities they otherwise could not afford. Florida CIO Warren Sponholtz said centralized cybersecurity services help governments achieve economies of scale and expand access to enterprise-grade protections. He also warned that artificial intelligence is speeding up vulnerability discovery and exploit development.

Ahern argued that continued federal investment is essential as states face increasingly sophisticated nation-state threats. Sponholtz called for close collaboration among federal, state and local governments. Lawmakers discussed potential changes to future grant programs, but the witnesses broadly agreed that sustained federal support remains critical. They also stressed continued investment in cyber workforce development, threat intelligence sharing and AI preparedness. The hearing reflected growing concern that as AI lowers the barriers to sophisticated cyberattacks, strong federal-state partnerships will become more important to protect government systems and the public services they support.

Articles.Title: States to Congress: Don’t Pull Back on Cybersecurity Funding as AI Raises the Stakes

stories.Headline: AI company accused of generating child porn claims it’s been ‘cooperating with law enforcement’ in Florida
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against A2E, an AI software that generates images, accusing it of producing sexually explicit pictures of children in violation of state law. The suit was filed in state Circuit Court in Sarasota County. The defendant named in the case is Rengstorff Consulting, a Nevada firm that owns A2E. Uthmeier announced the suit at a news conference in Orlando earlier this week. The 26-page suit alleges that A2E committed unconscionable, deceptive and unfair practices under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

The first allegation is that the product lets predators nudify non-consenting Floridians, including children, and allows users to alter images of adults to feature child-like appearances. The suit cites a Tampa man arrested earlier this year who Uthmeier alleges created more than 100 sexually explicit images of his 6-year-old stepdaughter and 10-year-old stepson. In 2025, Florida lawmakers approved a measure requiring social media companies to delete deepfakes, which are AI-generated sexual depictions of people created without their consent. A2E said it learned about the news and is consulting with its legal team. The company said it has always treated child sexual abuse material very seriously since the very beginning.

It also said it has been cooperating with law enforcement to detect and prevent all kinds of CSAM, contrary to the attorney general's claim. Uthmeier said that creating the vehicle does not give exemption from liability, and that the software is the manufacturing hub churning out the child porn content. He said the state wants to make them pay and shut them down. Uthmeier's suit claims the Tampa predator was arrested thanks to the efforts of law enforcement and that the defendant never reported the abusive and criminal images. The articles do not say what happens next in the case beyond the filing and the company's statement that it is consulting its legal team.

Articles.Title: AI company accused of generating child porn claims it’s been ‘cooperating with law enforcement’ in Florida - Orlando Weekly

stories.Headline: UBS says AI investment boom remains intact despite growing scrutiny of spending
stories.Summary:
UBS published a report on Monday, November 2, 2026, saying the AI investment boom remains intact despite growing investor concerns about infrastructure costs, financing risks and whether technology companies can turn spending into profits. The Swiss bank said strong third-quarter results had reinforced confidence in demand for AI infrastructure. It raised its estimates for global AI capital expenditure to $1 trillion in 2026 and $1.4 trillion in 2027, and added a forecast of $1.5 trillion for 2028. UBS pointed to accelerating cloud growth at Alphabet, Microsoft and Oracle, with cloud revenue growth of 103%, 48% and 62% respectively in their latest reported quarters.

The report said higher investment has unsettled markets, with Alphabet and Meta shares falling sharply after investors focused on rising capital expenditure and negative free cash flow. UBS warned that financing pressures among specialist cloud infrastructure providers, known as neoclouds, could lead to project delays, repricing and industry consolidation, though it expects limited disruption because these companies account for only about 8% of its capital expenditure estimate. It also cited risks from AI replacing existing revenue streams, pointing to slower search revenue growth at Alphabet as its AI Mode currently generates less revenue. For investors in the US and UK, UBS said the AI theme remained attractive but recommended greater selectivity, diversification across the AI value chain and exposure to financially strong companies with pricing power and reasonable valuations. It favours foundries, computing and power infrastructure, and also recommends diversifying into industrials, healthcare and financials.

TechCrunch reported on October 30, 2026, that Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft had outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year. Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion, and it expects to spend up to $205 billion this year. Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months and expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter and is guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. Microsoft recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected, which it blamed on delays in capacity from third-party providers.

According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. TechCrunch said the anxiety spilled across the market on Friday, with the Nasdaq falling 2.9% and chip stocks also dropping. It said the muddied waters could complicate Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO, after the AI company filed to go public earlier that week, and that the Financial Times reported Blackstone had warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO. UBS expects greater volatility as investors shift their focus from AI spending commitments towards monetisation and returns.

Articles.Title: UBS says AI investment boom remains intact despite growing scrutiny of spending

stories.Headline: AI giants are offering billions in bonds, competing with European governments for investor capital
stories.Summary:
Four of the biggest US technology companies, Amazon, Alphabet, which owns Google, Meta and Oracle, have sold about $250 billion in dollar bonds since the start of 2025, according to a tally of US regulatory filings by AI Industry Reviews. They have sold a further €37 billion, or $41 billion, in euro bonds. Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, recently joined with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars. More than $1 trillion, or €900 billion, is pouring into the artificial intelligence build-out.

Goldman Sachs expects total new AI hyperscaler bond sales to reach $420 billion next year, with about €60 billion issued in euros according to the Dutch bank ING. France, Germany and Italy have seen sovereign bond yields rise sharply in recent months, straining public finances. France's public debt stands at 119% of gross domestic product and its deficit is still above 5%, and yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5% over the past six months. France's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at BNP Paribas, called the phenomenon bond abundance and told DW the hyperscalers' presence in the euro bond market is already high enough to create competition within the corporate sector and between companies and governments for fixed income funds. Economists at the European Central Bank said in August that the euro bond market was adapting well but warned the AI giants could make it harder for other companies and sectors to access finance. They questioned whether the bloc's markets can smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment. Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, co-author of a study for the OECD published in January, told DW that in the United States AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, while the opposite appears to hold in several European countries.

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies, finding that interest costs as a share of sales among Stoxx 600 firms have risen by nearly half since 2022 and cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period. European firms could face pressure to cut investment in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments. Cities and regions, whose borrowing funds schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects. The article says AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, but that US Big Tech's appetite for capital could add further pressure next year because of the additional billions in new bonds planned.

Articles.Title: AI giants are offering billions in bonds, competing with European governments for investor capital

stories.Headline: Sources: the US DOJ has inquired about the impact of Nvidia's Hugging Face deal on AI competition, as antitrust enforcers continue to probe Nvidia's conduct (Reuters)
stories.Summary:
The two articles supplied give almost no detail about the inquiry itself, so this account is limited to what they show. According to a headline carried by Techmeme and credited to Reuters, sources say the US Department of Justice has asked about how Nvidia's deal with Hugging Face affects competition in artificial intelligence. The same headline says antitrust enforcers are still probing Nvidia's conduct more broadly. The Techmeme page is dated October 28, 2026, and the text of the Reuters report was not included.

Because the articles do not describe the deal or the questions put to anyone, there are no figures, dates or terms attached to the inquiry to report. The headline does not say what Nvidia agreed to with Hugging Face, how much was involved, or whether any approval or remedy is being sought. It also does not say which officials made the inquiry, when it began, or who was contacted. Nothing in the material indicates that the inquiry requires any change by either company at this stage.

On responsibility, the only attribution is to unnamed sources cited by Reuters, who say the Justice Department has been asking about the deal's competitive impact. Neither Nvidia nor Hugging Face is quoted in the supplied material, and the Justice Department's own position is not given. The Techmeme page is mostly a roundup of unrelated technology news, chiefly Apple's launch of a touchscreen MacBook Pro, so it adds nothing further on this story. The inquiry is described only as part of continuing scrutiny of Nvidia.

The second article offers some background on Hugging Face, though nothing about the inquiry. Cheddar published a video interview on October 26, 2026, in which Irene Solaiman, the company's Chief Policy Officer and SVP of Strategy, discusses open-source AI, model sharing, safety and the fight for transparency. Its headline describes Hugging Face as changing who gets to build artificial intelligence. Neither article says what happens next, so how the Justice Department's questions might develop, or whether they could lead to formal action, is not addressed in the material provided.

stories.Headline: Oracle Announces Fusion Agentic Applications for Supply Chain Featuring Fusion Claw
stories.Summary:
Oracle announced new agentic applications for supply chain work that feature Fusion Claw, in a release dated October 26, 2026 in the United States and published in Japan on November 2, 2026. The announcement came at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas. Oracle described Fusion Claw as a governed agentic execution platform that lets Fusion Agentic Applications reason, calculate, adapt and act on specialized work such as detailed research, calculations, simulations, modeling and continuous replanning. The new Claw-powered applications are built into Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications.

The applications are available in Oracle Fusion Cloud Supply Chain & Manufacturing and include three named ones. Supply planning allocation weighs production lines, work centers, finished goods, components and business tradeoffs to decide how limited materials and capacity go to competing demand. Shipment load planning evaluates consolidation opportunities across timing, transport capacity, service commitments, cost and other constraints to cut transport costs and meet service levels. Procurement spend analyzes spend, supplier contracts and purchasing data to detect off-contract spending and deviations, explain root causes, quantify savings and recommend corrective actions for review and approval.

S.Y. Shenoy, Oracle's senior vice president of application development, said supply chain leaders need a connected view across products, plans, procurement, logistics and costs to decide faster and with better information. Shenoy said the Claw-powered applications let supply chain teams move to acting under governance across key processes and rethink how work is done. The applications reason across Oracle Fusion Applications data, weigh options and tradeoffs, coordinate the work needed to meet business goals and put approved actions into effect, Shenoy said. That helps leaders drive stronger business outcomes faster and with consistency and confidence, according to Shenoy.

The applications run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and use industry-leading LLMs, and they extend the Fusion Applications suite from assistance toward governed execution of work. They are part of a wider Fusion AI ecosystem centered on Oracle AI Agent Studio for Fusion Applications, whose no-code and pro-code features let organizations build and manage agentic applications using reusable Oracle, partner and external agents. Built-in observability, ROI measurement and security management are designed to help organizations monitor agent activity, apply safeguards and run agents responsibly at scale. Oracle's release did not say when the applications would become generally available or how they would be priced.

Articles.Title: Oracle Announces Fusion Agentic Applications for Supply Chain Featuring Fusion Claw

stories.Headline: Bills could control how ‘surveillance pricing’ impacts what you pay for products
stories.Summary:
Michigan lawmakers have introduced bills to restrict surveillance pricing, the practice of companies using consumers' personal data to set individual prices. The legislation is led by Reps. Steve Frisbie, R-Battle Creek, and Rylee Linting, R-Grosse Ile, and was introduced earlier this year. The bills passed the House and are now pending in the Senate Economic and Community Development Committee. The practice draws on data such as online browsing history, location and shopping patterns to set prices for individual customers.

The Federal Trade Commission has also looked into the practice. In a January 2025 report, the agency said third-party pricing services can use consumers' location, demographics, browsing habits and shopping history to tailor prices and promotions. The FTC said the findings raised questions about how companies use personal data to determine what consumers pay and called for further investigation. In August, the agency sought public comment on a proposed enforcement policy statement saying undisclosed uses of personal data to set prices could violate federal law against unfair or deceptive practices.

Kyle Zawacki, legislative director of the ACLU of Michigan, said surveillance pricing is when tracking cookies and information collected by websites and social media are used to charge people more because they need something. He said the worry is that consumers may not know how their information is used or whether it affects the prices they pay. He said it is a problem if people are charged more because of who they are, the color of their skin or their zip code. The ACLU has been advocating for a legislative solution and argues the issue is not how companies gather information but how they use it to manipulate consumers' economic choices.

The Michigan Retailers Association has warned Congress not to lump together all variable pricing. The association contends that proposed limitations should clearly differentiate surveillance pricing from other methods, including discounts, seasonal sales and price changes based on supply, demand or inventory. It has urged policymakers to consider how proposed restrictions could affect retailers. The state Attorney General's Office administers Michigan's Consumer Protection Act, which bans unfair or deceptive business practices and lets the attorney general investigate and file lawsuits.

Articles.Title: Bills could control how ‘surveillance pricing’ impacts what you pay for products - The Manchester Mirror

stories.Headline: Fujitsu and partners launch AI pilot to standardize packaging damage assessment and cut returns
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu, the Home Appliance Supply Chain Council, the Distribution Economics Institute of Japan and SoftBank Robotics announced on November 2, 2026 that they have started a joint pilot project. The project aims to clarify and standardize criteria for judging packaging damage across the home appliance industry and to use AI to assess such damage. The goal is to cut unnecessary product returns during delivery. The work is run by the Council for Sustainable Home Appliance Logistics, made up of the Council and the Institute, and has been adopted under a Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism subsidy for promoting behavioral change in shippers and logistics operators using digital technology.

The pilot runs from November 2, 2026 to January 15, 2027. The Council and the Institute will plan the project, develop industry-wide packaging damage criteria based on existing criteria from manufacturers, mass retailers and logistics providers, and supply packaging image data and operational expertise. Fujitsu and SoftBank Robotics will provide AI technologies and data analysis. Fujitsu will contribute its Kozuchi platform and Amalgamation AI for Vision, which recognizes images with little data and can give reasons for its assessments, while SoftBank Robotics will provide a solution that analyzes smartphone photos of cardboard packaging and records the results for later review.

The partners will evaluate the accuracy of the AI damage assessment model and ways to standardize the assessment criteria. They will also check how feasible the system is in real logistics settings and analyze how well it reduces returns and redeliveries. They will assess whether it could be applied to optimize the whole supply chain. The project intends to publish the packaging damage criteria and explore use beyond the home appliance industry.

The background is that the logistics industry faces labor shortages and rising delivery costs. In home appliances, products are often returned or redelivered over minor abrasions or dents in cardboard even when the appliance itself is undamaged. Criteria vary by company and often depend on the subjective experience of onsite staff, so the same damage may be judged differently by location or staff. This can cause inefficiency, higher transport costs, more CO2 emissions and excess resource use.

Articles.Title: Fujitsu, Home Appliance Supply Chain Council, Distribution Economics Institute of Japan, and SoftBank Robotics launch pilot project to standardize packaging damage assessment and reduce product returns using AI

stories.Headline: Larridin Raises $30 Million in Series A to Prove AI’s Impact Across the Human and Agent Workforce
stories.Summary:
Larridin, Inc., an AI value measurement platform based in South San Francisco, announced on November 2, 2026 that it raised $30 million in Series A funding. Pelion Ventures led the round, with existing investors Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures taking part. New investors included GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Alumni Ventures and Cougar Capital. The financing brought Larridin's total funding to $47 million.

The company said it has measured more than 2 billion AI sessions and tracked more than 82,000 workflows end to end. Across its customers, Larridin reports a 47% average increase in measurable team output and a median $2.4 million in AI spend optimized within the first year. Larridin said it will use the funding to speed up product development and expand its teams. It also announced a quarterly Engineering AI Impact Report, drawing on data from more than 1,000 engineers.

Russ Fradin, the CEO of Larridin, said enterprise AI has moved from an innovation budget to financial accountability. He said the investors share the company's conviction that firms must prove tangible business value from rising AI spend. Jeff Kearl, a General Partner at Pelion Ventures, said Larridin gives leaders transparency into AI and ties each dollar spent to measurable outcomes. Alex Rampell, a General Partner at a16z, said the company's growth and customer partnerships show it has built an indispensable platform.

Larridin's customer data shows why traditional adoption metrics fall short, according to the company. At one customer, 92% of engineers were active AI users, yet a single engineer accounted for roughly 65% of the team's AI spend in one week. At another, Larridin found a 66x difference in cost per shipped engineering change between two comparable AI tools. The report also found that AI-assisted pull requests rose from 35% in April to 62% in September, while median wait times for initial human code reviews grew by 50% over the same period.

Articles.Title: Larridin Raises $30 Million in Series A to Prove AI’s Impact Across the Human and Agent Workforce

stories.Headline: AI Use Has Reached 90% in Internal Audit. Is Assurance Keeping Up?
stories.Summary:
A 2026 survey by Sikich, the 10th edition of its U.S. Internal Audit Priorities Survey, found that 90% of internal audit functions now use artificial intelligence, and 77% include AI assessments in their audit plans. The findings were published in an article by Jamey Loupe, a principal and Risk Advisory practice leader at Sikich. The survey also showed that 35% of internal audit leaders now name AI and automation as an emerging risk, up from just 3% in 2022. Cybersecurity has been the most frequently selected emerging risk for the past five years, reaching 43% in 2026.

The survey found that 64% of respondents reported higher internal audit budgets, 43% expect to increase headcount, and 82% use external partners to add specialized expertise. Only 53% of respondents auditing AI review operational effectiveness, 40% address ethical use and bias, and 36% include model validation. The article says internal audit should ask whether AI systems perform as intended, whether outputs are accurate and appropriate, whether human oversight is meaningful, and how risks are handled when data, models or use cases change. It gives accounts payable as an example, where auditors should test exception handling, how often humans override the AI's coding, and whether accuracy is reviewed after vendor model updates.

Loupe writes that AI adoption is no longer the central issue and that internal audit must now determine whether its assurance practices are keeping up with rising risks. He says the goal is not deep technical expertise but enough understanding of AI risks, controls and governance to assess whether assurance remains effective. He lists five questions leaders should ask, covering where AI is used, whether the right risks are prioritized, whether assurance goes beyond governance and security, whether the right skills exist, and whether AI risk is reassessed as use changes. A separate Deloitte article by Vipul Patel and Peter Low says internal audit's core assurance role has not changed, but the subject matter has become more sophisticated, and that AI assurance usually builds on traditional frameworks with an added layer of AI controls.

The Deloitte article says 2026 marks the enforcement phase of major AI regulatory frameworks, and the EU AI Act calls for governance transparency and explainability. It says AI systems are adaptive and produce probabilistic outputs that can shift over time, so internal audit should assess how controls perform as models change rather than testing a point-in-time control. It recommends starting by verifying an enterprise-wide AI use-case inventory, then reviewing model risk management, monitoring, controls and ethical considerations such as bias. The Sikich article says internal audit functions are investing in their ability to keep pace, and that chief audit executives will need the right expertise and flexibility to adjust their approach as uses and risks grow.

Articles.Title: AI Use Has Reached 90% in Internal Audit. Is Assurance Keeping Up? - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: AI in Practice: Fiserv Former CLO Wants Legal to Be the Company's AI 'Super Users'

Fiserv’s legal department is using artificial intelligence to speed up document-heavy legal work, spot suspicious activity and eventually help track where deals get bogged down, according to an article published on November 3, 2026. Adam Rosman, who until recently was chief legal officer of the financial technology company, set a bigger goal for the department. He wanted legal to be one of the company’s heaviest users of AI. The article was written by Trudy Knockless for Law.com.

The article does not give details of the tools Fiserv uses, the number of people involved or the cost. It names no dates for when the work began beyond the November 3, 2026 publication date. It gives no figures on time saved or deals tracked. The only named person is Rosman, and the only named company is Fiserv.

Rosman is the person responsible for the push described in the article, and he set the goal of making legal one of the company’s heaviest AI users. The article does not include direct statements from him beyond that goal. It describes his aim as a bigger one than the department’s current uses. The article does not say what he said about the tools themselves.

The article is part of a series of candid conversations about how AI is changing the way in-house lawyers work, lead and deliver value. It appears in Law.com’s legal technology coverage.
