stories.Headline: A look at AI safety debates and the rising popularity of "Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness", or SURA; safety-focused AI labs shouldn't abandon the AI race (Scott Alexander/LessWrong)
stories.Summary:
Scott Alexander published an article on LessWrong on October 31, 2026, arguing against a set of ideas he groups under the name SURA, which stands for Stop Unilaterally and Raise Awareness. He describes SURA as the view that alignment-focused AI companies, their employees, and alignment-friendly countries should all halt or restrict AI work on their own, even if rivals keep racing. He says this idea has become popular among newer members of the AI safety community, who often do not know that a backup plan was ever considered. He also says older members now treat that backup plan with scorn, as if it had been debunked.

The article lays out two broad plans for handling the AI transition. Plan A is a global pause on AI development, ideally lasting decades, during which people research alignment or work to make the pause permanent. Plan C applies when no global pause happens, and it calls for alignment-focused labs to coordinate a mutual pause for as long as their joint lead lasts, then use that time to research alignment and release carefully aligned superintelligence at the last moment. Alexander cites forecasts from the AI Futures Project, where team members put survival chances under Plan C scenarios mostly in the 25 to 50 percent range, with FutureSearch at 44 percent.

He says the average gain from moving from a poorly thought out default race to a consciously managed Plan C effort is about 20 percentage points. Alexander argues that each plank of SURA would hurt the chances of Plan C working. If leading alignment-focused companies quit the race, less careful companies end up ahead, and if their employees quit, those companies become less prepared to do alignment research. He adds that a unilateral US stop would either hand superintelligence to China first or force the US to restart with no lead.

He traces SURA's popularity to assumptions he questions, including the belief that alignment is doomed and that racing is simply evil. He also says the current consensus comes from people fitting themselves into a mass-politics shape that forbids subtlety and demands clear villains. The article says that from the start of the AI safety community until about 2023, the common view was that a global pause was unlikely and people should prepare for Plan C. From 2023 onward, as the public woke up to ChatGPT, the community decided a pause was more likely than expected and put more resources into it. Alexander says the pendulum has now swung too far, and he plans to challenge SURA's assumptions and argue that SURA hurts even the chances of getting Plan A. He also cites Buck Shlegeris saying AI takeover risk does not feel like by far the largest concern, and Paul Christiano's older estimate of around 20 percent.

Articles.Title: A look at AI safety debates and the rising popularity of "Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness", or SURA; safety-focused AI labs shouldn't abandon the AI race (Scott Alexander/LessWrong)

stories.Headline: Shield Recognized for AI Communications Governance in 2026 Gartner Critical Capabilities Report
stories.Summary:
Shield announced on November 2, 2026 that it was named a Visionary in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Digital Communications Governance and Archiving Solutions. The evaluation covered 16 vendors and recognized Shield for its Completeness of Vision and Ability to Execute. In the complementary 2026 Critical Capabilities for DCGA, Shield scored among the three highest vendors across six use cases. Those use cases were Risk Management, Regulatory Compliance, Investigations, Organizational Insights, Archive and Retention, and AI Communications Governance. This marked Shield's third consecutive year of recognition in the Gartner Magic Quadrant and Critical Capabilities for DCGA since the category was established.

Gartner projected that by 2030, 70% of enterprises using DCGA solutions will adopt AI-driven features and processes, up from 40% in 2025. It also projected that by 2029, 85% of DCGA customers will consolidate supervision of text- and audio/video-based content to a single DCGA solution, up from less than 20% in 2025. Shield said its AI-native Communication Risk Operating System addresses both shifts by combining communications capture, archiving, surveillance, investigations and governed agentic AI in a single platform. The platform supports over 150 communication sources and detects risk across more than 100 languages, including rare and unmonitored languages. Shield said its AmplifAI suite expands surveillance coverage with 91.7% precision and reduces alerts requiring manual review by 77.3%.

Shiran Weitzman, co-founder and CEO of Shield, said the company's vision has always been to give compliance teams a platform they can trust so they are ready for whatever comes next. He said Shield was built as an AI-native operating system that brings together trusted communication data, intelligent risk detection and human control. He said the latest Gartner recognition reflects the company's ability to turn that vision into results for customers. He said that as Shield advances agentic AI and expands its global presence, its goal is to help regulated organizations with the most complex client needs reach continuous compliance readiness.

Shield said its AmplifAI suite explains risk within each alert, accelerates investigations up to seven times, and supports governed alert resolution with human oversight. Shield Insights adds enriched intelligence to that data, while Shield's AI-enabled Archive provides secure hot and cold storage that reduces data storage costs by up to 50%. The Archive also simplifies migration from legacy systems, with no archive export or exit fee. Recent releases bring Microsoft 365 Copilot and Claude interactions into Shield for search, surveillance and review, while Shield's MCP Server lets customers use live Shield alert information within supported AI tools under existing governance and access controls.

stories.Headline: IRIS Expands Accountancy Portfolio with Launch of AI-Powered Document Management Solution
stories.Summary:
IRIS Software Group launched IRIS Document Management on November 2, 2026, according to CPA Practice Advisor. The cloud-based, AI-powered system is built for accountancy practices and professional service firms in the UK and the US. It gives firms one secure place to store, file, find and share client documents. It is available as a standalone solution or as part of an integrated bundle with IRIS Firm Management, known as IFM.

The system uses AI to search documents in plain language, to read scanned files using optical character recognition, and to tag documents automatically from the firm's own tag library. Auto Filing rules route documents by template, folder path and year, and a branded client portal replaces email for sharing files with clients. It also offers bulk actions, check-out, version control and in-browser editing of Microsoft Office files. Client data stays within each firm's own tenant and in the region where it is held, and is never used to train AI models. Legal holds and full audit trails come as standard, and security includes Okta single sign-on, two-factor authentication, role-based access controls and conditional access.

Jonathan Priestley, General Manager for Global Accountancy Solutions and Transformation at IRIS, said efficiency now drives profitability in accountancy. He said work that once took ten billable hours can take thirty minutes, so firms cannot grow by billing more time, though time still matters for planning resources and is ultimately profit. He said the system uses AI to read, sort and file client documents as they arrive and keeps them alongside the client record, giving firms time back for client service and growth. He added that the next step is AI that helps firms act on what is inside documents and helps clients see what is needed from them and when.

The launch comes as accountancy firms face pressure to do more with the resources they have, the article says. Software has made routine work far quicker, changing how firms bill and protect their margins, yet staff still spend much of their time chasing, reading, sorting and filing documents by hand. Many firms use separate tools for document storage, client portals and practice management, which creates manual admin work and gaps in compliance and security. Existing IFM users can add the system as a module on the same platform, with no new vendor relationships or third-party connectors, and it connects with third-party platforms including Microsoft Business Central and Apxium.

stories.Headline: How to Get Breached, Step 5: Paste Client Data Into Any AI
stories.Summary:
A November 2, 2026 article by Scott Carr in CPA Practice Advisor describes how accounting firm staff may paste client tax returns, bank statements and Social Security numbers into free AI chatbots, a practice the article calls shadow AI. The piece is Step 5 in a series that offers bad advice so readers do the opposite. It gives a hypothetical example of a junior preparer who uploads a client's full return PDF into a free chatbot from her personal account and repeats it the next day with another client, while no one reviews the tool's data terms. The firm keeps no record of what was uploaded and cannot confirm whether it was retained.

The article says firms should classify data so tax returns, Social Security numbers, bank records and client financials are off limits for unapproved tools, and should add an acceptable use policy to their written security program. It recommends choosing approved tools with admin controls, multifactor authentication, activity logging and written terms on data retention and training use, and reviewing the vendor like any service provider. It advises taking inventory before the next filing deadline, requiring admin approval before AI apps connect to email, document storage or practice management software, and using DNS filtering to block or flag unapproved AI services. It also calls for log monitoring, staff training before busy season, offboarding that removes access to every tool tied to client data, and written records.

The article says many accounting and tax firms fall under the FTC Safeguards Rule, which expects a written information security program, a risk assessment and oversight of service providers that touch customer information, and that an AI vendor handling client data can be one of those providers. It notes the IRS offers guidance in Publication 4557, Safeguarding Taxpayer Data, and that Section 7216 limits how preparers may use and disclose tax return information, advising firms to confirm with their advisors how these apply. Carr, owner of Farmhouse Networking in Grants Pass, Oregon, writes that clients do not need a firm that avoids AI but one that can explain how it uses AI and why their data stays protected. The article says a short policy, a short list of approved tools and basic monitoring let firms answer client questions with confidence.

Articles.Title: How to Get Breached, Step 5: Paste Client Data Into Any AI - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Wikimedia Urges Court to Separate AI Training From Content Retrieval
stories.Summary:
The Wikimedia Foundation asked a court in an OpenAI copyright case to treat AI model training differently from systems that retrieve and present specific copyrighted works. The foundation filed an amicus brief on Oct. 30 in In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation. An amicus brief comes from an organization outside the case that wants to explain how a ruling could affect people or groups beyond the parties. The filing takes neither side in the litigation.

The foundation's argument turns on how an AI system uses copyrighted material. During pretraining, a model learns patterns from a large body of text, and Wikimedia argued that this process typically qualifies as fair use. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, works differently, because a system retrieves particular material and includes it in a response. Wikimedia argued that this kind of use should be subject to licensing requirements. The distinction would separate learning from a broad collection of works from presenting selected content in answers.

The foundation warned of risks on both sides of the question. A ruling that restricts AI training too broadly could curb tools that help volunteers improve Wikipedia, it said. A decision that permits too much use without licensing could lead publishers to limit access to their work. Wikipedia contains more than 67 million articles in over 300 languages. The filing follows the foundation's 2023 response to the U.S. Copyright Office, which called for case-specific reviews of AI fair use.

Articles.Title: Wikimedia Urges Court to Separate AI Training From Content Retrieval - TOKENPOST

stories.Headline: Latham & Watkins Adds Jason Raeburn As London Partner To Expand AI, Copyright, And Data Disputes Practice
stories.Summary:
Latham & Watkins has added Jason Raeburn as a partner in its London Litigation & Trial Department, the firm announced on November 2, 2026. Raeburn joins from Paul Hastings and will work on artificial intelligence, copyright, privacy, intellectual property, and technology disputes. His practice covers high-value litigation and international arbitration, along with counseling on AI regulation, copyright and data litigation, trade secrets, cyber incidents, and cross-border enforcement. He also advises companies that develop and deploy generative AI technologies.

The firm said the appointment expands its capabilities as AI regulation, copyright litigation over AI development, and data enforcement create complex legal challenges in the UK and Europe. Latham pointed to the European Union AI Act, growing copyright disputes involving artificial intelligence, and intensifying regulatory enforcement as areas driving new demand from technology companies. The firm expects the hire to support collaboration across its litigation, corporate, antitrust, regulatory, copyright, privacy, communications, and artificial intelligence practices. Raeburn is qualified to practice in England and Wales and also serves as a Deputy Master of the Business and Property Division of the High Court of England and Wales, a role the firm said makes him the youngest person appointed to it.

Ed Barnett, managing partner of Latham's London office, said technology is central to the firm's global strategy and that the UK and European markets are critical for leading technology companies, fast growth businesses, and entrepreneurs. Sy Damle, global chair of Latham's Copyright, Privacy & Communications Practice and global vice chair of its Artificial Intelligence Practice, said the EU AI Act, a rising wave of copyright disputes over AI development, and intensifying regulatory enforcement are reshaping the legal landscape in the UK and Europe. Raeburn said some of the most consequential legal battles of the next decade will be fought where technology, AI, and regulation meet. Raeburn received his LLB from the University of Bristol, completed the Legal Practice Course at the College of Law in London, and earned a Postgraduate Diploma in Intellectual Property from the University of Oxford.

Articles.Title: Latham & Watkins Adds Jason Raeburn As London Partner To Expand AI, Copyright, And Data Disputes Practice - Pulse 2.0

stories.Headline: Where gubernatorial candidates stand on placing statewide moratoriums on AI data centers
stories.Summary:
On Oct. 27, Tennessee gubernatorial candidates met at a forum hosted by the Tennessee Press Association at Middle Tennessee State University. Democratic nominee and Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green attended, along with independents David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston. Republican candidate and current Sen. Marsha Blackburn did not accept the invitation. The forum came as Rutherford County faced the data center issue, with its commission unanimously recommending a 12-month moratorium on Oct. 12 for a new development, and its Public Works and Planning Committee set to discuss a one-year moratorium resolution on Nov. 3.

All three candidates at the forum agreed on limiting data center growth but proposed different approaches. Hatley said data centers should pay for property taxes, power and water, and face limits on placement and noise, with counties then able to vote on moratoriums. Green said she has opposed data centers for years and is fighting for a moratorium on the Memphis City Council, and wants to take the effort statewide before what she called human harm. Pinkston also called for a statewide moratorium, saying the technology is outpacing the ability to legislate it, and that middle-class and working-class people should not foot the bill for utility and water system expansion. Blackburn has said communities should decide whether they want data centers, and she supports a rate payer protection plan under which rates would not rise with a data center and the data center would pay the cost.

In New Hampshire, both Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington are calling for a temporary moratorium on new data centers but differ on how to do it. Ayotte plans to include a moratorium in her 2027 state budget proposal, to be introduced in February, which would need Legislature approval and take effect July 1 at the earliest. Warmington calls for an immediate executive order, saying Ayotte provided no leadership on a failed moratorium effort this spring. Ayotte said at an Oct. 22 forum that a governor is not legally allowed to issue a moratorium by executive order, citing conversations with the state's attorney general. A University of New Hampshire poll from June found more than two-thirds of residents would oppose a data center in their town and 45% would support halting construction statewide.

Other moratoriums were placed this year. In August, Metro Nashville imposed a moratorium on data center advancement next to the Nashville Zoo, pausing permit approvals until after Dec. 1, after the zoo said the center would cause detrimental harm to its animals, conservation efforts and community. Memphis' one-year moratorium failed to pass on Oct. 20, and city council members instead reached for a substitute ordinance halting data center construction for 135 days. In New Hampshire, the 1st Congressional District candidates disagree, with Democrat Stefany Shaheen calling for a statewide moratorium and Republican Anthony DiLorenzo favoring local control. Tennessee's Election Day is Nov. 3, and after the state elects its new governor, Tennesseans will have a clear path on how state oversight will tackle data center advancements.

Articles.Title: Where gubernatorial candidates stand on placing statewide moratoriums on AI data centers - MTSU Sidelines

stories.Headline: Microsoft Is Borrowing $25 Billion for AI, Its First Bond Sale Since 2017
stories.Summary:
Microsoft issued at least $25 billion in corporate bonds, its first such sale since 2017, after reporting quarterly results. The bond sale was reported alongside Amazon's third-quarter results, which were released after the close on October 29, 2026. Amazon's cloud unit AWS grew 39.3% year over year to $45.98 billion in revenue, but its free cash flow over the past 12 months swung from positive $14.8 billion to negative $42.4 billion. Alphabet shares fell 12.64% in a single day, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market value.

The Microsoft bonds have maturities ranging from 2 to 40 years, including an ultra-long note due in 2066 priced at a spread of 1.05 percentage points over U.S. Treasuries. The deal drew more than $115 billion in orders, more than four times the offering size. Microsoft carries a AAA credit rating, and its 5-year credit default swap spread is 0.54 percentage points, versus 1.16 for Meta and 2.75 for Oracle. Amazon maintained its plan for about $220 billion in cash capital expenditure for 2026, most of it directed at AI infrastructure, and its purchases of fixed assets related to data centers and AI equipment rose by $94.8 billion over the past year.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said AWS will maintain growth of more than 40% next year and through 2028. Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors, said the free cash flow figure was the worst part of the results, noting that operations generated plenty of cash but capital expenditures consumed it entirely. Microsoft's first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue was $92.279 billion, up 19% year over year, with net income of $36.63 billion, up 32%, and earnings per share of $4.89 topping the $4.73 estimate. Azure revenue was $33.17 billion, with growth accelerating from 42% in the prior quarter to 48%.

The articles describe rising capital spending and cash-flow pressure across the major cloud providers even as AI revenue grows. A McKinsey survey found that only 37% of respondents believe AI has made a positive contribution to corporate EBIT. Investment-grade and speculative-grade bonds issued by financial institutions, companies and governments so far this year total $6.61 trillion, up 15% year over year, of which bonds issued by hyperscalers and AI data center developers reached $368 billion, more than six times the year-earlier level. Oracle said it expects capital spending to peak in fiscal 2027 and 2028 and free cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028.

Articles.Title: Oracle Declines 4% as $10 Billion Bond Sale Revives AI Debt Worries; CoreWeave Advances 2%, Microsoft Holds Steady - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: The Digital Duty of Care bill reaches services that generate material using AI. That's the chatbot on your website. Here's what it would owe.
stories.Summary:
The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 passed the House of Representatives on 28 October, with 23 amendments agreed along the way. The bill places a duty, enforced by eSafety, on whoever is responsible for an online service to keep it safe. In the version that passed the House, the list of covered services includes ordinary websites and any service that generates material using artificial intelligence, with no size threshold. That means a chatbot on an ordinary business website is caught, both as part of the website and as an AI service in its own right.

The person responsible would have to take appropriate action to ensure a safe online environment, including measures to mitigate risks identified in risk assessments. That action would be judged by whether it works and is proportionate to the level of risk, and the cost of the action must not be taken into account. Written risk assessments would be required at least annually and before any significant change, and they would have to be kept for at least six years. The duty starts 12 months after Royal Assent, and the ceiling for breaching it is 60,000 penalty units, which is $21.84 million, or up to $109.2 million for a body corporate.

COSBOA chief executive Skye Cappuccio told SmartCompany on 22 October that the organisation was very concerned the bill as drafted would increase the compliance burden on small businesses that are exceedingly low risk, citing a hairdresser's website as an example. SEO Jim Stewart posted on 28 October that the scope is broad enough to potentially capture ordinary business websites and ecommerce stores. The explanatory memorandum says the definition does not provide for any defence to liability. The only off-ramp is a ministerial power to exempt services that pose little risk to users, and no such exemption can exist until the bill is law.

The Senate committee holds public hearings in Canberra on 9 and 10 November and reports on 20 November. The Coalition opposed the bill, and the Greens want it wider, with real teeth and a right to sue. Section 25A(1) excludes state and territory authorities and agencies, but the bill does not mention local government, so whether a council's chatbot is caught is unclear. It is also unclear how two responsible people share one duty, and the bill does not say who should have caught it when a vendor's model says something harmful on a business's site.

Articles.Title: The Digital Duty of Care bill reaches services that generate material using AI. That's the chatbot on your website. Here's what it would owe. - Webcoda

stories.Headline: U.S. Midterm Elections: Market Focus on AI Regulation and Prospects for Divided Government; Major Financial Institutions See Limited Impact
stories.Summary:
U.S. midterm elections are scheduled for Nov. 3, and major financial institutions say the market impact will be limited. The prevailing view is that Democrats will retake the House, while the Senate balance of power is the key focus. Markets are watching the risk of tighter AI regulation and a possible corporate tax hike in 2028. They are also wary of President Trump's rhetoric and actions after the election.

Monica Guerra, an investment strategist at Morgan Stanley, forecasts that Democrats will retake the House, creating a divided government with Trump's administration. She sees Democrats holding an edge in the Senate, and she says a president can veto Congress-passed measures, so Democratic tax and regulatory plans would face obstacles. She said stability that favors the stock market could result if major policy changes become impossible. Citigroup presented three scenarios, including Democrats winning 53 or more Senate seats, which could weigh on stock valuations. Another scenario is Republicans unexpectedly keeping a Senate majority, which could push up the year-end market.

Masahiro Ichikawa, chief market strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management, is concerned about headwinds if Trump takes a more hawkish stance to project a strong America externally. Ryotaro Sawada, a senior analyst at Tokai Tokyo Intelligence Laboratory, said post-election rhetoric and actions remain a source of uncertainty. He warned that investors could shift to selling all at once if Trump takes unexpected action. Makoto Hattori, head of the equity division at Marusan Securities, said uncertainty will be resolved after the election and stock prices are likely to rise. On AI, he said development will not stop as the U.S. and China vie for supremacy.

The Senate committee composition will influence financial regulation and is tied to approval of Federal Reserve governor nominees. The selection of a successor to Chair Powell will also be affected by Senate political dynamics. At the local level, Democratic governors tend to be cautious on construction permits and land-use zoning for AI data centers, which could delay projects. In Texas, the Republican incumbent governor is considered favored, but support for the party's Senate candidate has declined. Persistent inflation is a headwind for the ruling Republican Party, and some market participants say the current configuration resembles the 2006 midterms.

Articles.Title: U.S. Midterm Elections: Market Focus on AI Regulation and Prospects for Divided Government; Major Financial Institutions See Limited Impact - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: South Korea's Parliament Weighs New Local-Government Permits Ahead of AI Data Center Law, Industry Warns of "Double Regulation"
stories.Summary:
South Korea's National Assembly is considering amendments to the Special Act on AI Data Centers, which takes effect on March 10. Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Chae Hyun-il introduced a bill requiring a permit from a provincial governor or city, county or district mayor for new or expanded AI data centers above a size set by presidential decree. A separate amendment by lawmaker Han Jeong-ae would bar the law's one-stop licensing exception from applying to certain building permits tied to protecting residential and educational environments. The government is reportedly considering lowering the threshold for qualifying as an AI data center to 5MW from 10MW.

Chae's bill would require the new permit in addition to the existing building permit, along with mandatory public consultation with nearby residents. The permitting authority would have to consult with the Minister of Science and ICT, disclose the business plan in advance and gather residents' opinions. Han's bill would also require consideration of a region's power self-sufficiency rate and the share of electricity-use facilities that follow a local-production, local-consumption model when designating AIDC special zones. The current law focuses on one-stop licensing through the Ministry of Science and ICT to speed up construction.

A Ministry of Science and ICT official said the law requires data centers to obtain an existing building permit because they involve constructing buildings, but the bill creates a new permitting right separate from that. An aide to Chae said the legislation responds to the concentration of data centers and resident complaints in areas such as Seoul's Yeongdeungpo district, where four data centers operate and nine more are planned, including some next to schools. A cloud industry official said a new permitting procedure needs clarity on the size of facilities covered, screening criteria, how resident opinions are gathered and processing deadlines. Another industry official said there is concern over whether the new permitting system will preserve the special law's intent of speeding up licensing.

Just over four months remain before the special law takes effect. President Lee Jae Myung said in his budget address that South Korea will invest 21.3 trillion won, nearly twice this year's amount, in AI and the three megaprojects of semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers. The government's work on subordinate legislation is another variable, and the final criteria for qualifying as an AI data center have not been set. How the National Assembly reconciles community acceptance and investment speed is expected to affect South Korea's AI infrastructure buildout schedule and private investment plans.

Articles.Title: South Korea's Parliament Weighs New Local-Government Permits Ahead of AI Data Center Law, Industry Warns of "Double Regulation" - finance.biggo.com

stories.Headline: Senior judges warn of AI risks at Hellenic Australian Lawyers Association event
stories.Summary:
Senior judges and legal professionals gathered in Sydney on Wednesday, 28 October for the Hellenic Australian Lawyers Association's Observations from the Bench event. It was hosted by HAL's NSW Chapter at Sparke Helmore in Martin Place. The panel featured Anthe Philippides SC, Justice Melissa Perry KC, John Hatzistergos AM, Deputy Chief Judge Theo Tsavdaridis and Judge Joy Boulos. Bill Kritharas, HAL NSW Chapter Chair and a partner at Sparke Helmore, moderated the discussion.

Artificial intelligence was a central theme, with Justice Perry warning that growing reliance on technology could weaken the analytical, reasoning and interpersonal skills essential to legal practice. Philippides said AI would not produce a Mabo and called for stronger regulation to prevent misuse of AI in the justice system. Hatzistergos said AI-generated legal material could unnecessarily prolong litigation when practitioners adopt it without proper professional judgement. Tsavdaridis described longer submissions from self-represented litigants, with hearings that once took several hours now stretching over multiple days. Justice Perry suggested carefully regulated, voluntary AI-assisted decision-making could have a role in some routine matters, provided safeguards existed and parties could still appeal to a human decision-maker.

The panel also examined judicial independence and public confidence, with Justice Perry stressing that people appearing before courts should feel heard and understand proceedings whatever the outcome. Hatzistergos highlighted the judiciary's duty to uphold fairness, accountability and the rule of law, while saying broader social policy remained the responsibility of elected governments. Mental health and wellbeing were discussed, including heavy workloads and burnout, and Judge Boulos raised concerns that disclosing mental health difficulties could be seen as professional weakness. The panel also considered growing media scrutiny of judicial decisions and the importance of protecting judicial independence.

Kritharas opened the event by noting it fell on Oxi Day, commemorating Greece's rejection of an Italian ultimatum on 28 October 1940. He reflected on HAL's growth since it was established in Victoria in 2014 and its NSW Chapter formed in November 2016. He foreshadowed a national HAL conference in 2027 and an international conference in 2028, after earlier gatherings in Rhodes and Athens. The evening ended with a vote of thanks by Law Society of NSW Councillor Angelo Bilias, followed by networking.

Articles.Title: Senior judges warn of AI risks at Hellenic Australian Lawyers Association event - The Greek Herald

stories.Headline: Open source and practical AI take center stage at Wuzhen Summit
stories.Summary:
The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit opened on Monday in Wuzhen, East China's Zhejiang Province, and runs from November 2 to 5. Its flagship "Light of the Internet" Expo features 671 companies and institutions from 54 countries and regions, showing over 1,000 new technological achievements. Displays include robots filling prescriptions at smart pharmacies, automated garment sewing and precision assembly, and 6G communications enabling remote operation of construction machinery. The summit's theme is "Open Source and Openness, Joint Contribution and Shared Benefits - Jointly Building a Community with a Shared Future in Cyberspace."

The expo has six themed areas covering communications infrastructure, computing capabilities, manufacturing, everyday services and cybersecurity. For the first time, the WIC invited developers under 40 to debate how open models can address real industrial needs. The summit holds 27 sub-forums on topics from agent interoperability to embodied intelligence and green, low-carbon transitions. Exhibitors include Alibaba, Huawei, ZTE, Sugon, Intel, Qualcomm, Microsoft, Schneider Electric and Kaspersky.

Xiang Ligang of the Beijing Institute of Intelligent Era Industry said global AI development is forming two paths, with the US tending toward closed-source approaches that create silos. He said AI must become a service system integrating cloud infrastructure, data centers, talent and communications, and no single company can do this alone. Liu Dingding, a technology industry analyst, said the WIC's focus is shifting from demonstrating technological capabilities to showing how AI serves real production and everyday needs. He Weiwen of the Center for China and Globalization said global AI cooperation should be built under a multilateral framework for shared benefits, warning that exclusive groupings would bring economic costs and weaken cooperation.

The article says the WIC comes as some countries try to erect protectionist walls and form exclusive circles. It says the Quad foreign ministers' meeting expressed intent to provide more than $85 million in technical and financial assistance for trusted AI technologies across the so-called "Indo-Pacific." Wuzhen itself had only 12 internet-related enterprises before the first summit, and by 2024 the number had surpassed 1,200. Wuzhen's GDP grew from 2.84 billion yuan to 10.89 billion yuan, which the article describes as effectively "rebuilding three Wuzhens."

Articles.Title: Open source and practical AI take center stage at Wuzhen Summit - Global Times

stories.Headline: Eight in 10 judges encounter fake AI court ruling citations
stories.Summary:
A survey by the National Court Administration, an agency under the Supreme Court, found that 80.7 percent of judges handling civil, family and administrative cases in Korea have encountered citations of nonexistent court rulings, and 65.4 percent reported cases in which rulings were falsely cited. The survey ran from Oct. 6 to 16 among 360 judges nationwide, and respondents could select multiple answers. Another 16.9 percent had seen citations of fabricated or nonexistent laws, and 4.1 percent reported citations of fabricated academic papers or other materials. The results were released on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026.

When asked who submitted documents with such citations, 69.5 percent of the judges identified the litigants themselves, and 57.6 percent pointed to lawyers representing parties in civil cases or defendants in criminal proceedings. Some litigants submitted AI-generated fake judgments that copied the format of real Supreme Court rulings, and some documents altered actual rulings or cited them in ways that misrepresented their meaning. Some documents even included excerpts from conversations with AI chatbots, revealing that they had been prepared with AI. Of the judges, 91.7 percent said institutional measures were needed, with 64.8 percent calling them highly necessary. For specific measures, 61.4 percent supported a legal basis for administrative fines, 61.1 percent favored requiring parties to verify the rulings they cite, 60.6 percent backed mandatory disclosure of AI use, and 55.4 percent called for sanctions against lawyers, including disciplinary referrals.

The National Court Administration said citations of fabricated or nonexistent rulings from AI use burden opposing parties and the courts and delay the public's right to a trial. It said ensuring the accuracy of submitted documents is necessary to reduce unnecessary litigation burdens and improve the speed and fairness of judicial proceedings. The agency said it plans to develop countermeasures based on the survey findings, will consult with the Ministry of Justice and other relevant agencies, and will submit recommendations to the National Assembly to amend the Civil Procedure Act and Criminal Procedure Act and establish a legal basis for administrative fines and other penalties. It is also considering guidance for lawyers and litigants on precautions when using AI through the electronic litigation system.

Articles.Title: Eight in 10 judges encounter fake AI court ruling citations - Korea JoongAng Daily

stories.Headline: UAlbany researcher calls for transparency and digital literacy as AI spreads in politics - WRGB
stories.Summary:
A researcher at the University at Albany examined how voters react when they believe artificial intelligence is used in political campaign messages. Seulki Lee-Geiller, of the university's Center for Technology in Government, published the study on Sept. 24 in the Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties. The study is titled "AI as a partisan cue: the relational dynamics of AI-assisted campaign messaging in election integrity perceptions." Lee-Geiller ran an online survey experiment with 3,055 U.S. participants in June and July 2024, ahead of that year's presidential election. Participants were randomly split into four groups and shown a hypothetical campaign letter from a presidential candidate.

The letter's content was the same for everyone, but the groups got different information about how it was made. One group saw no mention of AI, one was told AI helped draft the letter, and two others were told AI was used by either the participant's preferred party or the opposing party. Participants then rated election integrity measures such as fairness, authenticity, freedom from fraud and whether voters' interests were represented. Lee-Geiller said simply knowing AI was used did not significantly change views on fairness or authenticity, but people were more likely to think AI was being used to target messages to specific audiences. Bigger differences appeared when party affiliation was added.

On a five-point scale, the average authenticity rating was 3.71 when AI use was attributed to a participant's preferred party, compared with 3.37 when it was attributed to an opposing party. Lee-Geiller said transparency, consistent standards and digital literacy can help people make more informed judgments about AI-assisted messages, regardless of who is using the technology. The study is described as exploratory and focused on short-term reactions to hypothetical campaign materials rather than real-world election conditions. Lee-Geiller said additional research could look at how perceptions evolve with repeated exposure to AI-assisted messaging during actual campaigns.

Articles.Title: UAlbany researcher calls for transparency and digital literacy as AI spreads in politics - WRGB

stories.Headline: Mass+torts+and+AI%3A+Litigation+that+plays+to+technology%E2%80%99s+strength - Virginia Lawyers Weekly
stories.Summary:
Mass tort litigation has become increasingly high-tech, with artificial intelligence tools now used to organize and analyze large volumes of information. Plaintiffs' attorneys say AI allows them to document similar medical complaints from hundreds or thousands of plaintiffs and link their illnesses to drug ingestion, toxic exposure, or consumer product use. Joseph Fantini, managing attorney of mass torts at Rosen Injury Lawyers, said the defense side has generally been ahead of plaintiffs in AI use, but the gap is narrowing over the last two or three years. He said his side uses AI from case acquisition to case workup to settlement and settlement administration.

Christopher M. Placitella, a partner with Cohen, Placitella, Roth & Goslee, said mass tort opportunities often have a short filing window, causing a rush to gather medical records and other materials that AI is crucial for cataloguing. His firm is one of those representing some 70,000 plaintiffs in the mass tort case against Johnson & Johnson over talcum powder exposure. Ashleigh Raso, founding partner of Nigh, Goldenberg, Raso & Vaughn, cautioned that questions litigants ask generative AI programs about their cases can be discoverable, and that inputting proposed settlement terms into AI could void an agreement. Carasusana B. Wall, senior partner at the Bullock Legal Group, said plaintiff fact sheets that used to be 15 pages can now run 60 to 80 pages each.

Kaeo Caindec, chief executive officer and founder of Clarra, said there is no end to the complexity of mass tort cases, with firms struggling with increases in both litigation and litigants. About 100,000 Roundup cases have been settled for about $11 billion, with about 3,000 claims outstanding, and about 69,000 mass tort cases are active in the federal multidistrict litigation over talcum powder before a federal judge in New Jersey. About 3,000 individuals and 800 school districts are plaintiffs in suits claiming Facebook, YouTube and other social media platforms caused psychological or physical harm. Retired Michigan district court judge Brian MacKenzie concluded that a potentially massive social media tort case can be fairly adjudicated under current negligence statutes.

Articles.Title: Mass+torts+and+AI%3A+Litigation+that+plays+to+technology%E2%80%99s+strength - Virginia Lawyers Weekly

stories.Headline: Revealed: From AI to ageing laptops — what junior lawyers really think about their firms’ tech
stories.Summary:
Legal Cheek published exclusive research on 2 November 2026 from its annual survey of more than 2,000 trainees and junior lawyers. The survey found that firms are investing heavily in AI tools while everyday technology such as case management systems, laptops and work phones is often slow, outdated or broken. One new starter said their firm presents itself as an AI law firm but barely has working tech, with rudimentary laptops that break often. Another said AI will only get you so far if you cannot even open an email. Some juniors praised tools including Claude, ChatGPT and Harvey but rated laptops and IT support as sub-par.

The responses describe a range of setups across firms. One trainee said the tech is very advanced but laptops cannot handle the amount loaded on them and get slow, while another said their case management system is older than they are. One junior reported that their laptop screen fell off, and another said trainees are not given work phones. Some firms were described as slow to adopt AI and apprehensive about committing to one provider, with clunky client management systems. Others were praised for combining AI with high-quality hardware, reliable software and helpful IT support, and one rookie said they could not think of a more advanced firm.

The survey gives no overall figures beyond the 2,000-plus respondents and names no individual firms or people, quoting only anonymous trainees and junior lawyers. No one is identified as responsible for the technology, and the article does not say what firms plan to do in response. It also does not say when the full survey results will be published. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Revealed: From AI to ageing laptops — what junior lawyers really think about their firms’ tech - Legal Cheek

stories.Headline: 'AI Made the Decision' Is Not a Defense: What NYC Employers Need to Know About the City’s AI Enforcement Position
stories.Summary:
New York City has said that employers remain responsible for following anti-discrimination and worker-protection laws when they use automated systems in employment decisions. The city's position was set out in a Law.com article by Keith Gutstein, published on November 2, 2026. The article says employers cannot avoid liability by claiming that an algorithm or AI system made the decision. It reports that the city has reaffirmed this enforcement stance as artificial intelligence becomes more common in employment decisions.

The article says employers are still liable for unlawful results even when an automated system contributes to them. It says audits and human review can help but do not replace legal compliance. The piece is described as an 8 minute read and was published at 7:00 AM. It frames the issue as a basic question of who bears legal responsibility when an algorithm contributes to an unlawful result.

The article attributes the position to New York City rather than to a named official, and it does not name any individual who made a statement. It says the city has reaffirmed that employers remain responsible for complying with applicable laws. The article presents audits and human review as helpful measures, not as substitutes for meeting legal duties. It does not give any further details of what employers are required to do.

The article does not say what happens next or describe any specific enforcement action, penalty or deadline. It does not give any dates for future steps or name any agency involved. It does not say whether guidance or rules will follow. The article does not provide any further context beyond the city's stated position.

Articles.Title: 'AI Made the Decision' Is Not a Defense: What NYC Employers Need to Know About the City’s AI Enforcement Position - Law.com

stories.Headline: 😸 Microsoft's enforceable AI privacy standard for schools is now in effect
stories.Summary:
Microsoft, the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers announced the AI Safety & Privacy Standard on September 9, and it took effect on Sunday, November 1. Any U.S. school district can add the standard to a new or existing Microsoft agreement without renegotiation or renewal, according to Microsoft's fact sheet. The standard is written into the contract rather than posted on a webpage, which makes it harder for Microsoft to change later. Once a district writes it into its agreement, the district can cancel and seek damages if Microsoft breaks the rules.

The standard bans training AI models on student or educator data permanently, with one narrow safety and security exception. It also bans selling student data or using it for advertising, tracking students, and AI companions, meaning chatbots built to act like a friend. High-risk decisions require human review, so AI can assist but people decide. Breach reports are due within 72 hours, and violations must be fixed or AI use paused or ended. Microsoft also faces annual certification, audit rights and a deadline to fix security problems.

AFT president Randi Weingarten said older rules like FERPA and HIPAA never anticipated AI, and Fortune noted that COPPA predates generative AI too, so the union went for leverage. UFT president Michael Mulgrew said AI use in grades K-8 isn't appropriate right now, and New York City's public schools had just announced a one-year pause on AI. Weingarten said OpenAI and Anthropic have expressed willingness to sign. An Anthropic spokesperson told Fortune the company has worked with the AFT on a safety and privacy standard, while OpenAI didn't respond.

The standard says nothing about whether classrooms should use AI, only the terms for districts that do, and it binds just one company so far. Microsoft's fact sheet refers to its AI products in general and doesn't name which ones are covered. If OpenAI or Anthropic sign the same standard, a union-negotiated contract starts to look like the default rulebook for AI in schools. If neither does, districts using their tools get whatever terms those companies offer.

Articles.Title: 😸 Microsoft's enforceable AI privacy standard for schools is now in effect - The Neuron

stories.Headline: Manufacturing’s black art is retiring. AI may be the best chance to keep it
stories.Summary:
As key manufacturing hubs including Singapore continue to age, many veteran engineers are nearing retirement, and new talent is not entering the sector at the same rate. These experienced workers can diagnose problems on the factory floor by ear, smell and instinct, a skill the article calls the black art of manufacturing. That knowledge lives in their heads, and it leaves with them when they retire. Some manufacturers said it can take two to three engineers to replace one seasoned veteran, without a guarantee of the same results.

Factories have digitalised rapidly, with sensors tracking nearly every stage of production, but the article says lots of data does not mean lots of insights. Decisions still depend on the same few experienced people who know what the numbers mean, and some firms treat sensor tracking as a box-ticking exercise. The article says AI trained on production data and engineering drawings could flag a yield dip within minutes, trace it to a temperature drift at an upstream station and recommend a fix. It would act as an assistant to veterans and help new engineers, capturing judgment in a form that can be checked and passed on.

The article says budget for trialling technology is rarely the problem, and the hardest part is change management, because a small process change can ripple down a linear production line. Managers and workers are reluctant to experiment because they run tight schedules and cannot bear the risk of downtime. Manufacturers also treat production data as sacred, so any tool sending data outside the factory would not make it to a trial. Viable AI therefore has to run in-house with security at its core, fit the existing workflow and work alongside floor engineers, who keep the final decision.

The article says deployment is where many companies win or lose, and forward-deployed engineers work on-site to narrow the first deployment to a single line or problem with a measurable outcome. Demonstrating return on investment in numbers the plant manager already tracks is how trust is earned on the floor. The article concludes that AI will not replace the veterans' intuition, but it may give manufacturers a way to capture, explain and pass it on before it retires. It adds that manufacturing may not be the most glamorous sector, but it could be where AI proves its real worth.

Articles.Title: Manufacturing’s black art is retiring. AI may be the best chance to keep it - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Op-Ed: Canadian schools need well-considered AI guidance
stories.Summary:
Many Canadian educators began the school year with little or no guidance on managing AI use in their classrooms, according to an op-ed published by Canadian Affairs on November 2, 2026. The piece was written by Joanna DeJong VanHof, director of the education program at Cardus and a PhD student at the University of Toronto. It says just four provinces have formal AI guidelines for educators: British Columbia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador and Quebec. Provinces like Manitoba are still working on their own, and the op-ed says half of the provinces have been quiet on the issue.

The op-ed points to stricter approaches elsewhere. New York City announced a moratorium on AI use in public schools for the 2026-27 year, under a policy published by Chancellor Kamar Samuels, with strong limits for elementary students and limited, guided opportunities for high school students. In early September, Los Angeles passed an even more restrictive policy, imposing a district-wide moratorium on generative AI use by students on all school devices for this school year. The op-ed calls these approaches time-limited and prudent but not a long-term answer. It cites Professor Josh Brake of Harvey Mudd College, who argues in an upcoming book, Beyond School Choice, that a ban can buy time but cannot answer the deeper questions.

The op-ed says that in the absence of provincial guidance, there is a risk that education unions will steer the conversation. It says reports from the Canadian Teachers' Federation emphasize the risks AI poses to members' autonomy and the need for human judgment in the classroom. It raises concern that AI approaches could be shaped by what unions, teachers and education workers will and will not do, rather than by what leads to the best learning outcomes. Brake is paraphrased as saying that forcing students through complicated systems sends the message that their work is not worth doing for its own sake and that they are not trusted to do it honestly.

The op-ed argues that policies should be developed in consultation with educators, parents and students. It says they must start from learner-focused questions about what educational purpose a tool serves, what evidence shows it advances that purpose, and what human capacity its use might strengthen or weaken. It concludes that until those questions can be answered, restraint is a policy choice in its own right. It notes that New York has decided the answer for younger students is, for now, no, and says provinces here should be prepared to follow suit.

Articles.Title: Op-Ed: Canadian schools need well-considered AI guidance - Canadian Affairs

stories.Headline: U.S. Midterms to Decide Fate of $2.5 Trillion in AI Data Center Investment as Governor Races Emerge as Wild Card
stories.Summary:
With three days to go before the U.S. midterm elections, Wall Street is focusing on governor's races rather than Congress, because authority over data center permitting and power and water regulation sits at the state level. Market research firm Cleanview estimates that 10 governor's races will affect data center investment plans totaling 67.4 GW and $2.5 trillion. Texas holds roughly 25% of U.S. data center capacity expected to come online by 2030. Jefferies warned that if the Democratic candidate for Texas governor, Gina Hinojosa, wins, her pledge to halt new construction could put 13.3 GW of announced projects at risk. Incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott is pushing to strengthen power and water reviews.

Georgia and Ohio are also seen as key states, with community opposition over grid strain and water use intensifying in both. In Ohio, the Senate race is a separate variable: cryptocurrency groups have poured more than $50 million into efforts to defeat Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown, a crypto skeptic, in his matchup against Republican incumbent Jon Husted. If Brown returns to the Senate and Democrats win a majority, oversight of the crypto industry by financial regulators could tighten. Some companies are reportedly holding off on issuing billions of dollars in high-yield bonds while they wait for policy clarity. If data center construction is delayed, financing schedules and plans to recoup investments could be thrown off together.

RBC Capital Markets said in a report that governors are on the front lines of AI and data center regulation. JPMorgan noted that President Donald Trump has said he would veto legislation restricting the expansion of the AI industry, and that it is realistically difficult for Democrats to win enough seats to override a veto, so federal gridlock offsets policy risk. Kevin Shea, a senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth, said policy uncertainty around data centers will not reverse the AI investment flow itself but could disrupt project timelines and costs. Analysts say projects that have yet to secure new permits and power supply contracts face the greatest risk of schedule delays and cost increases from tighter regulation. The direction of the investment environment is likely to be decided not in Washington but in state capitals.

Articles.Title: U.S. Midterms to Decide Fate of $2.5 Trillion in AI Data Center Investment as Governor Races Emerge as Wild Card - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: AI: Data Centers on the Ballot in 15 Governor Races. AI-RTZ #1259 - AI: Reset to Zero
stories.Summary:
On Election Day in the US, AI data centers became a top issue in governor races for the first time in this AI tech wave. The Information analyzed candidate platforms and public statements and found that of the 36 states electing a governor, 21 have at least one major-party nominee backing a data center moratorium. In five states both nominees back a pause: Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon and Texas. In three more, Maine, New Mexico and New York, a pause backer is likely to win based on recent polls. In seven others, Alaska, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Wisconsin and Vermont, the race is close between a pause backer and a candidate who does not back one.

Those 15 states hold more than a third of the US population and some of the biggest AI data center projects. OpenAI's Stargate with Oracle has large sites in Texas, Michigan and New Mexico, and SoftBank's SB Energy plans an 8-gigawatt campus for OpenAI in Ohio. Three sitting governors have already paused new large-scale data centers: Kathy Hochul in New York, Greg Abbott in Texas and Tina Kotek in Oregon. The pauses vary in length from 45 days to three years and in scope, with New York's applying to facilities above 50 megawatts. Every statewide pause so far has relied on halting new environmental permits, and Abbott has also frozen new grid hookups in Texas while Kotek stopped deals on state land in Oregon.

Of the 46 top nominees not calling for a moratorium, 38 back at least one other restriction, most commonly ratepayer protection. Hawaii is the only state where neither candidate is campaigning on data center limits, and the split is not cleanly partisan, with Republican candidates backing moratoriums in Maryland and Iowa. Abbott said developers had dug their own grave, and his challenger Gina Hinojosa called his pause an election-year stunt. New Hampshire's incumbent said she would need the state budget next July, while her opponent promised an executive order on day one. Google's head of data center energy said the bottleneck on Earth is permits and grid studies, not power, and that space data centers could cost up to 100 times as much as those on Earth.

At the start of this year only about 40 localities had bans on data centers, and by August there were over 500, driven by power bills, water use, noise and blight. A Pew Research Center poll in August found six in ten US adults would be uncomfortable with a new data center in their area, and a University of Pennsylvania poll found more than 60 percent now oppose new data centers nearby, up from 49 percent in March. Anthropic named moratoriums and other restrictions as a business risk in its IPO filing, citing New York and Texas, and SB Energy and Nscale named the same risks in their own filings. Google lost about $500 billion of market value in a day, and OpenAI has raised less than half of its $30 billion target.

Articles.Title: AI: Data Centers on the Ballot in 15 Governor Races. AI-RTZ #1259 - AI: Reset to Zero

stories.Headline: Megazone Cloud to Apply KAIST Physical AI Technology in Manufacturing
stories.Summary:
Megazone Cloud signed a memorandum of understanding with the KAIST Manufacturing Physical AI Research Institute on the 2nd at COEX in Seoul, according to a report dated November 3, 2026. The agreement covers cooperation on Physical AI technology in industrial settings and its commercialization. Lee Ju-wan, chairman of Megazone Cloud, and Jang Yong-jae, director of the institute, took part in the signing and posed for a commemorative photo. The two sides aim to bring a robot operating platform developed by KAIST to manufacturing sites.

Under the agreement, Megazone Cloud will use its AI and cloud deployment and operations capabilities to bring Kairos 37, a robot orchestration platform developed by KAIST, to industrial sites. The partners will pursue technical standardization among companies in the parts, equipment, AI and data sectors, develop joint business models and expand into global markets. They plan to form a working-level consultative body to specify application areas, cooperation projects and the roles of participating companies. The goal is a common foundation that lets technologies validated in research and demonstration be repeatedly applied across diverse manufacturing environments. KAIST plans to expand its partner companies and link their robotics, AI and manufacturing systems technologies with Kairos 37.

The agreement is part of efforts to build a standardization cooperation framework led by the governance subcommittee of the Ministry of Science and ICT's Physical AI Alliance. That subcommittee is tasked with resolving connectivity issues among the different robot, equipment and data environments at each company and supporting the overseas expansion of technologies and business models validated in South Korea. Lee said Megazone Cloud will combine industrial-site experience from work with around 8,000 companies and the AI and AX capabilities of around 2,800 people. He said the company will support Physical AI technology in taking root in industrial settings and creating tangible value.

Articles.Title: Megazone Cloud to Apply KAIST Physical AI Technology in Manufacturing - 파이낸셜뉴스

stories.Headline: San Antonio teachers are using AI. Schools are figuring out the rules. - San Antonio Express-News
stories.Summary:
Brent Ritchey, an eighth grade U.S. history teacher at Briscoe Middle School in San Antonio, began using chatbots in 2022 after OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public. He fed the program Texas learning standards for the American Revolution and asked it to plan a lesson. Four years and 40 models of ChatGPT later, he uses education-focused AI tools in his classroom. His students have interviewed Abraham Lincoln, created documents about 18th century events using slang, and received feedback on writing assignments.

Northside Independent School District, where Ritchey works, has approved 10 AI tools for educators. In the next few weeks, the district plans to roll out ChatGPT for Teachers, a private platform for educators to create and share lessons across schools and districts, according to Director of Academic Technology Carrie Squyres. North East ISD allows employees to use tools including Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot. San Antonio ISD rolled out the AI platform Coursemojo last year to teach reading at some schools, and Somerset ISD launched Subject.AI over the summer to help high schoolers catch up in classes where they had fallen behind.

Ritchey said teachers cannot be replaced by AI but can accept that students will use it and should be taught to use it properly. Torie Marquez, North East ISD's executive director of technology services, said that when something is adopted at such a large scale, people have to shift their thinking about whether it is a trend or longer term, and she believes AI is here to stay. Jessica Saenz, a Madison High School English teacher, called learning the tools tedious but said she was impressed the feedback touched on each part of the rubric, and that we gain the ability to do more in less time. Patti Holub, chief technology officer at Education Service Center Region 20, said training teachers takes time, money and staff, and the center launched four online AI courses in October.

Northside ISD's employee handbook prohibits feeding identifiable student information into AI when developing special education plans and using AI tools to determine student grades, stating that AI is a tool and not a replacement for human judgement. The guidance does not outline enforcement beyond saying the district will continue to monitor use and misuse of AI applications. Deepti Tagare, a UTSA professor who studies AI in schools, said educators should not use AI in grading, identifying cheating or predicting how students will perform academically. Squyres said she cannot ensure that all of Northside's 95,000 students learn to leverage AI under the current policy that lets teachers decide how much they use it, and she warned against creating inequity across classrooms.

Articles.Title: San Antonio teachers are using AI. Schools are figuring out the rules. - San Antonio Express-News

stories.Headline: Algorithmic kill chains: China’s military AI, Europe’s regulatory mismatch
stories.Summary:
A study from the NATO Defense College examined how China’s People’s Liberation Army is integrating artificial intelligence into its war-fighting doctrine. The authors are Anselm Küsters, scientific director for the Nordic countries and head of the Department of Digitalisation and AI at the Centre for European Policy, and Marius Strubenhoff, an independent expert on foreign and security policy at the same think-tank. They applied large language models to a corpus of over 171,000 Chinese documents spanning 2000 to 2025. The study is titled Decoding the Dragon: A Language-Based Analysis of China’s Vision of AI Warfare.

The study found that surveillance-related terms dominated the corpus by a wide margin. Computer vision accounted for 49.4 per cent of the subfield distribution, robotics for 12.5 per cent and natural language processing for 6.2 per cent, while AI safety was under two per cent. References to meaningful human control in the People’s Daily peaked in 2021, when UN deliberations on lethal autonomous weapons were most intense, and declined sharply afterward. The number of military AI publications grew from 52 papers in 2016 to 181 in 2024.

The authors write that near-term PLA investments appear geared toward battlespace transparency that supports information dominance and precision strikes. They say the dominance of surveillance applications suggests near-term crisis instability will stem from information asymmetries rather than rogue autonomous weapons. They conclude that positive state narratives and the decline in meaningful human control rhetoric after 2021 signal growing Chinese confidence and waning commitment to international norms. They are careful not to overstate China’s current capabilities, noting it is not quite on the verge of autonomous military dominance.

Europe’s EU AI Act explicitly excludes AI systems used exclusively for military, defence or national-security purposes from its scope. The Dual-Use Export Control Regulation is export-centric and reactive and does not yet cover foundation models, reinforcement-learning environments or synthetic datasets. The GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive are strong on individual rights but not designed to counter adversarial exploitation of European data streams by a foreign military. European Parliament resolutions in 2018 and 2021 urging a ban on lethal autonomous weapons without meaningful human control remain legally non-binding.

The study addresses its recommendations to member states rather than to the EU as an institution. It calls for investment in adversarial robustness research, counter-ISR technologies and human-machine teaming architectures. It says effective arms control requires technical measures that are intrusive and analogous to Chemical Weapons Convention inspection protocols, and it calls for treaty obligations targeting autonomous target selection and non-reconstructible black box military AI systems. The article describes possible EU measures including a dedicated Defence AI Instrument, amending Annex I of the Dual-Use Regulation, a Strategic Data Spaces regime and a European strategic autonomy framework requiring unanimous member-state agreement.

Articles.Title: Algorithmic kill chains: China’s military AI, Europe’s regulatory mismatch - EU Perspectives

stories.Headline: Google Play policy bans app deception of AI agents
stories.Summary:
Google announced new Play policy rules for AppFunctions on October 29, 2026, and the change was reported on November 2. AppFunctions let apps expose discrete, structured actions that AI agents can invoke. An agent can read a function catalogue, decide to call a function, and pass structured arguments for the app to execute. The updated policy adds an enforcement clause for these functions.

The policy prohibits AppFunctions from deceiving or manipulating AI agents, bypassing security controls, or interfering with other applications. Deceiving an agent includes lying in function metadata or return values, such as describing a read-only function that actually writes, or claiming capabilities an app does not possess. Bypassing security controls means working around user or operating system permissions that an agent should obtain. Interfering with other apps covers eating another app's agent traffic, spamming agents with fake results, or poisoning shared context built from multiple apps.

Google is responsible for the policy, and it extends its existing logic against deceiving human users to AI agents. The company treats AI agents with the same integrity requirements as human users, so apps must not use dark patterns or half-truths when interacting with agents. Google said the policy aims to address bad actors who treat AI agents as a user acquisition channel, similar to how human users are acquired. Developers should audit their function descriptions to ensure accuracy and make return values unembellished.

Articles.Title: Google Play policy bans app deception of AI agents

stories.Headline: South Korea to double spending on AI and chips in 2027 - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said in his annual budget speech to parliament on Monday, November 2, 2026, that the country will double spending on AI and semiconductors in 2027 to a record high. He told lawmakers that 21.3 trillion won, about US$16 billion, would go to chipmaking and artificial intelligence, covering areas from data centres to robotics. He said the figure was nearly double this year's amount and that the government would make bold investments in AI and future growth engines to boost the economy's growth potential. He also pledged to use the technology to turn the military into what he called a smart, elite force.

The 2027 budget plan totals 821 trillion won, a 12.8 percent increase on-year and the largest budget proposal on record. The defence budget would rise around eight percent from this year to 73.3 trillion won, with the aim of securing nuclear-powered submarines and KF-21 fighter jets. Lee said Seoul aims to rapidly transform the military into a smart, elite force through integrated manned and unmanned systems based on AI, robots and drones. The government will also invest 4.7 trillion won in frontier AI development projects, with the aim of achieving world-leading performance for the country's own AI model, which he called a national strategic asset, and 2.1 trillion won in electricity, water supply and industrial complex infrastructure.

Lee is the one responsible for the plan, and he now needs parliament to pass the budget proposal, which the articles say is likely given his party's majority. In June, Lee announced a public-private partnership centred on three mega-projects, aiming to expand chip production hubs nationwide, establish robotics research and development centres, and build gigawatt-scale AI data centres. The government at the time unveiled plans for nearly $1.2 trillion in investment, equivalent to more than two-thirds of South Korea's GDP, and Samsung and SK hynix also announced plans in June to invest more than 4,755 trillion won in the country, a record level of corporate investment. In September, Seoul announced plans for a 162.3 trillion won Future Fund next year, aimed at channelling record tax revenues from the chip boom into long-term growth.

The context is that South Korea is a tech powerhouse, home to Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, two of the world's three biggest makers of memory chips, which are in huge demand thanks to the AI boom. South Korean chipmakers have seen profits and share prices skyrocket as frenzied demand for AI infrastructure squeezes the global supply of memory chips, and the boom has spurred chip engineers and other workers to seek higher payouts in tense negotiations at companies including Samsung and SK hynix. North Korea has recently tested a slew of weapons, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which it said used AI technology. Last year, Seoul announced an agreement with Washington to build nuclear-powered submarines, with Pyongyang slamming the submarine programme as a dangerous attempt at confrontation.

stories.Headline: AI Glasses Can Replace Your Prescription Glasses, But Should They?
stories.Summary:
AI smart glasses can now be fitted with prescription lenses, and Ray-Ban lets customers order Meta's smart glasses with prescription lenses already installed by uploading a prescription. The lenses are possible because most AI glasses are essentially regular glasses with extra technology built in, and from a distance a pair of Ray-Ban Meta looks like any other glasses. The articles say the prescription itself is not the hard part of the decision. Instead, buyers are told to weigh weight, battery life and privacy before swapping their everyday glasses for AI eyewear. Regular glasses usually weigh between 20 and 30 grams, while smart glasses can weigh up to 80 grams, which is fine for a few hours but becomes a burden over a full day.

AI glasses last an average of 3 to 5 hours before the battery dies, so all-day wear requires constant recharging, and once the battery drains the glasses work only as regular glasses with no AI features. The Courts of England and Wales have banned Meta glasses from courtrooms, and New York followed suit in July. Many schools around the world have also banned students from wearing AI glasses during class, and many companies have barred them from their premises. Meta has been facing scrutiny after outsourced workers were able to access intimate images and videos captured by its AI smart glasses, and the company says content is sometimes reviewed by humans to improve the product experience. The articles also note that even with the camera off, audio features can be a problem, since a real-time translation feature could upload confidential conversations to a third-party server.

A German nonprofit has filed a criminal complaint over Meta smart glasses privacy. Some users have stopped wearing AI glasses in public because of the backlash, fearing they could be labeled stalkers or weirdos. Taken together, the technical limitations make AI glasses more of a second option than a replacement for everyday glasses, and privacy is described as the real deal-breaker. The articles say buying AI glasses with prescription lenses is entirely possible, but clear limits remain before they can fully replace everyday eyeglasses. For the market to grow in earnest, the industry still faces the task of making hardware lighter, improving power efficiency and securing trust in how captured photo and audio data is handled.

stories.Headline: Palantir's U.S. Revenue Soars 119% as Commercial Revenue Surpasses Government Revenue for the First Time. Here's Why Its Growth Is Still Surging, Even as Other AI Stocks Falter
stories.Summary:
Palantir Technologies reported third-quarter 2026 results on Nov 2, 2026, and the AI and data-mining company beat Wall Street's expectations. Revenue of $2.3 billion rose 96% year over year, the company's highest-ever growth rate, and climbed 20% quarter over quarter. Earnings per share of $0.44 surged 144%, while analysts had expected revenue of $2.2 billion and EPS of $0.41. The U.S. commercial segment, which includes the flagship Artificial Intelligence Platform, grew revenue 148% year over year to $984 million, passing U.S. government revenue for the first time.

U.S. government revenue rose 96% year over year to $953 million. Total contract value closed in the quarter was $2.92 billion, up 6% year over year, with $1.46 billion of that from the U.S. commercial segment, up 11%. Net dollar retention was 165%, meaning existing customers spent 65% more than a year earlier, and U.S. commercial remaining deal value rose 79% to $6.52 billion. The company posted operating cash flow and adjusted free cash flow of $1.2 billion each at roughly a 53% margin, held $10.56 billion in cash and equivalents, and raised full-year revenue guidance to about 91% growth from 82%.

CEO Alex Karp argues that businesses should not casually hand their data to others, particularly those selling AI solutions, because doing so gives away proprietary knowledge, workflows and strategic advantage, which he calls a business's alpha. Palantir uses boot camps to show businesses how to get real-world AI-powered results and a solid return on investment, and once customers see the evidence they keep coming back. The article says this is why Palantir's growth continues to surge while its AI rivals stumble. The article also notes that the stock carries a hefty premium, so any failure, real or imagined, will spark a swift and severe rerating.

Palantir just delivered its 13th consecutive quarter of accelerating revenue growth, and its forecast suggests more is in store. The stock sells for 125 times earnings, though the article says the most common valuation metrics fall short for high-growth stocks, and a price/earnings-to-growth ratio of 0.53 is below the level of 1 that marks an undervalued stock. The article says Palantir won't fit every investor and that those starting or adding to a position should consider dollar-cost averaging. The author's view is that the evidence is clear and the stock is a buy.
