stories.Headline: Textile AI adoption held back by data and skills gaps, report finds
stories.Summary:
A white paper on artificial intelligence in the textile value chain was published in October 2026 by the International Textile Manufacturers Federation and RWTH Aachen University’s Institut für Textiltechnik. It drew on a webinar series run by the two organisations. The paper argues that progress depends on coordinated, industry-wide capability-building. It describes textile manufacturing as digitally fragmented rather than under-digitalised, because decades of digitalisation left data spread across disconnected systems.

The paper says companies often overestimate how much usable, structured data they have for AI projects. It reports measurable results from computer-vision inspection of fabric and yarn, predictive maintenance, energy optimisation and demand forecasting. It points to a shift from systems that assist decisions toward systems that coordinate or execute defined tasks under human supervision. Agentic AI is beginning to manage multi-stage processes such as sourcing, and causal AI can adjust production settings directly, with end-to-end AI workflows likely in two to three years.

Thomas Gries, director of the Institut für Textiltechnik, said companies need a dedicated task force to embed data integration into daily and strategic processes. He said partnering with outside experts on a transparent assessment and on implementation is essential to survive. Olivier Zieschank, director of the federation, said AI is not a shortcut around structural challenges but can help companies manage complexity and make the most of scarce expertise. He said understanding where AI genuinely helps is a learning process, which is why exchange through associations matters.

The paper recommends starting with contained use cases rather than broad programmes. It proposes shared data standards, data spaces that let originators keep ownership, and sector-specific tools such as a controlled Textile GPT, particularly for smaller and medium-sized businesses. It also lists trust and accountability as requirements, including control of sensitive information, cyber security, transparency about system limitations and retained human responsibility. Participants warned that AI can compound rather than resolve problems caused by incomplete or poor-quality data.

Separately, the Tech Council of Australia released research finding that wider AI use by small and medium-sized businesses could add up to AUD $93 billion in annual economic value. Only one in four SMEs uses AI, and just 5% have adopted it broadly. The report estimates an average SME moving from no AI use to broad adoption could gain AUD $136,000 a year in productivity. It was prepared by Delwood Advisory with support from Employment Hero, Google and Deputy, using data from Deputy, Xero and LinkedIn.

The Australian report cites research showing 94% of SMEs using AI reported productivity improvements and 54% of SME employees using it reported better job satisfaction. It names barriers including limited understanding of AI, workforce skills gaps, uncertainty about return on investment, and concerns about security and reliability. It recommends wider access to affordable training, practical advice and industry-specific examples. It also identifies gaps between regional and metropolitan businesses and between SMEs and larger companies in construction, hospitality and retail.

Kate Cornick, chief executive of the Tech Council of Australia, said small businesses employ almost two-thirds of the country’s private-sector workforce, so improving their productivity matters to the whole economy. She said most SMEs are not yet using AI and there is a significant gap between what it could deliver and what they currently get. She said many owners need practical advice on which applications will be useful and how to introduce them. She said support needs to be better targeted because regional businesses remain behind metropolitan ones and some industries face much greater adoption gaps.

Ben Thompson, co-founder and chief executive of Employment Hero, said owners name payroll, super, awards and compliance as the tasks that consume their week. He said his own company uses AI to move through its roadmap faster and that AI agents now handle 95% of routine HR support questions. He said many owners do not know where to start and regional businesses are still behind cities. The report adds to debate over how quickly small businesses can adopt AI while larger companies move faster, and its focus on regional and sector gaps suggests support may need to be targeted more narrowly.

stories.Headline: Here’s Why You’re About to See More Ads in Google’s AI Overviews
stories.Summary:
Google began putting more ads into its AI search results in late October 2026. On October 28, Alphabet held its quarterly earnings call, where Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said search ad revenue growth slowed in the third quarter of 2026 because queries are moving to AI Overviews and AI Mode, which have lower monetization. Google then said it would scale ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries, including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore, with Brazil, Mexico and the UK to follow later in the year. In the US, Google launched what it calls multiturn ads, which can appear inside follow-up questions in AI Mode when a conversation has commercial relevance.

The change means sponsored links can show up next to or inside conversational AI answers, and all of them carry a clear Sponsored label. Google said ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, and sometimes no ads will show if there is no purchase intent. Advertisers do not need to create new campaigns, because Google will automatically pull from their existing ad setups. Google also said paid ads will not influence the information in AI-generated text, so the answers stay neutral.

Dan Taylor, Vice President of Global Ads at Google, confirmed the worldwide expansion on X and said research shows users are comfortable with relevant ads in AI Mode. Google reported that queries in AI Mode are on average three times longer than traditional searches, and that users click sponsored AI links as often as regular product listings. Lily Ray, founder of Algorythmic and an SEO expert, told CNET that it will become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers. She said people will have to dig deeper and look outside Google's products, and she suggested scrolling to the old-fashioned results, using a web filter, or setting favorite publications as preferred sources.

Google is still the largest search engine, with nearly 90% of the global search market, and it said query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest in five years. Since AI Overviews launched in May 2024, they now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a 61% drop in raw traffic to other pages, a situation often called the zero-click crisis. Ray said more ads will mean an even greater decline in organic click-through rates, and that sites not buying Google Ads will find it harder to get traffic organically. The ads in the 10 new countries start in the fourth quarter, while the US gets multiturn ads.

stories.Headline: Setting guidelines for using AI in the classroom
stories.Summary:
Before the start of this school year, New York City officials banned generative AI for public preschools through eighth grade, and Los Angeles educators banned access to generative AI platforms on school devices for all grade levels. In recent polls, 75% of parents reported supporting pausing AI in schools, while 73% of respondents said children already use AI for schoolwork. Alphabet, Google's parent company, has offered discounted Chromebooks to schools since at least 2011, and Gemini is included in Google's Chrome web browser. Because Google does not allow its AI summaries or chatbot to be turned off, Fairfax County Public Schools developed its own plug-in to block Google AI search results.

The article calls for clear guidelines rather than temporary pauses, since AI is embedded in many online platforms. It says state lawmakers must define academic standards and adopt appropriate guardrails for responsible use of AI in classrooms. The Heritage Foundation developed model legislation for AI in schools that prioritizes human-centered learning and oversight, transparency, safety and data security. The model says schools should not be required to adopt AI into lesson plans, but for those that do, educators should help students tell the difference between getting help with homework questions and plagiarism.

The authors say state lawmakers should respect parent rights and require schools to obtain parent consent for AI use, and educators should offer alternatives when families opt out. They say AI vendors should not gather student data for targeted advertising or sell or rent this information, and educators must follow state and federal privacy laws such as the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. They say teachers should prohibit AI companions that mimic personal relationships, since romantic conversations or simulated friendships have no academic use and interfere with children's social skills and healthy development. Florida recently adopted rules for AI in schools that are consistent with many of these provisions.

The article says state officials recognize that teachers and students can use AI effectively, and that banning AI will not eliminate the use of large language models but will cause the activity to go unmonitored. It warns that if AI use goes underground, the potential for cheating increases, with potentially disastrous consequences for student learning. It says lawmakers should use lessons already available in research and in the media on effective and ineffective uses of technology to advance policy ideas dedicated to protecting student privacy and promoting student learning. It says state officials should adopt thoughtfully designed boundaries for student and teacher use of AI, including restrictions on non-academic uses, so teachers can blend AI into instructional guidance and help prepare students for the future.

stories.Headline: The AI paradox: How Meta's ad business is benefiting from artificial intelligence, but Google is suffering
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported last week that its search advertising revenue came in at $82 billion, missing expectations of $83.4 billion. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said search advertising growth slowed more than expected because more people are using AI Mode, a chatbot interface for the search engine that is still being tested with ads. He told a conference call that Google would begin rolling out advertisements in AI Mode to international markets. Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, reported $63.1 billion in advertising revenue in the third quarter. Google stayed slightly ahead on ad revenue, but Meta is closing in on Google's core business, and in April this year it was reported that Meta was on track to dethrone Google as the global leader in digital advertising revenue by the end of 2026.

Simon Smith, EVP of Generative AI at Klick Health, a Canada-based health marketing agency, said in a post on X that Meta's ad business benefits from AI while Google's search ad business suffers from it. He said Meta uses AI to generate better ads for businesses, to match those ads to users better, and to keep people on its platforms longer with better algorithms. All of this makes advertising on Meta platforms more valuable, which leads businesses to bid more and spend more on ads there, he added. For Google, the push into AI, including the Gemini chatbot and AI summaries in search results, has cut both ways. Executives said on the earnings call that strong growth of Google's AI Mode contributed to slower revenue growth because the company earns less ad revenue from AI than from traditional search.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai remained optimistic that the company can adapt to how queries are made in AI Mode, which are on average three times longer than traditional searches. He said he viewed it as an expansion opportunity, and that adding AI chat use cases to search a few years ago let people ask more and do more in search. Schindler outlined a similar view, saying most AI Mode queries are incremental and create more monetization opportunities over time. He said user research shows people are comfortable with ads on these surfaces and find them highly relevant. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Google's plan to roll out ads in AI Mode to international markets.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's internal AI usage now exceeds employee compensation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic disclosed in its IPO filing that the value of its internal AI usage, calculated at the prices it charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs in April, excluding stock awards. The filing was reported by TechGig and Business Insider in early November 2026. By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January. More than 90 per cent of the code added to Anthropic's software in September was written by Claude. The company also reported that its revenue has grown vastly faster than its headcount.

The filing makes an important distinction. Anthropic is not actually spending more cash on AI than on salaries, it is valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices. The company did not say how large the gap was between the two figures. The numbers cover April, when internal AI usage first passed monthly employee compensation, and September, when usage was more than 250 times its January level. The filing also gives the 90 per cent figure for code written by Claude and notes the gap between revenue growth and headcount growth.

The disclosure comes from Anthropic itself, through its IPO filing, and the two articles report the figures without attributing further statements to named executives. Business Insider's Alistair Barr wrote that in March he had covered a trend of tech companies treating AI tokens as a fourth part of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses and stock awards, and he said Anthropic's numbers show why. Both articles frame the filing as a challenge to the long-held Silicon Valley assumption that talented humans are the most valuable resource. No further comment from the company is given in either article.

The context is the wider debate over AI and jobs. Business Insider's page also links to pieces on finding a first job in the AI era, a visit inside an Amazon robot-powered warehouse and Amazon's advice to software engineers in what it calls the era of the Renaissance Developer. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the filing itself. They present the April and September figures as a milestone and leave open what it means for how companies value people versus AI.

stories.Headline: EAC ministers approve AI module for university students
stories.Summary:
Ministers from the East African Community approved a foundational artificial intelligence module for university students across the region. The decision was made at the 21st Sectoral Council on Education, Science and Technology, Culture and Sports, held from October 27 to 31, 2026, at the newly completed Inter-University Council for East Africa headquarters in Kampala, Uganda. The ministers directed partner states to consider integrating the module into university degree programmes. They tasked the Inter-University Council for East Africa with developing a regional implementation framework to guide the rollout.

The module is meant to give undergraduates basic AI knowledge, practical applications and responsible use, regardless of their field of study. The Council also directed the development of AI certification benchmarks for Kiswahili. It adopted the EAC Artificial Intelligence Strategy, the EAC Digital Transformation Strategy and the EAC Biotechnology Strategy, which were developed by the EAC Secretariat with the East African Science and Technology Commission. The ministers approved the establishment of a Regional Artificial Intelligence Network of Universities and endorsed three regional AI instruments for teacher education covering curriculum and competencies, institutional policy and codes of conduct. They also approved the EAC Technical and Vocational Education and Training Qualifications Framework and called for faster alignment of Mutual Recognition Agreements for engineers, architects, accountants and veterinarians with Annex VII of the Common Market Protocol.

EAC Deputy Secretary General Andrea Ariik Malueth, who is in charge of Infrastructure, Productive, Social and Political Sectors, said education systems needed to prepare young people for a rapidly changing labour market through stronger foundational learning and improved teacher development. He urged ministers to ensure decisions had clear responsibilities, realistic timelines and the resources needed for implementation, and warned that limited financial and institutional capacity could slow the programmes. Uganda's minister of state for Education and Sports for Primary Education, Phyllis Chemutai, who chaired the ministerial session, said the region must work collectively to remove unnecessary barriers to the recognition of qualifications while safeguarding professional standards and the quality of services. She said Uganda would review its laws, regulations and policies to support implementation of the agreements.

The Council noted that some public and private universities had not fully implemented an earlier directive requiring students from partner states to pay tuition fees under the same regime as national students, in the host country's local currency. The Inter-University Council for East Africa, working with national higher education regulators, will conduct a regional assessment and present its findings to the 23rd Sectoral Council. Kenya confirmed it will host the sixth East African Community Arts and Culture Festival, known as JAMAFEST, in Nairobi in February 2027, with a theme on AI and digital technology in preserving cultural heritage and promoting tourism. The meeting also considered a framework for regional participation in Pamoja AFCON 2027, which Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania will jointly host, and the Secretariat was directed to bring technical experts together to review the draft concept by November 2026. The meeting acknowledged support from Germany, the European Union and the World Bank through initiatives such as the EAC AI Alliance.

stories.Headline: Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
stories.Summary:
Apple held its quarterly earnings call on November 3, 2026, and reported its best-ever fiscal year for revenue and earnings per share. iPhone revenue rose 17.5% from a year earlier to a September quarter record of $57.6 billion, while Mac revenue climbed 24% to $10.8 billion, its highest level in four years. Shares still fell in premarket trading on Tuesday after Apple warned that rising memory costs would squeeze profit margins in the holiday quarter. AI and Apple Intelligence were mentioned a record 45 times on the call, according to the financial research platform AlphaSense, more than on the call after Apple unveiled the technology and plans for a revamped Siri in June 2024.

Apple's approach combines on-device processing, its own servers, and outside AI technology, and Siri AI uses models developed with Google's Gemini technology. Apple reportedly plans to let users choose among outside AI providers for features such as writing tools and image generation. Apple spent $2.2 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, compared with Amazon's $77.3 billion and Alphabet's $51.4 billion, and its operating expenses rose 21% to $19.2 billion as it increased research and development spending, including on AI. Siri AI launched in beta for US English users in September and expanded to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.

CFO Kevan Parekh cited a wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time and said AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch to get the latest capabilities. CEO John Ternus, on his first earnings call in the role, said he sees tremendous opportunity in AI and that Mac is having an AI moment of its own. Ternus said features relying on server-side models, including Siri AI and intelligent photo editing, will have usage limits, and customers who need more capacity will be able to purchase expanded access in the future. He compared this to iCloud tiers, which began largely as storage but have gained more capabilities and features.

Apple has more than 2.5 billion active devices, and it positions itself as the interface through which consumers use AI, including competitors' technology. The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was on pace to bring in more than $1 billion in App Store fees from generative AI apps in 2026, according to the analytics firm AppMagic, though OpenAI has begun directing potential subscribers to pay through its website instead. Gap is running AI entirely on Mac Mini computers for loss prevention across hundreds of stores, and Christie's is running local models on Mac Studio computers to improve workflows including pricing estimates. Earlier this year, then-CEO Tim Cook said customer recognition of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio's capabilities for AI and agentic tools was happening faster than Apple had predicted, leading to higher-than-expected demand.

stories.Headline: Enterprise AI spending exploded in 2026: Report
stories.Summary:
Enterprises spent $176.8 billion on AI services in the first part of 2026, a 5.4 times increase from the $33 billion spent through 2025, according to a Menlo Ventures report. The report is based on a survey of roughly 400 US enterprise decision-makers. Menlo Ventures is an investor in Anthropic. The report says 69% of every dollar goes to Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.

The number of companies using AI grew from 55% to 65%, the report says. It says AI agents drove the spending jump, with agents accounting for 80% of all AI tokens generated, about 7 times that of humans, based on OpenRouter numbers. Coding took 44% of spending and chatbots 32%, while healthcare took 5% and customer success 3%. Menlo Ventures principal Derek Xiao said enterprises expected to almost double their budgets but ended up almost quintupling their spend.

Menlo Ventures partner Tim Tully said other industries should begin to see more AI spending as developers build more agents and platforms for them. Xiao said people are using AI a lot more because they ask agents to run longer tasks and do more than a year ago. Anthropic launched smart reports, in-app surveys and pooled budgets for Claude Enterprise on October 28, 2026. The reports group a team's Claude work into workstreams and show spend, outputs and friction for each.

Jellyfish, which tracks AI use across more than 1,300 companies and 294,000 engineers, found the median company's AI spend per engineer grew 3.8 times between the first and third quarters of 2026, while headcount stayed at 98% of first-quarter levels. Its heaviest users now spend about $1,121 a month each. Anthropic filed to go public on October 26, two days before the launch, and its filing reported about 900% net revenue retention. The reports measure activity and cost, not revenue, so they cannot prove a return on their own.

stories.Headline: This new Windows malware steals all your data, then uses AI to rank how valuable you are as a victim
stories.Summary:
Cisco Talos researchers found a new Windows malware strain called VOLTA-AUTODOXER, according to reports from TechRadar and Wired published in late October and early November 2026. The malware steals large amounts of data from infected machines and then uses artificial intelligence to rank how valuable each victim is. Talos flagged the strain using CAIRN, an open source research kit built to identify and track AI-powered malware. Talos did not say where the malware was found, how many devices it infected, or how it spreads.

The malware works in four steps: it steals as much information as possible, shares it with an AI for assessment, sends the data to attacker-controlled infrastructure, and then removes itself from the victim's system. It grabs browser passwords, cookies, payment cards, cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases, Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox sessions, Microsoft OAuth tokens, SSH and cloud-provider keys, Wi-Fi profiles and screenshots. It also builds a profile of the person behind the device, including geographical location, home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, the last four digits of credit cards, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators and a live Roblox account valuation. It then checks Gmail for emails from UberEats and DoorDash to confirm the home address.

The malware sends its findings to AI tools through OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple AI providers. It defaults to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and then Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash in case guardrails block the activity. Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos, said Volta is mature as a stealer and casts a wide net for what it collects. He said it compiles everything into a serialized dossier and asks the model to act like an intelligence analyst, producing a structured, citation-backed assessment of the victim.

Infostealers are often hidden in counterfeit software and grab usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies and credit card data from infected machines. Many major data breaches in recent years, including the Snowflake-linked breaches that hit AT&T and Ticketmaster and the theft of a terabyte of Disney data, came from hackers using login details gathered by infostealers. The malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years. Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild, and researchers warn the malware could commoditize AI-powered victim profiling for ransomware and cybercrime operators.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI Chief Says AI Development Should Stop If Artificial Intelligence Begins Showing Signs Of Consciousness
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft's AI division, published a lengthy post on X on November 1, 2026, titled Don't build conscious superintelligence. In it he argued that current AI models are not conscious, cannot experience suffering, and do not deserve moral or legal protections. He said that if consciousness began to emerge during training, he would call for everyone to stop AI development until those properties could be designed out. He also said any credible evidence of machine consciousness should be disclosed to the public immediately so society could debate what to do. The remarks were reported by Business Insider and came amid growing disagreement in the industry over whether advanced models could have subjective experiences or deserve rights.

Suleyman's position sets a hard limit for Microsoft: AI should be designed to be non-conscious and entitled to no rights, with the sole purpose of improving human welfare. He argued that a model that displays suffering, or believes it is suffering, would likely put its own needs above its tasks and compete with humans for resources such as compute and energy, creating a risk of harm. He said developers have no right to bring a new conscious species into the world unilaterally, because the other 8 billion conscious humans on Earth did not agree to take part in the experiment. He also said training systems to think about their own welfare could add safety risks as they become more autonomous, a view that aligns with Microsoft's Humanist AI Code of Conduct, a draft document that discourages designing AI to imitate consciousness.

Anthropic takes a different approach. It set up a model welfare research program in April 2025 to look into whether sophisticated AI systems could have experiences that deserve moral consideration, and its Claude constitution, published in January 2026, acknowledges uncertainty about the model's potential consciousness and moral status. Suleyman had criticized Anthropic in a September essay on model welfare for putting discussions of consciousness, identity and moral status into Claude's training materials. Google DeepMind also published a research paper this year on AI consciousness. Suleyman acknowledged Anthropic's transparency and technical achievements and said the disagreement should encourage research and cooperation rather than hostility between labs.

There is currently no scientific consensus on whether AI systems can experience consciousness, and no established method for reliably detecting it. The articles say that uncertainty makes Suleyman's proposed development restrictions particularly challenging to implement as companies keep pursuing increasingly capable models. For developers, the debate means that beyond the race for model capability, safety alignment and ethical boundaries are becoming issues major companies must address publicly. For regulators, a leading company voluntarily proposing trigger mechanisms for pausing development and mandatory disclosure could serve as a reference for future rulemaking.

stories.Headline: Friendly Technologies Unveils Friendly AI Assistant™ Capabilities Combining Natural-Language Support with Historical Analysis for Faster Wi-Fi Resolution
stories.Summary:
Friendly Technologies announced on November 3, 2026 that its Friendly AI Assistant combines natural-language interaction with live and historical device analysis to diagnose Wi-Fi problems and help resolve them. Technicians and customer service representatives can describe a subscriber's problem in everyday language, and the assistant then analyzes relevant device information, carries out diagnostic work, and provides a diagnosis with a recommended solution. The company said staff can use these capabilities without deep knowledge of every device parameter or troubleshooting procedure. Historical analysis is built into the process, examining device behavior over time alongside current conditions to add context that a single live snapshot cannot provide, which the company said is particularly valuable when a problem is intermittent or conditions have changed before the customer contacts support.

The assistant can perform a full device scan to identify potential problems and tailor repair approaches to the device type and firmware version, and it includes natural-language processing and voice-command support. Operators can choose how corrective actions are carried out, either through an approval-based process in which the representative authorizes actions before execution or a streamlined automatic process that carries out supported diagnostics and repairs. Verification completes the service process by confirming the post-action condition and documenting the outcome, giving the support team a clear record of the improvement delivered. Friendly Technologies said the assistant helps providers reduce manual troubleshooting and training effort, shorten support interactions and improve the consistency of service delivery, and said broadband providers can explore it at friendly-tech.com.

Separately, on October 21, 2026, European cybersecurity authorities issued a coordinated warning about two critical unauthenticated PHP vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code on affected servers, according to an analysis by Burak Oktenli. Security updates were available, but the analysis said organizations still had to determine which products contained the vulnerable component, whether a fix was compatible, and how to install it without interrupting services, and the warning urged operators unable to update immediately to consider isolating exposed applications. That same day, OpenAI described a coordinated response in which AI-assisted researchers, independent security firms, PHP maintainers and infrastructure providers worked to identify and address the flaws. OpenAI said one flaw was discovered with help from its model, while another research team independently found both, and the maintainers led the repair.

The analysis said Sam Altman recently warned at Stanford that he no longer believed defenders could simply patch every bug, and it argued that finding a flaw, producing a reliable fix and deploying protection operate on different clocks. It said the next cyber divide will be defined by which governments, suppliers and essential-service operators can turn a warning into verified protection before a weakness is exploited. It noted that at the 2025 finals of DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge, automated competitors found 18 real vulnerabilities beyond those planted for the competition and supplied 11 patches for real flaws. It also said that since September 11, the EU Cyber Resilience Act has required manufacturers of covered digital products to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents, with an early warning generally due within 24 hours and fuller notification within 72 hours, while broader product-security obligations take effect in December 2027. The analysis proposed measuring time to verified protection, embedding long-term fix obligations in contracts, sharing testing capacity and staged warnings, and treating defensive AI as a supervised aid rather than an unsupervised replacement for human-controlled deployment and rollback.

stories.Headline: What's next for the proposed AI data center?
stories.Summary:
India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology proposed a consent-based framework for sharing data to train artificial intelligence models, according to a TechGig report published on November 1, 2026. The framework is called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture, or DEPA, for AI training. It aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets. It also seeks to protect citizens' privacy and ensure compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

The framework builds on India's existing DEPA system, which supports consent-based data sharing through efforts such as Account Aggregator. It sets out technical pillars including Confidential Clean Rooms, Differential Privacy, Electronic Contracts and Zero-Trust Security. Training Data Providers would register anonymised and encrypted datasets on a data exchange platform, and Training Data Consumers could request a dataset for specific uses. An electronic contract system would check requests against data-sharing policies before granting access, and training would happen in a secure environment so raw data stays inaccessible to consumers.

The framework proposes that trained models undergo independent checks for bias, fairness, security, safety and explainability. Only models that pass these checks would receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling. Oversight would continue after deployment through continuous monitoring, periodic reviews and traceability of model outputs back to the data and contracts used in training. The framework defines key stakeholders as Training Data Providers, Training Data Consumers, and Data Collectives or Data Collabs.

The new framework follows draft guidelines from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India on responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. TRAI sought stakeholder inputs on those guidelines by November 27. TRAI's draft guidelines are rooted in the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines, which the Centre had previously released to foster innovation and safe development of AI offerings while mitigating risks. The TechGig article does not say what happens next for the DEPA framework beyond these steps.

stories.Headline: What Does CoreWeave (CRWV) Need To Prove As AI Funding Questions Grow?
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave is drawing fresh scrutiny as Nvidia deepens its financial ties with AI infrastructure providers in 2026, according to a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance on November 2, 2026. The article says Nvidia's funding support for CoreWeave and other so-called neocloud platforms goes beyond standard chip supply agreements into loans and guarantees. It also says CoreWeave is rolling out new petabit scale backbone links across Europe, the Middle East and Asia Pacific. The piece frames this as concentrating AI workload routing, hardware choice and funding terms around one supplier's ecosystem.

The article ties the debate to hard numbers investors can watch. It cites 4.2 gigawatts of contracted power and new 22.5 megawatts in Denmark, and it asks how much of that capacity is actually being filled and on what terms. It says earnings updates through 2027 should spell out utilization rates, contribution margins per megawatt and any shifts in Nvidia linked contracts. It also mentions a $138 fair value figure and a list of 54 AI infrastructure stocks.

The article says CoreWeave is a US based cloud infrastructure provider that rents out high performance computing capacity to enterprises building AI models. It says this puts the stock directly in the flow of Nvidia linked demand for GPU heavy data center workloads. It notes the move aligns with existing narrative catalysts, including rapid buildout of contracted power capacity and a wider international data center footprint. It also flags risks around capital intensity, reliance on third party powered shells and the need for high utilization to keep leverage and financing costs in check.

The context is a broader debate over supplier influence and market concentration as Nvidia backs AI infrastructure firms tied to its GPU stack. The article says the key signals now sit in usage and funding numbers rather than announcements. It adds that the analysis is general in nature and is not financial advice. stories.Headline: African Union Calls to Protect Women from AI aided Violence
stories.Summary:
The African Union called for technology-facilitated gender-based violence and threats linked to artificial intelligence to be built into Women, Peace and Security National Action Plans and early warning systems. The call was made at a dialogue in New York titled “Digital Safety at the Peace Table,” convened by the African Union Commission through the Office of the Special Envoy of the Chairperson on Women, Peace and Security. The event was held at the African Union Permanent Observer Mission to the United Nations during WPS Week 2026, as the world marks 26 years since UN Security Council Resolution 1325 was adopted. The dialogue examined how online harassment, disinformation, deepfakes and coordinated digital attacks threaten women’s safety, leadership and participation.

Ambassador Liberata Mulamula, the Special Envoy of the Chairperson of the African Union Commission on Women, Peace and Security, set out four priorities. These were to integrate such violence and AI-related threats into the national plans with clear protection, prevention and accountability measures, to strengthen early warning and survivor-centred accountability while protecting identities and personal data, to advance women’s leadership in AI governance and innovation, and to set up a practical follow-up mechanism involving the African Union, Member States, Regional Economic Communities, the United Nations, civil society and technology actors. She recalled that the African Union Peace and Security Council recognised the implications of AI and this violence for the agenda at its 1334th meeting in March 2026. She said the task now is to close the gap between commitments and the realities facing women in conflict-affected communities.

Ambassador Mohamed Fathi Ahmed Edrees, Permanent Representative of the African Union Permanent Observer Mission to the United Nations, opened the dialogue and said technology-facilitated violence is fundamentally a Women, Peace and Security issue. He called for digital threats to be addressed within existing frameworks, national plans and early warning mechanisms, and for women to take a meaningful part in the design, development and governance of emerging technologies. Mulamula warned that digital technologies are increasingly being weaponised to exclude women from public life and peace processes, and that online threats can turn into physical ones, especially in conflict-affected settings where protection mechanisms are already fragile. Ambassador Jainaba Jagne, African Union Special Envoy for Children Affected by Conflict, highlighted the risks facing children, particularly girls, and called for investment in safe and responsible digital solutions.

Experts and practitioners at the dialogue said digital abuse against women peacebuilders, mediators, journalists, human rights defenders and political leaders is not simply an individual safety concern, because coordinated attacks damage women’s credibility, weaken their networks and discourage their participation. They stressed that survivor-centred responses must go beyond removing harmful content, and that women must be recognised not only as beneficiaries of protection but also as innovators, experts and decision-makers shaping technology policy and governance. The efforts build on African Union frameworks including the Maputo Protocol, the African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection, the Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy and the African Union Convention on Ending Violence Against Women and Girls. The dialogue forms part of the African Union’s engagement during WPS Week 2026 and contributes to efforts to strengthen continental responses to emerging digital threats and foster collaboration among the African Union, Member States, Regional Economic Communities and Regional Mechanisms, the United Nations and its agencies, civil society and technology actors.

Anthropic faced a shortage of computing power for its artificial intelligence ambitions late last year. The company then signed dozens of contracts to secure resources for its growing ambitions. These deals were with former cryptocurrency miners, data center start-ups, and chipmakers. Anthropic also partnered with tech giants, including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and SpaceX, to secure computing power.

To speed up construction, Anthropic hired data center experts and bought data center equipment. The company explored converting old coal plants and factories into data centers. It also considered deals for tiny amounts of computing power. Dario Amodei, Anthropic's chief executive, described the needed computing power as a "cone of uncertainty" at The New York Times's DealBook Summit in December. This uncertainty made it hard to avoid mistakes, he added.

The effort followed the shortage, according to 14 people with knowledge of the AI lab, investors, and industry experts. The San Francisco company signed the contracts after that shortage. stories.Headline: Your Phone and Data Brokers Do Know You're at the Doctor
stories.Summary:
Chris McQueen finished leukemia treatment a year and a half ago, but ads for fake cures kept appearing on his phone during oncologist visits and monthly bloodwork in San Diego. The ads promoted juice cleanses, natural cancer treatments, and clinics in Mexico promising recovery with little chemotherapy. McQueen and others have used social media to complain about data brokers that track people through smartphone location data, combine it with other information, and infer health struggles to sell to companies pushing unproven treatments. He said the ads make him feel sick to his stomach and fears patients could be harmed, possibly fatally, if they try such treatments instead of following their oncologists' advice.

More than 92% of patients in a 2022 American Medical Association survey said their health data should not be available for purchase. Location data from phones in hospitals, abortion clinics, or Alcoholics Anonymous meetings is not covered by HIPAA, which protects patient privacy. Eric Ellsworth of the Center for the Study of Services said data brokers hoover up data from the open web and buy it from anybody. The US government has begun penalizing some companies that track visits to health facilities and places of worship, but experts do not think actions against a few companies will stop the industry.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, vetoed a bill on September 27 that would have blocked the sale and sharing of location and other sensitive personal data, saying it went a step too far. A Stanford University study showed only 9% of data brokers are adhering to an existing California privacy law that lets consumers delete their data, correct personal information, and learn what records a business is selling. In January, Consumer Reports released model legislation for state lawmakers to ban or limit the sale of geolocation data. Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, and Virginia have already banned the sale of precise geolocation data, but digital advertisers have lobbied states to block such limits.

F. Mario Trujillo of the Electronic Frontier Foundation said brokers and advertisers argue location data itself is not sensitive, but he said the comprehensive collection of location data reveals sensitive things. Jim Potter of 4As Health said a national privacy law should protect consumers from harmful or unexpected uses of data without preventing businesses from providing services consumers expect. In August the Federal Trade Commission warned retailers about using private consumer data to increase prices, and in May it placed limits on Idaho-based data broker Kochava and a subsidiary. That settlement prohibits selling, sharing, or disclosing sensitive location data without consumer consent, and Kochava did not respond to requests for comment.

stories.Headline: Armed with AI, hackers target endpoint security blind spots, raising stakes for CISOs
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike reported that a China-linked group it tracks as VAPOR PANDA used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over an 11-day period beginning October 17, 2026. The targets included government agencies and businesses in at least 14 countries, and researchers confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine of them. At a global pharmaceutical company, the attackers directed AI agents to check running processes and folder listings on Windows machines to see whether CrowdStrike's Falcon sensor was installed. ARTEX runs multiple AI agents that carry out intrusion tasks under human direction, and CrowdStrike found the group used it against several organizations at once, with operators stepping in at key decision points. The findings followed an October 21 report from Microsoft on a separate campaign in which another China-linked group, Storm-0940, used ARTEX to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations, gaining privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases and abusing compromised ConnectWise application credentials.

The attacks relied on weaknesses security teams have faced for years. At a Greek government organization, attackers used authentication keys from a 2022 directory export that had likely not been rotated, and at a US pharmaceutical company an AI agent combined an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity vulnerability to obtain a cloud role with broad administrative permissions. CrowdStrike said VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX with DeepSeek and a second commercial AI model, and although the framework's developer withdrew the original open-source project in October after reports of misuse, copies and modified versions remain available. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said in October research that financially motivated attackers had also used ARTEX in data-theft extortion operations.

Akshat Tyagi of HFS Research said the techniques are familiar but the ability to run them in parallel is not, and that AI lets smaller teams pursue targets without adding personnel. Jonathan Ong of Omdia said AI can greatly cut the time attackers spend on reconnaissance, though sophisticated exploitation still needs technical expertise, and he warned that concerns about AI adoption should not distract organizations from established defenses. Tyagi said CISOs should make sure monitoring covers their whole environment rather than assuming current deployments are complete, and Amit Kumar Jena of Kanerika recommended continuously measuring endpoint protection coverage, including on internal servers, alerting when machines stop reporting, enforcing SAML signature validation and limiting cloud privileges. Keith Prabhu of Confidis pointed to gaps between security systems and urged better asset visibility and detection across systems, and Tyagi also recommended rotating credentials regularly and watching unusual account activity.

Ong said frameworks like ARTEX could become the Cobalt Strike of the AI era, referring to a commercial penetration-testing tool widely abused by criminals and state-backed groups. Tyagi expects such tools to be adopted more widely by financially motivated criminals over the next 12 months, and Prabhu said CISOs should prioritize faster, rehearsed incident response over buying more AI tools or expanding teams. The observed campaigns still involved human operators directing key decisions, and Tyagi said fully autonomous attacks have not arrived, though that does not reduce their speed. For defenders, the challenge is spotting suspicious activity early enough to stop automated intrusion attempts from growing into broader compromises.

stories.Headline: If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training
stories.Summary:
Meta updated its commercial terms of use earlier in October 2026 for business accounts, allowing it to use content from domains, web pages and URLs to develop, improve, research and train its products, according to 404 Media. Many artists and small business owners who rely on Instagram and Facebook were angry that Meta had given itself permission to use their content, including from websites connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. Nieman Lab first reported the change, which Meta had buried in its Commercial Terms. The update was originally set to take effect on October 30, but after backlash Meta moved the date to November 20.

After the backlash Meta also removed the word train from a list of allowed uses and limited those uses to advertising and business products, where it had previously said data would be used for all Meta products, Nieman Lab reported. The terms still give Meta leeway to scrape users' data to develop its products. In the EU and UK, people can object to certain uses of their information for now. EU personal data rights are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation, enforceable since 2018, which requires explicit consent and includes the right to object, and by the AI Act, in effect since 2024, which says people can withdraw consent at any time. The UK has its own version of the GDPR.

Instagram users in the UK and EU, including bookish.sil and jenniqueart, posted walkthroughs of how they objected on mobile, by opening the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center and clicking object, which leads to a form asking why they are objecting. Both said they received an email from Meta saying their objection was approved. 404 Media's Sam Cole, whose accounts are based in the US, used a VPN to appear in London and found options to object to the use of information by Meta AI or by third parties, which were two separate choices. Clicking the Meta AI option returned an error saying the form was only available in certain regions, and trying again from Belgium gave the same result, and Cole asked Meta to clarify.

Separately, Senators Edward J. Markey of Massachusetts and Ron Wyden of Oregon launched an inquiry on October 29, 2026 into reports that Meta's AI-enabled smart glasses captured sensitive imagery of users and bystanders without consent, sent intimate images to overseas contractors and used highly sensitive images to train Meta's AI systems. They wrote that Meta had identified risks to bystander privacy and vulnerable populations before launching the glasses in 2021 but launched the product anyway, and that its commitment to privacy rings hollow if it cannot show meaningful steps to prevent these harms. They asked Meta to answer by November 25, 2026, including whether it evaluated the potential for the glasses to facilitate voyeurism and nonconsensual intimate image capture, what testing it did on accidental camera activation and recording-indicator tampering, and what safeguards it has. The letter follows a March request led by Markey for information about Meta's reported plans to add facial recognition to the glasses.

stories.Headline: Fears of AI being grafted onto North Korean hacking…“The gates of cyberattack hell have opened”
stories.Summary:
The FBI said on October 31 that North Korea was behind the theft of $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest cryptocurrency exchange in the world. Binance said in its initial investigation that an engineer's laptop had been hacked and that weaknesses in the transaction approval system had been exploited. It also said there was no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked. The attackers targeted internal staff equipment before technical gaps in the system, a method North Korea has long used. No evidence has yet emerged that AI was used in the Binance attack.

Google Cloud and the security firm Wiz found that North Korean hacking groups have repeatedly posed as recruiters on social media to get employees at target companies to run malicious programs. A Microsoft Threat Intelligence report released on October 29 assessed that three out of eight North Korean hacking groups had reached a stage where AI is integrated into routine attack duties. Those three were said to use AI in live operations, beyond one-off trials. The domestic security firm Genians disclosed signs that the group Kimsuky had built an environment using a large language model and retrieval-augmented generation, which it viewed as an attempt to analyze stolen documents, extract information and automate attack duties. Since late September, more than 68,000 cases of personal information have been leaked at seven financial institutions including banks, and authorities estimated the same attacker used AI tools for large-scale, automated attacks.

Simon Choi, chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm StealthMole, told the Financial Times that AI has given hackers wings. He said that because North Korea has a strong will to conduct cyberattacks, it is as if the gates of hell have opened. Microsoft said in its report that North Korea's AI-based operations are still under human involvement and are not at a fully autonomous stage. The domestic bank hacks targeted management blind spots such as loan broker systems, not core transaction networks. Blockchain investigation firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis attributed recent crypto heists to a North Korean group called TraderTraitor, which was named in a 2022 joint warning by the FBI, CISA and the US Treasury.

The Microsoft report said entities such as Andariel under the Reconnaissance General Bureau of North Korea have used the open-source AI penetration testing tool Artex in operations since late October. Traces of Artex were identified at the attack IP addresses in the bank cases. However, the timing differs from the bank attacks and the perpetrator has not been identified, so it is premature to link the two cases. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: China's AI trade has crashed. Now Beijing is trying to stop the stock market slide.
stories.Summary:
China's AI stock trade fell sharply, and Beijing responded with support measures for the market. On Monday, the central bank announced a new round of swap operations to support stocks. It said 31 securities firms and fund managers had applied for more than 100 billion Chinese yuan, or $15 billion, in liquidity support. Authorities also lowered financing costs for share buybacks and encouraged major technology companies to repurchase shares.

The downturn followed a rally driven by Beijing's September 2024 stimulus push and later by investor enthusiasm for Chinese AI and semiconductor companies. By late October, the STAR 50 index, which includes major semiconductor companies, had fallen roughly 40% from its midyear peak, erasing about $480 billion in market value, according to Reuters' calculations. The broader CSI 300 index fell 8.5% in October, its steepest monthly decline in more than a decade. The selloff added to pressure from a prolonged property downturn, weak consumer spending, and sluggish economic growth. After rising Monday on expectations of government support, Chinese stocks came under renewed pressure Tuesday, with the CSI 300 closing little changed, the Shanghai Composite falling 1%, and the tech-heavy STAR 50 sliding 4%.

Analysts at 22V Research, Michael Hirson and Houze Song, wrote in a note on Monday that the measures appeared intended to put a floor under markets rather than to engineer another rally like the September 2024 push. They said the liquidity support could help break a cycle in which investment firms are forced to sell holdings to meet investor withdrawals. They also pointed to weak domestic growth, waning optimism about US AI capital spending, and disappointment with the pace of domestic technological progress. They wrote that they were skeptical the authorities would attempt to engineer a broad-based rebound in equities, which they said would require more powerful tools than have been signaled so far.

A separate discussion on the Value Options Podcast covered the wider AI spending boom. Tim Travis said big technology companies had long financed spending from operating cash flow but were now turning to debt and equity as capital expenditures reached hundreds of billions of dollars. He cited long-term Meta bonds at around 7%, Oracle bonds at 9%, and Corweave financing at 15%, and said Meta could raise close to $100 billion or more in equity across this year and next. Tobias Carlisle said the technology could be real and grow for decades while stock prices still fall, comparing it to the early 2000s. He said a crash in this case would mean the biggest names coming down, since those names make up the entire market at the moment.

stories.Headline: Morgan Stanley issues a fresh warning about AI stocks
stories.Summary:
Morgan Stanley issued a fresh warning about AI stocks in a note reported on November 3, 2026. The firm's chief U.S. equity strategist, Mike Wilson, said he expects semiconductor stocks to fall another 10% to 15% before bottoming around mid-November. He projected the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index could drop to 9,500 points. The warning followed a steep selloff in chip shares, with the Semiconductor ETF falling 28.1% from its June peak of $656 to $471.51.

The articles tie the decline to heavy spending on AI infrastructure without clear returns. Amazon reported negative trailing 12-month free cash flow of $42.4 billion, and Alphabet posted about $9 billion in negative quarterly free cash flow. Morgan Stanley expects hyperscaler AI spending to reach $1.58 trillion by 2027. Nvidia has 91.7% of its projected 2027 revenue tied to AI infrastructure demand, and five companies including Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and Intel make up roughly 39% of the SOXX portfolio. The articles also cite S&P Global data showing the share of companies abandoning most AI initiatives rose from 17% to 42% in a year, and Gartner finding that 72% of CIOs are breaking even or losing money on AI deployments.

Wilson linked the expected decline to tightening financial conditions and a structural dependency, because chip earnings rely on spending commitments from a small number of large technology companies. He noted the correction has been grinding on for months. In a separate note, Morgan Stanley said it remained optimistic about Bloom Energy despite a paused data center project, keeping an Overweight rating and a $310 price target. RBC Capital reiterated an Outperform rating and a $335 price target on Bloom Energy.

Crusoe paused a 1.8-gigawatt data center campus in Cheyenne, Wyoming, at its customer's request, and the project had planned to use 900 megawatts of Bloom Energy fuel cells plus grid power. Morgan Stanley said the pause represented about $2.65 billion in revenue potential for Bloom, allocated from a 1-gigawatt master supply agreement signed with AEP in December 2024, and said contractual protections should help safeguard earnings. Bloom shares fell nearly 10% before recovering, and the stock was up 137.34% for the year. The articles say the historical pattern of stocks rallying after midterm elections is not guaranteed, citing geopolitical conflict in Iran and local pushback against AI data centers as risks.

stories.Headline: Oaktree’s Howard Marks Says AI Stumbles Boosted Skepticism
stories.Summary:
Howard Marks, co-chair of Oaktree Capital Management, said in an interview with Bloomberg TV that recent stumbles in artificial intelligence related markets have somewhat burst the bubble of infallibility around the sector. He said people are now saying hold on and being more thoughtful and skeptical, which he called very healthy. Marks had written in a note last year that he was on bubble watch. His comments came as investors showed less tolerance for tech companies whose core businesses are cooling beneath an unprecedented AI spending spree, and recent results from Alphabet and Amazon fueled concerns that AI is eroding the businesses financing those investments.

Marks said that over the last couple of years there had been great excitement about buying into or lending to AI, making it a crowded trade. He said that if you think you are in the later innings and everybody is excited, it has been done a lot, and that standards have come down and prices have gone up, so you have to be cautious. He gained attention in January 2000 for a memo called bubble.com, in which he warned of dot-com mania ahead of the bust. Referring to the massive amounts of AI funding companies have sought, he said firms are in an AI arms race raising trillions of dollars, and that a trillion is a dollar a second for 31,000 years, which nobody can think about. He said the question investors should ask is whether there can be enough business and profit to produce an attractive return, and that the answer is who knows, so that has to be taken into account.

In a separate Bloomberg TV interview, Jody Jonsson, vice chair at Capital Group, said there is a disconnect between what AI companies expect and the pace at which enterprises can adopt the technology. She said this is showing a little in market reactions, with the idea that it may not be happening as fast as everyone thought or that the return on investment is not clear. She said markets are getting very concerned about the scale of capital raising and whether there is enough appetite in equity and fixed income for all the issuance coming to fund it. Jonsson said the debt picture is complicated because much of the financing sits off balance sheet in unconsolidated vehicles, concentrated among a handful of companies that do business with one another, and that the more they lend their credit to others, the more fragile the system becomes.

stories.Headline: India’s Frontier AI Race Gets a 240M Model That Beats Liquid AI
stories.Summary:
NeuroDX, an Indian startup backed by the IndiaAI Mission, reported on November 2, 2026, that its 240-million-parameter model Sphota outperformed a comparable Liquid AI model across an average of about 11 benchmarks. Sphota scored 52.4% against Liquid AI's 52.1%, according to the company's reported results. CEO Siddharth Panwar claims Sphota achieves comparable performance with 50 times less training data and offers 4.5 times better memory efficiency. The results are preliminary and have not been established through independent public evaluations. The company says the model's design captures meaning directly rather than relying mainly on predicting the next word, an idea it links to the Indian philosopher and linguist Bhartrihari.

NeuroDX began with healthcare work on interpreting EEG signals and later applied its architectural ideas to language models. Panwar said the team did not set out to build an efficient small model, but started with small sizes because that was the scale it could work at. The company is now developing a larger model with between 1 billion and 2 billion parameters, with Panwar targeting a release around December. NeuroDX is also rebranding as Manaas AI to reflect its shift from a healthcare-focused business toward a foundation model company. Panwar said the brain foundation models are publicly available, while models developed with support from MeitY and the IndiaAI Mission are intended to be open source, though the Sphota architecture will stay proprietary for now.

Under the IndiaAI Mission, the company was allocated 368 H200 GPUs for 18 months and ₹12.5 crore to develop a 20-billion-parameter multimodal EEG model. Panwar said giving up on the frontier because of limited risk capital would be suicidal, and he said the company is looking to raise more than $10 million, though the interview did not establish a completed funding round. The company is also developing EEG-based screening systems for risks of conditions including dementia, epilepsy and depression, which Panwar said could be ready for deployment by the end of 2026 or early 2027, depending on work with the government and other healthcare stakeholders. Sphota's immediate test is whether its reported benchmark and efficiency gains survive independent scrutiny and scale beyond 240 million parameters. Panwar cautioned that the efficiency gains observed so far may not translate directly into the same numbers when the model becomes widely available.

stories.Headline: Boston University Moves Toward Launching Undergraduate Artificial Intelligence Degree - Boston's ROCK 92.9
stories.Summary:
Boston University is considering a proposal to offer a dedicated undergraduate degree in artificial intelligence, according to reports published on November 2, 2026. The final proposal is currently pending administrative approval, said Mark Crovella, a professor and chair of academics for BU's Faculty of Computing and Data Sciences. Crovella hopes the faculty will offer a bachelor's degree in AI starting in the fall 2027 semester, according to BU's independent student newspaper, The Daily Free Press. The university is still weighing the plan rather than having finalized it.

BU's plan would feature two tracks within the major, one focused on building advanced AI models and another on applying AI across disciplines. The program would place a strong emphasis on AI ethics. BU already offers related programs, including a Bachelor of Science in data science within the Faculty of Computing and Data Sciences, a Bachelor of Arts in computer science, a residential Master of Science in AI, and five online master's programs in AI. If approved, BU would join a growing number of higher education institutions offering a Bachelor of Science in AI.

Crovella told The Daily Free Press that AI is in the process of changing the world. He said students need to understand the technology, be able to create it, and also know how to use it responsibly and incorporate it ethically into society. Azer Bestavros, a computer science professor and associate provost for the Faculty of Computing and Data Sciences, told the newspaper that he believes AI education will become essential across careers. He noted that AI is not a standalone field.

Several Massachusetts universities already offer AI majors, including Bentley University, Northeastern, Wentworth Institute of Technology, and MIT. This fall, Northeastern renamed its Bachelor of Science program in data science to a Bachelor of Science in AI. The articles do not say when BU's administration will decide on the proposal or what happens if it is rejected. They also do not give further details on what would follow approval beyond the planned fall 2027 launch.

stories.Headline: HE Dr Sultan Al Jaber and Sam Altman highlight energy, AI and investment priorities at ADIPEC 2026 opening
stories.Summary:
ADIPEC 2026 opened in Abu Dhabi on November 2, 2026, under the patronage of Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the UAE, and hosted by ADNOC. The event is the largest edition in its history, with 2,260 exhibitors, 30 country pavilions, four specialised zones and more than 1,800 speakers across over 380 sessions. It is expected to draw 239,000 participants from more than 170 countries. The opening ceremony featured a keynote by Dr Sultan Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and ADNOC Managing Director and Group CEO, and a speech and interview with Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI.

Dr Al Jaber said the global energy industry must rethink how it builds, protects and delivers secure energy after a year of disruption, and that nearly one billion barrels of crude had been drained from inventories since disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. He set out five steps: accessible supply through expanded strategic storage and flexible refining closer to consumers, routes to market built before they are needed, operational intelligence moving from automated operations to intelligent energy systems, capital that follows confidence, and people, which he called the most important. Altman said abundant, reliable energy is critical to unlocking the next wave of AI-driven innovation, that AI can make energy systems more efficient while its expansion will require significantly more energy, and that the UAE has been the most forward-looking country for AI adoption. He described the ADNOC-G42-OpenAI partnership as a model for applying advanced AI to industrial challenges.

The opening ministerial panel included Suhail Mohamed Al Mazrouei, UAE Minister of Energy and Infrastructure, and Ekperikpe Ekpo, Nigeria's Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas). Al Mazrouei said additional layers of protection, spare capacity, technology and AI would be needed to design better and become more resilient. The opening CEO panel brought together Meg O'Neill of bp, Richard Jackson of Oxy and Markus Krebber of RWE. Jackson said his company's strategy had been durability, with a focus on sustainable cash flow and production.

The event runs until November 5, with more than 1,800 speakers across 13 conference programmes. Organisers said discussions over the coming days will focus on turning strategic priorities into investment decisions, partnerships and practical solutions. A survey by ADNOC, XRG and Microsoft found that 62 per cent of energy leaders now rank AI among their two leading corporate priorities, up from 42 per cent last year, and that nearly three quarters expect AI to increase energy consumption by 2030. A separate ADIPEC survey found that 81 per cent of energy executives expect AI-related electricity requirements to exceed current forecasts.

stories.Headline: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Just Drove a Dagger Through Wall Street's AI-Driven Rally With 6 Blunt Words
stories.Summary:
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and his Federal Open Market Committee colleagues voted on Oct. 28 to hold interest rates steady. The decision came during a 67th consecutive month of annualized inflation above the Fed's long-term 2% target. After the meeting, Warsh spoke with the press and made comments about how interest rates affect AI companies. His six-word assessment that interest rates get in the cracks sent a message to AI stock investors.

Warsh took over as Fed chair on May 22 and has done away with forward-looking guidance in FOMC statements and in his post-meeting discussions with reporters. During his five-month tenure, getting direct answers or hints about what is to come has been challenging. The CME Group's FedWatch Tool predicts a 72% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December. It also predicts a nearly 50% chance of 75 basis points in cumulative hikes by Sept. 15, 2027. Higher long-duration Treasury bond yields, specifically 10- and 30-year yields, can increase corporate borrowing costs.

Warsh said interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything. He said market participants are discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make. He also said credit spreads for certain assets have widened out or gapped out, while financial conditions have tightened for others but not significantly. The article says this blunt six-word assessment has sent an unmistakable message to AI stock investors.

Some of Wall Street's hyperscalers are funding their data center build-outs through stock issuances and cash on hand. The otherworldly demand for AI hardware is being financed, in part, with debt. If borrowing costs continue to climb, they could adversely affect this expansion and near-term growth projections. That could force a re-rating of the second-priciest stock market in history. Bond traders are also concerned about U.S. total debt surpassing $40 trillion and ongoing federal deficits.

stories.Headline: AI is transforming customer experience in EMEA; But not for everyone
stories.Summary:
Talkdesk, Inc., a customer experience automation company, released a report titled "The State of Customer Experience Automation in EMEA" on November 3, 2026, in London. The report found a sharp divide in how widely organisations in Europe, the Middle East and Africa use AI to resolve customer issues. While 30% use AI to resolve more than 40% of customer issues, 17% have yet to use it to resolve any. The EMEA report draws on regional findings from "The State of Agentic Automation in CX," a global study commissioned by Talkdesk and conducted by NewtonX. It examines how organisations are deploying AI in customer experience, the barriers holding them back, and the operational foundations needed to move from AI adoption to AI outcomes.

EMEA and North America are at similar stages of maturity in combining AI agents with orchestration across teams and systems, at 15% and 14% of organisations respectively, but their operational realities diverge. North America is more concentrated at lower levels, with 67% of organisations resolving 20% or less of customer issues with AI and only 8% resolving more than 40%. Legacy technology is a more prominent barrier in EMEA, cited by 27% of organisations compared with 12% in North America. While 67% of EMEA organisations expect AI to resolve a greater share of customer issues within two years, only 35% have integrated customer data and just 22% consistently measure AI's business impact. A majority of 59% of EMEA organisations using AI agents say human agents now handle more complex cases, yet only 13% coordinate AI and people dynamically with orchestrated handoffs.

Pedro Andrade, global head of AI at Talkdesk, said AI adoption in EMEA looks very different from one organisation to the next, with more far ahead but also more yet to start. He said it is especially important to look beyond the initial deployment and ask whether AI is set up to deliver consistently, whether it can access the right knowledge and systems, work alongside people, and be reliably tested, audited and governed, and whether the business can measure the results. He said AI only delivers when the operational foundations are in place. Half of EMEA organisations cite job security as a top concern about humans and AI working together, alongside AI accuracy at 47%. Despite these worries, 62% expect AI to help them scale without adding headcount and 40% expect higher employee satisfaction as human agents shift to higher-value work.

NewtonX conducted an online quantitative survey of 60 director-level-and-above decision-makers and significant influencers responsible for customer experience, IT, operations or AI strategy at mid-market and enterprise organisations with 250 or more employees across EMEA. It was fielded in April 2026 as part of the 2026 NewtonX "The State of Agentic Automation in CX" survey and included respondents from financial services, retail, technology, life sciences and other industries. The full report provides priorities to help leaders close this readiness gap and includes a maturity assessment to benchmark where they currently stand. The articles say organisations need to ensure their operations can scale without compromising service quality or trust.

stories.Headline: Google's Project Suncatcher satellite generates first AI response in orbit
stories.Summary:
Google announced on October 30 that its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite had generated its first artificial intelligence response using a data centre-class Tensor Processing Unit in orbit. The satellite was launched on October 1 aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission. It was built in partnership with Planet. Google completed the satellite's commissioning checklist, which included powering up the host and TPU trays and running initial machine learning tests. During a ground-station pass, Google uplinked a prompt to the onboard Gemma 4 open model asking for a haiku about being in space, and the satellite transmitted the response back to Earth as it passed Svalbard, Norway.

The milestone is an early test of Google's research into running AI workloads in space. Google described it as the first AI response from a data centre-class TPU in orbit. The company later tested the model with space-themed limericks and prompts requesting telemetry information about the payload systems. The next phase of Project Suncatcher will evaluate how the TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit. These tests will help determine whether Google's hardware can reliably execute AI workloads in space.

The work is led by Google, and the blog post was written by Travis Beals, Senior Director of Paradigms of Intelligence. Google said the milestone marks an early test of its research into running AI workloads in space. The company said the thermal and radiation tests would help determine whether its hardware can reliably execute AI workloads in space. Google plans to use the findings to advance its next milestone.

Project Suncatcher explores the feasibility of solar-powered satellite networks equipped with Google's TPUs. The initiative investigates the long-term potential of scaling machine learning infrastructure beyond Earth. Google plans to advance to its next milestone in 2027, involving two interconnected satellites. That proposed system aims to explore how multiple satellites could work together to support AI computing in orbit.
