He said AI is a game changer and that he uses it every day in his clinic to outline the critical structures surrounding a tumor. He said radiation treatment planning that used to take a long time can now be done in minutes with AI's help. He also said AI helps read images such as CT scans and mammograms, reads pathology slides, and detects cancer cells earlier.

Murshed said patients should not use AI to interpret reports or to diagnose conditions and get treatment recommendations. He said it is fine to use AI to learn medical terminology and medical conditions, and to prepare questions for doctor visits. He said AI can be a tool, but a patient's doctor should still be the one helping make medical decisions. He said he is most excited about AI compiling medical history, family history, genetics, blood and lab reports, and imaging reports to assess a person's risk of developing cancer later.

He said the goal is more personalized screenings, earlier detection and a better chance of survival. He said he sees AI making the biggest difference by taking all of a patient's individual information and helping doctors create a more personalized plan for screenings and preventive care. The article also said AI is being used to schedule appointments and to save doctors time on patient notes. The article did not say what happens next beyond Murshed's vision of AI going beyond treating cancer to potentially preventing it.

Articles.Title: MEDICAL MONDAY: How AI is being utilized in medical field

stories.Headline: Opinion: Do you have the right to refuse to use AI in the workplace?
stories.Summary:
In an opinion piece published by the Deseret News on Nov. 3, 2026, Valerie Hudson, a university distinguished professor at the Bush School of Government and Public Service at Texas A&M University, argued that people should be able to refuse to use artificial intelligence at work without being penalized. She wrote that the right to refuse is a foundational right, and that governments can punish people but cannot make them do what they refuse to do. She pointed to two people, Erin Maus and David Durman, whose cases she said set a precedent. Maus is a Unitarian Universalist who works as a software engineer, and Durman is a humanist who works as a research administrator at the University of Kentucky.

According to the piece, both argued that being forced to use AI discriminates against their religious beliefs and that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 gives them the legal right to an exemption. Hudson wrote that Title VII prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin, and that humanism is recognized as a religion under that law. She described their successful pursuit of the exemptions as precedent-setting. She also cited a study in which doctors first checked AI diagnostics and later deferred to them, and said their skills were worse than before when the AI help was removed. She mentioned a National Health Service report on maternity services that drew more than 10,000 responses and was summarized with Microsoft's Copilot instead of being read, and said important themes were missed.

Hudson wrote that Durman said in a letter to the University of Kentucky that substituting automated machine processing for human presence, authentic listening and personal responsibility conflicts with his obligation to uphold human dignity and flourishing. She wrote that he also said the work of thinking through situations, his ethics and how he handles other people is a key part of developing himself as a moral person, and that offloading that labor undercuts his ability to be a moral actor. Hudson said that if using AI makes Durman less capable of acting morally according to his sincerely held beliefs, he should not be forced to use it or penalized for refusing. She thanked Maus and Durman for sticking to their principles.

Hudson also wrote that AI can threaten the mind, heart or soul through de-skilling, or never-skilling, and that mastery needs time, experience and friction. She said people are hard-wired to offload cognitive tasks, that students using AI may never develop skills beyond writing a good prompt, and that frontier AI companies can no longer monitor their models in real time and have turned that task over to AI monitors. She said humans may eventually be unable to check AI outputs in any meaningful sense. She noted that Bill Gates of Microsoft said some will want to emulate the Amish and simply abstain from the new technology, and she asked whether U.S. law shields people who refuse. The article does not say what happens next beyond describing the exemptions as precedent-setting.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Do you have the right to refuse to use AI in the workplace?

stories.Headline: Why AMD Stock Is In Focus Before Q3 Earnings And AI Partnership Updates
stories.Summary:
Advanced Micro Devices drew attention after partners including Meta, Vultr and LeadDesk highlighted new deployments of AMD EPYC processors, Instinct GPUs, Helios rackscale systems and ROCm software. The deployments cover large AI training, inference and conversational workloads across data centers and cloud platforms. The article was published on November 2, 2026, ahead of AMD's third quarter earnings. The piece says these collaborations point to AMD technology being embedded deep in customer infrastructure. The article says this can influence utilization levels, product mix and long term demand visibility across AI accelerators, server CPUs and supporting software.

It says the Meta partnership points to deep alignment on roadmaps, while Vultr and LeadDesk highlight broader demand across cloud and enterprise AI. It also says the short term swing factors remain AI accelerator shipments, data center margins and how capital hungry the Helios and Instinct deployments are. The article notes the stock still carries a rich P/E multiple and that funding relies on higher risk sources. The article says the lowest analysts worry that if infrastructure spending cools, the path to about US$117.6b of revenue and US$31.5b of earnings by 2029 looks stretched. It says readers should consider the wide ranges as a prompt to explore multiple viewpoints.

It also says one fair value estimate suggests as much as 41% downside from the current price. The article states that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned and that the piece is not financial advice. The article says the updates show AMD silicon and ROCm software embedded in production AI workloads, which matters for utilization, follow on orders and how sticky these customers become. It says the wins do not remove the big issues in front of AMD investors. The article does not say what happens next beyond AMD's upcoming earnings.

Articles.Title: Why AMD Stock Is In Focus Before Q3 Earnings And AI Partnership Updates

stories.Headline: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
stories.Summary:
A growing group of alignment researchers is promoting an approach called reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, to keep powerful AI models in check, according to an article published by MIT Technology Review on November 3, 2026. The idea is to design rules and incentives so that following the rules becomes the most rational choice for an AI agent. The article describes work by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, with colleagues from Yale and Columbia, in a recent preprint paper, and by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton. The article says Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.

The approach starts from the premise that we may never fully understand the internal workings of frontier models, so instead of peering into an AI's "brain" or training it on values, researchers want to build mechanisms that reward wanted behavior regardless of what is happening under the hood. Morris's paper suggests rewarding a model for how well its answers predict what a second model will say, so that deliberately underperforming on tests, known as sandbagging, becomes a losing bet. It also suggests pitting agents against each other in competition, or pairing agents known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them when their outputs match. Hazan's approach has models take turns as solvers, which tackle problems, and auditors, which check the others' work, with solvers that get caught cheating punished and auditors that fail to catch cheaters also punished, and disagreements sent to a kind of trial that a human expert might decide. He says the risk of collusion can be handled by rewarding auditors well enough and by auditing the auditors, using techniques akin to mystery shoppers.

Morris says AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve, so cross-checking could work in practice. Hazan points to Nobel Prize winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the rational offender in the 1960s, and argues that criminals break the law when it is the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Hazan says alignment should not be thought of as a property of a model but as a description of its behavior at a particular moment, and he asks why we do not first talk about how humans are aligned. Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, asks whether it is even reasonable to assume AI models will respond to incentives, and Morris says AIs are not rational but are just algorithms at work, though treating them as rational could still help predict and control them.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a defense in depth strategy alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, and the article says many questions remain before the approach can be used in actual frontier models. It is unclear how the theories will apply to real models, whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another, and whether models could find loopholes no one anticipated. Hazan says any mechanism will ultimately have to fit into the biggest mechanism of all, the free market, and asks whether the current system of rules and regulations actually gives frontier labs an incentive to release a more aligned model if it is slower or more expensive than a less aligned one. He says the market is responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind but could ultimately be responsible for something very terrible, and the article suggests the entities really in need of a better mechanism design may be the labs themselves.

Articles.Title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

stories.Headline: Compliance spend on AI rising, but fears about accuracy, reliability remain
stories.Summary:
Organizations are putting more money into artificial intelligence to support compliance and due diligence work, according to a report from cybersecurity consultancy S-RM. The report is titled From Screening to Decision-Making: The Next Phase of AI in Compliance. It is based on a survey of 225 compliance professionals. The article was published by Compliance Week on November 2, 2026, and written by contributor Neil Hodge.

The survey found that 78% of the professionals expect spending on AI-enabled compliance and due diligence solutions to rise by nearly a quarter, or 24%, over the next one to two years. That would take spending from about $337,000 today to $416,000. Despite the planned increase, many of those surveyed remain wary of the reliability and accuracy of the technology's outputs. The report describes this as the next phase of AI in compliance.

The article does not name any individual who commented on the findings. It attributes the results to the S-RM report and the survey of 225 compliance professionals. No specific quotes from respondents or S-RM staff are given in the article. The concerns about accuracy and reliability are reported as a general finding of the survey.

The article places the findings in the context of compliance teams weighing greater AI investment against doubts about how dependable the tools are. It does not say what specific steps organizations plan to take next. It also does not say whether S-RM plans further reports or follow-up research. The article gives no timeline beyond the one-to-two-year spending outlook.

Articles.Title: Compliance spend on AI rising, but fears about accuracy, reliability remain

stories.Headline: Dow Jones Futures: AI Trade Dives As Apple Tumbles On Earnings; Midterm Elections Next
stories.Summary:
Futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the other major stock indexes traded mixed ahead of Tuesday's open, according to Investor's Business Daily. On Monday the Dow Jones industrials climbed 278 points, but the artificial intelligence trade suffered a blow with heavy losses. After the close, Apple and Palantir Technologies reported their respective quarterly earnings reports. Apple stock sold off more than 3%.

The articles give few further details on the results themselves. A related item says Apple posted a fiscal fourth quarter beat on strong iPhone and services sales. Another says Palantir's earnings topped views, with revenue beating by a slightly smaller margin. The articles also note that midterm elections come next.

The articles do not name executives or give direct comments from anyone responsible. They do not say who is accountable for the moves or what was said about them. Coverage instead focuses on the market reaction and the earnings reports. The context given is a rough stretch for stocks.

One related headline calls it a stock market smackdown week, citing elections, jobs data, Iran and earnings. Another notes AI stocks facing possible ballot-box backlash as financing fears mount. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the elections and jobs report being due. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Dow Jones Futures: AI Trade Dives As Apple Tumbles On Earnings; Midterm Elections Next

stories.Headline: Connecting AI Visits to Sales Could Sharpen Retail Investment
stories.Summary:
A PYMNTS Intelligence report released in October 2026 examined how merchants track shoppers who arrive from artificial intelligence platforms. The report, “The Agent Advantage: How Merchants Plan to Win AI Shopping,” surveyed 60 senior eCommerce decision-makers at established, digitally active merchants in the United States with annual revenue between $50 million and $1 billion. Among merchants selling through their own site or app, 37% identified a visit that came from an AI platform but lost the trail before a purchase. No surveyed merchant selling through its own site or app could fully and consistently connect AI-driven visits to completed purchases.

The report found that 51% of merchants identified some AI-originated visits but reported inconsistent attribution, and another 12% could not tell agentic traffic apart from human traffic. AI visibility was a high or critical priority for 80% of merchants, compared with 62% who said the same about identifying AI-driven visits and purchases. The report also found that 87% of merchants had taken at least one step to improve how their products appear inside AI platforms. Nearly all surveyed merchants expected to pay to participate in the agentic ecosystem through commissions, subscriptions or other fees, and 82% said AI-driven product discovery has helped their businesses.

The report described businesses preparing for agentic commerce while still developing the ability to measure AI’s contribution. It said connecting referrals to completed orders could help merchants determine which efforts generate business and deserve additional spending, and could help them compare AI investments and evaluate partnerships. It also said better measurement could show whether changes to product listings bring visitors who purchase, whether particular referral sources deliver completed orders, and where shoppers leave before checkout. The report noted that attribution would still require care, because a shopper may consult an assistant, visit several merchants and return directly to buy, and because AI influence on a purchase would not by itself prove the sale was additional business.

The report said each outcome points toward a different response. Visits that end on a product page might warrant examining the information presented there, and shoppers who reach checkout but leave could prompt a review of the purchase experience. Orders traced to a particular source would give merchants a basis for comparing its contribution with other channels. The report said connecting referrals to orders could help retailers weigh costs against the business received, and that comparing order value, fees and returns would provide a fuller commercial assessment than counting visits alone. It said more consistent sales attribution could turn reported benefits into evidence for choosing partners, setting budgets and expanding the AI investments that perform.

Articles.Title: Connecting AI Visits to Sales Could Sharpen Retail Investment

stories.Headline: Humane Society of Utah issues warning about AI-generated veterinary records
stories.Summary:
The Humane Society of Utah is warning about false veterinary records that claim pets are vaccinated when they are not. The group said it has seen more reports of fake vaccination records, which came from community businesses that spotted records that looked odd and were later found to be made by AI. The warning was reported by ABC4 on November 2, 2026. The Humane Society is asking boarding facilities, pet groomers, veterinary offices and anyone else who requests vaccination records to stay aware and to contact the group if they are unsure whether a record is valid.

The Humane Society said faking a record puts pets and other animals at risk. Guinnevere Shuster, the Director of Marketing and Communications for the Humane Society, said this includes rabies vaccination, which by law pet owners are required to have. She said an unvaccinated animal may have a disease or contact that disease, which puts animals in the community at risk. She also said it puts the organization whose name is on the documentation at risk and liable until proven otherwise.

Under Utah State law, using fraudulent vaccination certificates and forging a legal document are third-degree felonies. The Humane Society said that even if a person uses the name of a fake veterinarian, both the organization and the forger can face legal penalties. The group also said pets would appreciate actually being vaccinated and getting the preventative care they need instead of trying to lie about it badly. The Humane Society is asking anyone who is unsure about a record to contact them.

Articles.Title: Humane Society of Utah issues warning about AI-generated veterinary records

stories.Headline: Essay: How an orchestra's experiment with AI can make for a better democracy
stories.Summary:
The Boston Symphony Orchestra premiered Tod Machover’s “already and not yet” at Symphony Hall in late October 2026, a half-hour concerto for orchestra with electronics that uses AI. The piece was commissioned for the 40th anniversary of the MIT Media Lab, where Machover has worked since it began and now heads the faculty. An AI operator, Manaswi Mishra, was embedded in the orchestra to run the live AI system during the performance. Kent Nagano conducted the premiere, and the program also included Mendelssohn performances, including the Fifth Symphony.

The AI in the piece is not a data collector like commercial systems, according to the article, but a tool taught to listen and analyze so it can offer musicians new ideas. In the first movement, “SMASH UP,” the AI has little use as the world is a mess. In the second, “WAKE UP,” the players become individuals and the AI’s responses read as ordinary electronic mimicry, which the players can treat as a challenge. In the last movement, “STAND UP,” the machine is tamed and the music enters what the article calls a sonic wonderland.

Nagano was described as the ultimate listener, able to cut off the AI when it was not interesting, and he said after the performance that the orchestra was always game. The article says the orchestra is in revolt, and many players wore red flowers on their lapels at the performance the writer attended. The players are unhappy that the administration did not renew music director Andris Nelsons’ contract when it expires in summer 2027, after 13 years leading the BSO. The orchestra said it was broadsided by the announcement that management and Nelsons did not have a shared vision, and the players want a say.

The article places the premiere in a wider season of orchestral democracy events, including Wild Up’s “Democracy Sessions” in Los Angeles and a democracy weekend by the Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig ahead of a state election in Saxony-Anhalt. Nelsons, who signed a nondisclosure agreement, did not take part in Tanglewood’s democracy concerts, and in Leipzig his contribution was a program of Tchaikovsky and Dvorak standards. The article says the BSO and Gewandhaus share Nelsons as music director and that he has tried to bring the two orchestras together. It ends by asking whether AI-assisted art can save democracy and suggesting it first try to do something about the BSO.

Articles.Title: Essay: How an orchestra's experiment with AI can make for a better democracy

stories.Headline: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
stories.Summary:
Apple has begun beta testing AI features for the Apple Watch that can rewind and recap conversations, TechCrunch reported on November 3, 2026. The features are part of a set called Audio Intelligence, which was first announced at Apple's Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The beta is initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update. The set includes four opt-in features for Apple Watch Series 12 wearers: sound detection, song identification, conversation catch-up, and note-taking. Sound recognition helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells.

Song recognition uses Apple's Shazam app to identify music playing in the background. Live Rewind lets a user double-press the digital crown to see the last 15 seconds of speech as text on the watch face. Snippets are deleted automatically after 30 seconds if not saved, and a chime and animation signal that something was recorded. Siri Recaps summarizes a conversation in a short sentence and bullet points, without identifying speakers, saving raw audio, or giving word-for-word transcriptions.

Recaps delete themselves within seven days if not reviewed, and users can enable the feature manually or on a schedule and turn it off anytime from Control Center. Apple says the features rely on the S11 chip, the watch's microphone, Apple Intelligence models on the iPhone, and Private Cloud Compute. Raw audio is processed in a secure enclave on the watch and is accessible only to the paired iPhone, and condensed text sent to Private Cloud Compute is deleted immediately after the recap is made. Apple says recaps are accessible only to the user and are encrypted when synced across devices.

Apple also says Siri Recaps was designed to omit sensitive information such as government identifiers, financial and authentication data, and language promoting self-harm. The company says none of the features should affect battery life. The features follow backlash to AI recording devices such as Meta's AI glasses and other AI wearables, and Apple has tried to design them to respect the privacy of people nearby. The features will later roll out to a public beta for broader testing before becoming available to everyone.

Articles.Title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing

stories.Headline: Why Almost Every Corporate AI Transformation Fails
stories.Summary:
Kai-Fu Lee, founder and CEO of 01.AI and chairman of Sinovation Ventures, wrote a TIME Ideas article published on November 3, 2026, arguing that most corporate AI programs fail. He said most chief executives he meets cannot name a single result from their AI programs that a shareholder would care about. They can list activity such as pilots run, licenses purchased, employees trained and partnerships announced, but none of that is a result. He wrote that surveys repeatedly find most corporate AI programs deliver disappointing measurable returns.

Lee argued the problem is not the models, the data or the talent, but where companies point the AI. Today's systems can reason across an entire business, yet companies use them to handle tickets and summarize meetings, which he compared to hiring a business operations genius and making him an assistant. He said the place where AI can move the most money is the corner office, not the call center. He described companies as information systems where information degrades at every level, with bad news discarded going up and directives diluted or quietly vetoed going down, so a company of 10,000 ends up knowing less than a company of 10.

Lee said every company keeps two sets of records, an official one that is polished at each level and a second one of meeting transcripts, chat threads, edit trails, sales notes and code check-ins that shows what actually happened. Managers have always worked from the first because the second was too scattered to read, but he said a CEO-level agentic system can now wake up that dormant data. At his own company he had his team build management agents that sit in meetings, track commitments and read the data underneath what he is told, and people called the system Kai-Fu's Boss AI. He reported that it found a priority project reported on track every week with no code committed in five, a customer marked highly likely to renew whose account manager had not called in two months, and a draft contract that could not have been profitable.

Lee also said AI can surface hidden good news, especially talent. In a performance review last year his company set aside resumes, KPI decks and department heads' recommendations, agreed on what engineering excellence means when a machine can write most of the code, and scored a year of repository history against it. Several of the strongest names were people he could not have picked out of a meeting, including a vice president who wrote close to 300,000 lines with AI in a month against his own ceiling of 30,000 twenty years earlier. Lee said he regularly asks his agent what he got wrong in a meeting, whether his time went where he said his priorities were and what people are afraid to tell him, and he argued employees resist AI not because they doubt it works but because they suspect it does.

Articles.Title: Why Almost Every Corporate AI Transformation Fails

stories.Headline: SuperIT AI Agents Launch in North America With Free Tier To Fix IT Incidents Without Runbooks
stories.Summary:
SuperIT, an Australian AI startup, launched its AI agents for managed service providers and IT teams in North America on November 2, 2026, as part of global availability. The launch came ahead of IT Nation Connect in Orlando, held November 4 to 6. MSPs can sign up at superit.ai, connect their ticketing system and have an AI agent working real tickets within the first hour, with no sales call or contract. The company moved from early access with MSPs in Australia, New Zealand and the U.S. to general availability worldwide, with North America as its focus market.

The free tier has no expiry and includes unlimited AI ticket triage with fair-use limits, plus monthly credits for other AI features. Paid plans run from US$99 to US$9,900 a month on month-to-month contracts, with more credits on larger plans. SuperIT integrates with ConnectWise PSA, Autotask, HaloPSA and Accelo, and every command passes a security pipeline and a three-tier policy of allowed, needs approval or blocked. Every action is recorded in an append-only audit trail, and MSPs can require engineer approval for any command or category of action.

CEO and co-founder Christopher Sale said products should win on technical merit rather than contract lock-in, and that the days of signing a one- to three-year contract just to try a product are over. He said SuperIT is free to use with no time limit so MSPs can judge it on their own tickets, and that most AI in IT support stops at triage or a pre-written script. He said MSPs should not have to sit through sales demos or commit to big minimums to find out whether a tool works in their environment. Sam Gridley, CEO of Hawaii-based MSP Intech Hawaii, said his company tested many ticket remediation solutions and only SuperIT passed its accuracy tests.

In early evaluations across technician conversations reviewed with early MSP partners, the technician's goal was fully or partly achieved in 91.1%, and 74.1% were assessed as clearly useful or decisive. Fields written by SuperIT's AI triage were still unchanged at review in 99% of cases for ticket type, 96% for subtype, 93% for priority and 91% for item. Between July and September 2026, the number of customers MSPs have deployed SuperIT to grew 71%, tickets synced more than doubled and monthly autonomous agent runs more than doubled. North American customers will initially be supported by SuperIT's existing team and global platform, and the company plans to open a dedicated U.S. team in the first quarter of 2027.

Articles.Title: SuperIT AI Agents Launch in North America With Free Tier To Fix IT Incidents Without Runbooks

stories.Headline: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
stories.Summary:
A guest post published on Terence Tao's blog on 2 November 2026 argues that mathematicians should rethink the purpose of their work as artificial intelligence advances. The post was written by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai and Jie Xue, and Tao notes that it was converted from another file format using AI. The authors say the ideas are entirely their own, while acknowledging help from GPT Astra 6.0 and GPT 6.1 Sol in drafting the post. They describe themselves as still far from the egolessness they hold up as an ideal.

The essay draws a distinction between mathematics that we invent and mathematics that we discover. It says there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact, and that mathematical truth does not receive its authority from our recognition. It argues that formal correctness alone does not make a statement enlightening, and that mathematical taste matters when it reveals unity among things previously understood separately. It also warns that measures such as publications, citations and awards become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself.

The authors say anxiety about being replaced by AI is natural if mathematics is seen as output, but they argue the problem began before AI arrived. They write that we had already come to understand ourselves in terms suited to machines, and that AI merely exposes the consequences of this view. They reject seeking refuge in human abilities mainly because those abilities give an advantage over machines. They propose egoless mathematics, in which humility concerns the place from which we pursue knowledge, and they say the joy of understanding does not diminish when someone else discovers something first.

The essay says its aim is not to settle particular questions of policy but to offer a higher-level perspective to guide deliberation and action. It suggests this perspective can reconcile those who welcome AI in mathematics, provided appropriate processes and principles are developed, with those who prefer not to use it at all. The authors conclude that mathematics was beautiful before any of us were born and will remain beautiful long after we are gone. They end with a thought experiment asking whether Ramanujan, who reportedly said an equation had no meaning for him unless it expressed a thought of God, would be perturbed by AI's advances.

Articles.Title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era

stories.Headline: Anthropic S-1 claims it may "imminently meet" its RSI threshold and may fail to identify "significant acceleration" in its development until after it's occurred (Julie Bort/TechCrunch)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed an S-1, a public registration document, and in it the company said it may "imminently meet" its RSI threshold, according to Julie Bort of TechCrunch. The filing also said Anthropic may fail to identify "significant acceleration" in its development until after it has already occurred. The document was reported on November 2, 2026. The S-1 does not say exactly when the threshold would be reached.

The filing gives several figures for the third quarter. Anthropic reported revenue up 12 times year over year to nearly $17 billion. It reported a net loss of $23.3 billion, up from $12.1 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Operating expenses rose 292 percent year over year to $17.5 billion. The articles do not explain what the RSI threshold is or what reaching it would require.

The filing places the responsibility for spotting acceleration on the company itself, and it warns that this may not happen in time. Anthropic says it may not identify significant acceleration until after it has occurred. The articles do not name any executive who commented on the filing. No further statements from the company are given.

The context is that Anthropic made these disclosures in a registration document tied to going public. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the filing itself. They do not give a date for when the RSI threshold might be met. They also do not say how the company would respond if it were crossed.

Articles.Title: Anthropic S-1 claims it may "imminently meet" its RSI threshold and may fail to identify "significant acceleration" in its development until after it's occurred (Julie Bort/TechCrunch)

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike Scales Project QuiltWorks Across Europe, Advancing the Industry’s Response to Frontier AI Risk
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 2, 2026, at its Fal.Con Europe event in Barcelona that Project QuiltWorks is expanding across Europe. The company said fifteen partners are joining the coalition, including Almaviva Group, Atos, BT, Computacenter, Deutsche Telekom Security, Grant Thornton UK, iiTD, Intrinsec, Kudelski Security, Orange Cyberdefense, Serviceware, Stoïk, Strong-IT, Telefónica, and TIM AG. CrowdStrike is a publicly traded company listed on NASDAQ under the ticker CRWD. The announcement describes the partners as adding expertise and remediation capacity.

According to the article, the expansion is meant to help organizations cope as frontier AI changes how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited. CrowdStrike says Project QuiltWorks gives customers the AI, data, infrastructure, expertise, and financial protection to move from finding risk to fixing it before impact. The article describes the project as an operating model for frontier AI risk and as an industry coalition working to close what it calls the frontier AI vulnerability gap at scale. It also says the added partners extend the project's reach and depth of expertise across Europe.

Daniel Bernard, CrowdStrike's chief business officer, said AI is changing the economics of vulnerability exploitation and that the industry has to disrupt the economics of remediation. He said QuiltWorks delivers the tools and protection to take customers from finding risk to fixing it before impact. He added that expanding across Europe scales the crowd behind that mission. He said this gives customers more capacity to prioritize what matters and fix it faster.

The article frames the effort around the shrinking time between patch and exploit, which CrowdStrike lists among the risks its frontier AI services address. It presents the European expansion as part of the industry's response to frontier AI risk. The article does not say which specific countries the new partners will cover or give a timeline for the rollout. It also does not state the financial terms of the partnerships.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike Scales Project QuiltWorks Across Europe, Advancing the Industry’s Response to Frontier AI Risk

stories.Headline: Eyedaptic launches Eva, an agentic AI visual assistant for patients with retinal disease
stories.Summary:
Eyedaptic, a developer of vision-enhancement technology, announced on November 2, 2026 the launch of Eva, an agentic AI visual assistant built into its EYE7 Vision Enhancing Smart Glasses. The company said the release moves away from passive question-and-answer AI toward a proactive agent that supports users in real time. Eva pairs agentic AI with Eyedaptic's computer vision platform so the AI and the glasses work as a single system to help users see, understand and interact with their surroundings. According to the company, Eva showed greater than 99% reading accuracy and 97% command accuracy in internal testing.

Eyedaptic has been adding AI to its wearable platform for several years. In August 2024 the company unveiled the EYE6 with Ivy, a wearable vision aid for patients with age-related macular degeneration and other retinal disorders. The EYE7 followed in March 2026, launched alongside the Eyedaptic Visual Assistant Family, when Ivy was fully available and Eva was offered through an Early Access Beta Program. With the full launch, the company describes Eva as bringing three capabilities into one system, visual intelligence, reasoning based on agentic AI and direct control of the glasses' vision-enhancement functions, an architecture it calls Eyegentic AI. Eva is available now to all EYE7 users and can be installed through a remote software upgrade without new hardware.

Jay Cormier, CEO and founder of Eyedaptic, said in the release that Eva is more than an assistant and is an intelligent partner. Cormier noted that Eva was the name of his late grandmother, whose AMD inspired him to found the company. Eva runs on Eyedaptic's proprietary Simulated Natural Vision software, which is designed to go beyond conventional magnification to help patients with conditions such as AMD regain function in daily life. The company says its approach is protected by a portfolio of granted and pending patents and describes its platform as the only solution that integrates both advanced vision enhancement and agentic AI.

At the American Retina Forum annual meeting in August 2026, David Almeida, MD, MBA, PhD, FRCSC, presented an unsponsored real-world evaluation of the EYE6 in 19 patients with advanced retinal disease. Seventeen of the 19 patients, or 89%, showed measurable improvement in near visual acuity immediately after fitting, with a mean gain of 5.7 lines. The article notes that the reading and command accuracy figures come from the company's own testing and have not been independently validated or peer reviewed. It adds that real-world validation across varied patient populations will determine how well Eva performs outside controlled conditions, and that patient selection, training and realistic expectations remain central to successful low vision rehabilitation.

Articles.Title: Eyedaptic launches Eva, an agentic AI visual assistant for patients with retinal disease

stories.Headline: Apax co-CEO bets on India’s AI strengths, eyes faster investment
stories.Summary:
Mitch Truwit, co-chief executive of global private equity firm Apax Partners, said India's technology capabilities, education levels and intellectual capital will keep the country from falling behind in artificial intelligence. He spoke in an exclusive interaction with Mint during a visit to India marking two decades of the firm's investing in the country. He said India may not lead on large language models, but its strength lies in change management, which most companies lack. He added that Indian companies can help other businesses put AI to work and create efficiency.

Apax has invested around $4 billion in India and has returned more than $10 billion to investors, with an internal rate of return above 25%, Truwit said. The firm is currently investing from its eleventh fund of $12 billion and is targeting a first close by March for its twelfth fund, according to news reports. It may put around 10% of the new capital into India, up from under 10% of total investments now. The money will go to technology, consumer and healthcare businesses, and Harjot Dhaliwal, partner and India head, named supply chain management, cybersecurity and new age digital businesses as attractive areas.

Truwit said Apax does not set aside separate pools of capital for Asia and the US and invests from a single pool because it is a returns-based firm rather than an asset gatherer. He said India's GDP growth of 7% or 8%, along with inflation and currency issues, can look riskier, but the firm is patient capital and sees an opportunity. Dhaliwal said short-term headwinds such as geopolitics, oil prices and froth in the AI market are seen differently by public market investors, and that Apax bakes historical currency depreciation into its deals and cost of capital. He said the firm focuses on driving operational improvement and growth in businesses over a five to seven year view.

Truwit's comments come as many foreign portfolio investors have pulled money out of India over the past 12 to 18 months, while long-term investors such as private equity and buyout funds have raised their bets. Apax's current Indian portfolio includes iD Fresh, greytHR, Azentio Software and IBS Software, among others, and the firm has backed Fractal Analytics, Globalogic and Healthium in the past. It considers India one of its best-performing markets. The firm expects to step up its investment pace in India going forward.

Articles.Title: Apax co-CEO bets on India’s AI strengths, eyes faster investment

stories.Headline: AI platform detects alleged ₹5,700 crore GST fraud network involving 1,500 shell companies in India
stories.Summary:
Innefu Labs, an Indian artificial intelligence company, said its AI-powered platform Prophecy Eagle I detected a suspected GST fraud network involving more than 1,500 registered businesses across India. The company estimated the potential fraudulent input tax credit at about ₹5,700 crore. The suspected transactions took place during one fiscal year, according to the company. The findings were published in a report on 2 November 2026.

The company said the businesses showed no fraudulent GST registrations or late returns, which made the activity hard to spot through individual compliance checks. The platform combined GST data with identity and transport data to find links between the entities. It flagged the alleged reuse of the same facial identity across dozens of business registrations in different zones within a month. It also identified newly registered companies that appeared to move large volumes of input tax credit within weeks of registration despite little evidence of purchases, and circular trading in which credits passed among companies and ended up near where they started.

Tarun Wig, co-founder and CEO of Innefu Labs, said the network was hard to recognize because the businesses appeared compliant when viewed individually. He said the platform linked information from various databases to show patterns that would not be visible by looking at them individually. Abhishek Sharma, co-founder and CTO, said the system used identity correlation, behavioural analysis and network mapping to detect suspicious activity based on filing data. The company said the ₹5,700 crore figure is a suspected exposure and has not been verified or gone through due process by enforcement bodies.

The alleged network is part of ongoing efforts by tax authorities against fake input tax credit claims. The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs detected fake input tax credit worth ₹36,374 crore in 9,190 cases during FY23-24, according to a Finance Ministry press release dated 29 July 2024, and police made 182 arrests in the same period. The Directorate General of GST Intelligence reported in a press release dated 11 July 2025 that it uncovered fake invoices worth over ₹266 crore and over ₹48 crore in fake input tax credits from six shell companies. The company said its platform is designed to help enforcement agencies identify suspicious registrations, circular trading, carousel fraud and vanishing trader schemes.

Articles.Title: AI platform detects alleged ₹5,700 crore GST fraud network involving 1,500 shell companies in India

stories.Headline: Chinese AI models tumble down rankings after a crucial change to testing
stories.Summary:
Artificial Analysis, an independent firm that measures AI performance, recently overhauled its testing system to better reflect how people actually use the technology. One crucial change was that many of the tests are now kept secret, making it harder for AI companies to train their models specifically to perform well on them. Under the previous system, the best open-weight models trailed the overall leader by just three points. Under the new system, that gap widened to 12 points. The 12-point gap included Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro, and among models with publicly released weights the leaders scored just 32 points, compared with 58 for the then overall leader, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5.

The findings could have major implications for the AI industry and the billions of dollars investors are pouring into it. Chinese companies have been releasing powerful models that other businesses can download and adapt, often at lower costs than American alternatives, which fueled concern that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic could struggle to charge premium prices. The new rankings suggest that threat may have been overstated, potentially strengthening the investment case for Anthropic's planned IPO and a possible future OpenAI listing. Even Claude Haiku 5.5, a smaller Anthropic model, outperformed every AI model with publicly released weights.

Sridhar Ramaswamy, CEO of Snowflake and a former Google executive, wrote on X that the day benchmarks went private, the open-model gap went from 3 points to 12, and asked whether open models were catching up or the test was leaking. His point was that when AI companies know exactly how their technology will be tested, they can train it to excel at those particular tasks, which does not necessarily mean their models perform equally well in the real world. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other AI experts have called this benchmark hacking, and keeping the tests secret makes these hacks harder. Nathan Lambert, cofounder of Trillium Labs, said he did think the previous index was flattering the open weight models too strongly.

There is another reason to question the threat from open-weight models: how much people actually use them. Dax Raad, cofounder of software development company OpenCode, recently examined traffic through OpenRouter, a popular service that lets developers access AI models from different providers. He estimated that almost all the previous day's DeepSeek traffic flowing through OpenRouter could be handled by a single rack of powerful Nvidia computers, costing roughly $6 million to $7 million. OpenRouter represents only a slice of the market, so its figures do not capture all demand for open-weight models. Lambert said open-weight models remain highly competitive in areas such as software development and can offer businesses greater control and potentially lower costs.

Articles.Title: Chinese AI models tumble down rankings after a crucial change to testing

stories.Headline: Global players bid for design, planning of Bidadi AI township
stories.Summary:
The Greater Bengaluru Development Authority is finalising tenders for the design and planning of a proposed AI-powered township in Bidadi, according to The Hindu. Tenders were invited months ago through a Global Expression of Interest, and bids have come from global players as well as Indian ones. The Karnataka government has also completed final notifications for all nine villages needed for the project. The last two notifications, for Bairamangala and Kanchugaranahalli, were issued last week.

The project requires a total of 9,640 acres, and the government has now notified 7,357.36 acres of residual land. In Bairamangala, 1,142.25 acres were notified, of which 1,070.42 acres are residual land, while Kanchugaranahalli has 753.11 acres notified, including 731 acres of residual land. Farmers in Bairamangala are set to receive nearly ₹2.4 crore per acre, and compensation is already being paid to those giving up land. The selected consultants will work with the Project Management Unit at all stages of planning.

Farmers have protested the project for over 560 days and accuse the government of backstabbing them. Prakash H.G., a protesting farmer, said a committee was constituted on July 14 and had recently invited objections, yet notifications were issued before its report came out. Yashavantha T., general secretary of the Karnataka Prantha Raitha Sangha, said the Chief Minister had promised on record not to touch the project until the report was submitted. A GBDA official said work was not halted and that many farmers had pressed for the notifications because they were already receiving money.

Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar had set up a committee to assess the project's merits and demerits, which slowed discussions over the past two months. A GBDA official said the land acquisition documents went to the government before the committee was formed, and that the authority would proceed in line with the committee's recommendations. The official added that it would be unfair to make farmers in the two villages wait. Both land acquisition and the tendering process are now gathering pace.

Articles.Title: Global players bid for design, planning of Bidadi AI township

stories.Headline: Digital Agency offers AI app to help draft parliamentary answers
stories.Summary:
Japan’s Digital Agency has launched a trial of an artificial intelligence app that helps government officials draft answers to lawmakers’ questions in parliament. The agency started offering the app using its Gennai generative AI platform, which is available to about 180,000 government workers. The app also helps officials better understand the intent behind lawmakers’ questions before parliamentary sessions. The agency announced the trial on November 2, 2026, according to The Japan Times. When a lawmaker’s question is entered, the app organizes and analyzes its key points and generates multiple draft answers within minutes.

It draws on past government answers and minutes of Diet deliberations, and it can predict follow-up questions from lawmakers. The app includes a function that adjusts writing styles, such as a “policy explanation” mode and a “political judgment” mode. Officials can edit the draft answers directly. The agency plans to evaluate the app’s effectiveness during the current Diet session, with the aim of full-scale operation from next year’s ordinary Diet session. The agency stressed that officials will remain responsible for clarifying policy decisions, organizing the government’s views and finalizing answers.

It said decision-making will not be left to AI. Digital transformation minister Toshiharu Furukawa told a news conference on Friday that it is very good that work efficiency can be improved and that answers can contribute to deeper Diet deliberations. He also said he would like to hear feedback from other ministers. The articles do not say what happens after the current Diet session beyond the agency’s plan to evaluate the app and seek full-scale operation from next year’s ordinary session. They do not report any further response from lawmakers or other ministries.

Articles.Title: Digital Agency offers AI app to help draft parliamentary answers

stories.Headline: World of Warcraft: Forever Is Already Overrun with AI Slop
stories.Summary:
World of Warcraft: Forever, a reimagining of the original game meant to bring back the discovery and wonder players felt in 2004, comes out on Wednesday. Ahead of the launch, subreddits for the game are already full of AI-generated addons that copy longtime developers' work. Warcraft Logs, a site made by Archon.gg that lets players track and share logs of in-game fights, told 404 Media it is changing its API because of the flood of AI slop addons. The site makes its API available for free to other developers, and its CEO, who goes by Sildri Silentcrest, said the users used to be mostly hobby developers.

Silentcrest said there has been an explosion of development, with the site now averaging at least one commercial ask per day, and they are sure more projects are commercializing without approval. They described it as one new World of Warcraft analysis company every day. Warcraft Logs is changing its API to better align with the applications it wants to enable, favoring tools that help the community dive deeper into their data, such as ones that explain why a player died to a boss. It does not want tools that scrape lots of data from the site to show surface-level information elsewhere, a type Silentcrest said has become much more prevalent. The site is also introducing a paid commercial key so developers with commercial ambitions can support the foundation for their projects.

Plusmouse, a well-known addon creator, said people are making rip-offs of their work and copying their ideas. They gave the example of a particular nameplate design, the bars above an enemy's head, saying that before it released no addons used that style and now it feels like every AI addon uses it. Plusmouse said that in some cases the code is so similar that copyright complaints to Curseforge result in takedowns, while other times it is just different enough to get away with it. They said borrowing ideas is normal in addon development, but not on the scale AI permits, and they made some of their GitHub repositories private, which they believe stopped LLMs from using their code.

Silentcrest said that if they can be hopeful, the many services under development will let people pick their own experience, whether exploring slowly or rushing to endgame content. Their worry is lots of abandonware that frustrates users with out-of-date information, buggy software and vulnerabilities. They said Warcraft Logs staff feel pressure to do more, and the site has used some AI itself for research and some code review. Silentcrest said that two years ago about 200 developers used the API and two or three or four were abusive, while today 10,000 use it and 1,000 are abusive, and that policing API use has become a struggle.

Articles.Title: World of Warcraft: Forever Is Already Overrun with AI Slop

stories.Headline: Dartmouth admissions office has no plans to screen applicant essays with third-party AI detectors
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth's admissions office does not plan to use third-party artificial intelligence detectors to review applicant essays, according to an Oct. 19 email statement to The Dartmouth from Lee Coffin, the dean of admissions and financial aid. Coffin said no applications are read by outside vendors and that an admissions officer reads each essay. A college spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment on whether admissions has a formal policy on AI use in application materials. The Brown Daily Herald first reported on Oct. 14 that Brown University's admissions office also does not use third-party AI detectors, according to its dean of undergraduate admission, Logan Powell.

The Common Application, which is used by more than 1,000 colleges and universities including Dartmouth, bans students from submitting plagiarized essays or the substantive output of an AI platform as their own work. Jackson Sternberg, a senior public relations specialist for the Common App, wrote that the platform does not validate any aspects of student applications and does not use AI detection software. Fraud reviews are triggered by reports or allegations from a member college or a third party such as students, parents or school counselors, and the Common App legal and operations team reviews them. Joel Butterly, co-founder and chief executive officer of the New Haven based consulting firm InGenius Prep, wrote that a fraud finding can get a student blocked from the Common App and reported to every school on their list.

Butterly wrote that Dartmouth's silence on AI use is not permission for applicants to generate admissions materials with it, and he called the school a good example of a gray zone. He noted that guests on Coffin's own podcast, Admissions Beat, have repeatedly discouraged using AI on applications. In an episode titled "AI Can't Feel," Ben Baum, vice president of enrollment at St. John's College, said authenticity is important throughout an application and is the antithesis of AI. Butterly also pointed to a 2025 Kaplan survey of over 200 admissions officers that found 68% of colleges had no policy on AI use in admissions essays.

Karen Warwick, college counseling director at the Bay Area company AJ Tutoring, said most students in her experience draft an essay and then seek feedback from an AI platform, and that using AI to create an entire essay from scratch is more rare. Butterly wrote that his clients' AI use has increased every cycle, mostly for brainstorming topics and tightening drafts, and he recommended treating AI as a smart study partner that keeps ideas and voice the student's own. The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill stopped using Slate's Reader AI tool for the 2026-27 cycle because AI use in essays skewed its ratings higher, the Daily Tar Heel reported in October. Virginia Tech pairs one human reader with one AI reader to score essays, according to The Collegiate Times, and Butterly said he expects more schools to add video responses and live components and to read the essay less as a writing sample and more as evidence of thinking.

Articles.Title: Dartmouth admissions office has no plans to screen applicant essays with third-party AI detectors

stories.Headline: Cyberdefense needs military-style resilience mindset in AI era
stories.Summary:
The U.S. National Security Agency recently warned organizations to immediately patch security flaws in the PHP programming language, according to Nikkei Asia. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also urged companies to respond to the warning. The report, published on November 3, 2026, said artificial intelligence is letting cyberattackers find weaknesses in computer systems at unprecedented speed and scale. Security experts have long argued that it is impossible to prevent every hack.

The article says governments and businesses should strengthen their defenses on the assumption that intrusions are inevitable. It describes the goal as maintaining critical functions when defenses fail, not perfect protection. The report says the rapid evolution of AI makes this shift urgent. It does not give further numbers or dates beyond the November 3, 2026 publication.

The article attributes the PHP warning to the U.S. National Security Agency and says Takaichi urged companies to respond. It does not include direct statements from either beyond that. The report frames the advice around a military-style resilience mindset in the AI era. It does not name other officials or give further details on what was said.

The context is that AI is allowing attackers to identify weaknesses at unprecedented speed and scale, the article says. It notes that security experts have long argued no system can be fully protected from every hack. The article does not say what specific steps come next beyond patching the PHP flaws and adopting the resilience approach. It also does not give a timeline for further action.

Articles.Title: Cyberdefense needs military-style resilience mindset in AI era

stories.Headline: DRAM prices double in 2026 as AI focus squeezes PC makers
stories.Summary:
DRAM memory prices have risen to roughly double their level at the end of last year, according to Nikkei Asia. The report, dated November 2, 2026, says the main memory makers are prioritizing supply for artificial intelligence applications in data centers over commodity products such as personal computers. Shipments of personal computers in Japan fell 30% on the year in the April-September period, with memory supplies stretched. The article was written by Hitomi Izawa.

The shift means top memory makers are putting supply for US hyperscalers ahead of general-use products. The price of DRAM, a mainstay chip, has climbed to about twice its level at the end of last year. The squeeze has hit PC makers, with Japanese PC shipments down 30% year on year in the April-September period. The article gives no further figures on prices or volumes.

The article does not name which companies are responsible or include any statements from them. It attributes the change to manufacturers of the mainstay chips prioritizing AI supplies. It does not say what the companies said about the shift. No responsible parties or comments are given in the text.

The context is strong demand for AI in data centers, which the article says is drawing memory supply away from commodity products. The article does not say what happens next. It does not give forecasts for prices or supplies. It also does not say whether the trend will continue.

Articles.Title: DRAM prices double in 2026 as AI focus squeezes PC makers

stories.Headline: Investor scrutiny of the AI spending boom is rising, but Big Tech is unlikely to give up
stories.Summary:
Investor scrutiny of Big Tech's spending on artificial intelligence is rising, and it is pulling down stock prices and pushing up borrowing costs. Alphabet's stock fell by as much as 13% after its third-quarter 2026 earnings report on Oct 28, even though revenue grew 25% and Google Cloud revenue doubled. The company reported US$9 billion in negative free cash flow, driven by US$51.4 billion in capital expenditure, mostly on AI infrastructure. Chipmakers, many of them based in Asia, have also suffered.

Big Tech says it must keep buying computing capacity and chips to stay competitive, because compute capacity is the main driver of AI capability and speed. Alphabet said more than 100 significant Google Cloud customers, including Anthropic and Apple, now run AI on Google's own tensor processing units. Nomura estimates a 75% chance the AI spending race will not stop. Changwon Chung, joint head of APAC equity research at Nomura, said the industry's fear is that falling behind puts even the core business at risk, calling it a game of chicken nobody can quit.

The International Monetary Fund said global trade rose 8.3% between 2023 and 2025, a figure that would be closer to 4.6% without AI-related products. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said technology-related sectors accounted for around 75% of year-on-year GDP growth in the third quarter of 2026. Morgan Stanley economists Chetan Ahya and Derrick Kam said computing demand still outweighs supply and the imbalance is set to persist, and that US AI capital expenditure should be higher in 2027 than in 2026. Analysts expect more sell-offs like the one in October.

Articles.Title: Investor scrutiny of the AI spending boom is rising, but Big Tech is unlikely to give up

The chip consumes about 98% less power than similar existing chips. Aisin worked on the technology with Tohoku University. The company said the breakthrough is expected to help process large amounts of data more efficiently.

The chip incorporates MRAM, a type of magnetic memory, and draws on Tohoku University's expertise in efficient magnetic RAM. stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: Seoul shares down over 2 pct late Tues. morning on AI concerns
stories.Summary:
South Korean stocks traded more than 2 percent lower late Tuesday morning, led by technology losses over concerns about the fast pace of artificial intelligence spending. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index opened 2.46 percent lower and stood at 5,714.06 as of 11:20 a.m., down 145.02 points, or 2.48 percent. Overnight on Wall Street, the Nasdaq Composite closed 1.07 percent lower and the S&P 500 fell 0.51 percent ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday. Investor sentiment was weakened by worries that heavy spending on AI infrastructure is hurting tech firms' near-term profitability.

In Seoul, technology shares led the decline. Samsung Electronics fell 2.95 percent, and chipmaker SK hynix slid 3.8 percent. Hanmi Semiconductor dropped 4.17 percent, and SK Square, the parent of SK hynix, tumbled 4 percent. Steel giant POSCO Holdings slumped 5.3 percent, and oil refiner SK Innovation plunged 7.76 percent. The Korean won was trading at 1,341 won against the U.S. dollar as of 11:20 a.m., up 3.4 won from the previous session's close.

stories.Headline: Deoksu Palace brings imperial feasts back to life with AI exhibition
stories.Summary:
Visitors to Deoksu Palace in Seoul can use artificial intelligence to create banquet dishes inspired by the Korean Empire. The Korea Heritage Service's Deoksu Palace Management Office, working with Davero Art, will open the exhibition "Imperial Banquet of the Korean Empire, Prepared With AI" on Tuesday at Dondeokjeon Hall. It runs through March 28, 2027. The exhibition combines research into royal Western-style banquets with generative AI.

More than 60 artifacts and exhibition items related to royal banquets will be on display, including chandeliers with the imperial plum blossom emblem, iron cooking utensils and matching tableware. At the center are 30 ingredient models, including lamb, pheasant, salmon, truffles and caviar. Visitors place ingredients on a banquet table, where sensors identify them and generative AI produces images of the dishes. A large language model then creates menu names and culinary stories in Korean and English, and the experience takes about five minutes. A 27-meter LED media wall will show a recreated imperial banquet with Korean Empire officials and foreign diplomats.

The Deoksu Palace Management Office said it hopes the exhibition will help visitors understand imperial banquet culture in an accessible and engaging way. It also said the show offers a new experience of cultural heritage through digital technology. The project was developed through a public-private partnership with Davero Art, which was selected for the Korea Creative Content Agency's 2026 AI Content Production Support Program. The exhibition draws on a decade of research, reconstruction and exhibitions on the Korean Empire's royal banquet culture by the heritage agency.

Articles.Title: Deoksu Palace brings imperial feasts back to life with AI exhibition

stories.Headline: Indie studios hide their demos as AI copycats circle
stories.Summary:
Korean indie studio YNOT pulled the public demo of its upcoming restaurant management game Spookitchen, set in a spooky Halloween town, on Oct. 20 after being warned that someone planned to clone it with AI. About a month earlier, its two developers, who go by Sini Ming and Seori Ming, received two threatening emails saying the sender intended to borrow the game's mechanics and make it with AI, and telling them there was no stopping the copying, so they should not waste their time and should just share the release date and price. Sini Ming announced the closure in a thread on X on Oct. 20 and thanked users who had sent encouragement and advice. Japanese indie studio Alliance Arts canceled the public demo of its Russian roulette-style drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflux on Oct. 16, three days before it was due to go live for Steam Next Fest, and switched to closed play sessions for a limited number of participants. In September, Weasel Pit, developer of the indie game Iron Pilgrim, made public a threatening email it had received warning that a copy would go on sale first unless the developer handed over $200 worth of Steam content within 24 hours.

The article says anyone who knows a game's mechanics can now build a similar one with a coding AI, even without development experience, a practice known as vibe coding, with results Koreans call ttalkkak games. Copiers no longer need the original code and can study the look and gameplay shown in a demo or trailer. OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra, released in September, can create, host and share websites, web apps and games directly from a prompt. Clones were already a problem on user-generated content platforms such as Roblox and Fortnite, and the practice has now moved to the wider industry.

YNOT said it worried that a similar game made with AI could be accepted as the original simply because it came out first, and that the original could even be mistaken for plagiarism. Sini Ming wrote that closing the demo right away was only a temporary measure and not a fundamental solution, and that there is no way to stop it as individuals, but letting people know on social media might serve as a warning that Spookitchen is their game and that many people are watching over it. Sini Ming added a resolve to focus on development as usual. Alliance Arts cited concerns that a game imitating the demo's look and gameplay could reach the market before the original.

Some in the industry warn that if games built over years keep losing out to AI-made copies, the industry's foundations could start to crack. An indie developer with five years in the business likened recreating hit games with AI to a new kind of gold farming, saying someone could change only a game's appearance slightly with AI and release it over and over without doing any development. Kim Jeong-tae, a professor in the Department of Game Studies at Dongyang University, said developers increasingly want to hide their ideas rather than share them, and that the market is likely to turn into a battle of capital in which only big games AI cannot easily copy survive. Kim called for clear guidelines on what must not be done and a copyright safety net for indie and small and midsize game companies.

Articles.Title: Indie studios hide their demos as AI copycats circle

stories.Headline: AI chat content carried over verbatim into filings… 80% of judges have “experienced fabricated precedents”
stories.Summary:
A judge recently came across a Supreme Court precedent cited in a brief that looked odd, and a check showed the case number had been made up by artificial intelligence. The Supreme Court's Court Administration Office announced on November 2 the results of a survey on citations of false AI precedents. The survey ran from the 6th to the 16th of the previous month among judges at courts of all levels and drew 360 responses. Eighty percent of the judges said they had seen false or non-existent precedents cited in civil, family and administrative cases.

Among the specific types, citation of a non-existent precedent was most common at 196 responses, or 80.7 percent. That was followed by citation of a false precedent at 159, or 65.4 percent, false or non-existent statutes at 41, or 16.9 percent, and false papers or other materials at 10, or 4.1 percent. Multiple answers were allowed. Judges described parties submitting fabricated judgments that copied the format of Supreme Court decisions, and in extreme cases language from chats with AI or from litigation strategy talks appeared in filings exactly as typed.

Asked who was responsible, 164 judges, or 69.5 percent, most often chose the party personally, while 136 judges, or 57.6 percent, also chose an attorney acting as litigation agent or defense counsel. The Supreme Court said citations of false or non-existent precedents from AI use burden the opposing party and the bench and delay the public right to a trial. Of the respondents, 91.7 percent said an institutional response is necessary, with 64.8 percent calling it very necessary. The most common proposed measure was a basis to impose fines, at 215 responses, or 61.4 percent.

Other proposed measures were a duty to verify cited precedents at 214, or 61.1 percent, a duty to disclose AI use at 212, or 60.6 percent, and sanctions such as referring attorneys for discipline at 194, or 55.4 percent. The Court Administration Office plans to pursue responses through amendments to the Civil Procedure Act and the Criminal Procedure Act. It will consult with relevant agencies, including the Ministry of Justice, to establish a legal basis for fines over false-precedent citations and will submit its views to the National Assembly. It also plans to consider measures such as guidance on AI precautions on the e-litigation website.

Articles.Title: AI chat content carried over verbatim into filings… 80% of judges have “experienced fabricated precedents”

stories.Headline: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount
stories.Summary:
Blackstone President Jon Gray said on Tuesday that the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout will need more equity financing as lenders become more exposed to the companies driving it. He spoke at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Gray said the scale of capital required for AI is creating concentration risks for debt investors, both across the sector and at individual companies. He said lenders have limited upside compared with shareholders, because their returns are largely confined to interest and principal repayments.

Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman, speaking on the same panel, warned that the scale of AI financing could prove too much for markets to absorb. He said AI-related capital spending could reach around $10 trillion over the next five years, citing an estimate by General Atlantic CEO Bill Ford. Roman said about $550 billion in AI debt had been issued in various forms so far this year. He compared the amount required, even with a mix of equity and debt, with a global corporate bond market of roughly $20 trillion, and said that at some point it is going to be too much. Goldman Sachs wrote in a report on Monday that global data center demand will require about $8.5 trillion in capital spending over the next five years.

Gray said financing the buildout would require a combination of public markets, banks and private capital, with companies increasingly turning to structured transactions to limit the debt they take on. He said cash generated by hyperscalers would also fund part of the spending, and that creativity is needed because the scale of capital is enormous. Despite the financing challenges, Gray remained bullish on AI infrastructure, saying demand for computing power was running well ahead of supply. He said spending on AI models across Blackstone’s portfolio companies had risen 20-fold over the past year, as businesses saw financial benefits from uses including coding, customer engagement and content creation. Meeting that demand remains difficult, he said, as securing sites, permits, chips, power and capital becomes more challenging.

Articles.Title: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount

stories.Headline: Korea, India launch economic security talks on supply chains, AI
stories.Summary:
South Korea and India held the first meeting of their economic security dialogue in Seoul on Monday, the presidential office said. The meeting followed an April summit between President Lee Jae Myung and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, where the two leaders agreed to launch the dialogue. Song Ki-ho, vice chief of the Blue House's National Security Office, represented Korea. Pavan Kapoor, deputy national security adviser of India, represented India.

The two sides discussed ways to keep momentum in stabilizing supply chains and to advance cooperation in advanced technology. They also talked about jointly responding to shifts in the global economic security environment. They explored partnerships in shipbuilding, shipping and energy resources. They agreed to strengthen collaboration in strategic sectors including aerospace, critical minerals and AI.

Seoul's National Security Office said Korea plans to continue working with India to promote mutual growth and innovation amid growing global uncertainty. The office gave no further details on the next steps. The dialogue was set up to strengthen supply chain resilience and advance cooperation in cutting-edge technologies. The April summit between the two leaders produced the agreement to launch it.

Articles.Title: Korea, India launch economic security talks on supply chains, AI
