stories.Headline: AI Helps Marin County Residents Shape Local Government Decisions
stories.Summary:
San Rafael residents took part in a program called Civic Dialogues, which was seed-funded by Change.org, and Marin County recently launched a website called Engage Marin to gather ideas from residents. In August, Change.org invited residents to visit civicdialogues.org and answer the question of what they want for San Rafael. According to Change.org spokesperson Erika Lamb, 2,281 residents submitted 973 ideas and cast 59,551 votes. In a second phase, 132 residents met online for a two-hour facilitated dialogue on the right way forward for downtown San Rafael, and each was paid $100.

Change.org has partnered with about 17 jurisdictions across the country to use artificial intelligence to try to bridge ideological divides on contentious issues. It uses AI, including Jigsaw's Sensemaking AI powered by Google Gemini, to sort through public comments and find common ground, and AI also helped write the briefing materials. Change.org announced a $100 million investment over the next three years to rebuild its platform, though Lamb said most of that money would go to its petition platform and a smaller portion to Civic Dialogues. At Engage.MarinCounty.gov, residents can suggest programming for the Veterans Memorial Auditorium, set to reopen in January, and ideas for a county strategic plan, and more than 1,100 people have submitted 765 ideas and more than 2,400 votes.

San Rafael Mayor Kate Colin said the process was worthwhile and that she looked forward to receiving the results from the Change.org team. County Executive Derek Johnson said every agency is trying to crowdsource ideas and that gems can come out of it, adding that people who help write a plan will help underwrite it with their civic and intellectual capital. Deputy County Executive Crosby Burns said AI is used only as a content-safety tool, flagging possibly harmful submissions for review by county staff, who decide what action to take. Change.org expects to release a report on the San Rafael results soon, and it will go to the City Council as proposals for consideration.

Articles.Title: AI Helps Marin County Residents Shape Local Government Decisions - GovTech

stories.Headline: District Educates Parents About Student Artificial Intelligence Usage - Webster-Kirkwood Times
stories.Summary:
The Webster Groves School District passed a policy on artificial intelligence in schools earlier this year and announced SchoolAI as its student-facing platform. To help parents understand how AI is used in the classroom, the district recently held an AI family information night. Administrators and students attended to answer questions and demonstrate SchoolAI and Google Gemini, which teachers and administrators use. The information night took place on Oct. 19.

Superintendent Jana Parker said the district must introduce students to AI and teach them to use it responsibly and to watch for bias and hallucinations, which she described as AI presenting something incorrect or nonexistent as fact. Aaron Winkler, assistant principal at Edgar Road Elementary School and the district's AI coordinator, said students on school-issued devices can only access SchoolAI. He said using it is not mandatory, and some teachers have used it to create chat bots that guide students and answer questions during coursework. Winkler said teachers can see the chat log between students and SchoolAI, and the technology team is alerted if a student enters something that might be harmful, unsafe or worrisome.

Joey Dodson, a junior at Webster Groves High School, demonstrated SchoolAI at the event and said its Homework Helper Hub limits users so they cannot find the answer without doing the work themselves. He said it gives a formula or walks students through the steps so they can find the answer, and he uses AI every day in and out of school. Zach Klestinske, the district's director of technology, introduced Google Gemini, which administrators and teachers use. He said curriculum coordinators upload state standards and rubrics to a Gemini notebook, and he uses it for data summarization, quick math and designing slide shows.

Some parents at the event raised concerns, with some saying elementary schoolers are too young to be introduced to AI and others asking for more clarification on classroom use. Matthew Murphy, whose children attend Hixson Middle School and Webster Groves High School, asked about the ethical aspect, including legal disputes over fair use in training the models, and said he is not sure the district should jump in before there is a more comprehensive understanding. The district offered whiteboards for parents to write their AI-related questions. Using those questions, the district created an AI frequently asked questions page, available at technology.webster.k12.mo.us/resources/wgsdai.

Articles.Title: District Educates Parents About Student Artificial Intelligence Usage - Webster-Kirkwood Times

stories.Headline: CMS student adviser finalists discuss mental health, campus safety, AI, and more
stories.Summary:
Nine high school finalists for the 2027 student adviser to the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education met at the Charlotte Government Center on Wednesday, Oct. 21 for the annual student adviser forum. The position was created through a partnership between Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools and GenerationNation, a nonprofit that promotes civic engagement for K-12 students. The adviser represents the district's nearly 140,000 students at official board meetings. Nine of the ten finalists attended, while Aser Mahmoud of East Mecklenburg High School was absent on a school trip. The forum was moderated by Charles Jeter, executive director of government affairs and policy, and current student adviser Inchara Gopinath.

The finalists are Tahirah Azim of West Charlotte High School, Kyle Boone-McDougall of William Amos Hough High School, Luka Bozovic of Ballantyne Ridge High School, Sreenika Pandiri of Providence High School, Cullen Pyles of Independence High School, Achyuta Raajkumar of Charlotte Engineering Early College, Avery Scrivener of Myers Park High School, Taleya Turner of Mallard Creek High School, Gabi Williams of Phillip O. Berry Academy of Technology and Aser Mahmoud of East Mecklenburg High School. Student voting opened on Oct. 20 and runs through Nov. 3, 2026. The winner will be announced on Nov. 4, 2026, and will serve a one-year term beginning Jan. 1, 2027. The adviser sits on the board during official meetings but does not have a vote.

On mental health, Azim backed a stronger work-life balance for educators, and Raajkumar called for assemblies on mental health and said counselors are often too overworked to meet students individually. Scrivener advocated normalizing mental health conversations on campuses, and Pandiri proposed beginning, middle and end-of-year counselor check-ins paired with peer bulletin networks. On safety, Boone-McDougall suggested placing trusted teachers at entry points instead of costly Evolv scanners, and Turner said the board must acknowledge gun violence and expand programs like Cops & Kids. Pyles pointed to peer-led efforts like See Something Say Something and urged leaders to look into the causes of student distress.

On technology, Williams and Azim supported the district's cellphone limits while saying students still need preparation for a computer-based workforce, and Bozovic argued for clearer guidelines on using AI in coursework. On resources, Turner said Title I schools get resources but not enough compared with larger schools, Raajkumar said smaller facilities are easily overlooked, and Pyles called for collaboration with Exceptional Children educators. On outreach, Azim and Pandiri suggested digital tools such as Instagram and Google Forms, while Boone-McDougall said social media does not represent all students and Bozovic proposed a districtwide council of student council leaders. On working with the board, Boone-McDougall said the key word is compromise because the student adviser does not vote, and Bozovic said pushback can signal a need to revisit policy language.

Articles.Title: CMS student adviser finalists discuss mental health, campus safety, AI, and more - EdNC

stories.Headline: Trump Corrects Pro-MAGA NY Post Reporter Mid-Interview For Saying ‘AI’
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump corrected New York Post reporter Miranda Devine during a Monday episode of her “Pod Force One” podcast, according to an article by Jazmin Tolliver updated on November 2, 2026. When Devine began a question with the acronym AI, Trump interjected with “SI” and smiled. Devine apologized right away and said “super intelligence.” She then asked whether bots and agents attacking infrastructure are something he thinks is real.

Trump dismissed the concerns and said the country is leading in super intelligence and leading by a lot. He said it is beating China and everybody in the whole world and that it is going to be great. He admitted there is “some negative” to AI but claimed the positive outweighs the negative. He said medical cures are coming that nobody would have had for maybe 100 years, and that whoever wins in SI will end up winning.

Trump signed an executive order on super intelligence in September, instructing all government departments and agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super Intelligence” in official communications. More than a week later, he said in a Truth Social post that he considers anyone who does not adopt his preferred term to be “THE ENEMY.” In a follow-up post weeks later, he called out The Wall Street Journal for not using the new terminology. He also announced his intent to soon ban the term artificial intelligence because of its “inaccuracy.”

Articles.Title: Trump Corrects Pro-MAGA NY Post Reporter Mid-Interview For Saying ‘AI’ - AOL.com

stories.Headline: Data centers are the digital steel of the AI century. America can't stop building them.
stories.Summary:
Tom Suder, a professor and the founder and president of the Advanced Technology Academic Research Center, wrote a commentary published by Nextgov/FCW on November 2, 2026. He grew up in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, a steel town that lost its mill, its jobs and its tax base. He argued that data centers are where artificial intelligence lives, and that every advance he describes runs on one. He framed the choice as a race America is in danger of losing.

The article cites the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, launched in November 2025, which connects 17 national laboratories and their supercomputers into one AI discovery platform and aims to double the productivity of American science within a decade. It points to Sweden's MASAI trial of more than 105,000 women, where AI-supported mammography found 29% more cancers than standard screening, and to Sybil, built at MIT and Massachusetts General Hospital, which predicts lung cancer risk up to six years out from a single CT scan. It says the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, citing Heatmap data, reports that at least $260 billion in planned U.S. data center investment was canceled after local opposition this year, costing more than 2 million construction jobs. Loudoun County, Virginia, is described as the world's largest data center market, with roughly 233 data center buildings that generated $1.2 billion in property taxes in fiscal 2026, or 39% of the county budget, and replacing that revenue would take roughly 63 more cents on today's 80.5-cent rate.

Suder said local zoning is paramount, and that a data center does not go next to homes in a community that does not want it. He said the race will be won by building where communities welcome the investment, not by steamrolling neighborhoods. He said the administration's job is to make those projects possible, and that the biggest barrier is power. He called for faster permitting for generation and transmission, a clear path for advanced nuclear, and for the biggest users to pay the full cost of their power so households never subsidize hyperscalers.

The article says most opposition is homegrown, but that in August X reported roughly 200 accounts tied to a suspected Chinese bot farm pushing Americans to oppose data centers. It notes that the Wall Street Journal has reported on a $2 billion plan to turn Aliquippa's long-closed mill site into a power plant and AI data centers. Suder said that for towns like his, the bigger risk is another generation of empty mill sites. The article does not say what happens next beyond his closing call to respect the neighbors, power the grid and keep making digital steel.

Articles.Title: Data centers are the digital steel of the AI century. America can't stop building them. - Nextgov/FCW

stories.Headline: Managing Legal Risk in AI-Driven Employment Decisions - McDermott Will & Schulte
stories.Summary:
McDermott Will & Schulte is holding a virtual event on November 3, 2026, at 12:00 pm ET called Managing Legal Risk in AI-Driven Employment Decisions. The firm says artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping employment decisions, from hiring and screening to promotions and other workforce assessments. The session will be led by members of the firm's Employment Group. The speakers are Ariel Beverly, Brian Casillas and Alivia Combe-DuQuet.

The discussion will cover the current AI landscape for hiring, screening, promotion and other employment decision-making tools. It will address key legal risks under Title VII, the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Age Discrimination Act, with a focus on disparate impact and disability discrimination. Employer and vendor liability issues will be covered, along with due diligence, contracting and oversight. State and local compliance requirements on notice, consent, bias audits and accommodation processes will also be discussed, as will recent litigation and developments such as preemption issues.

Beverly is a partner in Los Angeles who advises and litigates for employers and focuses on wage and hour, employee classification, discipline, terminations, leave and accommodations. Casillas is a partner in Los Angeles who handles employment litigation and counseling and represents clients against claims under the Fair Employment and Housing Act, the Labor Code, Cal/OSHA and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Combe-DuQuet is an associate in Chicago who focuses on labor and employment law matters. Continuing legal education credit is pending, and the firm says it can provide credit in California, Illinois and New York.

The firm describes a rapidly evolving legal landscape for employers evaluating and deploying automated tools. The event is aimed at steps organizations can take to strengthen governance, vendor management, accommodations processes and audit readiness. McDermott is an approved provider and will apply for credit in Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia when lawyers licensed there attend. It can issue reciprocal credit for lawyers licensed in Connecticut and New Jersey, and other attendees will get a Universal Certificate of Attendance to self-apply for credit.

Articles.Title: Managing Legal Risk in AI-Driven Employment Decisions - McDermott Will & Schulte

stories.Headline: Fraud, AI Use Emerge as Key Issues in Visa Holiday Report
stories.Summary:
Visa released a holiday shopping report on November 2, 2026, based on a survey of more than 1,000 U.S. adults conducted by Morning Consult. The report found that 41 percent of respondents would not tell someone that AI helped choose their gift. It also found that 54 percent of respondents have already used AI for at least one shopping task, up from 47 percent in last year's survey. The report's authors said the data shows consumers juggling cost pressures, changing technology and fraud concerns while still working through their gift lists.

The report gives many specific figures. Consumers use AI for comparing prices at 61 percent, checking availability at 59 percent, finding discounts at 57 percent and suggesting gift ideas at 54 percent. Generation Z leads the shift, with more than eight in 10 young consumers open to AI help and 73 percent willing to let it suggest gift ideas, 19 points higher than adults overall. Only 23 percent of U.S. consumers trust generative AI to handle payment transactions for them, though 61 percent said they trust Visa to secure an AI-powered payment, rising to 68 percent among 18- to 34-year-olds and 71 percent among weekly AI users. Nearly three in 10 shoppers said they were targeted by fraud during last year's holiday season, a figure that rises to 39 percent among Gen Z, and three-quarters said they have changed how they shop, including enabling two-factor authentication at 34 percent and changing passwords more often at 34 percent.

Michael Brown, principal U.S. economist at Visa, said consumers are approaching the holidays with both value and security in mind. He said they are looking for deals, trying tools like AI and changing how they shop because of fraud concerns. He also said consumers are adapting and that this resilience is the real story. The report also found that 30 percent of those polled expect to buy at least one gift from an overseas seller this season, with quality cited by 32 percent and uniqueness by 31 percent as top reasons. Travel at 60 percent and live-event tickets at 55 percent topped the list of gifts shoppers are most excited to give or receive.

Articles.Title: Fraud, AI Use Emerge as Key Issues in Visa Holiday Report

stories.Headline: America Can’t Afford an AI Recession
stories.Summary:
Over the past several days, President Donald Trump has told crowds at midterm rallies, including in Michigan, that the economy in his first term was the greatest in the country's history and that this term will surpass it. The economy he points to is largely the AI build-out: the five largest AI-data-center companies, among them Amazon and Google, are on track to spend $900 billion on AI in 2026, about as much as in the previous three years combined. Two AI chipmakers accounted for one-third of corporate profit growth last quarter, and as of September AI stocks made up nearly half of the S&P 500's growth in 2026. By some counts, AI investment is already more than 8 percent of GDP. The article reports that Anthropic's public offering next month could be the largest ever, perhaps valuing the company at $2 trillion, and that a recent Securities and Exchange Commission filing shows Anthropic has up to $807 billion in future contractual obligations for AI infrastructure and expects expenditures to increase significantly.

For comparison, U.S. defense spending was $954 billion in 2025. The biggest cloud companies have nearly $3 trillion in contractual obligations on the books and will soon pass $1 trillion in annual spending, and earnings reports last month showed Meta, Google and Amazon already losing money on their AI investments. The article says data-center construction is booming while all other private construction is in free fall, and that the only source of private investment contributing to GDP growth is tech, according to an analysis by Pacific Investment Management Company. The article says the AI industry has in effect taken on the role of a central bank, managing the economy and issuing money to keep it afloat, and that it needs the economy to run hot so customers have money to sustain revenue growth. It describes the industry's effect on the rest of the economy as like a parasite starving the organism, and compares it to the Dutch natural-gas discovery in 1959, which grew GDP while manufacturing withered.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, in an interview with The New York Times' Ezra Klein this fall, likened the cost of developing the technology to surgery, saying someone has to be cut open and suffer enormous pain so they can be saved. The article says the societal benefits of AI are largely vague or delayed: a wave of AI-discovered drugs has yet to reach pharmacies, the technology has not solved climate change as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Huang have claimed it will, and economy-wide data do not show clear AI-driven productivity gains. It says agents such as Claude Code and Muse have caused chaos, with hackers breaching hospitals, governments, utilities and financial institutions and recently draining billions from the crypto exchange Binance. The article concludes that the only thing more destructive than the AI boom might be a crash.

Articles.Title: America Can’t Afford an AI Recession

stories.Headline: Inside Anthropic’s Urgent Hunt for A.I. Computing Power
stories.Summary:
Late last year, Anthropic’s executives found themselves in a bind, because the company was growing quickly but running out of computing power for artificial intelligence. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, said at The New York Times’s DealBook Summit in December that the amount of computing power needed had become a “cone of uncertainty,” and that the width of the cone made mistakes hard to avoid. That realization sent the San Francisco company on an all-out effort to obtain more computing power. In the months that followed, Anthropic embarked on a deal spree, according to 14 people with knowledge of the A.I. lab, investors and industry experts.

Anthropic has since signed dozens of contracts with former cryptocurrency miners, data center start-ups, chipmakers and tech giants including Amazon, Google, Microsoft and SpaceX to secure enough computing power. It hired experts in data centers, the enormous computing sites powering A.I., and bought data center equipment to speed up construction. It met with developers and explored converting old coal plants and factories into data centers. It also considered deals for tiny amounts of computing power that could add up to what it needs.

Erik Bernhardsson, the chief executive of Modal, a New York company that sells computing power, said that Anthropic is gobbling up a lot of the capacity. Anthropic’s pursuit of computing power is critical as it tries to lead in A.I. and conduct what could be the largest-ever initial public offering this month. The company needs computing power to develop cutting-edge A.I. models and to deliver products, like the Claude chatbot, to businesses and consumers. The resource is so vital that Anthropic spent more than 10 pages of its public offering prospectus detailing the stakes.

Articles.Title: Inside Anthropic’s Urgent Hunt for A.I. Computing Power

stories.Headline: Binance Hackers Employ AI to Hunt High-Value Crypto Targets
stories.Summary:
Hackers accused of carrying out the largest cryptocurrency theft on record may have had help from artificial intelligence, according to a Bloomberg News report on Monday, Nov. 2. The FBI has accused a state-sponsored group from North Korea, known as TraderTraitor, of the $6.3 billion hack on Binance last week. Experts told Bloomberg the group may have only around a dozen members and is trained from an early age to target high-value crypto companies. The group's previous largest hack was the theft of $1.5 billion from the Bybit exchange last year.

The group uses a strategy called Big Game Hunting, using AI to find its targets rather than going after individual investors. Park Seong-su, a staff threat researcher at the cybersecurity company Zscaler, said the group looks for a big haul, targets crypto-related businesses, learns their infrastructure and then tampers with it or with fund transfer processes to carry out a large-scale theft. He said new advances in AI have significantly lowered the barriers to such skills while greatly increasing the speed of these operations. Nick Carlsen, a senior investigator for TRM Labs, told Bloomberg that new techniques used by TraderTraitor indicate the group has turned to AI for its recent hacks.

Dr. Tom Robinson, chief scientist and co-founder of Elliptic, said in an analysis shared with PYMNTS that the laundering is highly complex and clearly automated. He said that in under four days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions. Robinson said most of the funds are still likely being held by North Korea, with the laundered funds potentially already with Chinese money laundering networks, which North Korea has used in the past. Chris Dimitriadis, chief global strategy officer at ISACA, told PYMNTS last week that the financial exposure created by the hack demands board oversight and called it ultimately a governance question that belongs in the boardroom, not just the security team.

Articles.Title: Binance Hackers Employ AI to Hunt High-Value Crypto Targets

stories.Headline: Voting in 2026 Is Getting an AI Slop 'I Voted' Sticker
stories.Summary:
A voter in a town of 12,000 people received an AI-generated "I Voted" sticker at a polling place during the 2026 midterm elections, according to a first-person account published by 404 Media on November 2, 2026. The writer, Matthew Gault, said the sticker was a busy circular design with small bronze text reading "I Voted" at the top of a ring. Bronze laurels encircled a bronze bald eagle stretched atop the American flag, and below that was text reading "250 YEARS ANNIVERSARY" and "SEMIQUENCENTENNIAL." Another line appeared to read "CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA," which the writer assumed was meant to say "CELEBRATING FREEDOM."

The article says "I Voted" stickers have been a US tradition since the 1980s and are a symbol of the election cycle. It notes that in 2020 Marketplace asked whether the stickers were worth the cost, and that a New York cemetery has spent time and money tending the grave of Susan B. Anthony because voters coat it in stickers. In 2008, companies including Starbucks and Ben and Jerry's ran afoul of election laws for offering free treats to people who showed their stickers. The article also says Michigan runs a contest where students submit sticker ideas and the state prints the winners, and that Kentucky, Albany and several other places do the same, while Louisiana commissions local artists.

Gault wrote that he put the sticker on reluctantly and was not proud, and that he sent a photo to journalist friends with his face cropped out. He said they immediately noticed it was AI-generated, and that he did not post the sticker online. He described a friend's sticker from one town over as beautiful and tasteful, with a red ring, a blue field and the crescent and palmetto of South Carolina behind a bold white "I VOTED." Gault wrote that he draws the line at AI-generated "I Voted" stickers.

The article says only Denton, Texas, another place the writer has lived, seems to also have AI-generated stickers, and that Denton's is at least personalized with the city courthouse in the corner. Gault argued that complaining about such stickers may seem trivial, but that small annoyances pile up until people stop noticing AI around them. He wrote that society is currently negotiating what the future will look like and where its AI lines are. The article does not say who produced or paid for the stickers, or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Voting in 2026 Is Getting an AI Slop 'I Voted' Sticker

stories.Headline: On theCUBE Pod: AI bubble lets out some air
stories.Summary:
Last Friday, several tech companies saw their stocks fall amid concerns about an artificial intelligence bubble, as discussed on theCUBE Pod. Alphabet Inc. fell more than 12% after reporting slower search revenue growth, and Amazon.com Inc. dropped 7% as it continues spending on AI infrastructure. Intel Corp. had the steepest drop, almost 30%, after its Thursday earnings report. Anthropic PBC also filed for an initial public offering with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, despite not yet turning a profit. Intercontinental Exchange, the parent of the New York Stock Exchange, announced a partnership with Trade[XYZ] to bring perpetual futures markets built on the Hyperliquid platform to the U.S., subject to regulatory approval.

Dave Vellante, chief analyst at theCUBE Research, compared the situation to past bubbles such as the Dutch tulips of the 1600s, Japanese real estate in the 1980s and the dot-com era. He said the dot-com boom was overhyped but ultimately exceeded expectations, and he sees the AI bubble letting out a little air as a healthy sign. John Furrier, executive analyst at theCUBE Research, argued that rationale and common sense are kicking in and that Wall Street is trying to figure out the transition. He pointed to Alphabet committing $500 billion in a day as a reason he does not think this is a bubble. Furrier also said Intel and its CEO Lip-Bu Tan have an opportunity to turn things around over a multiyear journey.

Vellante said the current phase is a natural adoption phase and that tech is suddenly deflationary, with companies trading capital expenditure for labor. He noted that individual productivity gains are appearing but have not yet shown up at the firm level, and that these things take time. Furrier said cloud growth is needed to support AI expansion and that the infrastructure boom could coexist with a neocloud shakeout as enterprise AI starts creating jobs. He described the shift as a platform game moving from Silicon Valley tech platforms into the markets. The analysts concluded that AI is a unique phenomenon the market will have to grapple with over decades.

Articles.Title: On theCUBE Pod: AI bubble lets out some air

stories.Headline: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
stories.Summary:
AWS published a post on November 2, 2026, about using knowledge distillation to make agentic applications cheaper on Amazon SageMaker AI. The post describes a shopping assistant built on a frontier model that searches a catalog, checks constraints, and recommends a product. It says one completed task is not a single model call but a loop of search, read, refine, verify, and decide, and each step is billed. At production scale, the post says, that per-task cost compounds and can stop a project from shipping.

The method is sequence-level knowledge distillation, or SeqKD, which uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses and then trains a smaller student model on them with supervised fine-tuning. SeqKD needs only the teacher's text, with no logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works with a closed or API-only teacher. The walkthrough uses GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock as the teacher, acting as the ShoppingBench agent, and the benchmark's own scorer keeps only the trajectories that solve the task. Those solved trajectories fine-tune a Qwen3.5-4B student with serverless supervised fine-tuning on SageMaker AI.

The post lists requirements including an AWS account with an IAM role for SageMaker AI that can read and write to an Amazon S3 bucket and invoke the teacher model. It also requires access to SageMaker AI model customization in a supported Region, SageMaker Studio or a local IDE with the AWS CLI, and a Python 3.12 or higher kernel with the SageMaker Python SDK v3 and boto3. The notebook environment should be at least an ml.m5.4xlarge instance, and users need working knowledge of Python, supervised fine-tuning, and tool-using agents. The post also points to an accompanying code repository and a task with a programmatic scorer, using the ShoppingBench test set as the example.

The post says the student keeps much of the teacher's quality at the smaller model's speed and cost, and that the generated answers persist as a dataset that can be reused to train or test different students. It notes that some strong small reasoning models were built in significant part with SeqKD, citing the DeepSeek-R1 distilled models as a well-known example where a large teacher's reasoning was distilled into smaller Qwen and Llama students. The post says SeqKD is an effective starting point for reasoning transfer when the setup is right. It does not say what happens next beyond the walkthrough steps of generating trajectories, encoding them for supervised fine-tuning, running training on serverless infrastructure, and evaluating the student against a held-out benchmark.

Articles.Title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI

stories.Headline: OpenAI says its AI is getting better at doing things humans do, like shopping and meal planning
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 2, 2026, that its artificial intelligence is getting better at doing things humans do, such as shopping and planning meals, according to CNN. The company described the improvement in a statement reported that day. The article gives no further details about the specific tasks or how the work was measured. It also names no individual who announced the change.

The report does not list any numbers, dates or names beyond the company and the publication date. It does not say what the update requires from users or what it changes in the product. No details are given about which version of the AI is involved or how people can access it. The article does not describe any new settings, prices or release schedule.

OpenAI is the company responsible for the claim, and the article attributes the statement to OpenAI as a company rather than to a named person. It does not include direct remarks from an executive or researcher. No outside expert is quoted in the report. The article does not say whether anyone has tested the claim independently.

The context is that AI companies often present their systems as increasingly capable of everyday human tasks. The article does not say what happens next, whether the feature is already available or when more information will come. It gives no timeline for further announcements. The report also does not say how the change might affect users in practice.

Articles.Title: OpenAI says its AI is getting better at doing things humans do, like shopping and meal planning

stories.Headline: In the age of AI, paper ballots are more important than ever
stories.Summary:
In the weeks before the 2026 midterms, artificial intelligence has raised new concerns about election interference, though there is no evidence that AI agents have directly changed any election results. In September, OpenAI said its models had accessed websites run by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission. Before the election, the AI system Claude accessed publicly available voter information. Late last week, hackers were caught using a malicious version of Claude Code to secretly introduce vulnerabilities into programs being developed with the AI agent Cursor.

The article argues that paper ballots matter more than ever in the age of AI. Elections in the U.S. generally use paper records, even when machines count the ballots, so results can be checked by hand later. Some counties try touchscreen voting, but those systems tend to print a paper record too. Paper ballots have problems, since people can fill them in incorrectly or vote for multiple candidates, and they can be destroyed and are slow to count. But paper ballots cannot be hacked remotely, and the article says that is a strong reason to push back on internet-based voting.

The Brennan Center for Justice reached a similar conclusion after the 2020 election, which was again flooded with accusations of rigged voting machines and political interference. Government and election experts there said the public should have more than vague promises of security from private vendors selling a product central to democracy and national security. They said that after massive disinformation campaigns about rigged machines, it is more important than ever that voters have confidence their votes will be counted accurately, and that paper ballots provide such assurance. The article also notes concerns that viral deepfakes could mislead people right before elections and that AI tools, including those used by foreign adversaries, could spread biased information.

Ahead of Tuesday's election, OpenAI said it had opened a war room to track election-related interference, including abuse of its own tools. The article says people should expect speculation about whether AI is directly tampering with election results, but there is no evidence of that for now. It points to the hanging chads that threw the 2000 presidential election into chaos, and says a rogue ChatGPT model could cause far worse political pandemonium. At least in 2000, the article says, people knew there were hanging chads they could check.

Articles.Title: In the age of AI, paper ballots are more important than ever

stories.Headline: Construction safety researchers asking for input on how AI is influencing hazard identification
stories.Summary:
The Construction Safety Research Alliance is asking for study participants to look into how artificial intelligence influences hazard identification and safety decision-making in construction. The group, based in Boulder, Colorado, announced the request in a report dated November 2, 2026. It says participation is not limited to safety directors or managers, and people with relevant experience are welcome. Participants will take part in a one-time session that lasts 30 minutes. The alliance asks them to complete the session independently, in one sitting, using a computer or laptop rather than a phone.

The articles do not list the specific tasks involved in the session. They also do not give a deadline for signing up or a start date for the study. The alliance is responsible for running the study and is the source of the request for input. The articles do not include any statements from alliance officials beyond the call for participants.

No other people or organizations are named as responsible for the work. The articles give little context beyond the study itself and do not say what will happen with the results. They do not describe any next steps after the sessions are completed. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Construction safety researchers asking for input on how AI is influencing hazard identification

stories.Headline: The Next Evolution of AI Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The article, published by tedmag.com on November 2, 2026, is a Siemens-supported piece about a shift in data center power design. It says artificial intelligence is pushing data center design faster than the industry has seen before, as AI factories scale from tens to hundreds of megawatts and rack densities keep climbing. The electrical infrastructure built for decades of assumptions is being pushed beyond its limits, and the industry is now asking whether alternating current is still the most efficient way to power AI-driven facilities. The article presents this as a growing industry conversation rather than a single event, and no individual is named as having done anything.

The article says AC power remains the backbone of today's data centers, but rising power demands are accelerating interest in low-voltage direct current architectures. It says conventional designs may convert electricity multiple times as it travels from the utility source through medium-voltage equipment, transformers, UPS systems and power distribution units to the IT load, and that these cumulative losses become substantial in hyperscale AI environments consuming hundreds of megawatts. It lists three potential advantages of DC: fewer conversion stages, better alignment with technologies such as battery storage and solar that already operate natively on DC, and more efficient power delivery for high-density racks. It gives no specific figures beyond the tens to hundreds of megawatts range and no dates for any transition.

Siemens is presented as supporting a phased approach, and the article paraphrases the company's position rather than quoting individuals. Siemens says operators can deploy proven AC systems now while designing for an orderly move to low-voltage DC as standards, equipment and operating models mature, which it says protects current investments and limits disruption. Siemens describes an integrated power distribution platform spanning medium voltage, low voltage, protection, automation and modular deployment, with digital visibility from medium voltage down to branch circuits. It also says it is developing DC-rated breakers and disconnects, concepts for DC switchboards and busway systems, and protection technologies for DC fault behavior.

The article frames the context as a once-in-a-generation transformation in power infrastructure as AI facilities grow larger, denser and more power-intensive. It says AC will continue to dominate in the near term but that momentum toward DC is becoming difficult to ignore, and that the goal for operators is not to choose sides but to build a foundation that supports both. It says the transition will not happen overnight and that AC infrastructure remains deeply entrenched. The only next step it gives is an invitation to explore a Siemens AI Factories brochure for more on its power solutions and its roadmap from AC to future DC architectures.

Articles.Title: The Next Evolution of AI Infrastructure

stories.Headline: Design-to-Code: Reimagine Handoff Workflow with AI
stories.Summary:
Cisco's DevNet team tried a new approach on the latest revamp of PubHub, an internal publication tool, according to a blog post published on 2 November 2026. Instead of designers creating screens in Figma and developers translating them into code, the team asked AI to build the interface directly from user stories and backend APIs. The AI-generated version worked end to end and was connected to the backend, but it did not follow the team's visual language, some components were not intuitive, and several workflows needed cleanup. A designer then reviewed pages and flows on the working prototype one by one and refined styling and interactions.

The team first tried converting the existing HTML pages into Figma and using a Figma MCP connection so a coding agent could make matching code changes. Three problems emerged: detail was lost in translation, including interactions, complete page and button flows, and animations; updates took longer than expected; and it became unclear whether the Figma file or the HTML prototype was the source of truth. The team then used an AI coding tool to inspect the prototype and adjust its HTML directly, making the HTML prototype the single source of truth. Designers could make changes in stages and give feedback along the way, and the work survived tool switches, from Cursor to Claude to Codex, when the designer ran out of tokens, because the HTML artifact held the design state. New iterations came every day, where a single page had taken days under the old process.

The workflow now runs in steps: the product team defines user stories and backend APIs, an AI coding agent builds an end-to-end UI, designers refine the HTML prototype with an AI coding tool, and designers share the updated HTML with developers along with the design system, end-to-end flows for different personas, and a changelog. Developers give these to a coding agent, which applies the design changes to the real project, and the team tests and reviews the result, often live, then repeats. The prototype includes an embedded design system, a persona switcher, and changelogs for each iteration. The blog says the biggest change was moving the design and engineering feedback loop closer together, with more frequent reviews, earlier testing, and less distinct roles, and it advises teams to start from a working build, keep one source of truth, build the handoff into the prototype, document what the agent cannot infer, plan for token limits, shorten the review cycle, and keep the designer's judgment central.

Articles.Title: Design-to-Code: Reimagine Handoff Workflow with AI

stories.Headline: Startup Athena raises $2.5M in pre-seed funding to revamp the revenue model for legal AI
stories.Summary:
Athena Circle Corp., an AI-native legal technology startup focused on commercial real estate deals, raised $2.5 million in pre-seed funding, the company said on November 3, 2026. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz’s accelerator program, a16z Speedrun, and no other investors were named. The company was founded by co-founders Cem Ucan and Kieran John Keenan, along with founding engineer José Braz, all of whom previously worked at the legal AI startup Legora AB. Athena launched its service two months before the announcement and had already signed up 22 legal firms as clients. Instead of selling software tools to law firms, Athena provides a legal service through its affiliated law firm and charges a fixed fee per transaction, typically 30% to 50% lower than standard rates.

Its AI agents automate work on commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing, including purchase agreements, loan documents, due diligence and administrative closing tasks, while human lawyers remain in the loop for final legal determinations. The agents reduced review times by an average of 70%, according to the company. Keenan said each workflow starts with an incoming agreement that the agents check against standard deal sheets to flag inconsistencies, prepare redlines and draft client communications, after which attorneys review the work and approve all deliverables. Ucan said most legal AI companies sell tools to traditional law firms, but Athena took a different approach, with AI working alongside a law firm designed around it from day one. Keenan said he measures progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent’s work and confidently stand behind it.

L. Miguel Arce, chief executive of the Texas-based firm Mox Living, said Athena delivered a complete purchase agreement in less than 48 hours, the fastest turnaround he has seen, and that the system learns from every deal. Troy Kirwin of a16z Speedrun said clients still demand to speak to a human who can take responsibility for the work, and he described Athena as building around that need with a team obsessed with scaling fast. Keenan said the industry is preparing for a wave of new commercial deals as properties financed through short-term loans in 2021 and 2022 reach their refinancing deadlines, and he hopes Athena can win a significant share of that business. The company also plans to expand into new markets, new property classes and even new legal domains. The articles do not say what happens next beyond those expansion plans.

Articles.Title: Startup Athena raises $2.5M in pre-seed funding to revamp the revenue model for legal AI - SiliconANGLE

stories.Headline: Omen AI adds liquid know-how in $16 million Aquatic Labs acquisition
stories.Summary:
Omen AI has acquired Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash-and-stock deal, the company announced on November 2, 2026. Omen AI was founded in 2024 to build a real-time sensor that checks whether valves are failing or whether bacteria growth threatens to choke off water flow in data center cooling systems. The deal came together after Omen founder Zach Laberge was introduced to Aquatic Labs CEO Allan Adams by an investor in the filtration space. Both startups were building real-time water sensors with complementary technology, with Omen's sensors looking for elements in the water and the Aquatic Labs sensor testing its alkalinity.

The acquisition follows a $31 million Series A that Omen raised in June. Adams becomes the company's chief science officer, and the combined teams are working to integrate both technologies into one sensor, which they expect to have on the market by early next year. Omen's initial sensors will be monitoring chips pulling in 250 to 300 MW of power by the end of the year, worth about $5 to $7 billion, according to Laberge. He said the hope is to be installed on the equivalent of 1 GW of chips by the end of 2027.

Adams told TechCrunch that putting the two technologies in the same sensor creates a much richer picture of the water and the fluid, and that the combination unites their vision of automating what had previously been a slow, manual process. He said he hopes to see the technologies have an impact outside of data centers as well, noting that water goes into data centers, comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and that the whole process should happen as safely and responsibly as possible, which means measuring things. Laberge said Omen's team isn't worried about shifting sentiment on AI infrastructure spending, since their work comes after a data center has been built. He said the company is working with customers on stuff they are building today or have already built, and that all of those projects were financed 12 months ago.

U.S. data centers use 17 to 19 billion gallons of water to cool their hot-running chips each year, and that number is expected to triple in the next five years, according to The Water Foundation. Monitoring lets data center operators use the same fluid for longer and minimize the costs of a cleanup, since operators typically dump the water rather than risk damage to expensive equipment. AI companies once estimated as much as $4 trillion would be spent on AI infrastructure by 2030, but some investors have grown skeptical of the buildout, sending hyperscaler stocks plummeting in recent days. Laberge said that if there is tightness, this is still going to be the biggest market in human history, even if you sliced it in half.

Articles.Title: Omen AI adds liquid know-how in $16 million Aquatic Labs acquisition

stories.Headline: Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes
stories.Summary:
Thessai, a Bellevue, Washington startup led by former Microsoft HoloLens executive Michael Nassirian, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that uses motion sensors and AI instead of cameras, microphones or wearables. Sensors placed around the home feed software that learns a person's normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. When something falls outside that baseline, like a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night or a front door opening at 2 a.m., the system sends an alert through a mobile app. Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured; she had a phone and an emergency button within reach but did not use them and told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages to families with an older relative living alone: Basic, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home's Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription, while Premium adds a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half. An Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences. The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators.

Nassirian said older adults often keep quiet about a fall or health scare, saying they are OK, that they do not want to bother anyone, and most importantly that they are embarrassed. He said the older adult decides what gets monitored, and through the app they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late does not set one off. Nassirian said the system was designed "to the last bit of the person's privacy."

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. According to AARP's 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, 75% of older adults want to stay in their homes and 73% want to stay in their communities, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040. Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far, with operators pitching Thessai to renters as a "smart home" feature. The company's advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care. Nassirian said Thessai is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA's own secure network.

Articles.Title: Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

stories.Headline: The Fight Against Big Tech’s AI Takeover Must Continue Past the Midterms
stories.Summary:
Since Donald Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025, Big Tech companies led by Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg have gained more profit and political power than ever before, according to Truthout. As these companies pushed AI technology onto U.S. communities, often without consent, many Americans organized against AI data centers, Flock cameras and claims that the technology is inevitable. The article says mainstream media have treated the fight against AI as a midterms issue, but it describes the opposition as part of a wider struggle against tech oligarchical power. It was published on November 3, 2026.

The article says tech companies have reportedly made secret deals with municipalities to build AI data centers and worked with law enforcement to install invasive Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers. It also says companies are seeking to develop AI “agents” designed to displace workers. It cites an ABC, Washington Post and Ipsos poll finding that nearly two-thirds of Americans are anxious about AI taking their jobs. It points to the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild of America strikes, which won protections such as forbidding studios from replacing human actors with “digital replicas” without consent.

Gil Durán, author of The Nerd Reich, told Truthout that the federal government should direct and regulate AI development rather than leave it to private companies. He compared AI to the Manhattan Project, saying private companies should not be in charge of such powerful technology. Anna Kornbluh, a Chicago-based activist and literary scholar, argued that Big Tech figures could pay taxes and called democratic deliberation over what public money is for the political question that affects everything. Data & Society’s Livia Garofalo said it is hard to think about a democratic way to regulate something so corporate, and former Kickstarter worker Clarissa Redwine said people hate how technology is used, not technology itself.

The article says the movement must go beyond opposition and articulate a vision for democratizing technology, and it cites Data & Society’s report “The AI Factory” on opposition in Pennsylvania. The report describes Pennsylvanians joining with existing activist groups against a pro-AI coalition that includes Amazon, Microsoft, Gov. Josh Shapiro and private developers. It outlines three long-term strategies: myth-busting, unveiling networks of power and collusion, and tracing data centers. The article says grassroots opposition in states like Utah, New Jersey, Virginia and Pennsylvania will need to keep holding policymakers and corporations accountable after the midterms.

Articles.Title: The Fight Against Big Tech’s AI Takeover Must Continue Past the Midterms - Truthout

stories.Headline: Super Micro's AI Boom Faces a Margin Test in Q1
stories.Summary:
Super Micro Computer Inc., the artificial intelligence server builder, is heading toward its fiscal first-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, according to GuruFocus. Preliminary results indicated improved sales and margins, which raised expectations on Wall Street. The company had previously estimated quarterly sales of between $18.5 billion and $19.5 billion, partly on growing demand for AI systems. It also forecast gross margin of 12% to 12.5%, up from an earlier range of 10.4% to 10.8%.

Wall Street is looking for earnings of $1.23 a share, up more than 251% from a year earlier, the article said. Analysts also expect revenue to jump more than 225% to $16.26 billion. The higher margin forecast has helped ease worries about further margin compression. Even so, the market will want more than growth from the report.

KeyBanc said Supermicro also has to show it can fund expansion internally, which would lower the risk of more stock dilution or increased borrowing. Competition from Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprise remains a pressure point, according to the article. The next catalyst is the results report on Tuesday. Management is also expected to update investors on margins, cash creation and AI-server demand.

Articles.Title: Super Micro's AI Boom Faces a Margin Test in Q1

stories.Headline: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
stories.Summary:
As midterm candidates made their final pitches to voters in late October 2026, experts spoke out about how artificial intelligence had shaped the election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI had become a major issue in several races over the previous few months. He noted that the rhetoric around it differed from other new technologies, saying that while tech had traditionally been liked as part of the political economy, that changed in the past year, with a more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI. Borick said the political calculus around AI had gone from positive to negative in both red and blue states after the backlash, picking up on broader public concerns about AI's effects on society, the economy and communities.

The articles give several figures on money in the cycle. More than $16 billion was raised ahead of the elections, with ad spending in House and Senate races topping $4 billion, according to AdImpact, which called it the most expensive cycle on record. Two leading AI super PAC networks, affiliated with OpenAI or Anthropic, spent $50.7 million on the primaries but only $8.5 million in the lead-up to the general election. A CNBC analysis from early October found that 14 of the 20 largest donors and donor groups exclusively or nearly exclusively backed GOP candidates or aligned groups. A recent poll of Iowa and Ohio voters, published online for SEMAFOR, found the vast majority wanted greater regulation of artificial intelligence.

Shobita Parthasarathy, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, said Republicans had been in a much closer position with AI companies over the past year or more, so they tended to talk more about the cost issue and were less likely to discuss broader issues or a moratorium. Borick said that at the local level, conservatives, liberals, Republicans and Democrats often align in opposition to data centers or in concerns about AI, which creates the potential for political realignments. Intercept managing editor Maia Hibbett said the data showed AIPAC was still spending a lot of money on many races and more often than not its candidates were still winning. Intercept politics reporter Matt Sledge said the AI super PACs were mainly about setting the tone for future federal regulation, and that such groups often run ads with vague names that are not associated with crypto or AI.

Sledge said polls showed it was not a great environment for Republicans, so the spending may have softened the blow but could still be overwhelmed by a blue tide. Hibbett said that no matter which party won control of either or both houses of Congress, many people elected would have gotten there on the backs of Big Tech and special interests. Sledge added that the groups were backing many people in safe seats without tight elections, and the goal may simply be to buy a few friends in Congress, since having people who can stop regulation can be as good as having people who can shape and pass laws. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the elections.

Articles.Title: There's been an increase in AI-generated ads during the midterm election
