OpenAI and other firms have argued that a licensing system for digital content would be too cumbersome, and the Justice Department has supported that argument for training AI models but not necessarily for outputs of AI queries. Hollywood's support comes as the Times has expanded its legal battle against the AI industry. The company, alongside other publishers, on Monday sued web browser Brave, alleging it scraped its copyrighted works and distributed them to AI firms.

Articles.Title: Hollywood backs NYT in AI copyright battle versus OpenAI, Microsoft

stories.Headline: Vintage fun: Prodding AI agents using retro hardware just because you can
stories.Summary:
Darko Mesaroš, an AWS developer advocate, connected a teletype to a modern command-line interface to interact with AI technology through a DECwriter and fanfold paper, or the display and keyboard of a computer whose heyday ended 40 years ago. His project involved AWS Kiro, a command-line interface and agentic coding service. The work was reported by The Register on November 2, 2026. Mesaroš used Hayes modem emulation for the serial connection and Agent Client Protocol for working with Kiro.

He used a WiModem232, which emulates a standard Hayes-compatible modem and was initially used to connect Commodore 64s to BBSes in the modern era. A simple Rust application took Kiro's output, obtained via ACP, and turned it into something a teletype or dumb terminal could handle. Kiro's CLI is not really suitable for a teleprinter capable of 30 characters per second. Mesaroš said the concept is portable and that any coding assistant or harness supporting ACP should work, so he could plug in Claude Code or Codex.

Mesaroš said the biggest problem is that the setup does not handle packet drops at all, and dropped packets are simply gone with no retries. He said there is no buffering, and information comes down through the serial device, which is itself the bottleneck. He had toyed with using GPIO pins on a Raspberry Pi but settled on the serial device because everything worked out of the box, calling it kind of cheating but also kind of good. He collects vintage hardware, including machines from Commodore and Sinclair, a 1974 Data General Eclipse minicomputer, Sun hardware and an old Decwriter, and he has learned soldering skills to keep old hardware operational.

He said he has a big peeve over modern computers that cannot be fixed, and it feels like a waste of resources that when his MacBook dies he has to drill a hole through it so nobody steals his data and throw it away. On his blog he wrote that the project absolutely serves no purpose. He said it provided a novel way of working out how the ACP protocol worked and taught him how to debug serial connectivity. He said it helps him stretch what he can do in the current age of AI coding and keeps his curiosity alive.

Articles.Title: Vintage fun: Prodding AI agents using retro hardware just because you can

stories.Headline: Marble Cognition Raises $3.75M: AI Learns Your Job [2026]
stories.Summary:
Marble Cognition, a Munich startup founded in 2025 by Felix Rösner and Christophe Schmit, raised a $3.75 million pre-seed round led by Heartcore Capital and Seedcamp, according to reports from Tech Funding News, Tech.eu and EU-Startups. The company builds a desktop app that watches employees work in business software, recording screen activity, mouse clicks and keystrokes, and turns what it sees into structured process maps that AI agents can follow. The agents, called Coworkers, then take over routine steps inside the tools a team already uses, with humans staying involved where a step needs judgment. The reports name EGYM, Mutares and Enam as clients, though they do not say whether those are paid contracts or pilots, and the valuation was not shared.

Angels in the round include a Datadog board member, a Personio founder, and executives from McKinsey, Mistral AI and Lovable. Rösner said every company he talks to wants AI to take over real work but nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done, so Marble solves that first by having Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. One report says Rösner claimed the round closed in under two weeks, a figure the article marks as unconfirmed. The reports do not say how long the app must watch a process before a model is ready, how it handles sensitive fields, or how many examples it needs.

The idea is not new: macro recorders have captured clicks and keystrokes for decades, robotic process automation let analysts record and replay tasks, and process mining read system logs to reconstruct workflows. Marble's bet is that software can do the shadowing that new hires normally learn by watching colleagues, which would cut the cost of deploying an agent because nobody has to interview staff and draw flowcharts first. If the extracted models need heavy human cleanup, the product becomes one more recorder. No public accuracy data exists yet, and Minicor's $3.8M seed for AI agents that drive legacy desktop apps shows the early field is already crowded.

Articles.Title: Marble Cognition Raises $3.75M: AI Learns Your Job [2026]

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s Claude AI Predicts a Monumental Move for SUI by 2027
stories.Summary:
An article published by Yahoo Finance on November 2, 2026, reported that Anthropic's Claude AI predicted a large move for the Sui crypto token, SUI, by January 1, 2027. The prediction was built on an intentionally extreme scenario, not a realistic base case, in which a consortium of gaming studios, social media platforms and AI application developers chooses Sui as the preferred blockchain for real-time consumer experiences and autonomous AI agents. Under that scenario, games, social apps and agent-based systems would run mainly on Sui's object-centric architecture, driving sustained transaction volume. The article described the idea as pure speculation and entertainment.

The article said SUI had been consolidating in the $0.88 to $0.91 region after a broader pullback, with resistance around $0.95 to $1.05. It said a sustained breakout above $1.20 to $1.40 would confirm intermediate strength in a standard bull market, with a longer-term recovery toward the prior all-time high near $5.35. Nearer-term supports were listed near $0.85 to $0.88 and $0.80 to $0.83. Under the extreme scenario, and assuming a full crypto bull market, the article said SUI could reach between $25 and $45, with a stretch target toward $70 or more by January 1, 2027.

The article attributed the prediction to Claude AI, made by Anthropic, and was written by Daniel Francis. It said the catalyst would require extraordinary coordination among major gaming, social and AI developers that is currently highly unlikely. It stressed that the outlook remains pure speculation and entertainment, not a realistic base-case forecast. It also listed external factors that could support the scenario, including resolutions to geopolitical conflicts, more accommodative central bank policy and continued Bitcoin and Ethereum ETF inflows.

The article did not say what happens next beyond the January 1, 2027 date attached to the prediction. It noted that momentum indicators sat in oversold-to-neutral territory with room to run into extreme overbought readings typical of parabolic advances. It said holding the listed support levels would keep the broader recovery structure intact. It presented the price range only as a speculative scenario tied to unlikely coordination and supportive market conditions.

Articles.Title: Anthropic’s Claude AI Predicts a Monumental Move for SUI by 2027

stories.Headline: Government Linux Servers Targeted With SysGoRAT and Suspected AI-Generated Scripts
stories.Summary:
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said it observed a cyber espionage campaign against Linux infrastructure tied to government entities and state-affiliated organizations between October 2025 and April 2026. The researchers, Roey Porat and Tom Fakterman, tracked the activity as CL-UNK-1211, with the letters standing for cluster and unknown motivation. The attackers used open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors and web shells, and tried to disable endpoint protections, wipe system logs and plant fake red-team markers to make the activity look like a legitimate security assessment. They also tried to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to reach social media accounts.

The campaign used malicious PHP and shell scripts that were likely generated with AI, according to Unit 42. The researchers said several scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes explaining the code's logic rather than standard developer documentation, which suggested the code was copied from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent. The attackers replaced the .bashrc file with a malicious version to steal passwords, injected code into PHP login pages to harvest admin credentials, and scanned configuration and command history files for cleartext email, SMTP and database passwords. They also deployed a custom Go-based remote access trojan called SysGoRAT, which connects over WebSocket to a hard-coded IP address, 104.194.158[.]65 on port 443, and supports commands to run arbitrary code, open an interactive shell, take screenshots, exfiltrate files and install persistence on Windows and Linux. A script named search_social.php searched email headers for social media keywords and displayed the file path, sender, recipient and subject, while a script called zip_mails.sh was meant to compress emails into ZIP archives but failed because of syntax errors.

Unit 42 said the campaign showed attackers combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows against government Linux server infrastructure, using AI to quickly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts while cutting manual developer effort. The report also noted that Google Threat Intelligence Group, Mandiant and Microsoft have documented threat actors abusing open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks such as ARTEX, PentAGI, Hexstrike and CAIRN. ARTEX was taken down by its author after reports of misuse but has spawned versions including a commercial offering called ARTEX PRO and a localized variation called ScopeWeaver. GTIG and Mandiant said such frameworks compress attack timelines to machine speed but currently trade stealth for velocity, since unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers and leaves distinct code-level traces that raise the chance of detection and mitigation.

Articles.Title: Government Linux Servers Targeted With SysGoRAT and Suspected AI-Generated Scripts

stories.Headline: The Democrat Shaping the Party’s AI Debate
stories.Summary:
In early November, a closed-door conference on artificial intelligence is expected to be held at the Four Seasons in San Francisco, in the brief window between the midterm election and the presidential-primary season. Presidential hopefuls are expected to sit for talks and dinners with leaders of the country's largest labor unions, donors to the biggest Democratic super-PACs, and political strategists. The host is Alex Bores, a two-term state lawmaker from the Upper East Side who lost the Democratic primary in June to succeed Jerry Nadler in Congress. Last year Bores was mostly unknown in national politics, and after sponsoring New York's RAISE Act in the State Assembly he campaigned on bringing similar regulation to the federal level.

The RAISE Act, as of January 1, will require AI companies to publish safety protocols and report incidents of potential catastrophic risk in their models. Bores's campaign prompted Leading the Future, a super-PAC that has received millions from an OpenAI executive, to spend roughly $8 million on an effort to defeat him. Bores received a surge of campaign contributions as a rival set of AI companies and tech-world figures who support regulation poured $18 million into the race to counter LTF. He lost the primary to Micah Lasher but became perhaps the most preeminent voice for AI safety. He is now launching a campaign to push the field of 2028 Democratic presidential candidates to write the rules for AI, through an advocacy organization he started months after losing his race called Who Decides, which raised $10 million at launch and has planned commitments of another $20 million.

Bores has already met with many would-be 2028 contenders, among them Kamala Harris and Pete Buttigieg, or their advisers. Who Decides is hiring dozens of staffers and placing them in the six early-primary states and the seven key swing states to meet with prominent local pastors, Democratic Party county chairs, and heads of Indivisible groups. Bores says he wants to make AI safety something a Democrat believes in by default, like marriage equality or being pro-choice, rather than an issue candidates split on. He says the group cannot match Leading the Future tit-for-tat in spending but will have public opinion and public support and will be shaping the terms of the debate. Chris Larsen, a crypto billionaire who gave Bores $3.5 million for his congressional run, says you cannot go like Sanders, calling that too simplistic and without a real plan.

Party strategists increasingly view AI as the central tension of the presidential-primary contest, partly because it touches on wealth inequality, the economy, the environment, and education. Concerns about data centers have morphed from a local land-use issue into a stand-in for the power of tech companies. Bernie Sanders has called for a moratorium on data centers and further AI research, and others on the left think AI companies should be treated as public utilities. David Shor, head of data science at Blue Rose Research, has urged his party to notice that national sentiment is not caution but rage, citing research that broad majorities, even among conservatives, favor heavily taxing AI companies to help people negatively impacted by the technology. Rob Flaherty, a digital director for the Biden White House and deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris in 2024, warns that if Democrats are weak and mealymouthed and Republicans do their demagogue thing, that opens up space for a conservative economic populist.

Articles.Title: The Democrat Shaping the Party’s AI Debate

stories.Headline: AI Ad-Placement Companies Rembrand and Whisper World Merge, Eye IPO
stories.Summary:
Rembrand and Whisper World, two companies that place brands into video after it has been filmed, are merging in a mostly stock-based deal expected to close in January. The combined company will be called WRLabs. Whisper World founder Manav Kapoor will be group CEO and co-chair, and Rembrand CEO Omar Tawakol will become co-chair. The two firms first met in June 2025 as partners, began merger talks that November, signed a term sheet in February and reached a definitive agreement this month.

WRLabs will act as the parent company and fund research into AI video editing, with Rembrand as the technology arm building a coding agent for visual effects. Whisper World, Spaceback and MRFactory will keep their names. Whisper World will keep selling in-content ads, Spaceback turns social posts into paid ads and MRFactory runs virtual production studios. The combined company will have about 450 employees in eight countries, work with roughly 3,000 advertisers and reach over 2 billion viewers a month, according to the company.

Tawakol said an IPO is absolutely on the table and that WRLabs will raise money after the deal closes. He said the merger will grow Rembrand about fourfold and make its in-content ad business instantly profitable, and that no layoffs are planned. Kapoor said the deal brings technology that can handle far more insertions without new hires and gives Whisper World an entry into the U.S. through Rembrand’s supply partnerships, which he said would take longer and cost more to build alone. Tawakol said the IPO plans are still early but he is bullish, arguing the company wins whether or not the market adjusts.

Whisper World, founded in 2013, puts virtual billboards into established shots after actors have left the frame, and it completes about 30,000 insertions a year, with Rembrand’s AI handling about 70% of them in South Africa and India. Unilever, Nestlé and Procter & Gamble have bought the format for five years, Kapoor noted. Tawakol founded Rembrand in 2022, and it raised $23 million in Series A in January 2025, bringing total funding to $31 million. He declined to give Rembrand’s current valuation but said the roughly $80 million figure that has been reported dates to that round, when the company had about $2 million in bookings, and it is now about 20 times that size.

Articles.Title: AI Ad-Placement Companies Rembrand and Whisper World Merge, Eye IPO

stories.Headline: ‘VRChat’ Faces User Backlash After Rejecting ‘AI-generated’ Content Label
stories.Summary:
VRChat released a survey earlier this month asking users whether the social VR platform should label AI-generated content, and the survey polled over 21,000 users. Japanese outlet Automaton reported that around 95% of responders wanted an AI-generated content label, which would make it easier to filter out AI content. In a statement last week, the studio said it would not implement the change. VRChat said some creators would honestly label their content, but others would try to pass generative or assisted work off as completely hand-authored.

VRChat said a label could create "sleuthing" behavior, where people try to sniff out AI content or harass creators who are not using AI tools at all. The company said this could create negative behavior spirals it does not want to encourage. Instead, VRChat has vowed to ban what it calls AI-generated inaccurate thumbnails used to advertise worlds. It is also adding a way to like and dislike worlds and a way to give feedback on worlds within VRChat. The studio said it is still debating an optional "Human-authored" mark that creators could apply when publishing.

VRChat said it has not decided on that mark, and that if it happens it would be optional and would only show on a world's detail page. The company said the mark would not affect discovery ranking, and a missing mark would never be an accusation or something users could report. VRChat said it leans toward a "Human-authored" mark over an "AI-generated" label, adding that saying you used AI can feel like a confession. Users have responded by review bombing the app on Steam. At the time of writing, VRChat has a "Mostly Negative" rating of about 4,000 users, a 33% positive rating over the past 30 days, which pushed its overall lifetime rating from "Mostly Positive" to "Mixed."

The negative reviews are smaller than the backlash over the studio's 2022 decision to add anti-cheat software, which led to over 33,000 negative reviews in July 2022 and about 8,000 more the following month, according to SteamDB. The article says AI content is a blessing and a curse, since it lets creatives make things without full knowledge of Unity or Blender but also brings a rush of slop. It says VRChat's creators are a big part of its identity, and for many long-term users it matters how avatars and worlds were made. The article says world generation will eventually become even easier, and asks how long an AI-generated content label will really be relevant when AI is in everything.

Articles.Title: ‘VRChat’ Faces User Backlash After Rejecting ‘AI-generated’ Content Label

stories.Headline: Japan can build defense edge on AI, Palantir CEO says
stories.Summary:
Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp said in an interview with Nikkei in New York on Oct. 28 that Japan could gain an edge in building its own AI stack for defense needs. The interview was published on Nov. 2, 2026. The comments signaled the U.S. big data analytics firm's willingness to supply AI systems to the Japan Self-Defense Forces. The article did not say that any deal had been signed.

The article gives no specific requirements, costs or timelines for such a supply arrangement. It also gives no dates beyond the Oct. 28 interview and the Nov. 2 publication. Related Nikkei headlines listed with the story say Japan is weighing the use of Palantir and Anduril AI systems for its defense forces. Another listed headline says Mitsubishi Heavy is to develop Japan-based defense AI with Preferred Networks.

Karp is the person named as making the comments, and Palantir is the company named as eager to supply the systems. The article paraphrases him as saying Japan's technological strengths could give it an edge in AI-enabled defense if the country is attacked. It does not give further direct remarks from him. No Japanese government official is named or quoted in the article.

The context given is Japan's interest in AI for defense, shown by the related headlines on weighing Palantir and Anduril systems and on reorganizing defense research around AI and cyber. The article does not say what happens next beyond Palantir's stated willingness to supply. It reports no decision by Japan. It also carries a related opinion headline urging Japan to think twice before entrusting Palantir with sensitive data.

Articles.Title: Japan can build defense edge on AI, Palantir CEO says

stories.Headline: Westpac AI Migration Halves Cost to $35M [2026]
stories.Summary:
Westpac said it used AI tools to move its legacy St.George data warehouse to its cloud platform, ADAPT, at about half the budgeted cost. The bank had budgeted about A$70 million for the migration and now expects it to cost around A$35 million, according to iTnews. Westpac also said the work finished more than two years earlier than expected. CEO Anthony Miller presented the figures to investors alongside the group's full-year results on November 2, 2026.

The bank said AI handled three jobs in the migration: code conversion, testing and documentation. Westpac expects about A$15 million a year in direct benefits, with booking to start in FY27, the same year it plans to decommission the old warehouse. The bank reported statutory net profit of A$6.8 billion for the year ended September 30, 2026, down one percent on the prior year. Westpac did not name the AI products, models or vendors involved, and it did not give an exact completion date.

Miller tied the project to UNITE, Westpac's multi-year technology simplification program. He said the team used AI tools to speed up code conversion, testing and documentation, which helped complete the migration more than two years earlier at half the cost. He also said the tools, methods and experience developed can be reused for other migrations. The articles note that the A$35 million is a forecast against a budget, not an audited final spend, and that no outside party has tested the claim.

ADAPT is Westpac's cloud data and analytics platform, built on Azure according to iTnews. Westpac has not said which of its remaining legacy platforms it plans to tackle next or in what order. The articles say reusable tooling only transfers if the next system resembles the first, and a warehouse on a different vendor stack may need fresh work. Westpac expects further benefits from reusing the capability on other migrations.

Articles.Title: Westpac AI Migration Halves Cost to $35M [2026]

stories.Headline: Is Alphabet's Massive AI Spending a Problem? The CFO Just Revealed Everything Investors Need to Know in a Single Sentence.
stories.Summary:
Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, mostly for its artificial intelligence compute build-out, and that figure could keep climbing in the fourth quarter and in 2027. The company raised $40 billion last quarter alone, part of tens of billions in equity and debt raised over the last few years. Shares fell after the third-quarter earnings release as investors worried the company was overextending itself on a speculative investment. On the earnings call, CFO Anat Ashkenazi said the company expects to generate an attractive return on invested capital that stays meaningfully above its cost of capital, along with strong cash flow from operations.

Alphabet is the only company with a full stack of AI products and services, according to the article. It designs Tensor Processing Unit chips for training and inference, develops its own frontier large language models, runs them on Google Cloud, and sells TPU systems directly to third parties. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said server spending, about 65% of total capex last quarter, has a payback period of less than two years, and the payback for its own TPU systems is half of that. Amazon has said its payback period for servers and networking equipment is nearly three years.

Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway began a position in Alphabet last year, and it has grown to the conglomerate's fourth-largest marketable equity holding. The article says his thesis was that Alphabet can earn a high return on capital while putting an enormous amount of capital to work. Analysts on average expect free cash flow to rise from around $50 billion, adjusted for stock-based compensation, before the investment cycle to more than $300 billion by 2031. The article also says investors should expect a deeper drop in free cash flow in 2027 as spending continues to ramp up.

Articles.Title: Is Alphabet's Massive AI Spending a Problem? The CFO Just Revealed Everything Investors Need to Know in a Single Sentence.

stories.Headline: FuriosaAI: US$2.9bn Korean Startup Accelerating AI Silicon
stories.Summary:
FuriosaAI, a South Korean AI semiconductor company, announced on November 2, 2026 that it had completed a KRW820bn (US$620m) Series D funding round. The round brought its post-money valuation to approximately US$2.9bn. The company was founded in 2017 and designs AI inference accelerators for data centres. Its second-generation chip, RNGD, entered mass production in January 2026.

FuriosaAI said it will use the capital to expand RNGD production, strengthen its software ecosystem and speed up development of its third-generation accelerator. It expects to produce 20,000 RNGD accelerators in 2026 and more than 40,000 in 2027. Customers deploying RNGD include LG Group, Samsung SDS and Upstage, and Samsung SDS launched its commercial NPU-as-a-service on RNGD in July. The company is also working with Broadcom on third-generation chips for frontier agentic models.

June Paik, Co-Founder and CEO, said the company's priority from the start has been inference accelerators that deliver performance, efficiency and programmability. He said RNGD has proven this through large-scale deployment with major customers. He added that the new investment will let the company ramp up RNGD production and build its third-generation chip. He also said RNGD targets models running at up to about 100 tokens per second per user, which he said matters most for enterprise workloads.

Korea's National Growth Fund committed KRW370bn (US$280m), and the Export-Import Bank of Korea, UAMCO and Hanwha Asset Management joined as new investors. All three original seed investors, NAVER through NAVER Ventures, DSC Investment and KDB Capital, contributed again, along with Korea Development Bank, Nextrans and Kakao Investment. Other backers named include Infinitum, Jericho Capital, QUDA Capital, Cisco Investments, NeoFort Holding and Worldline Capital. The company says it is expanding commercial deployments with enterprise and cloud customers globally.

Articles.Title: FuriosaAI: US$2.9bn Korean Startup Accelerating AI Silicon

stories.Headline: AI vs. Quantum Computing: Key Differences, How Each Works, and What Sets Them Apart
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is software that learns from patterns in data to make predictions and decisions, and it runs on ordinary computers using CPUs and GPUs. Quantum computing is hardware built on quantum physics, and it uses qubits that can hold a combination of 0 and 1 at once, a state called superposition. A well-designed quantum algorithm uses interference to raise the odds of the right answer and cancel out wrong ones, though this works only for problems with the right mathematical structure. The two technologies are distinct, but they could converge to solve intricate scientific problems in the future.

Quantum computers are still small and error-prone, but they are improving fast. In July 2026, researchers from IBM and the University of Chicago said they had verified computations beyond the practical reach of classical methods using error-corrected qubits. In 2025, Google said its Willow chip ran a physics algorithm 13,000 times faster than the best classical approach, then used the technique to study two small molecules. A large enough quantum computer could break the encryption that protects most online data today, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology finalized its first quantum-resistant encryption standards in 2024.

In October 2026, NIST set a plan to phase out today's vulnerable encryption methods after 2030 and stop allowing them after 2035. Quantum machines are not expected to replace traditional computers, and companies like IBM are building systems in which quantum processors work alongside regular supercomputers, with each handling different parts of a problem. AI is already helping build and run quantum computers, and Google DeepMind's AlphaQubit, a neural network, spots errors inside quantum processors more accurately than earlier methods. Researchers have proved theoretical advantages for using quantum hardware to speed up some machine-learning problems, but no one has shown what it would cost to put them to practical use.

The quantum acceleration of AI tasks could lead to possible breakthroughs in medicine and biotech, materials science, weather modeling, finance, and logistics. Most of these possibilities remain speculative, but early results are encouraging. AI is already everywhere, and quantum computing is less visible but could be at least as transformative. It could one day power breakthroughs in medicine, materials, and clean energy, and it is already forcing the world to upgrade its encryption.

Articles.Title: AI vs. Quantum Computing: Key Differences, How Each Works, and What Sets Them Apart

stories.Headline: Wood, Databricks partner to scale AI across energy asset lifecycle
stories.Summary:
Wood partnered with Databricks to help energy companies move AI from pilot projects into enterprise-scale use across the asset lifecycle. The companies announced the partnership on Nov. 3 in Abu Dhabi. It combines the Databricks Data + AI Platform with Wood's engineering, operational and asset expertise. The aim is to apply AI to complex industrial challenges, from project delivery through operations and maintenance.

The partnership builds on several years of work with shared clients. That work includes an AI-enabled engineering solution that, according to Wood, cut the time needed for critical-path document review and quality assurance by 75%. The companies said the solution sped up project delivery while keeping engineering oversight in place. The announcement gave no other figures or dates.

David Cole, chief operating officer, consulting, at Wood, said technology alone does not deliver outcomes. He said real value comes from combining advanced AI capabilities with deep engineering and operational expertise. He said the partnership will help clients move beyond AI experimentation and deploy practical, scalable solutions. Mustafa Ashraf, UAE country manager at Databricks, said many energy AI projects stall because the models lack the engineering and operational context of real-world assets. He said Wood brings deep expertise in how complex industrial assets are designed, built, operated and maintained, and the Databricks platform gives that knowledge a governed foundation to scale.

Ashraf also said the two companies are helping customers move AI out of the pilot phase and into the everyday work that drives safer, more productive and more profitable operations. The articles describe the partnership as building on earlier shared work rather than starting from scratch. They do not say what specific projects will follow or when new work will begin. They also give no financial terms for the partnership.

Articles.Title: Wood, Databricks partner to scale AI across energy asset lifecycle

stories.Headline: GE HealthCare Unveils Allia Celeo to Advance AI-Assisted Cardiac Imaging
stories.Summary:
GE HealthCare introduced Allia Celeo, a ceiling-mounted imaging system that uses artificial intelligence, automated positioning and predictive maintenance to support cardiac and other minimally invasive procedures. The company unveiled the system on Sunday at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics conference in San Diego. The launch expands GE HealthCare's interventional imaging portfolio as hospitals look to improve procedural efficiency and manage operating costs. The system follows the company's 2025 launch of the floor-mounted Allia Moveo, which became commercially available earlier in 2026.

Allia Celeo features a wide-opening C-arm, an X-ray device that captures images from multiple angles around a patient. Its ceiling-mounted setup gives clinical teams more room for staff and equipment, and automated positioning aims to reduce workflow interruptions. AI-assisted software adjusts imaging settings to balance image quality and radiation exposure, and a digital representation of the equipment lets clinicians preview its position before making physical adjustments. The platform also supports GE HealthCare software for visualizing coronary stents, guiding heart valve procedures and assisting with cancer treatments, extending its uses beyond cardiac care.

For maintenance, Allia Celeo integrates with OnWatch Predict, GE HealthCare's remote monitoring and predictive analytics technology, which flags potential equipment issues before they lead to breakdowns. The articles do not name any individual who spoke about the launch or give any statements from the company. They also do not say who at GE HealthCare is responsible for the system. No further details on responsibility or comments are provided.

The articles give little context beyond the launch itself and the earlier Allia Moveo system. They do not say what happens next, such as when Allia Celeo will become commercially available or how much it will cost. No timeline for future rollout or regulatory steps is mentioned. The only stated next step in the coverage is the system's introduction at the conference.

Articles.Title: GE HealthCare Unveils Allia Celeo to Advance AI-Assisted Cardiac Imaging

stories.Headline: Citi raises AI revenue estimates on hyperscaler demand strength
stories.Summary:
Citi raised its AI service revenue estimates for calendar years 2026 through 2028 on November 2, 2026, citing continued strength in artificial intelligence demand and monetization at major cloud providers. The firm increased its AI service estimates by 9% for 2026, 7% for 2027, and 17% for 2028. Combined revenue for AWS, Meta, Google, and Microsoft accelerated to 25% year-over-year growth in the third quarter. Cloud revenue growth for the top three cloud service providers accelerated to 56% year-over-year in the third quarter versus 48% in the second quarter and 39% in the first quarter.

Amazon called for AWS growth above 40% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028. Google Cloud Platform reported 2,600 customers consumed more than 100 billion tokens in the last twelve months versus 2,000 in the second quarter. Microsoft 365 Copilot customers using consumption-based billing grew more than 75% quarter-over-quarter, while Fortune 500 AWS spend increased nearly seven times year-over-year. Combined quarter-over-quarter backlog additions slowed to $128 billion versus $237 billion in the second quarter.

Hyperscaler backlogs grew 142% year-over-year, a nine-point deceleration versus the second quarter on a 14-point tougher comparison. Microsoft's commercial bookings declined 11% in constant currency, impacted by large Azure commitments in the prior year. Citi expects global AI capital expenditures of $1.68 trillion in calendar year 2027, up 64% versus 2026, with the top four hyperscalers accounting for approximately 64% of overall investment. SpaceX increased its year-end 2027 compute capacity target to approximately 13 gigawatts, up from its prior 5-10 gigawatt outlook, while targeting approximately 20 gigawatts of supporting power infrastructure.

Articles.Title: Citi raises AI revenue estimates on hyperscaler demand strength

stories.Headline: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
stories.Summary:
More than two dozen hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as "realising benefits" from Palantir's £330m federated data platform have told the Guardian they are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology. The 29 trusts said the system was either not live or they were not using any of its applications, according to more than 100 freedom of information requests obtained by the medical charity Medact. Epsom and St Helier said it was "not using FDP at the moment", Kent and Medway said the platform was "not currently live", Mersey Care said it had "not yet gone live", and University Hospitals of North Midlands said it did not intend to roll it out. NHS England says 137 trusts are "live" with the FDP, which began in 2024 and aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling.

NHS England has claimed that 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year, but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation ran an investigation. The OSR said it will now take the matter forward under its casework function. NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts "have now reported benefits", and it has previously said its list includes trusts using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than patient care. A Palantir spokesperson said the software was helping deliver better care, citing 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in people finding out whether they have cancer within 28 days.

A senior health official described the gap between the NHS claim and the trusts' understanding as "very misleading". Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir's contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned supplier, and the Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull the deal. Palantir's UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending the contract would be "putting politics above patients", and the company last month hired Labour's former deputy leader Lord Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytics Officers Network, said it was crucial for public support that benefits are reported accurately and transparently.

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the contract. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne asked whether ministers are being misled if they are using the claims to make their decision. Palantir has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump's homeland security crackdown, and its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy. Watson and Mosley have written to critical MPs in letters counting the times they have spoken out against the company, which Labour's Clive Lewis described as "very Big Brother".

Articles.Title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it

stories.Headline: Prada goes anti-AI for their new Christmas campaign - and it's working
stories.Summary:
Prada has released a Christmas campaign called "Drawing Prada: Animated By Hand," which uses traditional hand-drawn illustration instead of AI-generated images. The campaign was developed under the creative direction of Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, with Ferdinando Verderi overseeing campaign creative direction. Veteran animator John Pomeroy led a team of artists to create the animated characters and environments. The live-action scenes were photographed by Glen Luchford, and each frame was drawn by hand. The campaign combines live-action footage with hand-drawn characters and features celebrity ambassadors including Sadie Sink, Maya Hawke, Chen Haoyu, Luther Ford and Kelvin Harrison Jr. Pomeroy, best known for his work at Disney on films such as Winnie the Pooh and Tigger Too, The Rescuers and The Fox and the Hound, explained his commitment to traditional technique in a behind-the-scenes film.

He said he learned his craft with pencil and paper and that the team has remained faithful to that approach. He added that there is a distinct and purposeful reason to do hand-drawn animation, which is to show that handcrafted work is still alive today. A press release said that the sense of touch expresses a fundamental notion of humanity and a connection with craft that always lies at the heart of Prada's approach to creation. The article says the campaign feels like a direct response to those still using a technology that threatens human creativity and livelihoods. It notes that Coca-Cola's AI-generated Christmas advertisements faced criticism in both 2024 and 2025.

The article also says the "not-made-by-AI" approach has become a major selling point, and it reports online comments praising the campaign as a breath of fresh air with soul. The article says more people have grown wary of AI and that a growing backlash has led younger, digital-savvy generations to appreciate human creativity while older generations embrace traditional crafts. It says Prada's campaign has sparked enthusiasm online, with users saying they respect artists and that this is how an ad should be made. The article ends by addressing Coca-Cola, asking whether the company will pay real animators this year or produce another campaign based on artists' works used without permission.

Articles.Title: Prada goes anti-AI for their new Christmas campaign - and it's working

stories.Headline: AI security for OT and industrial environments
stories.Summary:
AI is starting to appear in industrial settings for reasons such as analysing alarms, summarising maintenance notes, supporting predictive maintenance and speeding up engineering tasks, according to a Security Bloggers Network post from Clear Path Security Ltd published on 2 November 2026. In OT environments the security bar differs from a normal business application, because the main concerns are not only confidentiality and integrity but also availability, safety and controlled change. A model that gives a wrong answer in a back-office workflow may be inconvenient, but the same model can create operational disruption or safety issues if it influences a setpoint, a maintenance decision or an operator action. For UK SMEs running plants, utilities, warehouses or industrial services, the post says the right approach is to treat AI as part of the control environment rather than as a standalone IT feature.

The post says AI is being introduced into industrial operations in a few common ways, including large language models that help engineers with documentation, shift handover summaries or troubleshooting. Others connect AI to historians, SCADA data, maintenance systems or engineering workstations to detect anomalies or recommend actions, and in more advanced cases AI is linked to workflow tools that can create tickets, trigger maintenance tasks or suggest control changes. The problem is that industrial environments are built around predictable behaviour, with long asset lifecycles, vendor-specific protocols and strict change windows, while AI systems are more dynamic and may depend on cloud services, external APIs, changing prompts, retrained models or retrieval from live documents. The post says this introduces a wider attack surface and more uncertainty, and that availability and safety matter more because downtime can stop production and an incorrect recommendation can be acted on by a human or an automated workflow.

The post names data poisoning as one of the most important risks, because an attacker or careless insider can influence output by inserting misleading records, manipulated maintenance notes or false examples into the data set. It also describes model tampering, where a changed model artefact, configuration, prompt template or orchestration layer can alter thresholds, instructions or how alerts are prioritised. Prompt injection is relevant where AI reads documents, emails, tickets, manuals or web content and then acts on them, and indirect prompt injection is particularly important in retrieval workflows because a harmful instruction may be hidden inside a document that looks legitimate. Shadow AI and unmanaged integrations create a quieter risk, since staff may use public AI tools outside approved channels and sensitive operational data can leave the environment without review.

The post recommends starting with segmentation and identity, placing AI services in a constrained zone with tightly defined conduits rather than on the same flat network as control systems. It says prompts, retrieved documents, uploaded files and API responses should be treated as untrusted, and that tool-using systems should have allow-listed actions and parameters rather than broad command capability. Model output should not flow directly into control actions, scripts or privileged workflows, and sensitive actions should require a meaningful human approval step in which the operator or engineer sees the source data, the recommendation and the reason it was produced. Logging and monitoring should cover prompts, retrieved sources, tool calls, model responses, user identity and any downstream action, and the post says operational data needs a clear handling model defining which sources are approved, who can add new sources and how changes are reviewed.

Articles.Title: AI security for OT and industrial environments

stories.Headline: Amazon vs. Home Depot: One Is Riding the AI Boom, While the Other Faces a Different Reality
stories.Summary:
Amazon reported third quarter 2026 revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, in results published around the end of October 2026. Its cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, grew 39% to $46 billion as demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence infrastructure accelerated, and North American retail sales rose 6%. Home Depot reported second quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $47.9 billion, up 5.7%, with comparable sales up 1.7% but customer transactions down 0.8%. The figures come from a Motley Fool comparison of the two retailers' last eight quarters, which also lists Amazon's revenue of $187.8 billion in the quarter ended Dec. 31, 2024, $155.7 billion in the quarter ended March 31, 2025, $167.7 billion in the quarter ended June 30, 2025, $180.2 billion in the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2025, $213.4 billion in the quarter ended Dec. 31, 2025, $181.5 billion in the quarter ended March 31, 2026, and $200.6 billion in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, and Home Depot's revenue of $39.7 billion in the quarter ended Feb. 2, 2025, $39.9 billion in the quarter ended May 4, 2025, $45.3 billion in the quarter ended Aug. 3, 2025, $41.4 billion in the quarter ended Nov. 2, 2025, $38.2 billion in the quarter ended Feb. 1, 2026, and $41.8 billion in the quarter ended May 3, 2026.

The article says Amazon draws revenue from global e-commerce, AWS, advertising and subscriptions, while Home Depot sells building materials, home improvement products and professional installation services to homeowners and contractors. Home Depot's management said consumers continued to favor smaller repair and maintenance projects as housing affordability pressures weighed on larger renovations. The article says higher spending per purchase, rather than more customer traffic, drove Home Depot's growth, and that elevated interest rates and housing affordability make sustained revenue growth harder for the company. It says AWS earns substantially higher operating margins than Amazon's retail business, so continued cloud growth could have an outsized effect on profitability.

The article is an investing analysis by RJ Fulton, published Nov. 2, 2026, and it draws no statements from Amazon itself beyond the reported figures. It says Home Depot remains a strong business with an established customer base and significant exposure to professional contractors, and that a recovery in housing activity could give its sales a meaningful boost, though the timing is uncertain. It calls Amazon the better buy for long-term investors, citing its multiple growth engines and expanding cloud business, and says Home Depot could benefit considerably from an eventual housing recovery. Home Depot had not yet reported results for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, according to the article.

Articles.Title: Amazon vs. Home Depot: One Is Riding the AI Boom, While the Other Faces a Different Reality

stories.Headline: Wall Street Veteran Dumps Most of His NVIDIA Stake, Warns of AI Spending Slowdown
stories.Summary:
Steve Weiss, founder and managing partner of Short Hills Capital Partners, said he sold most of his NVIDIA holdings, according to a CNBC interview on Friday reported by Benzinga on Nov. 2, 2026. He said he was concerned that AI infrastructure spending may be nearing a peak. He warned of significant over-ordering of memory chips, semiconductors and data-center capacity, and he compared the situation with earlier technology investment cycles. NVIDIA stock rose nearly 2% in Monday's premarket trading as technology stocks gained ground.

Weiss said AI investment is far from over, but he expects capital-spending growth to slow as companies assess their returns. He questioned whether hyperscalers can keep up their current pace of AI investment even though major technology companies continue to report strong growth. NVIDIA was set to report earnings on Nov. 17, with analysts expecting $2.48 per share on revenue of $109.17 billion, compared with $1.30 per share and $57.01 billion a year earlier. The stock carried a consensus Buy rating, with an average analyst price forecast of $342.08 across 50 analysts.

The article said NVIDIA traded 6.1% below its 20-day simple moving average of $221.46 and 6.2% below its 50-day SMA of $221.75, signaling near-term weakness. It sat 3.1% below its 100-day SMA of $214.52 but remained 1.7% above its 200-day SMA of $204.38, suggesting the longer-term trend remained intact. The MACD indicator stayed below its signal line, pointing to weakening momentum, with resistance near $235 and support around $190. NVIDIA shares gained 1.64% to $207.99 in Monday's premarket trading, according to Benzinga Pro data.

Articles.Title: Wall Street Veteran Dumps Most of His NVIDIA Stake, Warns of AI Spending Slowdown

stories.Headline: Can SpaceX Overcome the AI Trade Sell-Off?
stories.Summary:
SpaceX held its initial public offering in June, and its shares have stayed below the $150 opening price since then, trading at about $134.72 in the most recent session, down roughly 5% from that opening price. In the third quarter, which ended September 30, the company's AI revenue jumped 830% to $7.6 billion and made up 52% of total revenue. That AI segment includes the Grok bot and the rental of AI cloud capacity to customers. Even so, shareholders stayed skeptical and the stock has remained under its IPO price for months.

The wider AI sell-off has hit many tech stocks as investors question whether huge data center spending will pay off. Microsoft reported that Azure cloud revenue for its first fiscal quarter, ended September 30, rose 48% to $33.1 billion, and it said Azure revenue will grow by up to 50% this quarter. Alphabet's stock fell about 10% the day after its third-quarter results, when capital expenditures reached $51.3 billion and the company missed analysts' estimates for sales and earnings. SpaceX's own capital expenditures rose 185% to $19.6 billion in the quarter, with 83% of that going to AI, and the company says capex will reach up to $40 billion this year.

SpaceX is not entirely dependent on AI, since Starlink sales rose 69% to $5.2 billion with 13.6 million subscribers and the business is profitable. Its launch business grew too, with 12 launches in the quarter and a 6% revenue increase to $1.8 billion. Chris Neiger of The Motley Fool wrote that it is reasonable for shareholders and potential investors to be skeptical about the spending right now. He added that the pessimism about so much capex could hamper the stock for a while and that it is unlikely SpaceX will overcome the AI trade sell-off at the moment.

The article says investors are watching closely to see whether SpaceX can keep its AI sales accelerating as spending rises. Neiger wrote that the stock could struggle to gain ground if investors continue to doubt tech companies' AI investments. The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team did not include SpaceX among its 10 best stocks to buy now. The article gives no further details on what happens next for the company.

Articles.Title: Can SpaceX Overcome the AI Trade Sell-Off?

stories.Headline: Türkiye launches antitrust probe into Google over AI search features
stories.Summary:
Türkiye's Competition Authority opened an investigation into Google's AI-powered search features and ordered interim measures over suspected unfair practices affecting news publishers. The probe targets AI Overviews and AI Mode and will examine whether the features violate competition law, according to a statement on the regulator's website. The board said evidence of potentially discriminatory and exploitative practices had reached the level of strong suspicion, which prompted the interim measures. Google introduced both features in Türkiye in February 2026.

The interim measures require Google to set conditions that prevent discrimination among publishers and reflect the economic value of content used in its AI services. Google must also let publishers decide whether their material appears in AI Overviews and AI Mode independently of their visibility and indexing across other Google services. This is meant to stop publishers having to choose between appearing in AI-generated responses and keeping their visibility in conventional search results. The measures do not ban the AI features. The investigation also looks at whether Google's content-use agreements with publishers contain unfair terms and whether the features have exclusionary effects on publishers and AI chatbot providers.

The board is responsible for the probe and issued the interim measures through its statement. It said the evidence of practices affecting news publishers had reached the level of strong suspicion. The regulator's concerns center on how Google uses publishers' content and the possible impact on competition. Google has not commented in the articles.

AI Overviews shows AI-generated summaries at the top of search results, drawing on websites and linking to sources. AI Mode offers a conversational search experience for more complex questions and follow-up queries. Both are available in Türkiye, and their use of material from across the web has raised concerns about traffic reaching original publishers. Publishers that rely on visits for advertising and subscribers could see income affected if referral traffic falls.

Articles.Title: Türkiye launches antitrust probe into Google over AI search features

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike’s SafeMind pits AI attackers against AI defenders
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike has built a system called SafeMind that sets offensive AI models against emulated company networks and uses the traces of their attacks to train defensive models that can lock those networks down on their own. The work is led by CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab, which grew out of chief executive George Kurtz's ambition for the company to be the only pure-play cyber security firm doing frontier-style AI research. CrowdStrike unveiled SafeMind at its Fal.Con conference in Las Vegas in September. Bartley Richardson, CrowdStrike's chief AI and autonomous systems officer, described it as an "AI security factory" that turns out models, the harnesses that put them to work and the benchmarks used to evaluate them, with other parts to come online later.

The defensive models are trained by pitting them against offensive ones, an idea in machine learning that goes back to generative adversarial networks. The effort rests on 15 years of human-annotated adversary data collected by CrowdStrike and a harness that spins up emulated enterprise networks on real virtual machines, with 40,000 to 60,000 running at a time. CrowdStrike calls its offensive models Red Tempest and its defensive models Blue Solano. The red models are based on Nvidia's Nemotron family and open-weight models from Chinese developers including Zhipu AI's GLM, Moonshot AI's Kimi and Alibaba's Qwen, while the blue models rely largely on Nemotron, including its Ultra, Super and Nano versions. Nvidia is CrowdStrike's AI design partner on the project.

Richardson said the real goal of SafeMind from the beginning was to create the best defensive capabilities and tilt the advantage back to the defender, and that to create the best defence you must learn from the best possible offence. He said enough rounds of the loop make an attack intractable, and the aim is a defender model that understands the state of a network, including how misconfigurations compound, and acts as autonomously as possible. He said the company has a better understanding of the supply chain behind the Nemotron models and can run them in customer environments more easily. He also said the level of autonomy SafeMind gets in a customer's environment is up to that customer's risk appetite, so CrowdStrike keeps it tunable.

CrowdStrike is rolling out SafeMind in phases, starting with defensive models that will drive parts of its Falcon platform, with the first to be announced at Fal.Con Europe in Barcelona this week. More sophisticated customers will get direct access through Project QuiltWorks, which CrowdStrike launched in April as an industry coalition and is now shaping into its version of trusted-access programmes. The last phase is to make the emulation environment a product, with customers pumping Falcon telemetry into an emulated version of their network and getting detection content built for how that network is configured, without needing cloud access so long as they have enough compute. CrowdStrike is also training smaller models, including classifiers and small language models, to generate detection content and is looking into AI-powered honeypots, which Richardson said is in its early stages.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike’s SafeMind pits AI attackers against AI defenders

stories.Headline: Ed Yardeni Sees AI Chip Rebound, Year-End Stock Rally — Warns Of Midterm Election, Iran War Risks
stories.Summary:
Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, said in a CNBC-TV18 interview published Monday that the recent artificial intelligence sell-off was not a full-blown rout but was taking some air out of the AI bubble, which he sees as positive. He said he expects semiconductor stocks to rebound and that AI is a real technology that will become profitable, though picking the winning companies remains hard. His comments followed a Friday sell-off in which Intel stock plunged 28.6%, SanDisk fell 13.5% and AMD dropped 10.9%. Yardeni said investors were rotating from AI stocks into health care, financials and industrials rather than leaving U.S. equities.

Yardeni said the pullback has lowered valuations even as analysts raise earnings expectations for AI-related companies. He noted that semiconductor stocks trade at about 13.5 times forward earnings, below the S&P 500's 18.5. According to Yardeni Research, analysts expect semiconductor earnings to grow 114.3% in 2026 and 77.9% in 2027. The firm also said Microsoft, Oracle, Amazon and Alphabet have combined remaining performance obligations of $2.5 trillion, and that memory makers were sold out into 2029, giving them pricing power.

Yardeni warned that Tuesday's midterm elections and the possibility of renewed escalation in the war involving Iran could bring further volatility. He said his firm had advised caution since September 15 and suggested investors hold back cash for buying opportunities after the elections or any further escalation. He also warned that greater political division after the elections could make future debt and government shutdown negotiations harder, potentially creating risks heading into 2027. Despite those concerns, he expects a year-end rally in U.S. stocks between Thanksgiving and the end of December.

U.S. stock futures rose early Monday after a losing week on Wall Street, as investors looked ahead to earnings, jobs data and the midterm elections. S&P 500 futures gained 0.5%, Nasdaq 100 futures climbed 0.80% and Dow futures advanced 271 points, or 0.52%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the SPDR S&P 500 ETF fell to neutral from bullish a day earlier. Sentiment toward the Invesco QQQ Trust and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust remained bearish.

Articles.Title: Ed Yardeni Sees AI Chip Rebound, Year-End Stock Rally — Warns Of Midterm Election, Iran War Risks

stories.Headline: A profile of UCLA professor Terence Tao, who was once enthusiastic about AI's role in math but now warns of AI destroying the field's deliberative process (Rivka Galchen/New Yorker)
stories.Summary:
In early 2026, mathematicians and hobbyists using AI tools began solving some of the simpler unsolved Erdős problems, and in January GPT-5.2 Pro appeared to solve Erdős Problem #728 largely on its own, with Terence Tao and others verifying the proof. On May 20, OpenAI published a proof of Erdős Problem #90, the unit-distance problem, which top mathematicians had already worked on. On September 8, OpenAI announced it had solved the Navier-Stokes existence-and-smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, each carrying a million-dollar award. Tao, a UCLA professor who won a Fields Medal at age thirty-one and founded the Foundation for Science and AI Research in 2025, gave a talk at Caltech three days later.

Tao said solutions were being published with little explanation or detail, relying on mathematicians to verify and explain them for free. AI-generated submissions were overwhelming journals and databases, and the volunteer system of referees was collapsing under the weight of what the article calls slop. He said sometimes even the person submitting a paper did not understand it, and that answers matter less than the insights gained while working toward them. He said the field has to slow down and called the pace insane. Asked where new problems would come from, he said they emerge from the slow, deliberative process of working toward a solution, and that this is what is being destroyed.

Tao was once enthusiastic about AI in math, when many peers dismissed it as a toy that makes many mistakes. AI labs such as Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic use math problems as benchmarks because proofs can be digitized and objectively verified. AI tools scored at the silver-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad in 2024 and at the gold level in 2025. Tao said AI solves problems in ways orthogonal to how humans do, devoting pages to what would be obvious to an undergraduate and only a few lines to what is a large, cloudy move for a human. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: A profile of UCLA professor Terence Tao, who was once enthusiastic about AI's role in math but now warns of AI destroying the field's deliberative process (Rivka Galchen/New Yorker)

stories.Headline: How SF's AI boom is reshaping dating: founders treat first dates as interviews, use tech terms like "conversion rate" to track dates, and pay coaches $5K/month (Emmy Martin/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
San Francisco's AI boom has drawn a wave of young, ambitious people who are reshaping the city's dating life, according to a New York Times report by Emmy Martin published on Oct. 31, 2026. Start-up founders and engineers are dating less because they are working more as they try to build AI products and establish their fortunes. When they do date, they bring a high-stakes mind-set, so a first coffee can feel like a final-round interview. Mehul Agarwal, a 24-year-old co-founder of the AI start-up Koyal, wants to find a wife before he gets rich. He moved to San Francisco a year ago, when his AI filmmaking company, which has raised $3.4 million, joined the start-up accelerator Y Combinator.

Mr. Agarwal has strict criteria for a potential girlfriend. He said she must be smart, and that someone who went to Stanford or M.I.T. is great. She must be beautiful, which he distinguishes from hot, a term he considers shallow, and she must be kind and have a personality, which he said is very hard to find in San Francisco. She also has to like him back. He has never had a girlfriend, and he said he has told his parents that if he is 28 and has not found someone, he would love to enter the arranged marriage circuit.

This year Mr. Agarwal has been on a handful of dates. On one date, which took two months to schedule, he and his date were both exhausted from their jobs, since she worked at an AI start-up too. They were so practiced at professional small talk that the evening felt less like a date than a networking meeting. The report says founders treat first dates as interviews, use tech terms like conversion rate to track dates, and pay coaches $5,000 a month. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: How SF's AI boom is reshaping dating: founders treat first dates as interviews, use tech terms like "conversion rate" to track dates, and pay coaches $5K/month (Emmy Martin/New York Times)

stories.Headline: Bites, whose AI tools deliver personalized training to frontline workers via WhatsApp, SMS, Slack, and other channels, raised a $40M Series A led by PeakSpan (Meir Orbach/CTech)
stories.Summary:
Bites, an AI platform that creates personalized training for employees who do not work at desks, raised $40 million in a Series A funding round, according to a report by Meir Orbach in Calcalistech. The round was led by PeakSpan Capital, with participation from existing investors Vertex Ventures, Horizon Capital, Rittenhouse Ventures, Lyra Ventures and others. The new funding brings the company's total raised to $55 million. PeakSpan's Phil Dur and Charlie Reinkemeyer will join the company's board.

Bites was founded in 2020 by CEO Eran Heffetz, COO Tal Nagler Almog and CIO Hagai Horovitz. The company employs 30 people across its development center in Tel Aviv and its headquarters in New York. Its customers include Unilever, Coca-Cola, Shake Shack, Wynn Resorts, The Venetian and Compass Group, as well as Israeli companies in hospitality and retail. The platform turns documents and standard operating procedures into branded training videos within minutes, delivered through channels employees already use, including WhatsApp, SMS, Microsoft Teams and Slack.

Heffetz said his route into technology began with a problem he encountered while managing restaurants and bars in Tel Aviv, where he repeatedly had to retrain staff as employees left and new workers joined. He said running restaurants taught him that business performance comes down to what people do on the floor every day, and whether they have the knowledge and support to do it well. He said the company initially faced a slow adoption process, although sales continued, primarily in the United States, and he described the past year as a turning point as the product evolved to serve large enterprises. He said AI has served as a significant catalyst, and that to create effective content that actually drives action, the process must be data-driven and supported by automated tools.

The company cites an estimate that approximately 80% of the global workforce, or about 2.8 billion people, do not work at a desk. Each lesson, known as a "Bite," lasts up to 90 seconds and combines a short video with a question, a summary and a discussion, and the platform supports more than 150 languages. Bites says its customers typically achieve engagement rates above 90% within three weeks, and it reports net revenue retention of 161%. The company plans to use the funding to accelerate its expansion in the United States, develop its AI platform, grow its sales and customer success teams, build partner and reseller channels, and expand into banking, insurance and businesses that rely on external workers.

Articles.Title: Bites, whose AI tools deliver personalized training to frontline workers via WhatsApp, SMS, Slack, and other channels, raised a $40M Series A led by PeakSpan (Meir Orbach/CTech)

stories.Headline: SemiAnalysis launches GDPx, an agentic capability benchmark measuring 11 domains, including chip design, cybersecurity, and RSI; Opus 5.5 tops with a 12% score (SemiAnalysis)
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis launched GDPx on November 2, 2026, a benchmark for measuring how well frontier AI models handle agentic tasks across 11 domains. The domains are chip design, cybersecurity, biology, finance, legal, quant trading, recursive self-improvement, hardware design, materials science, alignment and software engineering. The benchmark was built by Max Kan, Andrew Megalaa and Dylan Patel with 14 specialized data partners, including Aria, Arcverex, Ergodex, Arithmetic, Latch Bio, Living Context, Chakra, Third Moment, Extrapolate, Beautiful Machines, ValenceForge, Emulated, Fleet and Datacurve. Opus 5.5 took the top overall score with just 12%, and SemiAnalysis says even the best model scores only 12%.

The benchmark gives each task a realistic environment rather than a single prompt. A finance example from Living Context is based on a real deal in which Bannock Capital buys about 62% of Haverly Snack Company for $880M plus an earnout, with Eakin Lowry as sell-side banker and Marbury Kline as accounting advisor, and the environment holds about 4,000 anonymized files. Cyber tasks are based on real zero days found by Arithmetic's engineers, materials science tasks run inside simulated laboratories, and hardware design tasks use live Siemens NX sessions tested on real AWS FPGA instances. SemiAnalysis says it forgoes industries such as government, real estate and insurance, and that finance and legal tasks are so hard that basically every model scores exactly 0.

SemiAnalysis says Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design and chip design, while Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model and edges out the win in software engineering, and GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is best for materials science. It says Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra had overall scores lowered by their safety classifiers, and that excluding cyber, biology and alignment changes the results. It also says Muse Wonder Full is the best available cyber model by a meaningful margin. SemiAnalysis argues OpenAI's GDPval, released September 25, 2025, is inadequate for today's agents because its tasks are non-interactive and spoon-feed context, and it cites noisy rubric-based graders with 71% human expert agreement on the gold subset.

SemiAnalysis says it started by picking the domains it believes AI will most accelerate in the next one to two years, tied to a demand model projecting OpenAI and Anthropic revenue in 2027 and 2028, and it reached out to more than 30 RL environment companies. It says partners went through a rigorous QA process, and that for some domains multiple partners wanted exclusivity and it selected the one with the highest quality tasks. It thanks Fireworks for inference on open source models, Modal for sandbox infrastructure and Abhijay Rana for sourcing partners and early QA. It says it cannot make all the comparisons in one newsletter and points readers to the official website to explore the data.

Articles.Title: SemiAnalysis launches GDPx, an agentic capability benchmark measuring 11 domains, including chip design, cybersecurity, and RSI; Opus 5.5 tops with a 12% score (SemiAnalysis)

stories.Headline: National Grid buys land in Teesside, UK, for 3.2GW substation to power AI data center
stories.Summary:
National Grid has bought more than 70 acres of land at Dorman Point in Teesside, in the north of England, to build a new substation. The company signed the deal last week with Teesworks, a local public-private partnership. The substation is expected to provide up to 3.2GW of capacity. Balfour Beatty and the utility firm Steel River Power are linked to delivering the power works.

The substation is meant to power an AI data center on the site of a former steel site in Teesside outside Middlesbrough. The site was chosen last year under the UK government's AI growth zone initiative and is described as the largest brownfield development in Europe. It is expected to span 500,000 square meters, or 5.38 million square feet. Teesworks is listed as the main developer, and the site has drawn interest from major US data center developers such as Google, though a preferred operating and investment partner has not been finalized.

Matt Pearce, National Grid's head of land, said in an emailed statement to MT Newswires that the deal marks an important step forward in the substation's development, part of the group's Great Grid Upgrade initiative. He said the company is committed to working closely with its partners to progress the development as quickly as possible. The site selection faced pushback from the oil and gas giant BP, which argued the plan would hinder its attempts to build a hydrogen plant in the area. The data center plan was approved last August despite the objections, and BP later scrapped the hydrogen project that year.

National Grid has announced or completed work on several substations to meet rising electricity demand from the data center sector. In November last year it began upgrade work at its Didcot substation in Oxfordshire to support data center growth in the region. It also started construction at its Uxbridge Moor substation in Buckinghamshire, which is expected to supply electricity to more than 12 new data centers. That substation, which will be the largest in the UK when built, is expected to be completed by 2029.

Articles.Title: National Grid buys land in Teesside, UK, for 3.2GW substation to power AI data center

stories.Headline: Nebius Stock: A Bloom Fuel Cell Powers Up in New Jersey as the AI Trade Pivots From Buildout to Payb - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
Nebius shares fell 4.0% on Friday, with one reading putting the daily decline at 4.1%, but the drop came from a broad technology selloff rather than anything the company disclosed. Media reports tied the weakness to Amazon's quarterly figures and Intel's outlook, which fed worries that money going into AI infrastructure is running ahead of the returns it will produce. Reuters reported that Amazon's sustained AI spending and Intel's warning about cash burn weighed on the wider market. Coverage of Nebius's decline linked the loss to that backdrop rather than to any fresh operational warning from the company.

On October 22, Nebius announced a $3.5 billion senior secured financing arrangement with Citi, with a 364-day term and proceeds earmarked for data center development, graphics processor procurement and general corporate purposes. The initial rate is Term SOFR plus 2.75% annually, with the spread stepping up to a maximum of 3.50%, and the facility matures on October 16, 2027, according to the SEC filing. On the operational side, Nebius activated the first Bloom Energy fuel cell block at its planned New Jersey data center site on October 25, and the site is designed for 300 megawatts. On October 21, Nebius introduced public real-time spot pricing for GPU compute and announced with NVIDIA a European expansion of its AI Builder Program, including more than $10 million in additional compute credits.

A report dated October 26 said Nebius chief Arkady Volozh acknowledged that some financing channels had temporarily become unavailable, while warnings from Elon Musk about failures and consolidation among neocloud providers weighed on the relevant stocks. According to the company, customers of its Physical AI Workbench, presented on October 21, reported development-time savings of up to 40%. Nebius announced Friday that its third-quarter 2026 results will be published before the market opens on November 12, followed by a conference call set for 8 a.m. Eastern Time. The articles say the key investor question is how convincingly Nebius ties investment, customer value and business results together, and that the figures will let investors set operating numbers beside the visible buildout milestones.

Articles.Title: Nebius Stock: A Bloom Fuel Cell Powers Up in New Jersey as the AI Trade Pivots From Buildout to Payb - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: County College of Morris to host free AI and Data Science Night on Nov. 19
stories.Summary:
County College of Morris will host a free, interactive event on Thursday, Nov. 19, called “AI and Data Science Night: Data Under the Stars.” It will run from 6 to 9 p.m. at the college’s Randolph campus, with check-in starting at 5:30 p.m. The event is open to students ages 15 and older, adult learners and working professionals. It will include hands-on workshops, career discussions and a planetarium presentation.

Attendees will take part in workshops led by CCM faculty and industry professionals. Topics include natural language processing, machine learning, AI cybersecurity, Python programming, statistical analysis, data visualization, vibe-coding and agentic AI. The evening will also offer networking, a panel with CCM students and alumni, and chances to meet representatives from four-year universities about transferring. Participants can also experience “Data Under the Dome,” a presentation inside CCM’s Longo Planetarium. People can learn about the college’s AI and data science degree programs, short-term credentials, certification exams, apprenticeships and internships.

CCM offers a five-course Certificate of Achievement in Data Analytics, on campus or fully online through its Virtual Campus. Admission is rolling, and credits may count toward an Associate of Science degree in Data Science. Representatives from CCM’s Center for Workforce Development will discuss noncredit training, including the Data Analytics and Visualization certificate and the AI and Data Science apprenticeship program. The center also offers courses such as AI Essentials, AI for Business Professionals, Business Analytics with Excel, Microsoft Power BI, SQL for Data Management, Introduction to R Programming and Tableau.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, data scientist employment is projected to rise 35% from 2025 to 2035. The median annual wage for data scientists was $120,230 in May 2025. No previous experience is required, but advance registration is mandatory. Those interested can view the agenda and register through Eventbrite.
